title: Personal testimony of clinging to childhood identity
text:
Leaving childhood and adolescence has been a difficult task for me; I’ve been in love with my image as a pubescent girl my whole life. It’s an image that has seduced me, that I’ve adored, and I’ve let it guide my life.

The attachment to childishness is more than a preference; it’s a lifestyle where the responsibilities never rested on me and my decisions but on circumstances, others, or the randomness of life.

CATI PRECIADO

It was easy to be forgiven for everything, because from my childlike attitude, I could pass as innocent; with this, I managed to get affection, privileges, and comforts.

Physically, I look much younger than I am. This allows me, even now in my fifties, to carry myself in front of others with a certain youthful air.

ROXANA ROSAS
summary: This chunk presents personal testimonies from individuals identifying with the self-preservation E2 subtype, describing a lifelong attachment to a childlike identity, the use of youthful appearance to gain affection and privileges, and the avoidance of responsibility through maintaining an innocent, dependent persona.

title: Parental conditional love and the E2 child's internalized role
text:
Origins

The self-preservation E2 internalized that they were loved mostly for being a pleasant, smiling and cheerful child; so they learned to hide feelings of sadness and displeasure.

When my father came home from work and saw me looking sad, he’d say, “I’ve got so many problems at work, so when I get home, all I want is my little ray of sunshine.”

My mother would tell me when I cried to save those tears for when she died.

ROXANA ROSAS

They received the ambivalent message of being the most important person in the family, at the center of their parents’ hearts. Parents who were always available to protect them and help them through life’s challenges. However, these parents set the condition that they should not express any negative feelings, and that they shouldn’t present them with problems they couldn’t be bothered with. These parents were always ready to meet practical needs, as long as the child didn’t make contact with anger, sadness, or any form of lack, and as long as they remained the most important people in the child’s life. The reward was a lack of boundaries and clear rules, which translated into the false sense of freedom, sense of having no limits. The privilege a child may have translates also, in adolescence and adulthood, into the obligation to remain in this role of the parents’ little girl or boy, who brings joy and doesn’t cause any problems.

The paradox of this privilege lies in being a child while also having the task of emotionally caring for, and sometimes even practically supporting, the parent. As they grow, they will be overwhelmed by a deep sense of guilt for leaving their parents behind and for not fully appreciating the privilege of being the protected child, and thus enjoying the security it provided. A quiet humiliation accompanies the frustration of growing up, particularly the challenge of stepping into the role of a man or a woman in their own right, since they cannot escape the inevitable transition into becoming an “adult.”

People of this character live with the impression that no one will love them if they express their sadness, anger, or any form of open displeasure, so joy and optimism become their ways of navigating the world, with their almost eternal smile being their greatest asset. They develop social skills like eye contact, a genuine smile, and physical closeness, but by not showing their sorrow or anger, they leave undeveloped their ability to set healthy boundaries.

The only way they can express discomfort is through temper tantrums, behind which they hide their anger, which in turn feeds into the privilege of claiming and occupying their place at the center of the world.

They create the illusion of deep intimacy, making others feel uniquely special, as if they reserve this level of closeness just for them. But, of course, they expect the same treatment in return. In every relationship, they repeat the lie they learned: “I will always be by your side, your source of light and joy, and in return, you will forever grant me the role of a special, irreplaceable person, who can do everything they want.”
summary: This chunk explores how self-preservation E2s internalize conditional love from parents who reward cheerful compliance and punish emotional honesty, leading to a lifelong pattern of suppressing negative emotions, maintaining a childlike role to secure affection, and struggling with guilt and identity when faced with adult responsibilities.

title: Самосохранение E2: позиция ребенка и трудности взросления
text:
The childlike posture that “allows” them not to assume the consequences of their decisions becomes so rigid that, to maintain it, they have to disempower themselves; something that manifests, for example, in difficulty making money or excessive spending on “childish” things. It also shows in the acceptance of tasks without analyzing beforehand what they entail or their own ability to handle them. It’s common for them to learn as they go or abandon the task without daring to face it, feeling overwhelmed by it.

The self-preservation E2 tries to occupy the center of attention, seemingly concerned with others’ needs, being the first to ask what they need. Their attitude towards life is like a game of magic and charm, rather than something more human, raw, and adult.

Their actions are driven by the need to be necessary for others, which creates a feeling of debt around them.

I remember having dinner with Dr. Claudio Naranjo, Antonio Santamaría, several others, and myself. Claudio mentioned he had something written that might interest Antonio, and asked for his email. Since he took a while to respond, I immediately said, “If you want, send the paper to me and I’ll forward it to him.” This is how I place myself at the center of attention, acting as the one who facilitates the relationship. This very same thing makes it hard for me to ask for help, since I would have to share the spotlight.

ROXANA ROSAS
summary: Описывает поведенческие паттерны самосохраняющейся двойки: стресс из-за невозможности взрослеть, попытки удержать внимание через заботу о других, пример из жизни иллюстрирующий потребность быть посредником, а также цитату Роксаны Розос о бесконечной потребности и чувстве долга.

title: Психодинамика и иллюзия изобилия у самосохраняющейся E2
text:
It’s like a bottomless barrel that never feels satiated. This creates a sense of debt in the other person, which can never be repaid, as they struggle to find ways to satisfy the ever-needy self-preservation E2. Psychodynamically, it reinforces their inability to trust in the love of others, leading them to ensure their worth by making themselves indispensable.

As a child, they built bridges of love, harmony, and well-being between their parents, thus nurturing their experience of occupying a privileged place. They continue to offer help as a way to avoid being forgotten, which is why they so often gravitate toward caregiving and service professions, where their “passion” is warmly received.

Interpersonal strategy and associated irrational ideas

by Veronica Anton

Here, we will describe how the fixation on false abundance, typical of Type Two, manifests in the self-preservation subtype.

Self-preservation E2s develop an inflated sense of self and the belief that their own needs (often confused with desires) should always come first. Unless they are the center of attention, they don’t feel seen or valued, which leads to intense emotional swings, shifting between sadness and euphoria. Their neurotic need to maintain a position of privilege is tied to a self-image of someone who deserves to be the focus simply by existing.

As we have seen, they build their identity within their family environment by adapting to and responding to contradictory messages and expectations. On one hand: “You are a special child; you must be the joy of this house, and that grants you a privileged place.” But at the same time, their worth is only recognized if they remain in that childlike, dependent role, preventing any attempt at self-realization outside of what their parents have envisioned for them.

The demand to forever remain a child results in the suppression of any initiative toward becoming an adult. So, they feel both irreplaceable and constantly humiliated, never acknowledged for their right or ability to make their own choices and lead an independent life. Deep down, they come to believe that they are incapable of surviving on their own, that leaving will lead to hunger or illness, that they lack the tools to sustain themselves. These beliefs reinforce an underlying sense of lack and inferiority.
summary: Анализирует психологические механизмы самосохраняющейся двойки: иллюзия бесконечной потребности, чувство долга у других, компенсация через незаменимость, формирование идентичности в семье через противоречивые послания, подавление взросления и вера в собственную несостоятельность вне зависимости от близких.

title: Грандиозность и ложное изобилие как защита от реальных потребностей
text:
Self-preservation E2s deny frustration, neglect, and fear of independence by constructing a grandiose self-image based on their privileged relationship with a parent. This “special” relationship doesn’t have to be characterized by affection, seduction, or overprotection; conflict can also make a relationship feel special. What matters is being the focal point of attention..

Their grandiosity is not necessarily rooted in a belief that they are better than others, but rather in the idea that they deserve protection, help, and a special kind of treatment. The passions for privilege and false abundance reinforce each other.

Any “negative” experience (whether it be a lack of true emotional care, unmet deep needs, or struggles with independence) is dismissed as unimportant, not worth the effort, or avoided through resorting to fantasy. Instead of taking concrete steps toward growth, they comfort themselves with vague ideas that everything is fine as it is or that they will achieve something meaningful in the future, without ever making an actual plan. This highlights the confusion between desire and need: as children, self-preservation E2s had their desires fulfilled but received no real attention to their authentic emotional needs or developmental milestones. That’s why they easily adopt a demanding, capricious attitude rooted in their false sense of abundance, rather than asking for the kind of support that would genuinely help them grow—because doing so would mean recognizing their own limitations.

False abundance also manifests, as it does in other E2s, through the appearance of being generous, empathetic, and attuned to others’ needs. But in this subtype, it primarily takes the form of not needing anything more because life already seems to work for them. They believe they can always get what they need through their charm or by simply being their “precious” self. Their grandiosity is expressed not as a need to be famous or superior, but as the desire to maintain a unique place as someone loved, protected, and indispensable, a privileged position in the hearts of others that guarantees their existence.
summary: Объясняет, как самосохраняющиеся двойки используют грандиозность и иллюзию изобилия как защиту: отрицают реальные потребности, фантазируют вместо действий, путают желания с потребностями, проявляют видимую щедрость, на самом деле стремясь сохранить привилегированное место в отношениях через очарование и чувство собственной незаменимости.

title: Эмоциональная защита и иллюзии у самосохраняющихся E2
text:
Their intense, unstable emotions serve as a defense against the deep emptiness of not fulfilling themselves, of not growing, whether through moments of euphoria when they get their way or deep sadness when they feel trapped and unfree.

Self-preservation E2s pour all their energy into pursuing fantasies, chasing their imagined desires until they lose themselves, like a ship adrift. They are often ungrounded, moving from place to place, struggling to find stability or take control of their own lives.

Their distorted thought patterns, as Claudio Naranjo explains, give rise to deeply ingrained beliefs about life and themselves, forming a coherent mental framework. In the Enneagram model, these are known as crazy ideas. “Crazy” in the sense that they are subjective and incomplete interpretations of life experiences, yet they become absolute truths in the mind of the individual, who loses awareness that these ideas are just mental constructs designed to uphold their psychological defense mechanisms. They assume these beliefs are reality and take for granted that everyone else sees the world the same way. “Crazy,” then, in the sense that they’re disconnected from the actual context the person is living in.
summary: Описывается, как самосохраняющиеся E2 используют эмоциональную нестабильность и фантазии как защиту от внутренней пустоты, формируя искаженные убеждения («бредовые идеи»), которые они принимают за реальность, отрываясь от контекста жизни.

title: Страх abbandона и стратегии выживания у самосохраняющихся E2
text:
Interpersonal strategies, while shaped primarily by early life experiences, especially with parents, become ingrained as the default way of relating to others. For self-preservation E2s, abandonment and the feeling of loneliness associated with it are among the most intensely avoided experiences, as they are deeply imprinted in their body-emotional memory. This serves as the driving force behind many of their interpersonal strategies, which are often based on catastrophic fantasies about these fears.

Here is a personal account:

Through various sessions of regression therapy, I relived the moment of my birth. It involved deep abandonment and loneliness. It was the sensation of being alone, of not feeling another presence beside me in a moment of extreme vulnerability. In these experiences, I connected with the coldness of my body and its rigidity in response to the fear and sense of abandonment.

This has awakened in me a “survivor” mindset and reinforced the irrational belief that “I can take care of myself and survive without needing anyone else,” which has shaped my entire life. I developed a suspiciously high level of autonomy, an independence that emerged too early; an apparent confidence and efficiency in navigating the world, which could be mistaken for that of an E3 or a social E2.

VERÓNICA ANTÓN

The deep fear of reliving this abandonment and loneliness leads self-preservation E2s to overvalue their freedom and independence, to the point that it often interferes with their ability to form romantic relationships—unless their partner is entirely willing to fulfill their every wish. Their extreme sensitivity to frustration makes them appear “spoiled,” reacting with thoughts like: “If you don’t give me what I want, you don’t love me,” “If you set boundaries, you don’t love me,” or “if you can’t guess my desires, you don’t care about me."
summary: Рассматривается, как страх abbandона и одиночества, закрепленный в раннем опыте, формирует стратегии выживания у самосохраняющихся E2, включая гиперавтономию, зависимость от исполнения желаний в отношениях и эмоциональную реакцию на фрустрацию как на отсутствие любви.

title: Полярность欲 и потребностей у самосохраняющихся E2
text:
Self-preservation E2s, thus, constantly oscillate between neglecting their essential needs and moments when they cannot bear to have their plans disrupted. Understanding this polarity is key to avoiding the misconception that they are merely “spoiled children” who always demand to get their way.

Here, it’s also important to differentiate between desires (or will) and needs. This subtype is highly in touch with what they want in the moment but struggles to perceive their own needs, ranging from deep emotional ones to basic ones like food, water, and rest. This is why it’s difficult for them to be direct in their relationships.

This impulse to fiercely defend and fulfill their desires stems from a neurotic compensation for the frustration of not being able to meet their needs (due to a lack of awareness of them). For E2s in general, recognizing their own needs is a major blind spot, but what sets the self-preservation subtype apart is this particular form of compensation: an almost obsessive drive to avoid frustration by ensuring their desires are met. At any cost.

When asked, “Why do you want that?”, their response might be: “Why not?”, backed by underlying beliefs like: “I deserve everything,” “I can do anything,” “If I don’t get what I want, I’m worthless,” and “I have a right to what I want."
summary: Анализируется конфликт между желаниями и потребностями у самосохраняющихся E2: они хорошо осознают свои momentary желания, но не видят реальных потребностей, что приводит к нейротической компенсации через настойчивое исполнение желаний любой ценой, основанное на убеждении в своем праве на wszystko.

title: Фантазия независимости и её реализация в жизни самосохраняющихся E2
text:
A self-preservation E2’s core fantasy might be: “I don’t answer to anyone.” However, in reality, this illusion of independence coexists with deep emotional dependence in their closest relationships, especially romantic ones. The desire for independence is often present from childhood and translates into fantasies of complete self-sufficiency, living alone, and being entirely autonomous. In their teenage years, this craving for freedom and the thrill of escaping parental oversight, doing something behind their parents’ backs, can sometimes put them in risky situations.

Some testimonies illustrate this:

Ever since I was little, I wanted to be independent from my family. At nine years old, I imagined living alone, having my own money, and soon wanted to work.

I engaged in risky behaviors: driving before I was thirteen, sneaking out of school in high school, having a boyfriend at eleven. I felt I had the right to do whatever I wanted.

By eighteen, I had saved up to buy my first car. I needed something that was mine! I wanted to move around without relying on my parents or public transport.

My need for “independence” led me to move out at twenty-one, as soon as I had the money to do so. But I made sure I could afford a nice apartment first. I didn’t feel safe leaving otherwise. From that point on, I supported myself financially.
summary: Описывается основная фантазия самосохраняющихся E2 о полной независимости («не отвечать ни перед кем»), которая противоречит их реальной эмоциональной зависимости, иллюстрируясь личными историями о ранней тяге к автономии, рискованном поведении и постепенном достижении финансовой независимости, albeit с оглядкой на безопасность.

title: Личный опыт с независимостью и финансовой безопасностью
text:
At times, I’ve had difficulty managing and being fully self-sufficient; I always had someone to “back me up,” like my boss, and later, my partner. Even though I didn’t directly ask for money, just knowing I had access to their financial resources gave me peace of mind.

It took me years to realize that I spent money on clothes, food, gifts, trips, and entertainment, but never on things that would provide real security, like health insurance or savings for emergencies. I lived day to day, assuming I’d always have money, as if the future didn’t exist.
summary: Автор делится личным опытом, иллюстрирующим иллюзию финансовой независимости у самосохраняющегося E2: несмотря на внешнюю самостоятельность, человек полагается на поддержку близких и тратит деньги на немедленные удовольствия, пренебрегая долгосрочной безопасностью.

title: Подростковый возраст: омнипотентность, соблазн и манипуляции
text:
CATI PRECIADO

Teenage years, often marked by feelings of omnipotence, are a time when self-preservation E2s impulsively step into the world beyond their family environment. Their difficulty in recognizing limits and their disregard for danger become more apparent. Their seductive impulses emerge with a unique twist.

Women often enter romantic relationships with much older partners or seek to attract people who hold knowledge or power. Seduction serves as a way to reinforce their sense of omnipotence, sometimes by deliberately breaking social norms: seducing a priest, a teacher, their therapist, a married man... In some cases, this results in an early exploration of sexuality and a preference for social circles composed of older individuals.

These behaviors are driven by deep-seated beliefs such as: “If I seduce you, I’ll have a privileged position and you’ll protect me,” “If I seduce someone with power, I’ll have power,” and “If I can attract you, I’m worth something.”

Manipulating their environment plays a key role in how self-preservation E2s relate to others, and it manifests differently at various stages of life. As children, they may present themselves as “good kids”—adaptable, observant, soft-spoken, and sweet—often excelling in school. Later, as they step into the world of adult relationships, they maintain this image of “innocence” or “childishness,” while leading a double life, secretly engaging in rebellious or risky behavior.

This tendency to conceal, manipulate, charm their way out of trouble, and selectively present themselves reinforces their illusion of autonomy and omnipotence: “I can do and achieve everything I set my mind to,” “I don’t depend on anyone,” and “I have no limits.”
summary: Описывается подростковый период самосохраняющихся E2: их чувство всемогущества приводит к рискованному поведению, соблазну людей с властью и манипуляциям для укрепления иллюзии независимости и силы, поддерживаемой двойной жизнью и социальной маской 'хорошего ребёнка'.

title: Взрослая жизнь: применение стратегии во всех сферах и цена 'выживания'
text:
In my teenage years and early adulthood, I used this mindset mostly in romantic pursuits. But over time, I’ve applied it to other areas of life. As an adult, I often feel like I can achieve anything if I put enough energy into it. Even if it means ignoring my needs, pushing past my limits, or overexerting myself at a great personal cost.

This is how I’ve tackled “difficult” situations in life. Like emigrating to a country where I had no connections and leaving a good job behind, building a professional career from scratch in a new environment, or deciding to stay in that country after my breakup, despite being alone and without family. The “survivor” in me finds the internal resources to overcome almost anything.

VERÓNICA ANTÓN
summary: Автор описывает, как стратегия самосохраняющегося E2, выработанная в подростковом возрасте, переносится во взрослую жизнь: эмиграция, карьерные риски и выживание в одиночку становятся проявлением внутренней силы, но ценой игнорирования собственных потребностей и переутомления.

title: Проблемы в командной работе, конкуренция и иллюзия исключительности
text:
A recurring theme in the lives of self-preservation E2s is their difficulty in recognizing and considering others. Their impulse and desires take precedence over dialogue and collaboration, making teamwork and adherence to institutional rules a problem. They believe they are the “exception” to the rule, that their breaking it doesn’t count, not recognizing that they’re imposing their will on others in the process.

Unconsciously, they are constantly competing, justifying it with beliefs like: “Me first—just because,” and “I have the right to do what I want because I’m special.” This difficulty in group settings often originates in childhood dynamics—perhaps one parent subtly pitted them against the other. This unstable alliance might have given them a privileged position, but at a high emotional cost. As adults, they still perceive group relationships as a threat, feeling that someone will always be there to take their place. Even while competing, they fear exclusion, making it hard to ever fully trust in love.

They don’t recognize their limits or needs, pushing themselves too hard due to an excessive sense of obligation (many individuals of this subtype pursue multiple degrees or juggle various jobs). Yet, this overexertion is inconsistent, alternating with periods of indulgence, where only their desires matter—what can seem like a “spoiled” attitude.

Despite all the skills they develop, their independence doesn’t always translate into true adult autonomy, meaning a mature acceptance of life’s limits. Their self-image and narcissistic ideal prevent them from fully integrating their achievements into a solid foundation for long-term personal growth.
summary: Анализируются трудности самосохраняющихся E2 в групповой работе: их убеждённость в исключительности, скрытая конкуренция, страх exclusion и неспособность признавать чужие границы ведут к конфликтам, несмотря на высокие достижения и навыки, которые не трансформируются в зрелую автономию из-за narциссической самоидентичности.

title: Сложности в самостоятельной работе и иллюзия долгосрочной устойчивости
text:
When self-preservation E2s work independently as their own bosses, they often struggle with discipline, meeting goals, and valuing the effort they put in. They can easily lose track of limits, either overworking themselves to the point of neglecting their well-being or not putting in enough effort and justifying their mediocrity.

A self-preservation E2 can be so focused on immediate benefit that they struggle to follow through on their projects. It’s as if they can’t see the future, finding it difficult to build something stable for themselves, to plan ahead, or to see themselves as someone with lasting resources. They seem to live in the moment, which can be mistaken for spontaneity, but in reality, it’s a difficulty in connecting with their own needs. They often say things like, “I thought I could handle it all.” They get into debt, run out of money. There’s an absence of a superego. Or rather, their superego acts as an accomplice, preventing them from setting limits to bring a project to completion.

Another polarity: While they may have a false sense of “independence” from the outside world, in their closest relationships (especially in romantic ones) there is often a deep dependency, an insatiable need for affection, physical contact, and emotional fusion.
summary: Описываются парадоксы самосохраняющихся E2 в предпринимательской деятельности: несмотря на внешнюю независимость, они испытывают трудности с дисциплиной, долгосрочным планированием и оценкой усилий, живя сиюминутными выгодами, что ведёт к долгам и выгоранию, при этом в близких отношениях сохраняется глубокая эмоциональная зависимость, противоречащая иллюзии автономии.

title: Эмоциональная зависимость и страх фрустрации в отношениях у самосохранительной E2
text:
They may feel a desperate need for the other person to be unconditionally present, with no risk of disagreement, confrontation, boundaries, or frustration. These are the very things that trigger their core wound: the fear of abandonment from childhood—“If I’m alone, I’ll die.”

Within an emotional relationship, they view limits or frustration as a threat to the bond itself, which reactivates their primal wound of abandonment. Because frustration is so intolerable, they resort to all kinds of seduction and manipulation to get the other person to do what they want and fulfill their desires. The underlying, irrational belief is: “I won’t survive the pain of frustration.” It’s as if part of the E2 still experiences themselves as the helpless, abandoned child they once were, feeling extremely fragile, in a way that no longer matches their current reality.
summary: Описывает, как у самосохранительной E2 проявляется глубокая эмоциональная зависимость в отношениях, rooted in детской травме abbandона; фрустрация воспринимается как угроза, приводящая к манипуляциям и избеганию конфликтов из-за убеждения, что боль от фрустрации неприемлема.

title: Личная testimony: внутренний конфликт и манипуляции в браке
text:
A testimony:

In my relationship, it’s like I don’t want to make a wrong move, yet at the same time, I’m constantly manipulating. I did this for the first ten years of my marriage. I omitted information, maybe even projected my fears. I was the one fantasizing about leaving the relationship. I’d think, “Why am I even here?” “Why do I need this? I’d be better off alone!” But I never left, even though I really wanted to because of our differences and arguments. My partner always told me that I didn’t consider him, that I acted as if I were the only person in the relationship.

CATI PRECIADO
summary: Первая личная testimony от CATI PRECIADO, иллюстрирующая внутренний конфликт между желанием уйти и страхом остаться, постоянные манипуляции через умолчание и проекцию страхов, а также неосознанную самоцентричность в отношениях, несмотря на чувство одиночества.

title: Псевдо-независимость и избегание реальности через активность и ложь
text:
In their pseudo-independence, a self-preservation E2 is terrified of ending up alone or without the resources to survive. This fear of having no one can take over their life entirely. Without realizing it, they fill their days with obligations, people to care for, and activities (even ones they don’t truly enjoy), just to maintain a sense of connection.

On the surface, they appear adaptable, like someone who can go along with anything, but eventually, they’ll feel the need to retreat. They become exhausted from being immersed in other people’s lives rather than their own.

This tendency to surround themselves with others stems from their difficulty in knowing what truly nourishes them (not just what entertains them—because in that, they’re experts). They struggle to identify what helps them grow and mature. Entertainment provides an escape, keeping them from facing what they actually want in life. The excessive activity that “fills” their life only increases their disconnection from themselves and reinforces their own self-deception.

Lying also becomes a way to avoid frustration in relationships, minimizing, adjusting, and softening reality to create an illusion of harmony. But this strategy backfires, because when conflict inevitably arises, it amplifies feelings of shame and guilt, making it even harder to confront reality. And yet, facing reality is what would actually allow them to take responsibility and mature in their relationships.

Avoiding the truth often includes leaving things unsaid, especially anything about their flaws that others might notice. This is another way of avoiding frustration. Anything they perceive as a personal defect feels terrifying to reveal. If they identify something in themselves as undesirable, they exaggerate it: “No one would love me if they knew this…”
summary: Объясняет, как самосохранительная E2 создает иллюзию независимости через гиперактивность и заботу о других, избегая собственных потребностей; ложь и умолчание используются как защита от фрустрации и страха раскрытия недостатков, что ведет к усилению стыда и препятствует зрелости.

title: Иррациональные убеждения и их связь с E4: страх раскрытия и избегание ответственности
text:
Manipulating situations by withholding information becomes an attempt to avoid rejection, abandonment, or the loss of a privileged position in the relationship. They avoid true commitment and responsibility, afraid to fully reveal themselves and grow together in a more authentic connection. Their thinking follows this pattern: “If they see my flaws, they’ll reject me” and “It’s better to disappear than to show who I really am.” These irrational ideas highlight the connection between self-preservation E2s and E4, with whom they are often confused. This subtype of E2 has a stronger link to emotions of deprivation: shame, shyness, and the impulse to hide when they fear their false sense of abundance might collapse.

Working through these irrational beliefs involves recognizing them, daring to identify them, and understanding their cognitive, emotional, and relational mechanisms. It also means seeing how they keep self-preservation E2s trapped in mere survival mode rather than truly living.
summary: Детализирует, как страх раскрытия своих недостатков приводит к избеганию ответственности и настоящей близости, усиливая связь с типом E4 через共享 emociones de privación (стыд, застенчивость); преодоление требует осознания и работы с этими убеждениями, чтобы выйти из режима выживания.

title: Детские стратегии выживания и их устаревший характер во взрослой жизни
text: Their interpersonal strategies are remnants of an early hunger for love, contact, and protection. As children, these strategies worked; they helped them secure the affection and care they needed from parents and caregivers. But as adults, these strategies are outdated. Yet the self-preservation E2 clings to them, believing they are necessary to stay afloat, to ensure their survival.
summary: Объясняет, что зависимые и манипулятивные стратегии поведения у самосохранительной E2 — это выживательные механизмы детства, которые в зрелом возрасте становятся дезадаптивными, но человек продолжает ими пользоваться, ошибочно считая их необходимыми для выживания.

title: Вторая testimony: ранняя травма рождения и формирование стратегии «сладкой беспомощности»
text:
Let’s end the chapter with another testimony:

A key moment in understanding my personality happened during a SAT 3 regression exercise (rebirthing). I experienced my earliest emotional memory, immediately after birth, as one of deep sadness and rejection. It wasn’t about the specifics of my birth itself, but about the stark contrast between the comfort of the womb and the painful experience of life. I perceived birth as an injustice that victimized me. I reacted with rebellion and frustration, believing I had to get revenge for my misfortune, on whoever was responsible for it.

I was incapable of resisting the fact that I had been born, that I was alive, and that life came with pain and frustration. So I developed a strategy: appearing sweet and helpless so that my parents would protect me. I also made a sort of bargain with God, with “the mechanics of life”: “Okay, I’ll be a good child, obedient and proper. In return, I expect my needs to be met.”

But since life kept failing to hold up its end of the deal, my old wound would resurface, reigniting an unbearable feeling of rebellion and frustration, expressed in fits of rage, and temper tantrums.

FERNANDO RAMOS
summary: Вторая личная testimony от FERNANDO RAMOS, описывающая раннюю эмоциональную травму после рождения — ощущение abbandона и несправедливости — которая привела к формированию стратегии внешней покорности и helplessness в обмен на заботу, а также к циклу гнева и истерик при повторной активации травмы.

title: Зависимость и маскировка
text:
Of the three subtypes, the self-preservation E2 is the most dependent, though they often present a façade of being self-sufficient. They distance themselves from their family, thinking that the space will lessen their dependency, but it doesn’t. Instead, they compulsively form dependent relationships to ensure their own protection and survival. They’re chameleonic, with an intuitive ability that allows them to captivate others.

They seek out strong-willed people to compensate for their insecurity, but in doing so, they “lose” their freedom, becoming attached to the role of being loved for their cheerful demeanor.

They project their aggression because they don’t connect with the courage that would allow them to set boundaries, as they’re constantly focused on pleasing everyone.
summary: Описывает зависимый характер самосохраняющегося E2, его маскировку под самостоятельность, стремление к сильным партнерам, проекцию агрессии и трудности с установлением границ из-за фокуса на угождении другим.

title: Стеснительность и избегание признания
text:
Shy

Shyness is a very noticeable trait in this infantile personality. It comes from the fear of exposing themselves unless they are certain they will be recognized or acknowledged.

The passion for privilege hides a search for validation and a deep lack of self-esteem. Since this character doesn’t want to admit having limitations or face their low self-esteem, they tend to lie low if they’re not sure of success. They prefer to childishly hide behind phrases like “I don’t know,” or “I can’t” rather than admit feeling inadequate. Their shyness and embarrassment can be used as a charming, childlike seduction tactic to avoid confrontation.
summary: Описывает стеснительность как защитный механизм самосохраняющегося E2, связанный со страхом отвержения, низкой самооценкой и использованием детского поведения для избежания конфронтации и получения одобрения.

title: Самовиктимизация и идеализация
text:
Self-victimizing

They tend to project blame, as their seduction attempts are meant to show only what others want to see. The underlying belief is that “to be accepted, you must hide the bad.” Thus, they blame the world for their difficulties and problems, as facing the truth would require them to take responsibility for their actions and change. It’s easy for them to play the victim when they feel misunderstood or unappreciated, but most of the time, they’d rather close the chapter and leave the relationship.

Idealizing

As children, when they depend on adults in every way, they idealize them, seeing them as strong, capable, protective, independent, and decisive. If the adults around them don’t give them time to process what’s happening to them and make their own decisions, the self-preservation E2 learns to leave everything in their hands.

The issue is that when they reach adulthood, they have an idealized image of what it means to be an adult, assuming that once they are grown up, get married, have kids, or start working, they will automatically gain the qualities of an adult.

I used to dream that when I turned 18, people would start treating me differently. I was so disappointed when that didn’t happen.

During my teenage years, I looked in the mirror wishing to be a mature woman with a beautiful body. The years went by, and my body barely changed. I wasn’t growing, and people still called me “little” or “child.” I got used to it, and by the time I reached adulthood, I realized my appearance hadn’t changed much. I shifted my idealization of being an adult into wanting to look younger, mentally erasing the limitations that came with resisting maturity.
summary: Описывает тенденцию самосохраняющегося E2 к самовиктимизации (перекладыванию вины) и идеализации взрослых/взрослости, основанной на детском опыте зависимости, что приводит к разочарованию и поиску способов избежать взросления через внешность или иллюзии.

title: Сравнение, поиск подтверждения и фантазии
text:
Prone to comparing

This subtype of E2 has an excessively high standard for themselves, creating a perfectionist, obsessive ideal that drives them. This comes from feelings of inferiority, believing they are not lovable and instead, easily disposable. But unlike the E4, they use pride to earn love and avoid being abandoned. The problem here is that they’re always comparing themselves to everyone else, often in an unfair and unfavorable way. This leads to an attitude of disdain (nose in the air), as though they’re royalty looking down on others.

Validation-seeking

The underlying issue for the self-preservation E2 is that they don’t feel valuable or deserving of love. To counter this, they do things for others in order to feel needed, thinking that this will prevent them from being abandoned and that others will offer them protection in return. They don’t realize that they end up feeling overwhelmed and resentful when others ask for something from them. And because they don’t know how to set boundaries, they respond with rejection and annoyance, behaving more like a tantrum-throwing child.

Fantasy-prone

Many self-preservation Twos are avid readers from a young age, using books to feed their emotions. Claudio describes them in workshops as “constrained adventurers,” meaning they long for freedom, to travel, to do whatever they want. But since they can’t achieve this, they turn to reading (especially novels) that allow them to break free from the rules and expectations they feel “confine” them. They feel their reality is too narrow, so in their imaginations, they accomplish things they wouldn’t be able to in real life.

When I was about ten, I started reading Salgari. It was amazing to become the main character in his novels, fighting tigers with Sandokan, being part of his pirate crew, or becoming Captain Storm. Soon after, I devoured the Book of Genesis from the Old Testament, The Divine Comedy, and many other books; stories that I would recreate over and over, where I was always the protagonist. It made me feel alive, powerful, and, most importantly, like I didn’t need anyone’s permission.
summary: Описывает склонность самосохраняющегося E2 к социальному сравнению из-за низкой самооценки, поиск подтверждения через служение другим (с риском выгорания) и использование фэнтези и чтения как escape-механизма для обретения ощущения силы и свободы, недоступного в реальной жизни.

title: Юношеский образ и адаптация
text:
Tomboyish

They often have a youthful appearance, looking younger than they actually are. Women of this subtype typically wear little to no makeup and tend to connect more easily with men than with women, interacting with them in a non-sexualized manner.

By the time my friends were twelve, they had already transitioned from girls to women, but I hadn’t… They were starting to like boys, while I was still enjoying my girlish games.
summary: Описывает внешне юношеский вид самосохраняющихся E2-женщин, их неприязнь к традиционной женственности, предпочтение общения с мужчинами в непринужденной форме и задержку в психологическом и социальном созревании по сравнению со сверстниками.

title: Accommodating and Complacent Behavior
text:
Since self-preservation Twos believe they are only loved when they are pleasant and good, they tend to be overly agreeable, saying yes to everything without stopping to consider whether they truly want to do it. This often leads them to take on commitments they later regret, fulfilling them reluctantly or abandoning them without warning.

Their complaisance carries an undertone of disdain; they view others as inferior beings in need of support and affection. At times, this blends with humor, manifesting as mockery, sarcasm, or cynicism.
summary: Describes how self-preservation Twos exhibit excessive agreeableness to gain love, leading to regrettable commitments, while masking disdain through humor and cynicism toward others they perceive as needing their support.

title: Hypersensitivity to Criticism
text:
Hypersensitive to criticism

They struggle both to self-reflect and to accept criticism from others. Any critique triggers their deep-seated fear of being unworthy, often leading to irritability, tears, and feelings of misunderstanding and resentment. At its core, this reaction stems from their fear of rejection, which equates to a fear of not being loved.

It is very difficult for a self-preservation E2 to accept their own mistakes. Even if they acknowledge their shortcomings, that is far from being able to tolerate someone else pointing them out. This often results in outbursts of anger or emotional explosions, turning the blame back on the one who dared to criticize them.
summary: Explains how self-preservation Twos react intensely to criticism due to fears of unworthiness and rejection, often responding with anger or blame-shifting rather than self-reflection.

title: Envy and Fear of Envy
text:
Envious / afraid of being envied

At first glance, self-preservation E2s don’t seem envious, as they compensate for any internal feelings of inferiority by projecting an air of abundance and superiority. However, envy, an unavoidable human emotion, is hidden beneath the surface as a way to mask their own perceived shortcomings and maintain a competitive edge. It may slip out occasionally in moments of indifference or apathy toward those they secretly envy.

This type of person not only hides their envy from themselves and others but also fears being envied, as it makes them feel vulnerable. Sensing others’ envy exposes their power because it reveals that they have something others desire. And they fear the potential backlash. Being envied could make them a target for rejection, criticism, or a loss of affection. To protect themselves, they resort to flattery and downplay their privileges or most desirable qualities, even adopting a false humility to stay safe and unchallenged.
summary: Discusses how self-preservation Twos conceal envy while fearing others' envy, using superiority and flattery to protect their sense of being loved and avoid perceived threats to their status.

title: Tenderness and Possessiveness
text:
Tender

The term “tender” is often associated with affection, kindness, and warmth—qualities typically linked to childhood, evoking an image of innocence and docility. Self-preservation E2s embody this quality naturally, drawing others in with their gentle and soft demeanor. This tenderness serves a purpose: it attracts protection and care, ensuring they remain untouched by the harshness of life and relationships.

Possessive

The possessiveness of a self-preservation E2 stems from their deep desire to merge with another person, seeking the assurance that they will always be there for them. This helps them avoid the pain of abandonment and ensures their basic emotional needs are met.

Their possessiveness also reflects their difficulty in seeing others as independent individuals. The idea of someone existing separately from them is a threatening reminder of their own fear of emotional independence. Ultimately, they see others as objects over which they must exert control.
summary: Describes how self-preservation Twos use tenderness to attract care and possessiveness to prevent abandonment, stemming from a fear of emotional independence and a need to control others as sources of security.

title: Jealousy, Arrogance, and Sadism
text:
Jealous

Jealousy, common in emotionally driven personalities, is deeply tied to the self-preservation E2’s neurotic need to be the sole person in a place of privilege, at the center of the other person’s heart and life. Its roots often trace back to childhood triangulation, when a parent involved them in a competitive dynamic of jealousy against the other parent.

Arrogant and egocentric

The proud arrogance of this personality type is most evident in their belief that what they want or think must always be taken into account and validated. It’s not so much an intellectual arrogance as it is the entitlement of someone who insists on being in first place. A kind of capricious superiority.

Sadistic

At first glance, sadism might seem contradictory to the tenderness and agreeableness of a self-preservation E2. However, their sadistic streak becomes evident when they feel denied or betrayed (in the sense of not getting what they want). If someone is not attending to them or fulfilling their needs, they can become the target of raw anger and mistreatment, amplified by this type’s intuitive ability to pinpoint and exploit others’ weaknesses. Their sadism also shows in their ability to wound with calculated coldness, leaving the other person feeling powerless and unable to retaliate.
summary: Covers jealousy rooted in childhood dynamics, arrogant entitlement to primacy, and sadistic reactions when needs are unmet, revealing a darker side beneath the agreeable facade of self-preservation Twos.

title: Paranoia, Control, and Vindictiveness
text:
Paranoid and controlling

Paranoia emerges in an obsessive and emotionally blind manner when a self-preservation Two projects their own manipulative tactics onto others, using them to gain favor and secure a position of privilege. If they sense that someone isn’t offering them unconditional support or encounter someone they perceive as superior in any way, they immediately see them as a rival, a threat to their place. This triggers their aggressive and controlling instincts, fueling a delusional sense of entitlement to attack whoever threatens them, sometimes even imagining conspiracies against them.

Belittling and vindictive

If someone disappoints them or they perceive competition, they have a sharp ability to humiliate and undermine that person until they’re no longer a threat. This dynamic plays out most notably in romantic or sibling relationships, as if they believe the other person should pay a price for not submitting to their demands or whims. The same applies when they feel criticized, offended, or abandoned. Stripping the other person of their power becomes a form of revenge, a way to assert their own dominance.
summary: Explains how self-preservation Twos develop paranoia and controlling behaviors by projecting their own tactics onto others, and respond to perceived threats with belittlement and vindictiveness to regain dominance and security.

title: Self-Indulgence and Avoidance of Limits
text:
Self-indulgent

Since their personality is built on an idealized self-image, they forgive themselves for everything. This self-indulgence reveals their intolerance for limits and reinforces a childlike attitude where they believe everything should be allowed. It serves as a way to avoid frustration or facing their hidden low self-esteem, compensating for it with the same permissiveness granted to a child. This trait directly clashes with their fear of growing up.
summary: Describes self-indulgence as a defense mechanism where self-preservation Twos avoid limits and frustration by maintaining a childlike belief in entitlement, masking low self-esteem and fear of maturity.

title: Само indulgence как защита от фрустрации
text: Since their personality is built on an idealized self-image, they forgive themselves for everything. This self-indulgence reveals their intolerance for limits and reinforces a childlike attitude where they believe everything should be allowed. It serves as a way to avoid frustration or facing their hidden low self-esteem, compensating for it with the same permissiveness granted to a child. This trait directly clashes with their fear of growing up.
summary: Описывает само indulgence у самосохраняющихся Двойки как компенсаторный механизм, основанный на идеализированном образе себя, позволяющий избегать фрустрации и низкой самооценки через детскую permissiveness, противоречащую страху взросления.

title: Непоследовательность и избегание ответственности
text:
Inconsistent

A self-preservation Two resists discipline; any task requiring sustained effort or sacrifice feels unbearable. Naturally, they justify this by making excuses, dismissing the goal as unimportant, or simply delegating the responsibility to someone else. This pattern reinforces their dependence on others while feeding their pride. They’re completely unaware that this very intolerance is what prevents them from developing real inner stability as an adult.
summary: Рассматривает непоследовательность и сопротивление дисциплине у самосохраняющихся Двойки, которые оправдывают лень оправданиями и делегированием, не осознавая, что это подрывает их внутреннюю стабильность.

title: Эмоциональность и фантазия как защитные механизмы
text:
Emotionality and fantasy

by Fernando Ramos

In contemporary characterological literature, Enneatype 2 is often referred to as the histrionic character due to its ability to generate emotions. The self-preservation E2 projects a childlike tenderness to seduce the one they perceive as the love of their life. They need to fantasize about an eternal romantic love, much like a sexual Three, with the difference being that while a sexual E3 adapts to become the ideal partner for the other person, a proud self-preservation E2 fantasizes that the other person is exactly as they want and need them to be.

And though they may appear cold and controlled compared to a sexual Two, emotionality and fantasy are their primary defense mechanisms.
summary: Объясняет, как у самосохраняющихся Двойки эмоциональность и фантазия служат основными защитными механизмами, включая проекцию детской нежности и идеализированные фантазии о любви, в отличие от адаптивности сексуальной Тройки.

title: Личный опыт переполняющей эмоциональности
text:
I never considered myself very emotional; I always saw myself as cold and controlled. It was only after years of therapy that I began to understand my emotionality. Emotionality is an exaggeration of sensitivity to emotions. It overwhelms you until you can’t see anything beyond the emotion itself. In that state, you don’t think, or if you do, your thoughts only amplify the emotion you’re feeling.

Many times, I find myself consumed by sadness. It starts with a feeling of loneliness, followed by thoughts like: “No one loves me,” “I’m alone,” “No one is coming for me…” and the sadness grows until I’m completely lost in it. Everything is sadness. It’s immense, a bottomless pit.

But the same thing happens with joy. Something good happens, I feel happy, and the process begins: “Life is wonderful,” “I’m amazing”… and before I know it, it’s joy multiplied—euphoria.

ANONYMOUS

What’s most characteristic about emotionality, as this person observes, is that by exaggerating it so much, one gets lost in it and can no longer think clearly (sometimes, they can’t think at all) or feel their body. Everything becomes emotion.

The core issue is that this character structure either gets lost in overwhelming emotion or suppresses it completely to maintain control. There’s no middle ground. In a confrontation, when trying to come up with arguments to justify their actions, they feel like their attempt is useless; the other person has better, more solid arguments. They can’t find a reason, or they can’t express it. Suddenly, they connect with a deep sense of helplessness, their energy rises, and speaking becomes more difficult. That’s when the theatrics begin and emotionality takes over. A sequence of exaggerated gestures and shouting starts; internally, it feels like they’re dying. They say disrespectful things, insult, threaten. From the outside, it looks like a crime is being committed. It ends with desperate crying and, at times, total withdrawal.
summary: Первоисточник личного опыта описывает, как эмоциональность у самосохраняющихся Двойки приводит к полной потере контроля и мышления, вызывая крайние состояния отчаяния или эйфории, которые заканчиваются истерикой или отшествием, без среднего состояния.

title: Эмоциональная экспрессия как способ самоутверждения
text:
You could say that a self-preservation Two is “all heart.” Though there’s also a mental labyrinth where we get lost, making it hard to extract a clear message about our feelings, needs, and desires.

I speak from the “I feel…” rather than “I think…” My inner world is rich with emotions: sadness, sudden joy, anger… I can start crying uncontrollably without really knowing why. The emotion just comes, and I need to let it out. Many times, after a deep cry, I burst into nervous laughter to release the tension completely.

There are gray days when I wake up and just know it’s a day for “cleaning”—crying and crying, letting myself sink into sadness and anger. For me, it’s healthy to accept it and let it happen. Though, to be honest, I often amplify the emotion to make it feel more “real,” more intense. I find pleasure in it.

Other times, a sudden internal joy takes over. My eyes light up, sparkling, I laugh, I feel like jumping, laughing, screaming… I love feeling alive. And if the day before, in a gray haze, my world had collapsed, today I can see everything with boundless light and beauty... This ability has helped me rise from many falls.

It’s hard to untangle my “mental web.” I can come across as a sweet girl, sometimes hysterical… Inside, there’s a being full of internal contradictions, of introjected ideas about how things should be, about who I am to myself and to the world, or who I should be… Aligning my needs, my mind, my body, and my deepest desires has been the work of my life.

VANESA LUNA
summary: Личный рассказ иллюстрирует, как самосохраняющаяся Двойка живет через эмоции («я чувствую» вместо «я думаю»), испытывая крайние колебания между горечью и радостью, используя эмоциональные выпуски для снятия напряжения, несмотря на внутренние противоречия и лабиринт интроецированных убеждений.

title: Детские корни эмоциональной защиты
text: As we’ve already discussed, a self-preservation Two’s emotional world never found a true form of expression in childhood. In general, their mother took up too much space with her emotions, either through depression or histrionics. The child learned that emotions could be used to manipulate others’ emotional worlds. Tears of sadness could stop aggression or unsustainable demands. Melancholy could seduce or keep someone from leaving. Panic attacks could mask a deep fear of life itself. And an overwhelming emotional outburst could be a way to avoid facing problems or failures.
summary: Объясняет, как в детстве у самосохраняющихся Двойки эмоциональная среда была доминирована матерью, что привело к обучению использованию эмоций как инструмента манипуляции и избегания проблем через истерики, слезы и панические атаки.

title: Эмоциональная защита и подавление у самосохраняющейся двойки
text:
So, a self-preservation Two expresses an entire hysterical emotional world that completely covers up the pain of loneliness, the wound of abandonment, and the absence of love. Deep wounds are denied through a mix of overwhelming, chaotic emotional display, and when it comes to the fear of rejection and abandonment, a proud display of superiority shuts everything down. This reaction follows the unconscious command to “never grow up,” but it leaves no room to feel the real fears of childhood while maintaining the illusion of not needing anyone.

We’ve already explored the connection between shame and humiliation. It’s true that shame is an emotion self-preservation E2s often feel but work hard to hide. It’s not easy for them to connect with humiliation because it’s a childhood wound inflicted by the same parent who adored or seduced them. Often, it was a shocking and unexpected betrayal, something they perceived as a deep violation of their trust. It’s as if their parent lured them into a trap and then abandoned them. The memory of feeling “exposed” and ridiculed remains vivid, and a great deal of energy is invested in never returning to that place.

Anger is also not permitted because it would be an attack on their parents or an admission that they are not the cheerful, radiant child their parents wanted them to be. Expressing anger directly is taboo, so it gets dealt with through avoidance, petulant tantrums, or, in extreme cases, deep depression.

Often, the only escape is to disconnect and trap emotions in the body. It’s not uncommon for them to experience asthma, allergies, muscle pain, or gastrointestinal issues.

Ultimately, despite being such an emotional character, self-preservation E2s struggle to truly feel. They are imprisoned by the duty to radiate joy and good humor, without ever really asking themselves if they are happy.
summary: Описывает, как самосохраняющаяся двойка использует эмоциональную экспрессию и гордость как защиту от боли одиночества и’abandonment, подавляя гнев и стыд, что приводит к психосоматическим симптомам и отрыву от настоящих чувств из-за обязанности быть радостной.

title: Творческое фантазирование какEscape-механизм у самосохраняющейся двойки
text:
There is, of course, a form of creative fantasy. Fantasy that is not defensive, but which self-preservation E2s are experts at using as a means of escape, as a way to believe in something different from what actually is. Reality is never as good or wonderful as what they can imagine, and they want to return to that fantasy as soon as possible. Because of this, they undervalue reality, comparing it to the imaginary life they’ve built in their minds.

For example, they might imagine the perfect man—handsome, intelligent, wealthy, kind, and wonderful. In reality, no such man exists, and so the conclusion is that no man is ever good enough. Their fantasy also fuels a sense of self-overvaluation; in their imagination, they believe themselves capable of endless things, things they have only envisioned but never actually done. Because taking action is terrifying.

During adolescence, when I was too afraid to approach the boys I liked, I would imagine having boyfriends instead. I didn’t have them in real life, only in my mind. I had my first boyfriend at eighteen, and only because my mother practically pushed me into it.

ANONYMOUS

From early childhood, fantasy was where they lived most intensely. Life always seemed dull in comparison to what they could dream up. They developed the habit of escaping into fantasy both because they couldn’t express themselves and because they didn’t dare to take action in certain situations. In fantasy, they could feel free. It was also an antidote to loneliness or having no one to play with; they invented imaginary friends. But in real life, they were shy and struggled to make real connections. Fantasy also became a way to stay afloat emotionally. The great tragedy of fantasy is that it keeps them from truly feeling how bad things are. In many ways, it resembles an addiction.

Romantic fantasies, of being desired, of someone never being able to stop searching for me, needing me, of being their great love, their light, their inspiration.

ANONYMOUS
summary: Описывает, как самосохраняющиеся двойки используют творческое фантазирование как способ побега от реальности, создавая идеализированные образы (партнера, себя) и избегая действий из страха неудачи, что приводит к отрыву от реальности и эмоциональной зависимости от фантазий.

title: Фантазия как основа самооценки и избегание ответственности у самосохраняющейся двойки
text:
One of the most striking aspects of this tendency is seeing just how far they will go to avoid taking responsibility for their actions and desires. Compared to the other proud subtypes—who work hard to seduce through action, whether by drawing in groups (social E2s) or individuals (sexual E2s) to earn affection and admiration—the self-preservation E2 appears to be the least active in seduction. In most cases, their seduction remains confined to the realm of fantasy.

Like other E2s, in their imagination, they see themselves as devoted, admired, and generous. Fantasy is their primary tool for inflating the ego with a sense of self-importance, a way to cope with the frustration of feeling incapable and ineffective in the real world.

The rich inner world of a self-preservation E2 is overflowing with fantasy. Our imagination knows no limits. Many Twos are drawn to esotericism and spirituality, as these paths allow them to expand their imagination and fulfill the need to feel connected to God or something greater, not bound by the rules of conventional rationality.

Since I was a child, I have lived in a parallel imaginary world. I would play alone, pretending I was a secret police officer, different from the other kids. I was on an undercover mission at school to capture someone from the FBI… I was “someone special.” One day, my prince charming would come to pick me up in a huge luxury car, big enough to fit all the kids in my class, and they would marvel at my incredible luck. I imagined it so vividly that, to me, it was simply real, it was going to happen someday... I spoke with God, even with the Devil, and made my own secret pacts for things to happen as I wished… or to prevent terrible things from happening.

VANESA LUNA
summary: Объясняет, как самосохраняющаяся двойка избегает ответственности через фантазию, используя её для соблазна и самоутверждения вместо реальных действий, усиливая самооценку через воображаемые сценарии и обращаясь к эзотерике как способу расширения внутреннего мира.

title: Неуверенность и фантазия как защита
text: Self-preservation E2s feel deeply insecure about their abilities. They carry the painful memory of failure and repeated humiliation for their perceived weakness, which is why they prefer not to take risks, turning instead to fantasy. Their ability to take action is clouded by the fear that whatever they do will not be enough to be admired. In this, they differ from the other subtypes, who are more proactive in romantic seduction. While they, too, care about achievements and recognition, simply dreaming about them is often enough to inflate their ego.
summary: Описывает, как самосохраняющиеся E2 используют фантазию как способ компенсировать свою неуверенность и избежать рисков, в отличие от более проактивных подтипов.

title: Свидетельство о гиперчувствительности и самоунижении
text:
Let’s end with this testimony:

I would exaggerate or minimize things to an extreme degree. For example, a single look from someone could stay with me for years. I would imagine that person was in love with me just because of the way they looked at me… There was a deep shame in coming clean about the situation, or at least in admitting my own desires and feelings, in taking responsibility for them. So instead, I let that look become proof that I was beautiful, special, capable of making people fall in love from afar.

And just as I could magnify something to an extraordinary level, I could just as easily shrink myself down: I let insecurity wash over every thought and emotion. Just imagining that, from a single gesture or a distant look (or one I only imagined was distant...), I wasn’t liked or was being criticized… It would hurt me so much that I felt small and very fragile… unworthy, cast aside.

VANESA LUNA
summary: Личное свидетельство о тенденции к преувеличению или преуменьшению событий, связанным с самооценкой, где внешние сигналы интерпретируются как proof любви или отвержения, приводящее к эмоциональной нестабильности.

title: Страхи самосохраняющихся E2
text: Fear plays a crucial role. Self-preservation E2s experience deep fears in their relationships and social interactions: Fear of being alone. Fear of being ignored. Fear of having no one in their life. Fear of being exposed as incapable. Fear of not being able to handle a situation. Fear of being attacked. Fear of not being able to stand on their own. Fear of losing the support of loved ones. Fear of being seen as flawed or defective. Fear of being trapped in a situation where they cannot experience their pleasures and desires. Fear of losing their special place with another person. Fear of getting angry and showing that anger. Fear of acknowledging pain and vulnerability. Fear of being caught in their own lies.
summary: Перечисляет ключевые страхи, характерные для самосохраняющихся E2, связанные с одиночением, неприязнью, ощущением неполноценности и потерей поддержки.

title: Детство как идеализированное убежище
text:
Childhood

by Tania Rojo

For the self-preservation Two, childhood is something they idealize as magical. It’s a refuge from frustration and pain. At the same time, they cling to a childlike approach to life, embodying the role of the eternal child, whether they recognize it or not.

As they grow, they mold themselves into the ideal child that everyone wants to have. A child who radiates warmth and tenderness, something so often missing in families and society.

A note from my mother in my baby book: “In general, she is a healthy, playful, and well-behaved little girl. She doesn’t cry much. A bit bold for her age (one year old), she loves climbing on anything she can and reaching for things, whether they’re within her grasp or not. Sincerely, her mom.”

Since I was little, I always felt deeply wanted by my parents. I believed my older brother and I were their dream come true, the perfect duo: first a boy, then a girl. I had incredible energy, always dancing, never staying still. I wanted to hug and kiss everyone, always smiling, always eager. Before I turned four, I felt completely free, as if neither my spirit nor my body had any limits.

Chubby legs, playful movements, endless giggles. I left a good impression on people. They found me sweet and charming. I made a nice impression, evoking in their hearts warmth and sympathy. When I started talking, my voice was deep and raspy, which made me stand out even more. People saw me as different, both tender and strong. I felt bold, always daydreaming. I loved being physically close to people, sitting on their laps, receiving affection and compliments, soaking up their attention (and of course, I got it).

CATI PRECIADO
summary: Описывает, как самосохраняющиеся E2 идеализируют свое детство как время безопасности и любви, стремясь сохранить образ милого, обаятельного ребенка во взрослой жизни.

title: Последствия гиперопеки и утрата автономии
text:
Growing up wrapped in “cotton wool” seems common for a self-preservation E2, though that comfort comes with its own burdens and a price to pay. They may have been overprotected by one parent or had multiple parental figures (siblings, aunts, uncles, etc.), some of whom displayed ambivalent attitudes that the child struggled to interpret as genuine and selfless care. More importantly, these figures often did not provide the necessary emotional containment. This creates a deep distrust in love and a low tolerance for life’s challenges since they haven’t developed the internal tools to handle difficulty and hardship.

How is a privileged child brought into the world?

I was the first daughter, first granddaughter, first niece… Basically, I was spoiled from every direction. I got gifts, had my photos taken constantly. I was the center of attention. I even had a whole room just for my toys. I had a strong personality; I was the real authority in the family.

ANONYMOUS

It’s true that I’ve always felt privileged. I was the firstborn, very much wanted, and from what I’ve been told, a very smart and charming child. I started walking at nine months and talking soon after. I was deeply loved and pampered. I always had what I wanted, and more. My family seemed perfect, and with them, I felt invincible. I always felt protected.

Now I see that it wasn’t protection; it was overprotection. That’s why I struggle so much with frustration.

ANONYMOUS
summary: Обсуждает, как гиперопека в детстве приводит к трудностям с самостоятельностью и терпением к фрустрации, несмотря на ощущениеPrivileged и любви.

title: Родительская переопека как защита от собственных тревог
text: By overprotecting their child, parents aim to ensure that “nothing bad happens” to them. But really, they are trying to protect themselves from the uncertainties and challenges of parenthood. They don’t realize they are raising a child who will struggle to meet their own needs. Some are emotionally absent, while others are themselves childish and narcissistic, masking their own immaturity with superficial praise meant to boost their own egos. Some resort to gift-giving as a way to compensate for their inability to form a genuine emotional connection with their child and their discomfort with a bond that might impose limits or bring them frustration.
summary: Обсуждает, как родительская переопека у самосохраняющихся двойок направлена на снижение тревоги родителей, а не на заботу о ребёнке, приводит к эмоциональной зависимости и отсутствию навыков саморегуляции.

title: Внутренняя диссоциация и манипуляция как стратегия выживания
text: Little by little, the self-preservation E2 learns that it’s far easier to disconnect from their inner world and present their parents with the charming, entertaining child they want to see, an object to be displayed. They also develop the ability to shift responsibility onto others (mother, father), mastering the subtle art of manipulation. Over time, they become hesitant to try new things or take risks, because someone else has always stepped in to do things for them. As a result, they place more trust in others than in themselves, leading to deep insecurity. Internalized beliefs like “Someone else knows how to do it,” “Someone else has the solution to my problem,” “If I do it on my own, I might mess up,” or “It’s safer to let others handle it, that way I won’t fail” become ingrained in their mindset.
summary: Описывает, как self-preservation E2 отключается от собственных потребностей, учится манипулировать и переносить ответственность на других, что ведёт к неуверенности в себе и зависимости от внешней поддержки.

title: Идеализация родителя как источник ложной безопасности
text: I adored my father. He was always right. He was the strongest, smartest, and kindest father in the world. I told him everything. He explained to me how things were, who among my classmates was an idiot and who was worth my time. He even told me what I was feeling. Most of all, he told me about himself at my age; how much stronger, braver, and more daring he was. For the longest time, he was my reference point. He was the man, the one who knew everything, the one who had the right to judge what was good and bad. His approval was what I sought.
summary: Личный рассказ о том, как отец становится непререкаемым авторитетом и источником эмоциональной опоры, заменяя самостоятельное восприятие и чувства ребёнка.

title: Ложная зависимость и эмоциональная путаница в отношениях
text:
But this isn’t real trust. It’s an internalized set of parental messages designed to keep the child dependent, locked forever into the role of their little girl or boy.

This so-called overprotection fosters a deep sense of inadequacy when it comes to facing the outside world. At the same time, the unspoken expectation to remain “mommy’s precious child”—along with the privileges granted by one or both parents—creates confusion and ambivalence. The only way to cope is through avoidance or prideful defiance. That confusion grows even stronger when the parents use their favorite child as a weapon against each other.

The special place a self-preservation E2 holds in their parents’ lives often creates tension with their siblings. They become the target of envy and resentment, leading to emotional distance that, on an unconscious level, reinforces their feelings of loneliness.

This distrust of peers tends to repeat itself later in life, affecting relationships with classmates and friends. Many self-preservation E2s describe struggling to make close friends or experiencing painful rejection.

Their parents interpret the external world for them, telling them how things are and how they should feel, without ever genuinely engaging with their emotions. Often, their explanations are inconsistent, based on whatever the parent is feeling or needing in the moment. As a result, the child grows up expecting others to instinctively understand what they’re feeling, without developing the ability to listen to themselves or put their experiences into words.
summary: Анализирует, как переопека создаёт иллюзию доверия, но на самом деле усиливает зависимость, путает эмоциональные границы и приводит к социальной изоляции и трудностям в построении близких отношений.

title: Самоустранение и внутренний запрет на аутентичность
text:
Over time, the self-preservation E2 internalizes the idea that being themselves is not acceptable, that it’s better to hold back because who they are isn’t “right.” “If I don’t cause trouble and I behave, they’ll love me” is one of their unconscious beliefs. The consequence is the characteristic self-erasure of this subtype. They make themselves small, fade into the background, and become overly cautious about taking up space or being a burden.

My mother made all my decisions for me: what I should do, what I should wear, how I should act. Little by little, I learned to suppress my own desires and just wait for her to tell me what to do. The rare times I took initiative, she criticized me and told me how I should have done it differently. Eventually, I just stopped thinking for myself. I simply did what she told me. I obeyed without question.
summary: Описывает процесс внутреннего самоподавления, когда ребёнок учится подавлять свои желания и инициативу, чтобы заслужить любовь через послушание и угодливость.

title: Псевдо-отдача как способ вернуть контроль и ценность
text:
Self-preservation E2s learn early on that their needs come second, that they can wait. First, they must take care of others, mirroring the way their mother was always there for them, as long as they didn’t trouble her with their truth.

At first glance, there seems to be a contradiction between this tendency to withdraw and the arrogance of expecting others to love them unconditionally, serve them, and recognize their “natural” gifts. But in reality, there is no contradiction at all. Their pride in being special is the ego structure that not only hides their sense of lack but also provides an escape from insecurity. They take on the role of the child who cares for their mother and other adults—helping when they’re sick, handling practical tasks, and working for the benefit of others. This approach disconnects them from their own needs, but it allows them to reclaim a central place in others’ lives. Over time, this dynamic leads to the belief that “I don’t need anything,” making it hard to even recognize their own needs. In turn, they develop a sense of omnipotence, though at the cost of true individual freedom.

My mother talks a lot, all day long. It was unbearable. I could listen for a while, but then I’d get tired and zone out. I felt like there was no room for me to express myself, so I’d go to my room and imagine all the things I wanted to say.
summary: Объясняет, как self-preservation E2 компенсируют чувство недостачи через заботу о других, что маскирует собственные потребности и создаёт иллюзию всемогущества, несмотря на потерю аутентичности.

title: Самодостаточный двойка: Танцы для учителя и поведение по желанию матери
text: I became a child who learned to dance for my teacher and to behave exactly as my mother wanted, both at home and at school. As a little girl, I would eagerly seek my mother’s hugs and kisses, only for her to tell me to stop and be still. I felt shut down. I couldn’t understand how my mother could reject something as beautiful as the love I wanted to give her, and that she could give me. My father, on the other hand, was more receptive. He let me hug and kiss him, and that helped me feel less alone in the coldness I felt from my mother.
summary: The narrator describes childhood experiences where maternal affection was conditional and withdrawn, while paternal affection was warm and accepting, leading to feelings of emotional shutdown and confusion about love and rejection.

title: Самодостаточный двойка: Притворная счастье и искажение реальности
text:
As children, self-preservation Twos learn to uplift those around them, to smile, and to always appear happy. Or at least pretend to be. This tendency is closely tied to deception, based on the principle that if reality isn’t as bright and fun as it should be, they can always adjust it to make it more interesting. The goal, as always, is to attract attention, be loved, and feel protected.

It seemed like my birth brought joy to my entire family, without exception. There was no one my age in my family; even my cousins were adults. I lived in an adult world and had to adapt.
