I learned very quickly that if I made them happy, they would pay attention to me and spend time with me. I became very affectionate. They would ask for hugs and kisses all the time, and I happily gave them as long as it meant they would play with me and not leave me alone.
summary: Self-preservation Twos develop a habit of appearing happy and adjusting reality to gain love and attention. The narrator recounts how, as the only child among adults, she learned to seek affection through constant hugs and kisses to avoid being left alone.

title: Самодостаточный двойка: Очки сквозь розовые стекла и избегание неприятного
text:
This belief that they can reshape reality later transforms into a habit of seeing life through rose-tinted glasses, downplaying or omitting unpleasant facts, or reframing situations to make them seem more positive. It’s a refusal to see the “dark” or harsh side of life. That’s how the child responds to family demands that negative emotions are not to be acknowledged or displayed. They form a strong alliance with their parents to shield them from feelings of inadequacy or anxiety.

Being close to my mother and knowing everything she was doing, saying, and feeling was important to me. Sometimes I’d get annoyed or bored following her around, but I adapted because I knew that later she would do what I wanted. Many times, while running errands with my mother, I would daydream and make up stories to pass the time.
summary: Self-preservation Twos develop a tendency to view life optimistically by ignoring negative realities, especially when family discourages negative emotions. The narrator describes adapting to her mother’s presence by daydreaming during errands to maintain emotional connection.

title: Самодостаточный двойка: Страх разоблачения и потребность быть «хорошей»
text:
Alongside their need to bring joy to others to earn approval and love, self-preservation E2s also develop a strong desire to present themselves as “good, obedient, and always available.” Naturally, this comes with a deep fear of being exposed as a fraud.

I was always afraid of being judged or called out by adults. Deep down, I felt like I couldn’t control myself. I longed so much to be polite and well-liked... Every time I made eye contact with an adult, I couldn’t help but project, “I am good.” I craved their kind smiles, their protection, their approval...

My biggest goal was to be seen as good, especially by adults, because they had the power. One fear I remember vividly, and still have, is the fear of being caught. I felt intense shame when I was caught misbehaving. I was ashamed of lying, ashamed of how I looked in those moments. If I wasn’t good, then I wasn’t worth anything. I felt this constantly with my father.

There was also a clear duality in believing I was better, more good, than other kids. I remember once trading a toy car with my neighbor (she must have been five, I was eight) in exchange for letting me touch her private parts ten times. The next day, her mother came over to complain. My mother didn’t even ask me if it was true or not; she simply didn’t believe it. I felt immense relief because, at the core, I knew my mother’s love was conditional. The image of me as an innocent, pure child was so deeply ingrained that anything that deviated from that narrative was framed as an impulsive mistake, something unintentional, something I couldn’t be held accountable for. Admitting fault would mean falling from my pedestal, and that would threaten the one thing I feared most: losing the constant, special love I received.
summary: Self-preservation Twos fear being exposed as fraudulent and strive to be seen as good and obedient to earn love. The narrator shares a vivid childhood memory of shame and relief when her mother denied her misbehavior, revealing the conditional nature of love and the need to maintain a perfect image.

title: Самодостаточный двойка: Идеализация отца и конкуренция с матерью
text:
A recurring theme in this personality type, especially among women, is the figure of an absent father (either physically or symbolically) and his subsequent idealization.

My father traveled a lot, worked a lot… in short, he was hardly ever home. And I adored him. I used to say I wanted to marry him. Since he always asked about school and grades when he was home, I started studying obsessively. I wanted to be the best, to do something impressive enough for him to notice me and want to spend time with me. I became the top student in school, then the best in university, and eventually my boss’s right-hand. When you’re in that position, you can’t afford to lose it, you can’t fail. You have to push yourself harder and harder. It’s exhausting...

There’s also a strong sense of competition with the mother for the father’s attention. It reflects an unresolved Electra complex, as the father gives his daughter a special place (with her being in love with him) and fails to step into the role of a parent within the family unit.

My relationship with my mother was intense as a child. She tried to “tame” me, and I refused to stay inside the fence. At times, I seemed very polite and obedient, but then... I would want to have my own way. My mother struggled with my impulsiveness and stubbornness. Our relationship was shaped by her teaching me how to be a “good girl,” to obey, behave properly, do what was expected of me, and dress nicely. I created an image of myself as a country girl like Laura Ingalls, who just wanted to play, live life, and have fun.

What scared my mother most was my unpredictability: how I could change my mind, tastes, and direction, and how I couldn’t focus on anything for long. She felt uneasy about what I might do or what could happen to me, convinced that others would take advantage of me.
summary: Self-preservation Twos often idealize an absent father and compete with the mother for his attention, reflecting an Electra complex. The narrator describes her father’s absence, her academic striving to gain his notice, and her mother’s attempts to control her impulsive nature.

title: Отношения с отцом как источник легкости и одобрения
text:
With my father, it was always more like we were friends. He would play nice music in the car, buy us sweets, take us to the movies, and there were always huge ice creams. He’d suggest going to the theme park, and I’d play in the pool with him. My father taught me how to ride a bike and showed me how to be carefree, not to take life too seriously. I saw him as a very young guy. I remember his athletic figure in those bell-bottoms from the seventies. I liked seeing his mane of straight jet black hair, and trying on his glasses. His presence was like a balm of lightness and good humor.

I had my father’s skin color and nails. His philosophy was that fighting for something wasn’t worth it. I began to imitate his nonchalant, carefree attitude, giving in like him just to avoid conflict.

I remember defending my father from my mother; I felt completely aligned with him—his love of food, his tendency to go for walks, his curiosity about the world. I was always proud of his work; he was a pioneer in the field of computing. His stories about his trip to Chicago, where a computer took up an entire floor... were mind-blowing. I didn’t need to read stories. My father told them to me. I imagined a life of adventure.

My father showed me his affection through his words and permissiveness. He would call me “my little one,” “my brunette,” always praising my willing and friendly attitude. He’d go so far as to tell my mother, “Why can’t you be more like your daughter?” I remember feeling uncomfortable hearing those words. On one hand, I felt important, but on the other, my father was criticizing my mother’s way of treating us and him, and I felt like I was betraying my mother.
summary: Описываются теплые, дружеские отношения с отцом, который проявлял ласку через permissiveness и совместные занятия, но при этом создавал лояльностный конфликт, ставя дочь против матери через сравнения и восхищение ею.

title: Сенсуальное соперничество с матерью за внимание отца
text:
CATI PRECIADO

The girl truly feels that she has more power than her mother over the father, whom she wants as a partner or accomplice, responding to his suggestions. This creates a strong sense of competition with the mother for the role.

My focus was always on the male world, whether from early crushes or because at home I was already going after my father. Before I even knew how to ride a bike, I was already making advances toward my father and competing with my mother, posing sensually for the photos he took, showing my legs to seduce him.
summary: Девочка осознает свое преимущество перед матерью в борьбе за внимание отца, проявляя раннюю сексуализацию и соблазнительное поведение, стремясь занять роль его партнерши или сообщницы.

title: Последствия детской динамики для самосохраняющейся E2 во взрослой жизни
text:
ANONYMOUS

This disordered relationship with both the mother and the father leads, in the future, to the self-preservation E2 woman’s difficulty in finding her place among other women, as she tends to want to be the one and only. With men, she will always seek special treatment, and in relationships, she tends to adopt the role of the pleasing, submissive girl.

In this regard, it’s important for the self-preservation E2 woman to recognize both her place and her mother’s place within the family. By lowering her defenses, acknowledging the harm caused to the mother in this battle, and embracing gratitude, she can finally stop participating in a fight for a position that doesn’t belong to her. She must also recognize that her alliance with the father came at the cost of losing maternal nurturing. Although this is a challenging step, as her sense of self has been tied to this role, it will ultimately be incredibly liberating. It will allow her to change her relationship patterns with other women, bonding and sharing, rather than competing, and enable her to forge her identity as a woman in relation to men, leaving behind the role of the little girl.

Statistically, there are fewer men than women with this character. The future self-preservation E2 man often has a complicated relationship with his mother, who instills in him a sense of specialness and an erotized bond, causing him to see himself as someone unique, while also remaining a little boy at heart.

The relationship with the father can be in his case more distant and, at times, competitive, resulting in difficulties in relationships with men. He may feel proudly superior but internally unfit for the adult male role. This childhood experience often leads him to adopt a very sweet demeanor and a more “feminine” way of seducing, characterized by empathy, care and sensitivity.

Generally speaking, the self-preservation E2 had a seemingly happy childhood, filled with attention and role models who offered love and taught them about the world, albeit through distorted and irrational lenses. Beneath the surface, however, it was a childhood marked by emotional neglect and harmful exposure to the adult world. There was a disconnect between feeling both childlike and privileged, while also being entrusted with inappropriate confidences that weren’t suited for their age.

They learned to do whatever it took to be the center of attention and earn the admiration of adults, by being polite, good, and obedient. This is the price of love, as they understood it in childhood. Setting or accepting boundaries will be just as difficult for them as having self-confidence. When it comes to making decisions, they will rely on the opinions of others, people that held value during their formative years. Ultimately, they develop a deep distrust in this ambiguous love and the ability of adults to truly care for them.

In conclusion, because their self-expression is “restricted” or denied in one way or another, they will learn to suppress their true selves in reality and seek refuge in fantasy. In this fantasy world, they will embellish what isn’t quite good enough. They will quickly realize that one effective way to receive love is by being the source of joy in the household and avoiding being a burden. As a result, they will become adept at reading the emotional atmosphere of their family. They will be a child with an unresolved Oedipus or Electra complex, leading to competitive relationships with same-sex peers and difficulty finding their place as adults in romantic relationships.
summary: Анализируются долгосрочные последствия детской динамики для самосохраняющейся E2: конкуренция с родителем того же пола, подавление истинного себя, зависимость от одобрения, идеализация любви как заслуги, и необходимость осознания и интеграции для здоровых отношений во взрослой жизни.

title: Характеристики самосохраняющихся детей E2
text:
Self-preservation E2 children tend to be noisy, picky, disruptive, and unable to handle demands. They can be easily distracted and often distract others. Critical, boastful, and impulsive, they always want to get their way. Many of these traits will follow them into adulthood.

Or, quite the opposite: they might be shy, insecure, quiet, and sensitive children, who suppress traumatic events, rewriting reality through fantasy until they lose touch with their feelings of aversion, rejection, anger, and even hatred toward their parents or caregivers. Rebellion may appear in adolescence, once they’ve mastered the art of masking their true emotions. They begin to outgrow the image of the “good boy” or “good girl” and, in an effort to be noticed, seek attention at any cost, focusing not just on accomplishments but anything that allows them to stand out.
summary: Описывает две противоположные модели поведения у самосохраняющихся детей E2: шумные, импульсивные и требовательные, либо тихие, подавленные и фантазирующие, которые позже могут бунтовать, стремясь к вниманию.

title: Личная testimony: потеря матери и эмоциональная адаптация
text:
I will conclude with the testimony of my own childhood:

When I was five years old, my mother passed away, and my father decided, in many ways, to give up on life. In fact, just a few months later, he was admitted to a psychiatric hospital. It’s only now, twenty-eight years after his death, that I’ve been able to open that box full of pain, that chapter of my life which I once spoke of as casually as telling someone I had a cup of coffee. Now I can relive the panic I felt the night she died, how alone I felt, the responsibility of having to take care of my brother when I didn’t want to, when I felt it wasn’t my place to do that, when what I needed was to be taken care of. Now I can feel the pain in my chest, a sharp pain that cuts through… and then, the relief of not having to carry it anymore, of not having to endure this great sadness on my own, just within the armor of my chest.

In that moment, I felt the depth of pain my young self was capable of enduring. I remember crying endlessly at first, while hearing countless “don’t cry” from those who couldn’t bear their own pain from seeing me cry. It was then that I began to numb my chest, shielding myself from the emotions: the start of a deep sadness that still lingers within me.
summary: Автор делится личным опытом детской травмы — смерть матери и отстранение отца, описывая подавление боли, эмоциональное онемение и начало жизненной стратегии избегания боли через контроль и самодостаточность.

title: Стратегии избегания боли и формирование всесилие
text:
I’m starting to see all the effort, throughout my life, to avoid feeling pain, replacing it with two different strategies: one, to invent reality, distort it, and paint the world pink; and another, to push everything painful away, not to see it. With pride, I can freeze my chest without realizing that something is affecting me.

I wonder if the emptiness from my mother’s death led to the neurotic decision to appear “full.” Was it my way of escaping the immense envy I felt toward others for having mothers, and my shame for feeling so different from the other children? I answer myself: yes; for me, there is a clear connection between feeling this great lack and wanting to hide it.

It was also around this time that my drive to do everything perfectly was born, to be admired by my peers and loved by adults. I sought the privileged position by excelling in school. Getting good grades was a sure way to earn my teachers’ love, so I didn’t hesitate to put my heart and soul into it. I remember my first big moment of anxiety about my studies when I was ten, for not finishing all my homework on time. Would I lose the teacher’s love?
summary: Описывает психологические защиты: отрицание реальности и эмоциональное отключение, связывает чувство пустоты после потери матери с необходимостью казаться «полным» и идеальным, чтобы заслужить любовь и избежать отвержения.

title: Формирование спасительского комплекса и гетеросексуальной динамики
text:
I was always my father’s little princess. I felt that we had a special bond, and I competed with my mother for my father’s love. But she never put me in my place. She let me stay there. After her death, I immediately stepped into her role, becoming my father’s emotional support and fulfilling the Oedipal role. I took on the role of partner, and, in inheriting my mother’s position with him, I became his mother. Daughter, partner, and mother—all impossible roles to combine. Yet, when I felt omnipotent, I believed I could occupy them. It was then that my arrogance took root, the belief that “I’m worth more than you, and I’ll prove it.” Taking care of my father and placing myself above him made me feel more capable than the rest of the world. That’s when the mindset of “I’m the best” and “men can’t manage on their own” took hold.

I recently heard Albert Rams say that personality is formed to prevent something from repeating itself, and in a recent therapy session, I was able to see how I developed that sense of omnipotence to ensure my mother’s death wouldn’t happen again. I discovered that I felt more capable than God; my mother’s death was a mistake of His. At the same time, I feel the heavy burden of not having been able to save her. Another part of my trait appears: the savior. “I will save everyone,” that’s my deepest, craziest idea. It’s a defense against something I can no longer prevent. As if trying to save everyone I think needs saving (whether they ask for it or not) could heal my trauma.

I also didn’t want the wound of abandonment to repeat itself, when my mother died and my father was admitted to the psychiatric hospital. That’s when I promised myself, “I will never need anyone again.
summary: Описывает формирование комплекса всесилия и спасителя после потери матери: Übernahme роли матери по отношению к отцу, убеждение в собственном превосходстве, обещание никогда не зависеть от других как защита от повторения брошенности.

title: Усвоенные роли и стратегии получения любви через заботу
text:
It didn’t feel strange to me, as a child, to play the role of my brother’s mother. The environment helped. I clearly remember the praise from my family: smiles and compliments for being so good, responsible, for taking such good care of my brother, and for being so strong and brave! I was the perfect child they wanted me to be, I was so adorable...

I learned to always be available and to guess what was expected of me in order to please and receive love. I learned to disconnect from my fear and force myself to be strong. I learned that taking care of others was more important than taking care of myself. I learned not to ask for anything so as not to disturb or disappoint. I learned to believe I was so good and capable that I could be the best. And, of course, I learned to seduce with my gaze, my charm, and my eloquence.
summary: Описывает, как автор в детстве усвоил роль заботливого опекуна через похвалу за ответственность, выработал стратегию получения любви через самопожертвование, подавление своих потребностей и развитие очарования как инструмента влияния.

title: Privilege and its consequences
text:
This behavior earned me many privileges, both in my family and at school. I learned the joy of having privilege and how to seduce adults into giving it to me. Here’s an anecdote: At the daycare I attended, they would put everyone down for a nap after lunch. I didn’t want to sleep, so they let me stay with the teachers or in an area for older kids, playing. Until one day, when no one was looking, I decided to “free” the little ones from the nap area. I went and opened the door for them; the teachers arrived, alarmed by the noise, and saw that the two-year-olds were happily roaming around with the door wide open. That’s when my privilege ended.

“Privilege”... It sounds like heavenly music to my ears. It’s dazzling, a place that draws me in, traps me... Because it’s a trap, a double-edged sword. Only now can I see it that way. The price I paid for this privilege was high: with my father, always being available, forgetting about myself; his needs first, mine second. This would shape my relationships with men in the future.
summary: The author reflects on how childhood privileges, earned through caretaking and charm, became a trap that shaped her relationships with men by prioritizing others’ needs over her own, ultimately leading to self-neglect.

title: Separation of love and desire in childhood
text: Another thing that would shape my relationships with men is the separation of love and sex, which also started to form in my childhood. I remember being very in love with my father and how much I loved sitting on his lap, hugging him, being in his arms, kissing him... When I was little, I remember the physical contact with my father being open; we bathed together, probably until I was five. I don’t remember how we stopped doing it, although I do have the memory of one day during a shared bath when I asked him something about his penis. I began to view my childhood sexuality with shame and embarrassment. Something about my desire must have scared my father, and he stifled it. I started to sense that it wasn’t right; I could love him, but not desire him. This split between desire and love is something that still haunts me.
summary: The author describes how early physical affection with her father became intertwined with shame after expressing sexual curiosity, leading to a lifelong split between love and desire that continues to affect her relationships.

title: Persona and shadow in Jungian theory
text:
Persona and shadow: destructive to themselves and others

by Hanna Husseini de Oliveira

Jung called the image we present to society—at work, in school, or within other social groups—the “persona.” The more disconnected it is from our inner self, the more it becomes a mask, one that showcases qualities we may not actually possess.

And he referred to the “shadow” as the negative side of the personality—“that is, the sum of hidden and unfavorable traits, failed functions, and contents of the personal unconscious.”

In short, according to the Jungian theory, the shadow is concealed by the persona. This persona, which we create to protect ourselves from the outside world, is also used to hide from our own shadow. It is the first thing we see when we look in the mirror. But if, in an act of courage, we go beyond that reflection, we may glimpse the aspects of ourselves that we label as “bad,” the ones we refuse to accept. That is our shadow.

According to María Adela Palcos, the persona is the part of ourselves we identify with, shaped by the expectations of those who influenced us in childhood. Some traits become part of the persona because they align with those expectations. For example, a self-preservation E2 woman, who in her childhood was treated by her parents as the “prettiest and smartest” daughter in the family, will likely see herself as “the prettiest and smartest,” while traits like “dull” and “ugly” will be pushed into the shadow. However, if that same pretty and smart girl was also frequently told by her parents that she was “aggressive” and “restless,” she may incorporate those traits into her persona, while suppressing qualities like gentleness and calmness.

Therefore, according to Maria Adela Palcos’ theory, both the persona and the shadow can hold traits that are socially undesirable or self-destructive.
summary: This chunk explains Jung’s concepts of persona and shadow, how they relate to childhood conditioning, and how self-preservation E2s may develop personas aligned with parental expectations while repressing unwanted traits into the shadow, which can include self-destructive qualities.

title: Empathy as both gift and strategy in self-preservation E2s
text:
If self-preservation E2s have an essential gift, it is their ability to “empathize.” This could be called pseudo-empathy. They present themselves as warm and kind, and they believe this about themselves, all while concealing their true intentions. When they genuinely connect with the pain and needs of others from a neutral, internal space, they open themselves to humility. However, this same ability also fuels their strategies of seduction, ensuring they are liked and valued.

Self-preservation Twos, therefore, embody the role of “good girls,” or “good boys”; helpful, cheerful, attentive to the emotional needs of others… They use this image to secure a privileged and protected position.

However, this empathy has limits. If the other person becomes too controlling or dependent, self-preservation E2s may abruptly withdraw, as they cannot tolerate a lack of freedom. Since they do not grant themselves the permission to be truly free, out of fear of losing protection and facing loneliness, they may remain in relationships that suffocate them. Yet, their demeanor turns harsh and distant. And in their deep fear of abandonment, they may become the ones to abandon others first—coldly, or even through acts of betrayal they refuse to acknowledge. Thus, the same person who once appeared so sweet and attentive may suddenly become unavailable, distant, and entirely self-forgiving.

In close friendships or romantic relationships, they can also develop an aggressive sense of competition, making it nearly impossible for them to recognize their own selfishness or engage in meaningful dialogue. On the contrary, they may express strong disdain for the other person. And if they do acknowledge their struggles, this can turn into deep self-contempt. Finally, their most destructive pattern, both for themselves and others, is remaining in immature relationships that reinforce their low self-esteem and prevent them from achieving true freedom.
summary: This section explores how self-preservation E2s use empathy as both a genuine gift and a manipulative strategy to gain approval and security, but how this dynamic leads to emotional withdrawal, self-contempt, and destructive relationship patterns when autonomy is threatened.

title: Self-sabotage through fear of autonomy
text:
Self-preservation E2s are unwilling to be anything less than “special.” They often abandon personal goals out of fear that they will fail. At times, they even avoid success and self-fulfillment because they fear losing the protection of their parents, partner, or other loved ones. They fear that, by becoming autonomous, they will lose their privileged and protected status. It’s an extremely destructive vicious cycle.

I see my own self-sabotage. It’s very convincing. I would delicately persuade my parents that this or that job wasn’t right for me because the pay was too low. I lost count of how many job interviews I skipped that way.
summary: Describes how self-preservation E2s sabotage their own success and autonomy due to fear of losing protection and privileged status, illustrated by personal examples of avoiding job interviews and self-fulfillment.

title: Avoidance of limitations and false self-perception
text:
JÚLIA PESSOA HUSSEINI

One major form of self-sabotage is avoiding any confrontation with their own limitations—and, by extension, the possibility of failure. This subtype believes that they must be “the best at everything” and fears the rejection that adulthood may bring. They maintain the idealized notion that they “would have been able to pass that selection process” or that they “would have been accepted in that job interview,” using deceptive excuses to avoid moving forward with their personal projects. In this way, they never even take flight.

The greatest form of self-destruction for a self-preservation E2 is sabotaging their own independence. They infantilize adulthood, hiding behind justifications that sustain their childlike arrogance, the belief that they haven’t really failed, because they’ve never truly tried. They fear that becoming independent will mean losing their place in the system that once provided them with security.

It’s as if they were saying in their relationships, “I’ll make things easier for you, but in return, let me stay under your protection.” Their ability to “make things easier” requires a sharp intuition for others’ needs. They use their ability to “empathize” to feed their own neurotic need for love, privilege and security. A self-preservation E2 tells people exactly what they want to hear, gives them exactly what they need, and carefully weaves a web of deep dependency.
summary: Explains how self-preservation E2s avoid facing limitations through self-deception, maintain dependency by feigning helpfulness, and sabotage independence to preserve a protected, childlike position in relationships.

title: Empathy as a weapon and emotional disconnection
text:
In this sense, they not only harm themselves, they can also be destructive to those around them. Empathy (which should be a gift) becomes a tool of their shadow. At this point, they are blind, to their own real needs and to truly seeing others. The only thing that matters is maintaining their privileged position and feeling like the favorite. When their need for importance and love is unfulfilled, they weaponize their empathy, becoming deeply hurtful. They can turn cruel, demanding, and vindictive.

Another highly destructive trait is their ignorance, stemming from immaturity, their persistent refusal to see others, to acknowledge the world beyond themselves. This ignorance prevents them from taking responsibility for their actions, their impulses, and their outbursts. They struggle to read social contexts accurately, and their ability to reflect, discern, or exercise patience is limited.

A key part of their shadow is the denial of emotions that feel uncomfortable or threatening—deep distress that was, in reality, a cry for help from their own unmet needs. Sometimes it manifests as pain, other times as sadness, and also as helplessness—emotions that are difficult to acknowledge and process.

This emotional disconnection and willful ignorance are deeply self-destructive, preventing self-preservation E2s from forming genuine, transparent relationships, both with themselves and with others.
summary: Details how self-preservation E2s misuse empathy to control others, deny their own emotions and limitations, and suffer from emotional disconnection that prevents authentic relationships.

title: Narcissistic self-love and false intimacy
text:
Love

by Tania Rojo

When talking about love, it’s worth starting by saying that E2s “love” themselves above all else. Or rather, they are in love with their own narcissistic image. This creates fundamental difficulties in their relationships, as there is no genuine interest in other people. Recognizing this can be hard, as it’s an unpleasant realization for a self-preservation Two. Beneath it lies a great deal of shame and guilt, and often, a poor self-image disguised by a false sense of abundance helps conceal this self-infatuation.

I am incapable of truly seeing the other person. I’m not interested. Since I am the center of the world, I can’t see them. I only notice my own needs and demands. But because my personality traits are so strong, the initial image I project is wonderful: extremely receptive, kind, affectionate, almost ethereal… When I use my power of seduction, I feel radiant. I feel special, attractive, like someone people should feel pleasure being around, talking to… someone with charisma.

There is a lot of guilt in being the way I am, though it may not seem like it. The distance between myself and others, especially my partner, causes me deep pain. I picture myself sitting, surrounded by a mirrored sphere. I don’t see the world. Wherever I look, I only see myself. There is no contact, just me, reflected everywhere. No world, no people.

VANESA LUNA

I used to think I danced to seduce others, and maybe there was some of that. But now I see that I dance to seduce myself, to delight in how much I like myself when I dance, when I cook, when I sing. I catch myself looking in the mirror a thousand times a day, checking how beautiful I am, how beautiful I feel.

TANIA ROJO

False love defines this subtype. Like the other E2 subtypes, they appear to give everything, showing an exaggeratedly generous, selfless, even saintly love. But it’s “false” because it always comes with an expectation of repayment. Everything a self-preservation E2 gives is carefully logged, and at some point, they will demand compensation. In romantic relationships and close friendships, they offer an intense level of care (better described as pseudo-devotion): attention, time, affection, caretaking… neglecting their own needs and personal goals. But later, when they realize this self-abandonment, they turn it into resentment toward their partner.
summary: Explores how self-preservation E2s confuse self-love with love for others, use seduction to feed self-image, and engage in pseudo-devotion that masks expectation of repayment, leading to resentment.

title: О погружении в любовь и потере себя
text:
When I fall in love, I forget myself. I throw myself entirely into the other person, I feel them inside me: Ffffbbbbuuuuum! I’m already out there, eager to meet their expectations, watching, analyzing, blending in… If I usually struggle to recognize my own needs, when I’m in love, it becomes mission impossible!

I remember skipping university classes to go with him to work. My responsibilities came second; the most important thing was to be with him.

[...]

I could give him everything, make him believe I was completely devoted, but deep down, I knew I wasn’t showing even 50% of my real self.
summary: The author describes losing oneself in romantic relationships, prioritizing the partner over personal responsibilities and authenticity, revealing a pattern of self-abandonment despite outward devotion.

title: Ложная щедрость и динамика любви у self-preservation E2
text:
TANIA ROJO

According to Claudio Naranjo’s theory of the three types of love, self-preservation E2s enter relationships through compassionate love, like all E2s. Their false sense of abundance makes them seem generous, always willing to help and care for others. But this false generosity has a purpose: to create dependency, so they feel needed, which in turn feeds their false self-image.

Like other E2 subtypes, they also idealize erotic love. However, their sex life often remains more alive in their imagination, being repressed in reality. Having experienced ambiguous or harmful sexual situations in childhood, they may find themselves in unwanted sexual relationships, driven more by a need for affection and validation than genuine desire. In relationships, they frequently struggle with the divide between love and sex, unable to integrate the two due to a deep-seated fear of intimacy. They carry old guilt from having unconsciously seduced a parent, triggering jealousy in the other. As a result, they maintain a childlike stance where sexuality doesn’t seem to belong, even though they tend to eroticize their relationships.

Among E2 subtypes, the self-preservation E2 specializes in compassionate love, taking care of others in tangible ways, just as they learned to do with their parents as children.

A woman with this personality type will care for others by attentively meeting their needs with warmth and charm, until the other person feels captivated by having a “gentle geisha” by their side—someone emotionally supportive yet also capable in practical matters. Let’s not forget that, among the pride-based subtypes, the self-preservation E2 is the most hands-on, the one who puts the most energy into action. But they can also suddenly turn into a tyrannical child, using their seductive whims to manipulate others into doing their bidding.

I used sexual seduction to attract men, but I didn’t want to follow through with sex. I only wanted the attention, the feeling of being desired, not the actual contact. I was unconsciously repeating my childhood pattern, looking for parents everywhere I went. I thought I wanted a relationship, but in truth, I feared real physical closeness the way a child does.

ANONYMOUS
summary: This chunk explains how self-preservation E2s use compassionate and erotic love as tools to fulfill hidden needs for validation and dependency, often rooted in childhood trauma, resulting in repressed sexuality, manipulation, and a cycle of seeking parental figures in relationships.

title: Развитие истинной сострадательности как путь к исцелению
text:
Developing genuine compassion is essential for self-preservation E2s because, beyond the harm their selfishness causes others, the greatest damage is to themselves. Their lack of self-compassion stems from the harsh judgment of their inner critic. Learning true compassion allows them to connect with maternal love, helping them see others more fully, with both their pain and their joy. It also helps them develop self-love, increasing their ability to support themselves.

Working on compassionate love in SAT V changed my life. I felt as if my chest couldn’t contain all the love inside me. I could finally see people as whole beings, with both their light and darkness. I felt a deep respect for their journeys and struggles. That shift helped me see myself with greater compassion, allowing me to be kind to myself in moments when I would have previously torn myself apart.

TANIA ROJO
summary: The chunk emphasizes that cultivating genuine compassion is vital for self-preservation E2s to heal self-judgment, develop self-love, and achieve emotional wholeness, as demonstrated through personal transformation in the SAT V program.

title: Ложное восхищение и зависимость от власти
text:
In this character, admiring love is tied to securing a privileged position under someone with power. They may put a teacher, therapist, or any authority figure on a pedestal, seeking shelter in them, where they won’t feel threatened or, most importantly, powerless.

They also use these power-based connections to feel valuable, though they never fully believe it. Instead, manipulating someone powerful only reinforces their low self-esteem, leaving them feeling unworthy or incapable of living independently.

Self-preservation E2s idealize certain people but, as with the other subtypes, their admiration isn’t entirely genuine. It’s tainted by the belief that “I’m superior to the rest of humanity.” And, though they may adopt a childlike persona to charm others, deep down, they don’t feel they have much to learn from anyone. They offer admiring love only when they expect a reward. If the person they admire doesn’t reciprocate or grant them special status, their admiration quickly fades and turns into something far more destructive.

I used to admire some people intensely, while looking down on others I considered less important. I granted near-divine status to a select few, which left no room for faith in God or true devotion. My identity became entirely dependent on “I am because you believe in me,” leaving me stuck in place, unable to grow.

ANONYMOUS
summary: This section describes how self-preservation E2s use admiration of powerful figures to gain a sense of safety and worth, but this admiration is conditional and rooted in superiority and manipulation, ultimately hindering authentic growth and independence.

title: Поиск недостатков как способ утверждения собственного превосходства
text:
Whenever I’ve admired someone, I’ve tried to learn as much as possible to be like them—only so that later, when I spotted their flaws, I could feel superior. First, I put them through a rigorous test to see if they were worthy of my admiration. Then, I idealized them for a while. Eventually, I’d start searching for their weaknesses, just to prove they weren’t as great as I once believed, or as they claimed to be, so I could “cut off their head.”

TANIA ROJO
summary: The author reveals a pattern of idealizing others only to later devalue them by focusing on flaws, using this cycle to temporarily feel superior—a defense mechanism masking deep insecurity.

title: Self-preservation E2s in friendship: initial charm and eventual breakdown
text:
We’re talking about solitary people who find it difficult to share and, therefore, to maintain and deepen friendships. When it comes to making friends, they become chameleon-like. Their strong intuition guides them on how to captivate those they are interested in. They appear pleasant, fun, witty, talkative, with a touch of mystery that initially draws people in. They function better one-on-one than in a group, although in group settings, their powers of observation lead them to position themselves near the leader, which is a place of interest to them.

Self-preservation E2s struggle to maintain their act. They know that their hidden side will eventually surface when least expected. As long as the other person remains reserved, they face a challenge to overcome, and will continue to make efforts. But once the other person starts to trust them, their “good boy/good girl” image gradually fades. Euphoria takes over, they feel they have control of the situation, and they begin to play with the relationship. They invade, don’t listen, and show disrespect. They make heavy-handed jokes and insist on being right.

Ultimately, all the repressed emotions tied to the “good boy/good girl” image they’ve sold come to the surface. When the other person gets angry or disappointed with them, they fall into a deep void; they no longer feel understood. They immediately retreat into their beliefs, once again verifying that they cannot act freely, because when they do, others simply don’t understand them. They may limit themselves to playing the victim, theatrically blaming the other person, but most often they choose to give up and move on.

One of the main difficulties for people with this subtype is taking responsibility for the fact they’ve also caused pain, as their egocentric position makes it difficult for them to see the other person’s perspective. With their self-image, it’s hard for them to acknowledge they aren’t “perfectly good.”
summary: Describes how self-preservation E2s initially charm others in friendships using intuition and adaptability, but eventually reveal controlling and disrespectful behavior when trust is established, leading to emotional withdrawal and avoidance of responsibility due to their inflated self-image.

title: Self-preservation E2s in relationships: dependency and conditional giving
text:
I felt above others simply because I didn’t belong, because I wasn’t attached to any particular environment or person. This has been the story of my life; an overwhelming sense of displacement, concealed by pride.

ANONYMOUS

They are distrustful and controlling people, so in order to show themselves, they need to feel a lot of trust. They need to have confirmed that they are in a safe space where they can open up, be vulnerable, and reveal their weaknesses.

They are mainly driven by interest. They make contact in order to have their needs met, using seduction as a tool. They view relationships as business contracts, as games of favors. The explanation “just because” is hard for a self-preservation E2 to understand; someone simply calling to check in and see how they’re doing feels strange. Because of this, they often struggle to maintain friendships, pay attention to others, or show genuine interest.

As generally independent and solitary individuals, the internal mandate of self-sufficiency makes it hard for them to rely on others when they need help. On the one hand, they feel they must manage everything on their own, and on the other, they feel indebted to the person offering help. The same happens in romantic relationships, though it’s even more extreme.
summary: Highlights the self-preservation E2's distrust, need for control, and transactional view of relationships, where contact is driven by personal gain rather than genuine care, and independence is tied to a sense of indebtedness when help is accepted.

title: Romantic relationships and emotional dependency in self-preservation E2s
text:
Romantic relationships

The life of a self-preservation E2 revolves around (romantic) love. When they’re in a relationship, because they have it, and when they don’t have it, because they’re missing it. There’s a certain confusion here: they believe their happiness depends on being in a relationship, so they pass all the responsibility of making them happy onto their significant other (if they have one).

Their life tends to exist in an emotionally ambiguous state due to a combination of need and a desire for physical contact. They still experience a childlike dependence on someone they see as older, more capable, and organized, who provides them with both physical and emotional stability. Libido plays an important role in this mix. While their sexual drive can be intense, it often becomes muddled and loses its power, especially for self-preservation E2 males, when they project a maternal figure onto their women, toward whom they may have had an unreciprocated and fantastical erotic longing. Similarly, women of this subtype project a paternal figure onto their men.

There’s a need to re-balance the source of satisfaction, making it more internal and less external. Growth for a self-preservation E2 involves establishing an internal sense of security regarding their capabilities and autonomy, which they often delegate to their partner. They admire and are attracted to stable, secure figures, people to whom they feel they can give more affection than sexual energy.

Sandra Maitri explains that individuals with this character trait, after the loss of fusion with their mother, spend their lives trying to recreate that sense of oneness. This is what they experience when they fall in love: an overwhelming (yet fleeting) fullness in their hearts. They confuse happiness with the feelings a romantic partner provides them. Instead of channeling their energy inward to cultivate self-fulfillment and take responsibility for their own happiness (living a deep, non-romantic love), they direct their energy outward, seeking someone who can “fit” with them in order to feel complete.
summary: Explores how self-preservation E2s seek emotional completeness through romantic relationships, projecting parental ideals onto partners, confusing love with happiness, and relying on others for stability instead of developing internal autonomy, as described by Sandra Maitri.

title: Personal testimony on externalizing happiness in relationships
text:
I place my partner, or my potential partner when I don’t have one, as “the most important thing in my life.” I’ve idealized romantic love: it’s not just about walking a part of the path together; my partner has to make me happy. I place the responsibility for my happiness on the other person, and so I constantly blame them if something doesn’t feel right.

TANIA ROJO
summary: A personal account illustrating the self-preservation E2 tendency to idealize romantic love, place full responsibility for happiness on a partner, and blame them when expectations are not met.

title: Difficulties in self-care and relational dynamics
text:
The difficulty of taking care of themselves translates into difficulty in taking care of others, whose presence they interpret as a limitation to doing what they please. When they have children, attending to them, their partner, and themselves becomes overwhelming, as if they can’t be present with others and themselves at the same time. So, even though they seem so obliging and affectionate, it’s hard for them to find their own voice in the shared living space. It’s almost as if, in order to take care of themselves, they have to remove others from the picture. They end up hiding from their partner to do what they want: eat, go shopping, hang out with friends, or, if they dare, meet with a lover.

The partner becomes the authority, until the self-preservation E2’s interests feel threatened. That’s when a list of grievances or a sense of rebellion, stemming from feeling submissive and sacrificed, starts to come up. They don’t see submission as something they willingly do. And as for “sacrificing themselves,” they perceive it as denying their wants or whims to maintain the image of being accommodating and easygoing. They struggle to feel on equal footing with their significant other. It would imply being equally responsible, which, deep down, doesn’t feel right to them. If they took ownership of their own responsibilities, they’d be able to connect with their true needs.
summary: This chunk describes how self-preservation E2s struggle with self-care, often perceiving others' needs as limitations to their autonomy. They may hide to attend to personal desires, feel submissive in relationships, and struggle with equality and responsibility, ultimately needing to reclaim ownership of their needs to grow.

title: Idealization, blame, and relationship breakdown
text:
They idealize romantic relationships and don’t want to be alone. A person with this subtype wants company but without having to put in effort, as if they expect the benefits of being in a relationship to materialize on their own. They can tolerate various dissatisfactions, holding onto their idealization until it blows up in their face, and then blaming the other person, believing they’ve themselves given their share of affection and dedication. Since they lack self-criticism, when their partner points out something that bothers them, they feel deeply offended and believe it’s better to terminate the relationship than to possibly change themselves.

Some partners of self-preservation E2s feel like they’re being smothered or overwhelmed, as the E2 shifts from being fun to being impossible to please, always wanting more and never handling criticism well... At the same time, they’re attracted to their apparent lightness, freedom, and carefree, easygoing vibe of someone who doesn’t ask for anything to be happy and freely gives affection.

When the couple decides to separate, some self-preservation E2s are surprised and fail to understand the motivations of the other person. “How dare they leave me after I’ve given so much?” This confusion prevents them from acknowledging and processing their own part in the breakup. Likewise, when it is they who decide to leave a relationship, it can be very difficult for them to be alone, as they project their fear of loneliness and being hurt onto the other person. Sometimes, they even say they feel “sorry” for their ex. There is dependency and a deep difficulty in letting go of the idealized love that once existed in the relationship, or what they believe it meant to their partner.
summary: This chunk explores how self-preservation E2s idealize relationships, expect effortless fulfillment, and blame partners when expectations fail. They struggle with criticism, often ending relationships abruptly or being unable to cope with solitude, projecting fears and avoiding self-accountability.

title: Relationships "on top" – demands and disillusionment
text:
Relationships “on top”

The self-preservation E2 differentiates between relationships “on top” and “on the bottom.” A relationship “on top” refers to one in which they are with someone who clearly desires them. After a period of seduction and pleasing their partner to secure the connection, demands and expectations begin to surface. A cold, unpredictable side of them emerges, accompanied by an endless list of desires, most of which are material. One wish is quickly followed by another, creating a never-ending cycle. It’s almost as if they set up a series of challenges to prove to themselves and to their partner that they are not truly loved.

I had a relationship with a guy six years older than me, someone with a big and kind heart. What drew me to him was that he challenged me, and I kept pushing until I won. I fell in love, became dependent, cried for the moon, and he gave it to me. I constantly asked for demonstrations of love. He endured my fits of jealousy, my scenes... He fulfilled all my whims and demands, like dinners and trips... and I was always focused on what he wasn’t giving me or what was still missing.

VANESA LUNA

Since so much energy is invested in the conquest, they slowly realize that the persona they initially presented is not real, and they find it hard to keep it up. When they reach this point in the relationship, they feel the need to show the opposite side of the coin, and they swing to the other extreme. A sense of dissatisfaction takes over, manifesting in long faces, constant criticism, anger (not expressed through mature confrontation, but more like a child throwing a tantrum when their desires aren’t met), jealousy, accusations, and reproaches.

I put so many demands on the other person. In reality, it’s so much that they will never meet my expectations because a new crazy idea will always come up in my mind.

VANESA LUNA

I have staged countless scenes where I was hysterical, beside myself, and my energy was focused on destroying them, annihilating them.

ANONYMOUS

Logically, the other person doesn’t understand anything, because they’re facing someone completely different from who they had initially known. Nevertheless, the partner will often make an effort to understand and try to comprehend. But the self-preservation E2 will slowly begin tearing down their partner’s love, until they can confirm once again that they were never truly loved. They will force the relationship to end, often making sure their partner takes responsibility for it, because if they themselves ended it, it would tarnish their self-image as the “good” one.

I constantly test the other person until I have enough “proof” that it’s their fault, and I have a reason to leave them.

VANESA LUNA
summary: This chunk details the 'on top' relationship pattern where self-preservation E2s initially please partners to secure connection, then escalate demands, test loyalty, and ultimately destroy the relationship to confirm their belief of being unloved—protecting their self-image as the 'good' one by blaming the partner.

title: Идеализация и игра в отношениях «на дне»
text: These are relationships where the self-preservation E2 feels attracted to someone who is, in some way, out of their reach. They idealize this person to an extreme degree. They only focus on their positive, wonderful qualities, not seeing the person as a whole, and they fall madly in love with the image they’ve created. In this type of relationship, the self-preservation E2 no longer feels as secure. They fear being seen as just a sexual object, yet at the same time, they play with their sexuality (very actively) to trap their object of desire. In other words, they fear what they are doing—presenting themselves as a trophy—yet this game is also a way to gain false security in the relationship.
summary: Описывает, как самосохраняющаяся E2 идеализирует недоступного партнера, фокусируясь только на его положительных качествах, используя сексуальность как инструмент захвата и одновременно Fear being perceived как секс-объект, создавая ложное чувство безопасности через игру.

title: Личный опыт: секс-игрушка и отрицание боли
text:
“I’m all yours, you can do whatever you want with me.” A sex toy; your sex toy. How many times have I been fucked to the point of pain and said nothing? I put all my energy into not letting it show, especially not letting him notice; making it seem like I enjoy it...

I already knew something wasn’t right, but I couldn’t verbalize it; in fact, I denied it to myself. I did anything to maintain the status quo, no matter how painful, crazy, or surreal it was.

I felt the neurotic pleasure of being that sex toy, an image, an icon, a sex bomb, a porn star.

TANIA ROJO
summary: Цитата Tania Rojo описывает опыт самосохраняющейся E2, которая подавляет боль и дискомфорт в сексуальных отношениях, притворяясь, что наслаждается ролью секс-игрушки, чтобы сохранить статус quo и избежать конфронтации.

title: Требование обязательств и кризис отвержения
text:
In this type of relationship, the other person, who is simply looking to experiment, suddenly finds themselves dealing with someone they’re attracted to but who demands commitment right off the bat. This mistake often leads to a gradual distancing from the E2. And at this exact moment, the self-preservation E2 loses it. They don’t understand why they’re being abandoned and demand, angrily, that the other person comes back. It’s disastrous.

“The children of the enneagram” can’t stand being rejected, and they sink into misery for a while. In these relationships “on the bottom,” there are instances where their efforts to seduce this impossible love succeed, and they achieve their goal. However, their interest in that person dwindles just as quickly as the desire had built up when it wasn’t returned. Once they feel the person is theirs, that they’ve opened up, fallen in love, and are getting closer, the game ends. Because what truly mattered was the chase, the excitement of making the other person fall for them.
summary: Описывает, как самосохраняющаяся E2 требует немедленной приверженности от партнера, который ищет только экспериментов, приводит к отдалению, гневному требованию возврата и циклу, где интерес исчезает после достижения цели — важен был лишь процесс соблазна.

title: Зависимость от вызова и потеря себя в погоне за победой
text:
The challenge appeared: being able to make them notice me. Being able to seduce them, make them fall in love, make them crazy about me, so that there’s nothing more important in their life than me... And I became more and more insatiable as I achieved what I wanted. It excited me, fulfilled me. Overcoming it was more important than what I actually felt for that person. (Did I feel anything?) But it also blinded me, and I lost touch with what I truly wanted or felt. I didn’t even know I was out of touch with myself. The more difficult the challenge was, the more I said I was in love.

TANIA ROJO
summary: Tania Rojo описывает, как самосохраняющаяся E2 становится зависимой от вызова соблазна, где победа важнее реальных чувств, приводит к потере связи с собой и самообману, что она влюблена, несмотря на отсутствие искренней привязанности.

title: От эмаскуляции к самоподавлению: цикл унижения
text:
On the opposite end of treating the other person as an object (whether or not they succeed in their seduction), is a tendency to allow themselves to be treated as one and subjected to humiliation. Driven by the fear of loneliness following a breakup, they develop a remarkable ability to endure.

My game of seduction has been accompanied by emasculating men. Like with a guy I didn’t know very well. I admired him from afar because of his strong character, his cocky attitude, and his high status among other girls. I was drawn to him, but once I had him, I scorned him.

The guilt I felt for that behavior pushed me into a new game: submitting to humiliation. After that experience, I allowed myself to be humiliated by men many times, almost as much as I had tried emasculating them.

ANONYMOUS
summary: Описывает цикл поведения самосохраняющейся E2: от эмаскуляции партнеров из чувства вины к сознательному поиску унижения как способу справиться со страхом одиночества после разрыва.

title: Полное самоуничтожение и зависимость от abuse
text:
In this relationship, I completely erased myself. I let him completely dominate me, treat me however he pleased. I always blamed myself for everything, and naturally, he blamed me too. I felt incapable of anything unless I was with him. I became far more dependent than I had been in my previous relationship, even though he didn’t fulfill me, and I never felt comfortable with him. When I opened up about my thoughts or personal growth, he would use it against me in fights. I was always the “crazy one.”

After the psychological abuse came the physical abuse. I had to hit rock bottom, completely lose myself, in order to find myself again.

TANIA ROJO

The humiliation that the self-preservation E2 accepts from their partner is closely related to the dependency they feel.

As I became more “independent” from my parents, I became more and more dependent on my new relationship instead.

ANONYMOUS
summary: Tania Rojo и анонимный источник описывают, как самосохраняющаяся E2 стирает себя в отношениях, принимая психологическое и физическое насилие, виня себя, и как растущая независимость от родителей компенсируется crescente зависимостью от партнера.

title: Детская рана’abandonment и путь к пробуждению
text: The fear of experiencing the childhood wound of abandonment places them in a powerless, childlike position, where they are willing to endure all kinds of situations, whether or not they realize they’re not healthy for them. They need a strong jolt, a deep awakening, or someone to open their eyes and help them reconnect with their inner strength in order to break free from this pattern.
summary: Объясняет, как страх повторения детской травмы abbandona приводит самосохраняющуюся E2 к беспомощной, детско-подобной позиции, где она терпит нездоровые ситуации, нуждаясь в мощном пробуждении для восстановления связи с внутренней силой.

title: Брак и关系 тенденции самосохраняющейся E2
text:
Relationship tendencies

When it comes to marriage, many self-preservation E2s choose partners with whom they share a deep friendship, yet the relationship often evolves into something more like a child’s game than a genuine marriage, where each person focuses on their own interests, with little mutual commitment. However, it’s also common for them to enter relationships with individuals who possess a strong, confident character, compensating for their own insecurities. In doing so, they sacrifice much of the freedom they long for, submitting to the clear, well-reasoned direction of their partner. This can lead to an even greater loss of personal responsibility and a near-total self-annulment, all in an attempt to fulfill their neurotic need to secure the place of privilege they crave.
summary: Описывает тенденции в браке у самосохраняющихся E2: выбор дружеских партнеров, которые превращаются в детскую игру без взаимной приверженности, или поиск сильных партнеров для компенсации неуверенности, ведущий к потере свободы и самоаннигиляции в стремлении к привилегированному положению.

title: Паттерны отношений самосохранительного E2
text: The self-preservation E2 falls into their own trap, clinging to comfort, even if it means playing the role they assumed in childhood: to cheer up and decorate. This causes them to begin to distance themselves from their partner, whom, if female, they see more as a father figure than a lover, and by whom they feel neither understood nor loved. This type of relationship slowly drains their vitality, as they lose their sense of strength and identity as a woman, growing increasingly disempowered. In extreme cases, it can plunge them into a depressive episode, ultimately forcing them to abandon everything and start anew.
summary: Описывает, как самосохранительный E2 попадает в ловушку комфорта, повторяя детские роли в отношениях, что приводит к эмоциональному отдалению, потере идентичности и потенциальной депрессии.

title: Седективное поведение и его психологические корни у E2
text:
Seduction

I didn’t realize I was constantly exuding a seductive energy, but it made many people believe I was flirting, whether it was the way I walked, my tight pants, the way I played with my hair, my laugh, my gaze, or leaving sentences unfinished... At the SAT, I was stunned by the number of guys who thought I was “hitting on them” or that they had a chance with me. Naturally, this behavior led to many misunderstandings.

ANONYMOUS

Although it might seem like seduction is their art, the self-preservation E2 struggles to accept and learn how to use it because of the asexual self-image they’ve introjected. They rarely approach someone directly if they’re attracted to them, sometimes even pretending they’re not interested due to the shame of showing it. Or, in a burst of boldness, they may use all kinds of strategies to “make the other person understand” (at least, that’s what they believe) that they’re into them.

I never seduced “directly.” Many times I felt in that “privileged” position, being chosen by someone who held a high place in my internal hierarchy. But that wasn’t really what I wanted. I was actually attracted to another guy, but my inability to approach him and my deep shame made me avoid even crossing paths with him.

VANESA LUNA

What drives this constant seduction?

The intense need for connection, affection, and tenderness... The sense of emptiness is so near the surface that it quickly fades when someone comes along who provides all of that…

VANESA LUNA

They also fall into a cycle of compulsive sexual relationships, one after the other, during bouts of depression, which they can’t sustain. Faced with the frustration of a lost love or humiliation, they turn to sexual validation, often devoid of genuine pleasure, only to be left with deeper frustration and guilt, feeling as though they've betrayed the image of the “good” child who has disappointed their parents.
summary: Анализирует седективное поведение самосохранительного E2 как проявление глубокой потребности в связи и любви, коренящееся в стыде и внутреннем конфликте между желанием быть замеченным и страхом проявления интереса.

title: Динамика власти и подчинения в работе у самосохранительного E2
text:
At work, the self-preservation E2 charms their boss in much the same way they charm a potential partner, in order to secure a favorable and comfortable position relative to their colleagues. They dislike direct competition with their peers, which requires effort and action, knowing they may lose in such situations. They understand that if they win the boss’s favor, they’ll gain a significant advantage over their colleagues, but the privileges they receive may not sit well with others, ironically making things more difficult for them in the process. This leads to problems with team cooperation, prompting them to prefer working alone, on their own terms, with their boss’s consent.

The same thing happens when they hold coordinating or leadership roles that require direct confrontation with subordinates. They’ll feel uncomfortable in such a situation and turn to their superior if their subordinates don’t “fall in line,” since they themselves aren’t stepping into their rightful role.

In exchange for these privileges, they are capable of almost anything. They submit to the demands of someone who, rather than just their boss, serves as their protector, with whom they maintain an affectionate relationship, and sacrifice their personal life for the job, as though it were their own company. The compliments from their boss are like a reward for the “children of the enneagram,” driving their willingness to serve to unprecedented levels. They’re essentially recreating the privileged relationship they had with a parent they charmed, and reliving their sibling dynamics, with whom they didn’t directly compete but instead won over one of the parents.

The praise motivates me and makes me give everything for the job. To maintain my image as a good employee in front of the boss, I’m capable of going to extremes, working until I’m exhausted. But I don’t do it for the company; I do it because I don’t want to disappoint them.

ANONYMOUS

When a self-preservation E2 cannot charm their boss, they enter into a crisis, feeling lost. They lack motivation to work hard, don’t feel seen or valued, and don’t know how to be just one among many. They may give up easily.

I had a boss I couldn’t sweet-talk. I ended up hating him. At that time, there was an undeclared war between that boss and another from the department, so I knew I would team up with the other one to get back at him. In the end, we all managed to get him fired from the company.
summary: Описывает, как самосохранительный E2 использует charme и подчинение на работе для получения одобрения и защиты, воспроизводя детские динамики с родителями, что приводит к зависимостям и кризисам при потере благосклонности начальника.

title: Нерон как исторический пример самосохранительного E2
text:
Historical figures: Nero and Marie Antoinette

Nero

by Erika Marchetti

Nero: The Antichrist, the arsonist, the murderer, the matricide, the madman capable of any atrocity, the bloodthirsty tyrant. But also the artist, the musician, the performer, and the one who “oppressed the powerful but was gentle with the weak.” (Napoleon Bonaparte)

He was the fifth Roman emperor and the last of the Julio-Claudian dynasty. He ruled for about fourteen years, during which he won the love of his people, who were captivated and fascinated by his “boundless” generosity. At the same time, he was despised by the authorities, whom he boldly opposed by making daring political decisions, which were too ahead of their time.
summary: Представляет Нерона как историческую фигуру, потенциально соответствующую типу E2, подчеркивая его противоречивую природу: стремление к любви и признанию сочетающееся с бунтом против авторитетов и жаждой выдающегося самовыражения.

title: Современная переоценка образа Нерона
text: Historians, both contemporary and later Christian chroniclers, passed down the “black legend” that still haunts him. However, modern historiography, supported by recently discovered archaeological evidence and rigorous source analysis, presents a very different (and perhaps more accurate) image of an emperor who is likely not guilty of all the crimes attributed to him.
summary: Современные историки оспаривают «черную легенду» о Нероне, опираясь на археологические данные и критический анализ источников, предлагая более сложную и менее однозначную оценку его правления.

title: Детство и ранние годы Нерона: зависимость и контроль матери
text:
Nero remains a controversial and contradictory figure. On the one hand, his dependent nature is evident: the Nero who craved love, the “good boy” willing to sacrifice anything to fulfill his mother’s ambitions in order to shield himself from his own insecurities, external threats, and the fear of abandonment. At the same time, his seductive, theatrical, playful, irresponsible, and hedonistic side emerges—a man desperately trying to free himself from the power of others, from limitations and societal norms, obsessively pursuing an extraordinary image of himself. Over time, his darker side, marked by excess, despair, violence, and self-destruction, would come to the forefront, triggered by his fear of being alone and his constant sense of threat to his life and authority.

Nero belonged to an imperial dynasty steeped in deception, conspiracies, and crimes, where no one ever felt truly safe.

He was born on December 15, 37 AD. His mother was Agrippina the Younger, and his father, Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, was known for his arrogance and cruelty. It is said that when friends congratulated him on Nero’s birth, he remarked: “Any child born to me and Agrippina will have a detestable nature and become a public danger.” He never took an interest in his son and died when Nero was just three years old. Agrippina, excessively ambitious and power-hungry, was immediately exiled by her brother, Emperor Caligula, for her involvement in a conspiracy against him. She would not see her son again for four years.

Thus, Nero spent his early years deprived of close family affection. He developed a deep bond with his paternal aunt, Domitia Lepida, who raised him with love and nurtured his interest in art and dance. Years later, Agrippina, jealous of the affection between her sister-in-law and her son, and fearing it might interfere with her own plans, forced Nero to testify against Domitia in a political trial, which resulted in her execution.

Upon returning from exile, Agrippina managed to marry Emperor Claudius, despite being his niece and despite his marriage to Messalina. Meanwhile, she devoted herself to securing the best possible education for her son, pouring all her ambitions into him. Nero, desperate not to be abandoned again, understood that he was essential to his mother’s plans and paid a high price for the privilege of being the “chosen one.” At Agrippina’s insistence, he married his stepsister, Octavia, Claudius’ daughter, at the age of sixteen. His passion for art and sports was reduced to mere leisure activities, and he had little interaction with his peers during adolescence due to the constant threats and conspiracies orchestrated by his own mother.
summary: Описывается внутренний конфликт Нерона между стремлением к любви и независимостью, его ранние годы под сильным влиянием властной и амбициозной матери Агриппины, а также эмоциональная изоляция и манипуляции, формировавшие его личность.

title: Правление Нерона: искусство вместо власти
text:
At seventeen, in 54 AD, Nero ascended to the throne after Agrippina poisoned Claudius. Historical sources describe his early years of rule as prosperous and peaceful. Under the influence of Agrippina, the philosopher Seneca, and the Praetorian prefect Afranius Burrus, Nero implemented policies that favored the senators, aiming to restore their authority and secure their privileges. He was a moderate and diplomatic ruler who even rejected the title of Pater Patriae (“Father of the Fatherland”), saying, “I will accept it when I have earned it.” During this period, he suppressed his natural impulses and remained a devoted and obedient son, prioritizing his mother’s wishes above all else. He delegated much of his power to Agrippina and sought an almost symbiotic relationship with her. Coins were minted bearing their images together, he chose “Optima Mater” (Best Mother) as the password for his guards, and he even allowed his mother to secretly attend Senate meetings.

Nero was highly dependent on his mother; the role of emperor was too heavy a burden for his age, and he neither felt suited for it nor up to its responsibilities. Rome was a military powerhouse, where everything revolved around battles and bloodshed. However, Nero had a different temperament. He was affable. During his reign, he did not declare any wars of conquest; instead, he focused on defending the empire’s borders. He opposed the taking of life in general, and it is said that when he was forced to sign a death sentence—something he was deeply against—he sorrowfully remarked, “I wish I did not know how to write.”

He saw himself more as an artist than as a ruler. What truly interested him was art, and whenever he was allowed, he spent his time attending chariot races or practicing and performing in singing, acting, and poetry. When asked what he would do if he were deposed as emperor, Nero replied, “Art will always give me a way to live.” It is said that before he died, he uttered the famous words: “What an artist the world has lost in me!”
summary: В ранние годы правления Нерон действовал под контролем матери, проявляя зависимость и уступчивость, избегал войн, выступал против насилия и находил своё истинное призвание в искусстве, видя в нём смысл жизни.

title: Эгоцентризм и эстетическая одержимость Нерона
text: He had a deep passion for Greek society and culture, praising the importance of art and aesthetics. He never wore the same outfit twice, loved jewelry and fine fabrics, and spared no expense, feeling he deserved only the best. He was egocentric and demanding, like a spoiled child insisting on his right to happiness. When he performed, no one was allowed to leave the theater. Not even in an emergency, not even during an earthquake! Some women, it is said, were even forced to give birth in the audience.
summary: Нерон проявлял крайнюю требовательность к роскоши, внешнему виду и художественному самовыражению, требуя беспрекословного восхищения от окружающих, что свидетельствует о его эгоцентризме и потребности в постоянном признании.

title: Неро и его фантазия о материнстве
text: Nero lived in romantic fantasies, idealizing himself through them. Given his power, these fantasies sometimes became “reality.” One day, he became obsessed with the idea of experiencing motherhood. He desperately wanted to be pregnant and give birth to a child. He summoned Rome’s finest doctors to make his vision come true. Their detailed explanations about the impossibility of such a feat were useless, and to save themselves from a death sentence, the doctors devised a trick. They gave Nero a so-called “miracle potion” that secretly contained a small live frog. As it moved in his stomach, it would give him the sensation of an advanced pregnancy. Eventually, after enduring great “labor pains,” Nero “gave birth” thanks to a purge. The frog was then paraded through the streets of Rome in a royal carriage, followed by the aristocracy.
summary: Описывает фантазию Неро о беременности и родах, реализованную через обман врачей, которые использовали лягушку в зелье, чтобы создать иллюзию беременности.

title: Стиль и внешность Неро как эстета
text: Like a Hellenistic ruler, he paid great attention to his appearance, though in a unique and eye-catching way. He would appear in public wearing a simple, unusually short, ultra-fine silk tunic, without a belt, barefoot, with a scarf around his neck. His hair was well-groomed but rebelliously long, like that of a poet.
summary: Описывает эксцентричный и художественный стиль внешности Неро, подчеркивающий его идентичность как поэта и эстета, а не правителя.

title: Политика Неро: популизм и культурный расцвет
text:
Politics, on the other hand, was just a tiresome list of duties. Over time, he began to feel the effects of his mother’s oppressive control, the rigid discipline, and the dramatic choices imposed by his role. He longed to rule alone, desiring “absolute power” to be free to do whatever he pleased and to live a more carefree life.

He pursued a populist policy, granting extreme freedoms to all. He mingled with the public, enjoyed mixing with ordinary people, and at night, he would leave the palace to visit the slums. During the day, he entertained the masses with spectacles and performances, organized grand games and events, and handed out prizes. He banned the killing of gladiators in the arena. He ordered grain distributions during famines. He devalued the currency to stimulate the economy. He enacted tax reforms that favored business classes while penalizing the extravagant luxury of the senatorial elite and powerful imperial freedmen.

This approach proved useful and effective. He spent enormous sums to enrich the city with works of art and monuments, and under his rule, Roman society reached its highest cultural and artistic prestige.
