However, the senatorial class, which had been hit hardest by these reforms, became his sworn enemy.
summary: Описывает политический курс Неро: его стремление к автономии, популистские реформы, поддержку искусств и культурного развития, которые привели к конфликту с сенаторской аристократией.

title: Разрыв с матерью и рост тирании
text:
The final rupture came when his mother, Agrippina (who despised his artistic inclinations and extravagant behavior, considering them unfit for an emperor), began openly promoting his stepbrother, Britannicus, the legitimate heir of Claudius, as the true ruler. Suddenly, Nero was no longer the favored one. Despite his sacrifices and so-called “generosity,” he was now seen as replaceable. Terrified by his mother’s threats, deeply wounded, and feeling abandoned and undermined in his authority, Nero first poisoned Britannicus during a banquet and then exiled his mother—only to later order her assassination.

The murder of Agrippina was a pivotal moment in Nero’s life. By exiling her and stripping her of her power, he had severed his relationship with the most important woman in his life—the woman he had sacrificed himself for, who, for better or worse, had kept his feelings of vulnerability and inadequacy in check. In a way, he had destroyed the very foundation of his existence. He often claimed to be haunted by the image of his mother, by whips and the flaming torches of the Furies. Even his most loyal supporters began to distance themselves (though they remained complicit and continued to uphold his public image) because they could not forget the act of inhuman cruelty he had committed.

Given his deep dependence on his mother, he was only able to rid himself of her because he had found someone else to rely on: his second wife, Poppaea. A shrewd and ambitious woman, she (like Agrippina) understood the power she held over her weak and impressionable husband.

Alongside Poppaea, Nero appointed Gaius Ofonius Tigellinus as his advisor. He was a ruthless man, infamous for his cruelty, who shared Nero’s passion for excess. Tigellinus encouraged Nero’s paranoia and led him to distrust everyone, approving increasingly extreme measures against his enemies, both real and imagined.

Nero shed the last remnants of the gentle, art-loving child driven by a sense of justice. Overwhelmed by his need for control and self-preservation, he transformed into a tyrant.

Tigellinus filled Rome with spies. Any negative remark about Nero ended in murder or suicide. His ruthless vengeance after the Pisonian conspiracy became infamous. Nero eliminated his opponents without hesitation, including his own mentor, Seneca.
summary: Описывает конфликт с матерью Агриппиной, её убийство, замену влияния на Поппею и Тигеллина, и последующее превращение Неро из артистичного юноши в paranoicного тирана.

title: Пожар в Риме, золотой дворец и обвинение христиан
text:
In 64 AD, a great fire devastated Rome. Many blamed Nero, who, in his delusions of grandeur, wasted no time in building over the ruins: the Domus Aurea, the largest palace ever constructed by a ruler in the heart of the city, and a colossal 30-meter bronze statue of himself, in which he took on a divine likeness. Nero was likely falsely accused, as he wasn’t in Rome when the fire broke out. However, to divert suspicion, he placed the blame on the Christians, leading to the brutal execution of thousands in unspeakable agony.

In the years that followed, amid fierce repression, food shortages, and uprisings in Spain, Gaul, and North Africa, opposition to Nero grew stronger. The crisis might have been resolved, but Nero could only envision revenge or dream that the rebellious troops would be moved to remorse simply by his presence, unarmed and pleading before them.

The Senate deposed him, declared him a “public enemy,” and ordered his arrest and flogging to death. The Praetorian Guard abandoned the palace. Desperate, Nero knocked on the doors of his friends, begging for help, but found no one willing to aid him, or even to kill him. “So, do I have neither a friend nor an enemy?” he cried.
summary: Описывает пожар в Риме 64 г. н.э., строительство Неро Домус Ауреа и статуи себя как бога, ложное обвинение христиан, рост'opposition, падение власти и отстранение сенатом.

title: Смерть Нерона
text: Abandoned by all, he fled six kilometers from Rome to the home of a loyal freedman. Despite his despair, Nero hesitated, unable to take his own life and spare himself further humiliation. Only when he heard the Praetorians’ horses approaching did he finally act, driving a dagger into his throat with the help of his freedman, Epaphroditus. He died by forced suicide at the age of thirty-one, alone and tormented, realizing that this time, no illusion could save him.
summary: Описывает последние часы жизни Нерона: его бегство, колебания перед самоубийством и окончательный акт с помощью освобожденного раба Эпафродита, подчеркивая его одиночество и разочарование в иллюзиях.

title: Мария Антуанетта как представитель E2
text:
Marie Antoinette is a historical figure highly representative of self-preservation E2. As the Queen of Versailles, she made her personality traits remarkably visible.

Here’s how her most renowned biographer, Stefan Zweig, described her:

Marie Antoinette was neither the great saint of royalism nor yet the great whore of the Revolution, but a mediocre, an average woman; not exceptionally able nor yet exceptionally foolish; neither fire nor ice; devoid of any vigorous wish to do good and of the remotest inclination to do evil; the average woman of yesterday, today and tomorrow; lacking impulse towards the demonic, uninspired by the will to heroism, and therefore (one might fancy) unsuited to become the heroine of a tragedy.
summary: Представляет Марию Антуанетту как яркий пример самосохраняющейся E2, цитируя описание Стефана Цвейга, который характеризует ее как среднюю, незамечательную женщину без ярких добродетелей или пороков.

title: Детство и юность Марии Антуанетты
text:
Despite living in an era with rigidly defined roles and strict protocols, Mary Antoinette sought to live life on her own terms, attempting to break free from the obligations imposed on her time. In her pursuit of freedom and autonomy, she ultimately met a tragic end, which also symbolized the historical moment she lived in: a nation, desperate and starving, unseen and unheard, that decided to abolish the monarchy and, with it, everything it represented.

The birth of a young queen

Marie Antoinette was born on November 2, 1755, in the royal chambers of Vienna’s Hofburg Palace. She was the fifteenth child of Empress Maria Theresa of Habsburg. She was baptized as Maria Antonia Josepha Johanna, but within the family, she was affectionately called Antoine (or Madame Antonia). In her book Damned Queens, Cristina Morató notes: “The court chamberlain recorded in his notebook: ‘Her Majesty has safely delivered a small but completely healthy archduchess.’” At the time of Marie Antoinette’s birth, her mother, aged 38, ruled the Austrian Empire—a sovereign deeply devoted to governance, and one of the most powerful women in Europe.

Marie Antoinette’s childhood is often described as idyllic. She grew up in palaces surrounded by botanical gardens, collections of wild and exotic animals, and multiple residences where the family moved according to the seasons. She was particularly fond of one estate, where the children could enjoy a countryside setting with freedoms that were impossible within the formal constraints of the Viennese court.

Marie Antoinette’s father, Emperor Francis I, had a cheerful, relaxed, and easygoing nature, which contributed to raising his children in a manner more akin to that of a typical bourgeois family. He imposed no strict demands during their stays outside the palace, allowing them to behave with greater freedom:

Everyone indulged the charming Maria Antonia, including her father, who had a particular soft spot for her. Her mother, however, was less lenient, often describing her as rebellious, impulsive, and spoiled. Yet, Maria Theresa failed to see that the young girl, through her mischief and defiant behavior, was constantly seeking her mother’s attention [...] Feeling unloved by her mother, little Antoine found solace in her sister Maria Carolina [...] The two shared a special bond—they were both outgoing, talkative, and inseparable.

From an early age, the girl displayed artistic talent. She took part in performances where children would sing, dance, and act, all with the encouragement of her parents, who instilled in her a love for music. She was tutored by some of the best singing and dance instructors of her time.

Like all the queen’s daughters, Marie Antoinette was educated to become a future monarch, trained in the customs of the era. Her lessons emphasized modesty, submission, and the social graces expected of a royal. She was raised to embody the refined and dignified demeanor befitting her noble lineage.
summary: Описывает рождение, детство и воспитание Марии Антуанетты: ее idyllicное детство в Вене, отношения с родителями, художественные таланты и образование, направленное на подготовку к будущей роли монарха, с акцентом на скромность и социальные грации.

title: Подготовка к браку и ранние годы во Франции
text:
A child bride

At just twelve years old, her mother arranged for her to marry the Dauphin of France, Louis-Auguste of Bourbon. The Empress saw that Antoinette was a beautiful young girl, though she had a few imperfections that could be corrected, such as slightly crooked teeth, which were straightened with wires, and a forehead considered too broad, which a stylist helped to conceal.

While her appearance was not an obstacle to her future, her poor education was. She could barely write, and when she did, it was riddled with spelling errors. She had little interest in reading, history, literature, or languages. Though charming, lively, and cheerful, her lack of intellectual curiosity would shape her fate: “Spoilt, inattentive, high-spirited, vivacious to a fault, Marie Antoinette, though quick of apprehension, had never shown the slightest inclination to busy herself with matters of serious import.”

Her tutor, Abbé de Vermond, described the young girl in class:

She is more intelligent than has been generally supposed. Unfortunately up to the age of twelve she has not been trained to concentrate in any way. Since she is rather lazy and extremely frivolous, she is hard to teach.

At twelve years old, the carefree young archduchess learned that she was to become the Dauphine of France. In the months leading up to her departure, her mother spent more time with her, trying to prepare her for her future role as queen.
summary: Детально описывает подготовку Марии Антуанетты к браку в двенадцать лет: физические коррекции внешности, недостаточное образование, отсутствие интеллектуального любопытства и описание tutora Abbé de Vermond о ее лени и сложностях в обучении, несмотря на скрытый интеллект.

title: Брак и жизнь при дворе
text:
At thirteen and a half, France formally requested Marie Antoinette’s hand in marriage. The slender, small-breasted, and petite adolescent did not appear to be the most physically mature or prepared for such a role. However, upon meeting her, King Louis XV, her future father-in-law, found her charming, spontaneous, and childlike. He expressed his delight to her mother, Empress Maria Theresa, assuring her that the French royal family was pleased and considered Marie Antoinette a blessing.

As for the Dauphin (her future husband), he was an introverted and unattractive teen. When they met, he was formal and dutiful, without much enthusiasm. This set the tone for their early years of marriage, marked by indifference and a lack of passion. They failed to consummate their marriage, unable to become the ideal couple that both the court and the people longed for. With little excitement in her life, Marie Antoinette amused herself by playing with her young brothers-in-law, her days passing in monotony.

At first, she tried to adapt to court life with good humor. However, she quickly found the rigid rituals of Versailles to be a burden. From the moment she woke up until she went to bed, every aspect of her day was dictated by strict etiquette. Additionally, the ever-present court hierarchy oversaw her hygiene, clothing, hairstyle, and daily activities. She had around five hundred attendants of various ranks at her service, though she spoke to only a handful of them.
summary: Описывает брак Марии Антуанетты с Луи-Августом, их непривлекательные первые годы брака из-за фимоза мужа, а также её попытки приспособиться к строгому этикету Версаля, где она чувствовала себя обременённой избыточным контролем и ритуалами.

title: Поиск удовольствий и бегство от рутины
text:
Discovering adolescent pleasures

By the time she turned eighteen, Marie Antoinette had sought entertainment by attending the opera, theater, and horse races, often accompanied by her brother-in-law. She became increasingly drawn to amusement, even sneaking out of Versailles at night to spend long evenings in Paris.

Around this time, her husband, Louis XVI, began to take more interest in her, making admiring remarks and expressing pride in her. However, in the absence of a sexual relationship between them—due to the Dauphin’s phimosis—she threw herself into her distractions:

Year after year her sexual passions were fruitlessly stimulated in this unsatisfying, shameful and degrading way, without a single act of complete intercourse. One need hardly be a neurologist or a sexologist to recognise that her superlative liveliness, her persistent and unavailing search for new satisfactions, her fickle pursuit of one pleasure after another, were typical outcomes of unceasing sexual stimulation by a husband who was unable to provide her with adequate gratification. Because she had never been stirred to the depths and then profoundly satisfied, this wife who was not really a wife after seven years of married existence craved for an atmosphere of perpetual movement and unrest. By slow degrees, what to begin with had been no more than the high spirits of a spoilt child degenerated into a mania for pleasure, convulsive, morbid, regarded by the whole as scandalous—a vehement desire for pleasure against which Maria Theresa and all Marie Antoinette’s friends fought in vain.
summary: Описывает, как Мария Антуанетта, лишённая сексуального удовлетворения в браке из-за фимоза мужа, компенсировала это поиском удовольствий через светские развлечения и тайные поездки в Париж, что привело к росту её репутации как скандалистки.

title: Вознесение на престол и жизнь в Petit Trianon
text:
The dauphine becomes queen

A year later, King Louis XV died, clearing the way for Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette to ascend to the French throne. As queen, she spent her nights taking secret excursions to Paris with her closest companions, her petit comité. She also dedicated herself to decorating The Petit Trianon, a small château gifted to her by her husband. This private retreat, where no one could enter without her invitation, became her sanctuary for over a decade. Lavishly decorated with unlimited funds, it freed her from the rigid court protocol of Versailles. “To be queen meant no more to Marie Antoinette, for fifteen years or so, than to be admired as the smartest, the most coquettish, the best dressed, the most spoilt and above all the best amused woman at court.”

Marie Antoinette had no desire to leave a mark on history. She was a teenage queen with little vision for the future, her interests limited to her own person and her pleasures. She had no intention of contributing to political thought or ideology: “From earliest youth, her main characteristic had been a longing for independence. She did not want to dominate, but, on the other hand, she would not allow herself to be dominated or even influenced by others. To be queen meant for her nothing more than increased scope for personal freedom.”
summary: После смерти Луи XV Мария Антуанетта становится королевой, но видит в этом роли лишь возможность для личной свободы и удовольствий, укрываясь в Petit Trianon от этикета Версаля и избегая политической вовлечённости.

title: Роскошь, критика и утрата связи с реальностью
text:
Part of Marie Antoinette’s lack of interest in the world around her stemmed from her ignorance of the France of her time, a country in the grip of a severe economic crisis and widespread famine. Her detachment was further compounded by the intrigues and rumors spread by the late king’s sisters, who had always viewed her with hostility. Scandalous pamphlets began circulating, accusing her of affairs with both men and women, as well as of recklessly squandering the people’s money.

There was some truth to these rumors. Marie Antoinette went overboard with her extravagant purchases: dresses, shoes, and hats made of the finest materials, adorned with feathers and precious jewels. She not only set fashion trends but also took them to such extremes that the towering hairstyles she popularized forced noblewomen to travel on their knees inside their carriages to accommodate their elaborate coiffures.

From the outset, the Queen’s mistake was that she wished to conquer as woman instead of as queen. Her petty feminine triumphs were of more moment to her than any she might have achieved in the stupendous domain of history. Because, for her trivial mind, the royal position was only a matter of outward form devoid of spiritual content, in her hands what should have been a mighty task shrivelled to become a temporary amusement, and an exalted function was for her mere playacting.
summary: Описывает, как отрыв Марии Антуанетты от реальности Франции, её роскошный образ жизни и стремление к личному триумфу вместо государственного служения привели к росту ненависти и обвинений в расточительстве и моральном падении.

title: Материнство и начало перемен
text:
At the age of twenty-two, Marie Antoinette received a visit from her older brother, Joseph II, who had been sent by their mother, Empress Maria Theresa. His mission was twofold: first, to persuade his brother-in-law to undergo surgery for phimosis, allowing the marriage to be consummated; and second, to confront his sister about her reckless behavior. His visit proved successful, and within a year, the queen gave birth to a daughter.

Three years later, in 1781, she gave birth to her first son, the Dauphin Louis Joseph. Four years after that, her third child, Louis Charles, was born. In 1787, she had her last daughter, Sophie Béatrice, who tragically died of tuberculosis at just one year old.

With motherhood began the first transformation in Marie Antoinette, not so far a decisive metamorphosis, but the beginning of a decisive one. Her pregnancies necessitated several months’ abstinence from the life of unmeaning amusement; she soon began to find it more agreeable to play with her children than to stake money at the gaming table; the tender emotion which, for want of a better object, had been squandered upon carousals, had at length found a normal outlet. The way to a life of reflective self-knowledge seemed to be opening.
summary: Describes Marie Antoinette's experience with motherhood, including the births and deaths of her children, and how this led to a shift in her priorities from frivolous amusement to more meaningful engagement with her children, marking the beginning of personal transformation.

title: Неизменное отчуждение и растущая критика
text:
Yet, despite her new role as a mother and her fulfillment of the duty to produce heirs, rumors and criticism of Antoinette’s behavior did not subside. She remained unpopular, largely due to her favoritism toward a select inner circle. Her attitude toward political matters, thoughtless and detached from the needs of her people, only fueled the resentment. At a time when intelligent diplomacy was crucial to preserving the monarchy, particularly through engagement with the bourgeoisie and the common people, she remained indifferent to the growing unrest in a nation tired of being ignored:

The Austrian group was continually though vainly endeavouring to guide her into the courses of statecraft. One who aspires to rule, or to play even a modest part in the work of government, must spend a few hours every day in the perusal of relevant documents, but the Queen had no taste for reading. One who would make sovereignty effective must listen to ministerial reports and must think them over carefully, but Marie Antoinette found it tiresome to think. For one with her levity of temperament, merely to give careful hearing was a great exertion. “She scarcely listens to what I say,” wrote Mercy [the Austrian ambassador] to Vienna, “and it is almost impossible to discuss serious matters with her or to rivet her attention upon an important affair. The pursuit of pleasure holds her in thrall.”

Over the course of ten years, frustration and resentment continued to build. Discontent spread, not only among the common people but also within the nobility and segments of the bourgeoisie. Pamphlets circulated, fueling the growing opposition. Yet Marie Antoinette felt untouchable, convinced that she was in no real danger. She remained proud and dismissive of the accusations, even as the tide of public anger rose. “Smilingly she made light of the danger,” her critics observed. “To her way of thinking, words were but chaff in the breeze. A violent storm was needed to awaken her to a sense of danger.
summary: Highlights Marie Antoinette's continued detachment from political responsibilities despite motherhood, her aversion to reading and critical thinking, and the growing public resentment fueled by scandals and pamphlets, which she dismissed as insignificant.

title: Скандал с бриллиантовым ожерельем и его последствия
text:
Another scandal at court

Although her nighttime escapades in Paris had ceased, Marie Antoinette now devoted her free time to decorating. She acquired a new palace, once again angering the public and earning the nickname Madame Déficit. Her love of theater and being in the spotlight drove her to take part in a comedy based on The Barber of Seville, which she planned to perform in the palace’s private theater.

At the same time, a scandal erupted. She was asked to pay for an extravagant diamond necklace that she supposedly ordered, which was delivered to a woman claiming to be a close confidante of the queen.

Furious over the deception, she assumed the culprit was Cardinal Prince de Rohan-Guéméné, a man she already disliked. Without investigating further or considering the consequences, she had him exiled. This rash decision only deepened the public’s disapproval of the monarchy, further cementing the perception of the king and queen as unjust and corrupt rulers.
summary: Details the diamond necklace scandal, Marie Antoinette's impulsive reaction in exiling Cardinal de Rohan without investigation, and how this action worsened public perception of the royal family as corrupt and out of touch.

title: Пробуждение слишком поздно
text:
Although Parliament eventually exposed the real culprits in the affair of the diamond necklace, the damage was done. The scandal had permanently tarnished Marie Antoinette’s reputation.

Meanwhile, French society was waking up. The ideas of Voltaire and Rousseau challenged the monarchy’s privilege, fueling a new social consciousness. The people and the state were no longer shackled to the whims of kings and queens. For the first time, the country saw hard numbers: the financial deficit ran into the millions of livres.

Marie Antoinette began to react—but too late.

This violent thunderclap was requisite to startle Marie Antoinette out of her arrogant indifference, out of her hitherto invariable mood of ‘laisser-aller’—live and let live. Being thus awakened, she began to realise where she had gone astray, and, her nervous energy being directed into new channels, she made a hasty endeavour to atone for the worst of her errors. Instantly she cut down her expenditure. [...] For the first time Marie Antoinette’s ears were open. She had begun to ignore the old power, the fashion set by society, and was trying to guide her actions in accordance with the new power, that of public opinion.
summary: Describes how the diamond necklace scandal, combined with rising Enlightenment ideas and financial crisis, finally prompted Marie Antoinette to acknowledge her mistakes and attempt reform—though her efforts came too late to prevent revolution.

title: Transformation and regret of Marie Antoinette
text: Now, she feared everything she once dismissed. And she was deeply shaken: “Marie Antoinette has eaten the bitter fruit of the tree of knowledge, has lost the confident gait of the sleep-walker, for they only are fearless who do not know that danger threatens.” She withdrew from frivolous circles, preferring the quiet company of her children. She longed to turn back time, to undo her mistakes. But it was too late. The people and the bourgeoisie had not forgotten. And now, they were ready to punish her for years of indifference and scorn.
summary: This chunk describes Marie Antoinette's emotional transformation after the revolution began, detailing her regret, fear, and withdrawal from society as she confronts the consequences of her past indifference.

title: The revolution’s escalation and the queen’s isolation
text:
The revolution catches up with the queenly woman in the making

In the final moments before the Revolution, tragedy was relentless. On June 4, 1789, her eldest son, Louis Joseph, Dauphin of France, died of tuberculosis, leaving Marie Antoinette devastated. Though tensions in society were rising, she and the king remained oblivious to what the people were truly capable of: “Yet this arrogant, this unqualified condemnation of the Revolution, did not (at any rate to begin with), as far as Marie Antoinette was concerned, imply the slightest hostility towards the people. Having spent her childhood in the more genial atmosphere of Vienna, the Queen regarded ‘le bon peuple’ as comprising a mass of persons who were rather stupid, but thoroughly good-natured.”

On July 14, 1789, the Bastille fell, but the king and queen had no grasp of the magnitude of what was unfolding. Marie Antoinette’s closest friends began fleeing Versailles. Among them, the Duchess Yolande of Polignac, whom she had protected for years, granting her and her family prestigious positions, a move that had drawn harsh criticism. Now, they fled in the midst of the storm.

Ministers urged Marie Antoinette to leave the country, but she refused, determined to stay by the king’s side as the mother of the dauphin. Meanwhile, enemies of the monarchy and opportunists fueled the flames of rumor, spreading pamphlets that portrayed her as promiscuous, homosexual, wasteful, and, above all, a foreigner who had thrown the country into chaos.

The queen ignored these slanders, never considering them a real threat. She did not know her people; she had never stepped beyond her world of palaces and luxury. She neither understood nor cared for the country she ruled.
summary: This section covers key events leading up to and during the early revolution, including the death of her son, the storming of the Bastille, the flight of her allies, and Marie Antoinette's continued disconnect from the realities of her people despite growing threats.

title: The royal family’s failed escape and imprisonment
text:
On October 5, 1789, a mob, mostly women filled with rage and demands, stormed Versailles, hurling insults at Marie Antoinette. They broke into her chambers, forcing her to flee from direct violence. The next day, she and her family were forced to leave for Paris, where they were met with jeers and threats. They settled in the Tuileries Palace under constant watch.

Months passed as the royal family tried to maintain a semblance of normal life in the Tuileries. But reality set in—they were prisoners. Realizing their lives were in danger, they planned an escape to a province where they might be protected and restore order. The attempt took place under the cover of night, but they were discovered and captured. When they were brought back to the city, they faced furious crowds spewing insults and threats. Now, they were under surveillance and effectively confined to the palace.

Marie Antoinette aged rapidly under the weight of chaos and revolution. She was only thirty-six, yet she felt crushed by the burden of her mistakes. She and her husband had lost everything—the power and status they once believed were theirs forever. Summoning what strength she had left, she sought allies, writing letters to other monarchies, but they had abandoned her. In desperation, she wrote to Count Mercy-Argenteau, the Austrian ambassador to France and her former advisor for over twenty-five years, before he left to serve her brother, Emperor Leopold:

I do not know what action to take or what tone to adopt. Everyone accuses me of deception, of falsehood, and no one can reasonably believe that my brother would be so indifferent to his sister’s terrible situation as to remain silent. Hatred, distrust, and insolence are the only forces driving this country now.
summary: This chunk details the forced move to Paris, the failed escape attempt, the royal family's imprisonment, and Marie Antoinette's growing despair as she seeks help from abroad, highlighting her emotional toll and isolation.

title: The terror, trial, and final days of Marie Antoinette
text:
The terror begins

The royal family was transferred to a fortress after their palace was ransacked. They remained unaware that enemies of the Revolution were being executed. Among them, dear friends. In those dark days, Marie Antoinette wrote: “In misfortune, you discover your true nature,” vowing not to show weakness in the face of the terror gripping Paris.

The royal family was on the brink of annihilation. First, King Louis XVI was sent to the guillotine. Then, their only surviving son, Louis-Charles, was imprisoned in solitary confinement. He died two years later, malnourished and stricken with tuberculosis, just after his tenth birthday.

Marie Antoinette was taken to a dungeon, but not before saying a final goodbye to her daughter, whom she left in the care of her sister-in-law, Princess Élisabeth. After two months, she was brought to trial. Though frail and unwell, she faced her accusers with composure, neither denying nor justifying her actions. For a year, she remained imprisoned, defending herself with remarkable serenity at each hearing.

Slanderers and false witnesses paraded before the court. In one session, she defiantly proclaimed:

“Yesterday, I did not know the witnesses, nor what they would declare. And yet, not one has spoken a single word in my favor. I will say only this: I was the wife of Louis XVI, and I had no choice but to act according to his will.” When Marie Antoinette finally heard her sentence—death by guillotine—she barely reacted.

In her final hours, she wrote a letter to Madame Élisabeth, who was caring for her daughter. The letter never reached its destination, but it revealed her deep sorrow and regret:
summary: This section narrates Marie Antoinette's imprisonment, trial, and final writings, emphasizing her dignity, composure under duress, and expressions of sorrow and regret as she faced execution.

title: Последнее письмо Марии-Антуанетты
text: I beg pardon of all whom I know, and especially of you, my sister, for all the vexations which, without intending it, I may have caused you. I pardon all my enemies the evils that they have done me [...] Farewell, my good and tender sister. May this letter reach you. Think always of me; I embrace you with all my heart, as I do my poor dear children. My God, how heart-rending it is to leave them forever! Farewell! Farewell!
summary: This chunk contains Marie-Antoinette's final letter to her sister Élisabeth, expressing remorse for unintended harm, forgiveness toward enemies, and deep sorrow at leaving her children forever. It reflects her dignity and emotional depth in the face of death.

title: Смерть королевы с достоинством
text: In the final moments of her fragile life, Marie Antoinette carried herself with dignity, walking steadily toward her fate. As she ascended the scaffold, she accidentally stepped on the executioner’s foot and, with the grace of a queen even in death, murmured: “Pardon me, sir. I did not do it on purpose.”
summary: This passage describes Marie-Antoinette's composed and dignified demeanor during her execution, highlighting her grace and polite apology to the executioner even in her final moments, underscoring her regal poise.

title: Литературный пример: Нора из «Кукольного дома»
text:
Literary and cinematic examples

A literary example

Nora

From A Doll’s House, by Henrik Ibsen

By Marina Gutiérrez Requena and Fernando Ramos

What makes Nora’s character particularly interesting, as a prototype of the self-preservation E2, is the profound transformation she undergoes due to the events in the play. Here, we see the healthy path for this personality type, which almost always begins when a major disruption occurs in matters related to love, its central theme.

Beyond Ibsen’s remarkable ability to craft deep psychological portraits, A Doll’s House presents, through its protagonist (Nora), the playwright’s conviction that “our society is male-dominated, and until women are included as equals, humanity itself will remain incomplete.”

The play offers an excellent depiction of how Nora’s seemingly abundant, frivolous, and happy life gradually turns into a suffocating cage, constantly threatened by the revelation of a lie. The final act opens a door to change: Nora realizes she has been living for others and that the only way forward is to summon the courage to take action and assert her independence. After hitting rock bottom, she comes to understand that the only thing she can truly rely on is her ability to determine her own existence, to stand on her own feet, to take care of herself. She must abandon everything—the societal role imposed upon her—in order to become her true self.

She expresses this realization in the final scene:

HELMER: To desert your home, your husband and your children! And you don’t consider what people will say!

NORA: I cannot consider that at all. I only know that it is necessary for me.

HELMER: It’s shocking. This is how you would neglect your most sacred duties.

NORA: What do you consider my most sacred duties?

HELMER: Do I need to tell you that? Are they not your duties to your husband and your children?

NORA: I have other duties just as sacred.

HELMER: That you have not. What duties could those be?

NORA: Duties to myself.

HELMER: Before all else, you are a wife and mother.

NORA: I don’t believe that any longer. I believe that before all else I am a reasonable human being, just as you are—or, at all events, that I must try and become one. I know quite well, Torvald, that most people would think you right, and that views of that kind are to be found in books; but I can no longer content myself with what most people say, or with what is found in books. I must think over things for myself and get to understand them.
summary: This chunk presents Nora from Ibsen's 'A Doll's House' as a prototype of the self-preservation E2, detailing her transformation from living for others to asserting independence and self-responsibility. It emphasizes her realization that her primary duty is to herself, marking her journey toward authenticity and adulthood.

title: Исторический и социальный контекст выбора Норы
text:
When A Doll’s House premiered in 1879, it caused great controversy, mainly because of its shocking and unprecedented ending. For European audiences of the time, who lived in a progressive, bourgeois society, it was unthinkable that a woman would leave her home and marriage, especially over dissatisfaction and a newfound awareness of her reality.

Indeed, such an act was unheard of at the time. And yet, even today, we continue to bear the weight of patriarchal beliefs that dictate a woman’s place within marriage… and within the world. This is why Nora stands as the most fully realized and modern female character among those who have endured in 19th-century literature.
summary: This section discusses the societal impact and controversy surrounding 'A Doll's House' upon its release, highlighting how Nora's decision to leave her marriage was radical for 1879 and remains relevant due to persistent patriarchal norms, positioning her as a pioneering feminist figure.

title: Путь Норы к самопознанию и emancipation
text:
Throughout the play, Nora is tormented by the possibility of being exposed for forging a signature to take out a loan, which she did to fund a trip that would save her husband’s life. She constantly has to navigate a world where people pursue their own interests, often at the expense of others. Ironically, Nora is the only one acting “for others”... for her husband, for Mrs. Linde, for Dr. Rank… seeking recognition and validation, but never truly prioritizing herself.

By the time the forgery issue resolves, it’s already too late. Nora has had a brutal wake-up call, undergone a catharsis, and reached a point of no return. The happiness she thought she had (her husband, home, children, and indulgences) was nothing but an illusion. That’s why she leaves. She’s not running away; she’s making a conscious decision, fully accepting the consequences. She is becoming an adult, taking responsibility for herself without resorting to manipulation. She renounces the childhood fantasy she once clung to and embraces the value of authenticity.

Her refusal to see her children before leaving—a detail that shocked audiences at the time—signals that her decision is final, irreversible. She refuses to be trapped in emotional blackmail. Her eyes are now open; she recognizes her dissatisfaction and understands that it is she who must change her circumstances.

In this way, Nora becomes one of literature’s free heroines and, in a sense, a symbol of feminism. With this play, Ibsen opened the door to discussions on women’s emancipation and rights, giving voice to the fight against oppression, objectification, and psychological abuse.
summary: This chunk details Nora's internal struggle, the irony of her self-sacrifice for others, her awakening after the forgery scandal, and her ultimate decision to leave as an act of authenticity and self-liberation. It positions her as a feminist symbol who rejects emotional manipulation and embraces self-responsibility.

title: Двойственная натура Норы: шарм и манипуляция
text: Throughout the play, we see in Nora a mix of dependence, immaturity, and a childlike persona—along with a conscious and clever use of her own charm through manipulation and seduction. She craves being the center of attention, and by wielding these traits, she keeps everyone around her at her disposal. She is brilliant, charming, and humorous, seducing people with her girlish appeal.
summary: This segment explores Nora's dual nature—her childlike, dependent side contrasted with her conscious use of charm and manipulation to control her environment. It highlights her brilliance and humor, as well as her tendency to indulge in pleasures and break rules based on her subjective sense of justice.

title: Параллели с типами в психософии
text:
She is the princess of the household, participating in solving family problems, but only by her own logic. She has a tendency toward extravagance and generosity toward others, embracing a mindset of abundance. She secretly indulges in little pleasures and sometimes overindulges, especially in sweets. She breaks the rules whenever she wants, prioritizing her own subjective sense of justice in the name of Love.

She fully embodies the role of a childlike doll in need of protection and guidance, first from her father, then from her husband. (One could say her life motto is: “I am pampered, therefore I exist.”) This spoiled-doll persona subtly places her in the realm of irrationality, or at the very least, theatricality. When Krogstad pressures and blackmails her, she cannot comprehend that the world does not operate according to her values. She retreats into the fantasy that a miracle will happen—the miracle being that her husband will behave as she believes he should.

But when her world collapses, Nora does not resort to suicide or any other tragic end. Instead, with great courage, she slams the door behind her and chooses to take control of her life. If her wishes are not fulfilled, if the miracle she expects does not come to pass, she can become cold and implacable. She no longer loves her husband, the man she once would have sacrificed everything for; to her, he is now a stranger. And yet, this crisis, this destruction of her world, becomes her greatest opportunity. It allows her to see reality for what it is. Her greatest misfortune is also her greatest hope, because it forces her to recognize her own shortcomings and take control of her own destiny.

Loneliness will be an essential refuge, giving her the space she needs to rediscover herself, to embrace her existence as a human being—just like anyone else—and to finally mature:

And I—how am I fitted to bring up the children? Indeed, you were perfectly right. I am not fit for the task. There is another task I must undertake first. I must try and educate myself—you are not the man to help me in that. I must do that for myself. And that is why I am going to leave you now.
summary: Описывает трансформацию Норы от зависимой, манипулятивной 'куклы' к зрелой личности, которая принимает ответственность за свою жизнь. Подчеркивается её внутренний рост через кризис, одиночество как путь к самооткрытию и отказ от иллюзий в пользу реальности.

title: Подтипы личности: 'Любовный специалист'
text:
Below are several excerpts from the play that further illustrate the different aspects of this personality subtype. (The feminine gender will be used, reflecting the statistical majority of women with this personality type.)

Love specialist

The sweet, affectionate, and spoiled little girl. She looks younger than she is, with childlike features and mannerisms. She has a special talent for connecting with children and is deeply attached to her family, to the point where she might even fall ill for their sake. She resists growing up, clinging to the privilege of staying a child, believing that life should yield quick results with little effort. Cheerful, playful, mischievous, and utterly charming.

HELMER: When did my squirrel come home?

NORA: Just now. (Puts the bag of macaroons into her pocket and wipes her mouth.) Come in here, Torvald, and see what I have bought.
 […]
MRS. LINDE: How kind you are, Nora, to be so anxious to help me! It is doubly kind in you, for you know so little of the burdens and troubles of life.
NORA: I—? I know so little of them?
MRS. LINDE (smiling): My dear! Small household cares and that sort of thing!—You are a child, Nora.

NORA (tosses her head and crosses the stage): You ought not to be so superior.

MRS. LINDE: No?
NORA: You are just like all the others. They all think that I am incapable of anything really serious—

[…]

(The NURSE comes forward with the children; NORA shuts the hall door.)

NORA: How fresh and well you look! Such red cheeks!—like apples and roses. (The children all talk at once while she speaks to them.) Have you had great fun? That’s splendid! What, you pulled both Emmy and Bob along on the sledge?—both at once?—that was good. You are a clever boy, Ivar. Let me take her for a little, Anne. My sweet little baby doll! (Takes the baby from the MAID and dances it up and down.) Yes, yes, mother will dance with Bob too. What! Have you been snow‐balling? I wish I had been there too! No, no, I will take their things off, Anne; please let me do it, it is such fun. Go in now, you look half frozen. There is some hot coffee for you on the stove. (The NURSE goes into the room on the left. Nora takes off the children’s things and throws them about, while they all talk to her at once.) Really! Did a big dog run after you? But it didn‘t bite you? No, dogs don’t bite nice little dolly children. You mustn’t look at the parcels, Ivar. What are they? Ah, I daresay you would like to know. No, no—it’s something nasty! Come, let us have a game. What shall we play at? Hide and Seek? Yes, we’ll play Hide and Seek. Bob shall hide first. Must I hide? Very well, I’ll hide first.

(She and the children laugh and shout, and romp in and out of the room; at last Nora hides under the table the children rush in and look for her, but do not see her; they hear her smothered laughter run to the table, lift up the cloth and find her. Shouts of laughter. She crawls forward and pretends to frighten them…)
summary: Описывает подтип 'Любовный специалист' у Э2: детскость, привязанность к семье, манипуляция через очарование и заботу, использование детскости как инструмента влияния, а также реакции окружающих, подтверждающие её образ 'несерьёзного' ребёнка.

title: Подтипы личности: 'Лжец и манипулятор'
text:
Flatterer and manipulator

She gets what she wants without asking directly, fueled by an internal sense of entitlement, believing she deserves to be given what she desires, like in the famous slogan: “Because I’m worth it.” It’s not about fulfilling basic needs, as she’s disconnected from them. Instead, she fixates on whatever she whimsically deems necessary—hence, her capricious nature.

HELMER: Very well. But now tell me, you extravagant little person, what would you like for yourself?

NORA: For myself? Oh, I am sure I don’t want anything.

HELMER: Yes, but you must. Tell me something reasonable that you would particularly like to have.

NORA: No, I really can’t think of anything—unless, Torvald—

HELMER: Well?

NORA (playing with his coat buttons, and without raising her eyes to his): If you really want to give me something, you might—you might—
summary: Описывает подтип 'Лжец и манипулятор' у Э2: косвенное получение желаемого через лесть и ощущение собственной значимости, оторванность от реальных потребностей, капризность и скрытые манипуляции, маскируемые под скромность.

title: Nora asks for money and mentions Christine
text:
HELMER: Well, out with it!

NORA (speaking quickly): You might give me money, Torvald. Only just as much as you can afford; and then one of these days I will buy something with it.

[…]

NORA: Christine is tremendously clever at book‐keeping, and she is frightfully anxious to work under some clever man, so as to perfect herself—

HELMER: Very sensible, Mrs. Linde.

NORA: And when she heard you had been appointed manager of the Bank—the news was telegraphed, you know—she traveled here as quick as she could, Torvald, I am sure you will be able to do something for Christine, for my sake, won’t you?
summary: Nora asks Torvald for money to buy something later and brings up Christine Linde’s desire to work under a capable man, hoping Torvald can help her get a position at the Bank.

title: Description of E2’s emotional intrusiveness and need to be needed
text:
An overwhelming sense of subjectivity

She struggles with boundaries and can be physically intrusive, dominating conversations and interactions. She forms quick emotional bonds, even when the other person isn’t receptive. She needs to feel needed and show interest in other people’s affairs but often struggles to truly listen. Due to her rigid nature, genuine emotional surrender is difficult for her.

NORA (looking incredulously at her): But, Christine, is that possible? 
MRS. LINDE (smiles sadly and strokes her hair): It sometimes happens, Nora.

NORA: So you are quite alone. How dreadfully sad that must be. I have three lovely children. You can’t see them just now, for they are out with their nurse. But now you must tell me all about it.

MRS. LINDE: No, no; I want to hear about you.

NORA: No, you must begin. I mustn’t be selfish today; today I must only think of your affairs. But there is one thing I must tell you. Do you know we have just had a great piece of good luck?

MRS. LINDE: No, what is it?

NORA: Just fancy, my husband has been made manager of the Bank!

MRS. LINDE: Your husband? What good luck!
summary: This section describes the Enneatype 2’s tendency to overstep boundaries, form rapid attachments, and seek validation through being needed, illustrated by Nora’s interaction with Mrs. Linde where she shifts focus to her own news despite claiming selflessness.

title: E2’s demand for recognition and hidden expectations
text:
Demanding special treatment

She expects the highest reward in return for her sacrifices. She’s overprotective. Behind her altruistic façade, she hides her unwillingness to give up anything. She gives all the love and attention she herself craves, because her inflated self-image prevents her from recognizing her own shortcomings and asking for what she truly needs.

MRS. LINDE: Listen to me, Nora dear. Haven’t you been a little bit imprudent?

NORA (sits up straight): Is it imprudent to save your husband’s life?

MRS. LINDE: It seems to me imprudent, without his knowledge, to—

NORA: But it was absolutely necessary that he should not know! My goodness, can’t you understand that? It was necessary he should have no idea what a dangerous condition he was in. It was to me that the doctors came and said that his life was in danger, and that the only thing to save him was to live in the south. Do you suppose I didn’t try, first of all, to get what I wanted as if it were for myself? I told him how much I should love to travel abroad like other young wives; I tried tears and entreaties with him; I told him that he ought to remember the condition I was in, and that he ought to be kind and indulgent to me; I even hinted that he might raise a loan. That nearly made him angry, Christine. He said I was thoughtless, and that it was his duty as my husband not to indulge me in my whims and caprices—as I believe he called them. Very well, I thought, you must be saved—and that was how I came to devise a way out of the difficulty—
summary: This chunk explores how E2 frames self-serving actions as altruistic, expecting gratitude and special treatment in return, illustrated by Nora’s justification of her secret loan as a sacrifice for Torvald’s health.

title: E2 countertype: dependence masked as magnetism
text:
Not so self-assured

Within Enneatype 2, this is the countertype—the one who most needs others, inevitably drawing people in with a magnetism that compels them to protect and nurture her at all times. This dependence means she is not as self-sufficient as she may seem.

DR. RANK: To have loved you as much as anyone else does? Was that horrid?

NORA: No, but to go and tell me so. There was really no need—

DR. RANK: What do you mean? Did you know—? (MAID enters with lamp, puts it down on the table, and goes out.) Nora—Mrs. Helmer—tell me, had you any idea of this?

NORA: Oh, how do I know whether I had or whether I hadn’t. I really can’t tell you—To think you could be so clumsy, Doctor Rank! We were getting on so nicely.

DR. RANK: Well, at all events you know now that you can command me, body and soul. So won’t you speak out?

[...]

NORA (to Mrs. Linde): Well!

MRS. LINDE: Gone out of town.

NORA: I could tell from your face.

MRS. LINDE: He is coming home tomorrow evening. I wrote a note for him.

NORA: You should have let it alone; you must prevent nothing. After all, it is splendid to be waiting for a wonderful thing to happen.

MRS. LINDE: What is it that you are waiting for?

NORA: Oh, you wouldn’t understand. Go in to them. I will come in a moment.
summary: This section describes the E2 countertype as someone who appears nurturing but is deeply dependent, using emotional magnetism to elicit care, shown through Nora’s flirtatious exchange with Dr. Rank and her evasive conversation with Mrs. Linde.

title: Seductive manipulation and emotional games in E2
text:
Seductive…

Playing the game of seduction without taking risks; planting promises, charming people. Self-preservation E2 uses sensuality and sexuality but doesn’t fully take responsibility for it… “She’s weaving a web and letting the flies come to it.” (In cruder terms, she aligns with the stereotype of a “tease.”) She may be unfaithful in love and, in general, once she’s achieved her goal and feels secure, she’s capable of moving on to something else.

NORA: And heaps of port and champagne. It is sad that all these nice things should take their revenge on our bones.

DR. RANK: Especially that they should revenge themselves on the unlucky bones of those who have not had the satisfaction of enjoying them.

NORA: Yes, that’s the saddest part of it all.

DR. RANK (with a searching look at her): Hm!—

NORA (after a short pause): Why did you smile?

DR. RANK: No, it was you that laughed.

NORA: No, it was you that smiled, Doctor Rank!

DR. RANK (rising): You are a greater rascal than I thought.

NORA: I am in a silly mood today.

DR. RANK: So it seems.

NORA (putting her hands on his shoulders): Dear, dear Doctor Rank, death mustn’t take you away from Torvald and me.

DR. RANK: It is a loss you would easily recover from. Those who are gone are soon forgotten.

***
summary: This chunk characterizes the self-preservation E2 as using charm and seduction indirectly, avoiding responsibility while eliciting care, illustrated by Nora’s playful, teasing interaction with Dr. Rank involving laughter, touch, and emotional manipulation.

title: Фильм о юности королевы Виктории
text:
The film tells the story of Queen Victoria I of England, depicting her unhappy childhood and focusing on her coronation and the early years of her reign, up until the birth of her first child. Particular emphasis is placed on the moment in 1837 when, at just seventeen, she becomes the focal point of a power struggle as her uncle, King William, nears death without an heir. Kept away from court at her mother’s insistence, and with only her governess for support, Victoria realizes that she is now first in line for the throne.

The future queen is born in London on May 24, 1819, the daughter of Prince Edward, himself the son of King George III. Victoria loses her father when she is only eight months old and is raised under the strict supervision of her mother and her steward (and probable lover), Sir John Conroy, far from the royal family. During this time, she meets Prince Albert, who initially seeks to please his uncle, King Leopold of Belgium, by pursuing Victoria for marriage. However, Albert eventually falls in love with her, and it’s a relationship that proves pivotal in shaping Victoria’s personal growth.

When she was born, Victoria’s chances of becoming queen were slim. But within a few years, due to a series of premature deaths and failed marriages that produced no heirs, she found herself first in line for the throne. However, she quickly learned that privilege comes at a cost—she has little control over her own life, and many people approach her solely out of self-interest.
summary: Описывается биография юной королевы Виктории: её детство, изоляция, подготовка к трону и осознание ограниченной свободы несмотря на высокое положение. Подчеркивается, как внешние обстоятельства формируют её раннее восприятие власти и зависимости.

title: Детство Виктории как отражение самосохраняющейся двойки
text:
Some people are born more fortunate than others. Such was the case with me. But as a child, I was convinced of quite the opposite. What little girl does not dream of growing up as a princess? But some palaces are not at all what you’d think. Even a palace... can be a prison. Mama never explained why she would have someone taste my food. Why I couldn’t attend school with other children or read popular books.

When my father died, Mama and her adviser, Sir John Conroy, created rules. He said they were for my protection, and he called it the “Kensington System.” I could not sleep in a room without Mama or even walk downstairs without holding the hand of an adult. I learned the reason for all this when I was 11. My uncle William was the King of England. Yet he and his three brothers could boast only one living child. And that was me.

The film’s opening scenes portray a deeply lonely child, living under a glass dome, shielded from the outside world, and subjected to a rigid education designed to prepare her for her future role as queen. A “good girl”—obedient and emotionally restrained—who simply accepts her fate.

Victoria’s childhood reflects typical traits of self-preservation E2: isolation, the heavy burden of responsibility imposed by adults, and the suppression of her own needs due to a lack of support in developing self-worth. The turning point in her character’s emergence is the moment she discovers she is the heir to the throne. Yet, this revelation is not a joyful one; rather, it forces her to reevaluate the motives behind the restrictions, expectations, and deprivations she has endured. It also gives her an outlet—tantrums and defiant behavior—allowing her to seek revenge in her own way. The absence of a father figure, her loneliness, and a deep sense of betrayal by her mother lead Victoria to retreat into comforting fantasies where she envisions herself as stronger, more powerful, and ultimately, free.

“So I began to dream of the day when my life would change... and I might be free. And I prayed for the strength to meet my destiny.” In this scene, images of Victoria’s coronation are interwoven with moments from her childhood—alone in bed, whispering to herself: “I will be good.”
summary: Анализируется детство Виктории через призму самосохраняющейся двойки (E2): изоляция, подавление потребностей, чувство вины и ответственности, а также внутренний протест и фантазии о свободе как реакция на эмоциональное пренебрежение и контроль со стороны матери и консультанта.

title: Виктория как фигура в чужих играх
text:
Dragged into power struggles far beyond her control, Victoria soon becomes the center of everyone’s ambitions. Her mother and Sir Conroy hope the king will die before she turns eighteen so they can rule in her place as regents. King Leopold of Belgium plans to arrange a politically advantageous marriage between her and his nephew, Albert of Saxe-Coburg. Even the King of England considers marrying her off to one of his relatives.

VICTORIA: Do you ever feel like a chess piece yourself? In a game being played against your will?

ALBERT: Do you?

VICTORIA: Constantly. I see them leaning in and moving me around the board.

ALBERT: The Duchess and Sir John?

VICTORIA: Not just them. Uncle Leopold. The King. I’m sure half the politicians are ready to seize hold of my skirts and drag me from square to square.

She is at the center of attention, but only because of the role she is destined to play. Her privileged position comes with an inherent loss of personal worth. Who she is and what she feels don’t matter; only the function she serves within the system does. Whether in the family or, in this case, the nation, her value is measured by her utility. Her character is therefore shaped in response to this internal contradiction, as she builds self-confidence to counteract the sense of insignificance imposed on her.

The teenage Victoria embodies this proud and defiant nature perfectly. She appears arrogant, aloof, and self-assured. She allows herself to express suffering only when safely hidden from prying eyes, and she endures her mother and Sir John’s increasing pressure and humiliation as her eighteenth birthday approaches. Their tactics grow more forceful and transparent, but her moment of liberation is drawing nearer.

SIR JOHN: You’re too young! You’ve no experience! You’re like a china doll walking over a precipice!

VICTORIA: Well, then, I must smash! For it’s too late to mend my ways now!

SIR JOHN: Now this is what you will do! First, you will refuse the money and demand that it be given to your mother. Next, you will appoint me your private secretary from today. Finally, you will agree to be co-regent with the Duchess until your 25th birthday. Neither she nor I will accept less!
summary: Описывается, как Виктория становится объектом манипуляций со стороны матери, Сира Джона, короля Бельгии и других, стремящихся использовать её положение для собственной выгоды. Несмотря на внешнее признание, она чувствует себя фигурой в чужих играх, что вызывает внутренний протест и стремление к самоутверждению.

title: Виктория отвергает контроль Сэра Джона и affermирует свою автономию
text: VICTORIA: You may do what you like with the money. Now, get out of my way! (Turning to her mother) And if you think that I will ever forget that you just stood by silent and watched him treat me thus, you are dreaming!
summary: Виктория резко отвергает попытки Сэра Джона контролировать её финансы и действия, выражая гнев и разочарование из-за пассивности матери, утверждая свою независимость.

title: Вступление Виктории на престол и ранние годы правления
text: On the night of June 18, 1837, King William passes away, and Victoria—being an adult for just under a month—becomes queen. Having escaped the possibility of being placed under a regency, she immediately frees herself from the rigid rules that were imposed on her and quickly redefines the power dynamics within the royal household. During her first official speech before the Crown’s advisors, visibly anxious about the impression she might give, her ability to charm emerges: “I am young, but I am willing to learn. And I mean to devote my life to the service of my country and my people. I look for your help in this. I know I shall not be disappointed. Thank you.”
summary: После смерти короля Виктория становится королевой, избегая регентства, и в своей первой речи демонстрирует очарование и готовность служить стране, несмотря на внутреннюю тревогу.

title: Стратегическое очарование и самопрезентация Виктории как инструмент власти
text: Victoria chooses to appear fragile yet generous and determined. Her charm has a childlike quality, making her endearing while also shielding her from potential attacks. Her flattery of those present, attributing to them qualities she claims not to possess, is not a genuine plea for help but a strategic move to win them over. This self-image crafting, meant to make her more appealing, conceals a deeper truth: an inability to recognize her own needs and shortcomings. Victoria gives orders, empowered by her role as queen, but she does not know how to ask for help.
summary: Виктория использует притворную хрупкость и лесть как стратегию для управления впечатлением и получения поддержки, что скрывает её трудности в осознании собственных нужд и невозможность просить о помощи.

title: Эйфория свободы и растущая зависимость от лорда Мельбурна
text:
The early days of her reign feel like living in the fairy tale she has always dreamed of. Between travels and grand receptions, she captivates those around her, becoming the center of attention. Finally, she can savor the long-awaited freedom to do as she pleases. Completely absorbed in herself and the personal benefits of her new status, she surrounds herself with ladies-in-waiting who never leave her side and orders the guards to keep her mother and Sir Conroy at a distance. However, the throne comes with its own set of problems: pressing social and economic issues that require attention. Her ascent to power draws criticism, with many arguing she is too young and inexperienced to rule.

Feeling insecure, Victoria places her trust in Lord Melbourne, the Prime Minister, who quickly wins the young queen’s confidence. Before long, she appoints him as her personal secretary. He is eager to support, protect, and advise her on every matter. It’s as if the father who has abandoned her through death has finally returned. Lord Melbourne is affectionate, charismatic, and able to guide her through a world she barely understands. She falls in love with the sense of security he provides, allowing herself to be influenced to the point of losing control over her own decisions. Yet, Melbourne has his own political agenda and ambitions. He seeks to manipulate Victoria for his own gain.
summary: После обретения свободы Виктория наслаждается властью и вниманием, но чувствуя неуверенность, передаёт доверие лорду Мельбурну, который становится эмоциональной опорой, albeit с собственными мотивами, prowadząc do jej uzależnienia.

title: Психологическая динамика зависимости E2 и иллюзия независимости
text: Self-preservation E2 is a dependent personality type, unable to make autonomous decisions and drawn to figures of authority to avoid the dangers of solitude or the burden of making choices alone. Victoria fantasizes about freedom but is incapable of sustaining it. Having someone to relieve her of responsibility feels to her almost like a right, so she cannot tolerate anyone criticizing her for relying on Melbourne. She cannot acknowledge that she needs him, nor that her stubbornness is nothing more than a hollow display of strength, a vain attempt to prove a false sense of independence. “You are confusing stubbornness with strength, my dear,” her aunt tells her when, despite knowing she’s in the wrong, Victoria obstinately stands by her advisor.
summary: Описывается психологический профиль E2 как зависимого типа, который ищет авторитетных фигур, чтобы избежать одиночества; Виктория фантазирует о свободе, но не может её удержать, упорно отрицая свою зависимость и принимая упрямство за силу.

title: Переход от Мельбурна к Альберту: поиск защиты и основание брака
text:
When Lord Melbourne’s political decisions turn public opinion against her, she is ultimately forced to replace him. Until then, Victoria had never seriously considered marriage. Perhaps because what she truly lacks is a father’s protection rather than a lover’s affection. She imagines marriage as nothing more than a restriction on her freedom. But when she finds herself alone once more, she accepts Prince Albert as her husband, and eventually, falls in love with him. The turning point, as depicted in the film, comes when a supposed “rebel” attacks Victoria, and Albert saves her.

Victoria and Albert have been in contact since their first meeting years earlier, exchanging affectionate letters. They are genuinely drawn to each other, sharing a painful past, a deep love for the arts, and a mutual desire to help the less privileged.

Albert wins Victoria over by immediately admitting that their union had been strongly encouraged by the King of Belgium and that he had been groomed for the role of royal consort. However, he also assures her that his true wish is simply to be by her side and to be of service. Their marriage is passionate and romantic, yet also turbulent. Albert struggles with his subordinate role, while Victoria fears losing her place at the center of society’s attention. It is not uncommon for those with her personality type to seek out an “unequal” partner, who, by comparison, reinforces their own sense of superiority and exceptionality. Victoria rules a nation, while Albert is the “poor cousin” whose only job is to be the queen’s consort.
summary: После отставки Мельбурна Виктория находит в Альберте фигуру, сочетающую отцовскую заботу и партнёрство; их брак основан на взаимной привязанности, но отмечен дисбалансом власти и её потребностью в превосходстве.

title: Конфликт в браке: борьба за признание и контроль
text:
One scene in the film captures a heated argument between the two, highlighting Victoria’s fury at not being recognized in the way she expects, regardless of her actual actions. Ironically, she scolds Albert for treating her like a child while simultaneously behaving like a spoiled princess who cannot accept things not going her way.

VICTORIA: How dare you speak to me in that way before them. How dare you... talk across me, as if I were a child.

ALBERT: I… I did no such thing.

VICTORIA: Oh, no? Well, you’ve sorted this, you’ve sorted that. You and Sir Robert. You and the Duke. All without reference to me!

ALBERT: Victoria, I thought you’d be pleased.

VICTORIA: I will tell you what you thought. You thought that I was a woman! To be petted and passed over and ignored!
summary: В ссоре с Альбертом Виктория требует признания своего статуса и гневается на perceived игнорирование, одновременно проявляя детское поведение и требуя особого отношения, раскрывая её внутреннюю потребность вValidation и страх быть незамеченной.

title: Ссора Виктории и Альберта о власти и роли
text:
ALBERT: Would it were so simple then we might avoid more scandals of your making.

VICTORIA: Have you lost your mind?!

ALBERT: Do you wonder at it? Less than three years on the throne and you and your precious Melbourne have pushed this monarchy to the brink of an abyss!

VICTORIA: I’ve told you before and I will again, you are my husband here, and that is all!

ALBERT: And that is quite enough, believe me!

VICTORIA: I will not have my role usurped! I wear the crown. Any mistakes will be my mistakes, and no one else will make them. No one! Not even you!

ALBERT: I’m leaving before you excite yourself and harm the child.

VICTORIA: You will go when I dismiss you.

(Albert turns away.)

VICTORIA: I am your Queen, and I am telling you to stay.

ALBERT: Goodnight, Victoria.

VICTORIA: You may not go. You may not go! I order you to stay here in this room! Albert!
summary: Описывается конфликт между Викторией и Альбертом, где Виктория настаивает на своем превосходстве как королевы, несмотря на попытки Альберта поддержать ее как равного партнера, иллюстрируя динамику власти и зависимости в их отношениях.

title: Роль Альберта как поддерживающего партнера Виктории
text:
For the prince consort, Victoria is, above all, his wife—and only then, the Queen of England. He is the one who truly believes in her worth, encouraging her to take initiative independently and trust her instincts. Resisting the temptation to indulge her whims will be precisely what saves their marriage. And not just that.

Victoria is so absorbed in the role of queen that she never fully grasps just how much her choices and actions can have real consequences on the political balance of her kingdom, and on her own life. However, she is fortunate to have a partner, an ally who, by treating her as an equal but, more importantly, as an adult, allows her, at least occasionally, to step down from her pedestal and acknowledge that she needs help.

This has profound consequences, both in the film and in real history. Victoria enjoyed a long reign of nearly sixty-four years, which shaped the history of England and Europe for much of the 19th century. Her “empowerment” as a woman led her to become a national icon, a defining public figure who came to embody the model of strict moral conduct now known as “Victorian.” Her reign, the “Victorian era,” also marked the peak of the Industrial Revolution and the height of the British Empire’s global power and expansion.

In a symbolic final scene, Victoria has Albert’s desk brought over from Germany and places it across from hers.

VICTORIA: I hope you don’t mind, I had your desk brought in.

ALBERT: Don’t I have a say in this?

VICTORIA (embracing him, playfully teasing his stubbornness, and with confidence): No!
summary: Описывается, как Альберт поддерживает Викторию как равного партнера, помогая ей осознать свою взрослость и необходимость помощи, несмотря на ее коронарную идентичность, что способствует их браку и историческому влиянию Виктории как королевы.

title: Шутки и vignettes о самосохраняющихся E2
text:
Jokes and vignettes

This is how self-preservation E2s imagine they give to others.

Illustration by Juan Pablo Compaired

title: Процесс трансформации и терапевтические рекомендации для самосохраняющихся E2
text:
Transformation process and therapeutic recommendations

by Ana Escoda, Cati Preciado and Rosa Medina

Transformation comes from the Latin transformare, meaning “to change form.” The transformative conversion of character, as described by Dr. Naranjo, occurs when passion is placed in service of life, of Being. This process seems to unfold when the “holy war” against the ego has accumulated enough battles, truces, dialogues, and integrations that it becomes a resource for living without self-deception, or with as little as possible.

For the self-preservation subtype of E2, the idea of actively engaging in inner work is generally unappealing, as they are always seeking comfort and operate from a mindset in which hostility is external, located in others rather than within themselves. Because of this, there is little hunger for transformation or any significant change in their way of life beyond moving from discomfort to a state of lesser discomfort and adversity.

Perhaps this is why they are sometimes mistaken for an E4 or an E9, as they endure situations that, from the outside, may appear masochistic or self-deprecating. However, this E2 does not consciously register suffering, submission, or the anger that slowly builds up, remaining latent due to heavy repression and denial.

The privileged position in which the self-preservation Two lives effectively masks the downsides of their relational dynamics. Privileges function like sweets given to children to assuage hunger, irritability, and the desire for autonomy.

When this character seeks transformation and commits to it, they must “burn their boats”—renounce their previous life. This is not merely about change but about gradually abandoning the internal structure that has sustained their infantilism: the relational patterns and mechanisms of alienation that have kept their bubble of an ideal world intact.

In a true transformation process, deconstruction must occur, gradually dismantling behaviors, communication styles, beliefs, emotions, and interaction dynamics, so that reconstruction can take place in favor of life. This journey is often fraught with fears and resistance. But it is not about destroying the ego; rather, it is about placing it where it is needed, not allowing it to reign as master and ruler.

The process requires great courage, tolerance, patience, and the willingness to step out of one’s comfort zone. It may threaten their emotional bonds with family, romantic partners, or work… anything that provides them with security and privilege.

The first realization they may come to is how difficult it is, as a self-preservation Two, to truly build something, especially to build an adult self, a life that resembles that of other human beings. This difficulty in constructing affects all types of relationships: friendships, work, family, and romantic connections. It also impacts their ability to fully develop a career or even embrace motherhood.

They may feel like a butterfly flitting from flower to flower, without clear direction, never leaving a lasting imprint, moving through life superficially, without deep commitment, without accumulating meaningful experience.
summary: Подробно описывается процесс трансформации для самосохраняющихся E2: их сопротивление внутренней работе, механизмы подавления, необходимость разрушения инфантильных паттернов, трудности в построении взрослой жизни и влиянии на отношения и карьеру из-за страха потерять безопасность и привилегии.

title: Recognizing the false self-image
text:
A key initial step in therapy is recognizing their false self-image, as this character is convinced of their spontaneity. They must come to see their neurotic need for universal approval, their intolerance of criticism, and their tendency to interpret boundaries as rejection or humiliation.

It is crucial that they reclaim the true essence of their inner child while also realizing that, as children, they were exploited, and that their privileged position came at a cost.
summary: This chunk discusses the initial therapeutic step of recognizing the false self-image in self-preservation Twos, including their need for approval, intolerance of criticism, and the reclamation of the exploited inner child.

title: Resistance to wounds and therapist boundaries
text:
This will not be easy. When faced with their own wounds, they will feel the impulse to escape in order to maintain their idealized self-image. The realization that they are not indispensable—and, above all, the recognition of the absurdity of their infantilism—may lead them to retreat into their familiar and limited world of relationships or to somaticize their suffering into physical symptoms.

The therapist must offer sincere empathy for the exploited child while also setting firm boundaries with the tyrannical child, constantly balancing both aspects.

The self-preservation Two will try to seduce the therapist by appearing needy, wounded, and incapable of moving forward. Holding space for the depth of their childhood suffering is not easy, so one must remain highly vigilant: offering open arms while firmly resisting their whims.
summary: This chunk describes the resistance self-preservation Twos show when confronting their wounds, their tendency to escape or somaticize, and the therapist's role in balancing empathy with firm boundaries against manipulation.

title: Learning to appreciate reality
text:
Reality

Learning to appreciate reality and striving to live with awareness of it allows for deeper connections with others and fosters a genuine motivation to listen. True listening increases awareness of another’s suffering. However, this character is oriented toward pleasure; they neither know how to accept nor endure pain. Yet pain is part of life—our own and that of others. Fleeing from pain means disconnecting from the richness of the emotional world. Trying to cover it up with excessive positivity only feeds infantile magical fantasies and deepens the fear of adulthood. For the self-preservation Two, being an adult means having no one to tend to their wounds.

This is an incredibly difficult step, often requiring therapeutic support to recover (or perhaps build for the first time) the experience of a child who, step by step, learns under the guidance of an adult to face the risks of life. Depending on their level of disconnection and fragility, therapy must help these patients develop trust in the therapeutic relationship so they can sustain a realistic and constructive view of their limitations. Over time, the ego must also learn to withstand more direct and substantial confrontation. For the therapist, it is essential to remain attuned, allowing themselves to be touched by the sweetness of the patient’s inner child without succumbing to manipulation. They must also maintain absolute clarity regarding the boundary between sexuality and affection.
summary: This chunk emphasizes the challenge of embracing reality for self-preservation Twos, their avoidance of pain, the need for therapeutic support to build tolerance for life’s risks, and the therapist’s role in maintaining attunement without manipulation.

title: Reflection and cognitive awareness
text:
Reflection

For the self-preservation E2, it is crucial to delve into the cognitive underpinnings of their character, paying close attention to how emotions are shaped by irrational beliefs (crazy ideas) and distorted convictions. This means becoming aware of how they allow themselves to be carried away by chaotic feelings, treating them as absolute truth, and how these emotions drive impulsive behaviors (acting outs) because they do not take the time to deeply feel, process, and assign a broader meaning to their experiences.
