They must learn to recognize the irrational belief behind their experiences and begin to see it as a subjective truth rather than an objective reality.

Taking time to reflect is essential. This is closely linked to the ability to manage anxiety, to observe thoughts, and, at times, to resist rigid mental patterns and open up to new perspectives.

Although discipline is particularly challenging for this character, meditation can be an invaluable tool in this process, helping to foster reflection and contain anxiety. A structured and gradual approach to meditation can help them grow accustomed to simply being, to stopping their racing mind, just as Claudio Naranjo taught in the SAT programs.
summary: This chunk focuses on the importance of reflection for self-preservation Twos, highlighting how irrational beliefs shape emotions, the role of meditation in managing anxiety, and the need to observe thoughts without impulsive reaction.

title: Seeing, listening, caring
text:
Seeing, listening, caring

Self-preservation E2 must recognize that one of their gifts is bringing joy to others, but that this isn’t just about laughter. It’s about truly seeing people, listening to them, and caring for them. Paying attention to what others share and what they’re going through helps avoid misinterpretations and fosters genuine empathy that benefits others rather than creating dependency. More importantly, it allows them to take a more peripheral position in relationships and to learn how to set boundaries, shifting the misguided belief that when someone sets limits, it means they don’t love them. It’s about opening up to love without being so attached to being loved.

It’s also important to become aware of how often seduction is used to gain affection or admiration. When seduction returns to its true nature—a way to experience intimate and erotic pleasure with another—there is hope for reclaiming a deeper sense of joy and sexual freedom.
summary: This chunk explores how self-preservation Twos can transform their gift of bringing joy into genuine empathy through seeing, listening, and caring, while redefining seduction as intimate pleasure rather than a tool for gaining affection.

title: Equanimity and realistic self-perception
text:
Equanimity

They need to recognize that, like everyone else, they have both strengths and flaws, and that trying to hide their flaws to showcase only their virtues prevents them from truly knowing themselves. Acknowledging that learning, in all aspects of life, is an ongoing journey helps silence the idealized self-image that craves only recognition. The goal is to see oneself realistically, both in shortcomings and talents, while also building resilience against frustration and failure. Naturally, this means letting go of the childish self-perception and embracing adulthood as a space of internal power, one that doesn’t depend on external validation.
summary: This chunk discusses the development of equanimity in self-preservation Twos, emphasizing the acceptance of strengths and flaws, the ongoing nature of learning, and the shift from external validation to internal power in adulthood.

title: Order and chaos
text:
They must understand that chaos leads to misery. True creation can only emerge from order. And order isn’t dull. It is a blank canvas for creativity. This is a crucial realization, as they have lived an internally chaotic life, believing that this chaos made them unique, fun, spontaneous, that it set them apart from conventional norms.

When I started a family, I realized that such chaos is incompatible with a life shared with a partner and children. Changing this requires resisting the allure of comfort and self-indulgence and instead incorporating order and discipline into my daily life.
summary: This chunk discusses the necessity of order over chaos for true creativity and stability, particularly in the context of family life, and reflects on how the speaker's internal chaos was mistaken for uniqueness but is incompatible with shared responsibilities.

title: Spiritual practices and self-reflection
text:
ANA ESCODA

Here’s another perspective:

One practice that often soothes this deep-seated wound is recognizing my own smallness in the vastness of the cosmos, through the practice of gratitude. Seeing life as an opportunity rather than a burden.

Rebuilding what Claudio called “devotional love,” which, from the start, had been distorted by opposition to life’s natural flow and by rebellion against any authority that imposed a will greater than my own. I am learning to admire those who embody this quality of love, who can feel small before grand, abstract ideas, not as a way of bargaining or seeking control, but with the serenity and trust that life can be more than a vale of tears. Prayer, certainly, can be a great help. So can meditation.
summary: This chunk presents personal spiritual practices—gratitude, prayer, meditation—as tools to heal emotional wounds by cultivating humility, surrender, and appreciation for life, reframing love as devotional and free from control or rebellion.

title: Humility and ego work for self-preservation E2
text:
FERNANDO RAMOS

This description illustrates how recognizing one’s abilities and accepting one’s true “size”—combined with the practice of admiring love—helps self-preservation E2 build real confidence. In other words, acting as if they were humble (humility being the virtue that counters Pride). Sounds simple enough. But in reality, this is a daunting task for someone who has survived by positioning themselves above everything and everyone. Recognizing their own arrogance and the deeply ingrained patterns of the self-preservation E2 system is not a one-time effort but a lifelong, evolving process.

At first, the key is to ruthlessly expose oneself to the tricks and traps of this personality structure: the whims, the longing for protection, the expectation of privilege, the victimhood used as a strategy to appear virtuous, the ways they make others feel guilty for their misfortunes, the tendency to seek rewards without effort, the desire to be admired without earning it, the self-serving manipulation disguised as kindness, and so on.

Through repeatedly seeing these ego traps for what they are, their grip weakens. The illusions begin to fall apart. The same patterns may still resurface, like an automatic reflex, but they become more obvious, more absurd, and less convincing. In those moments, smiling and letting it go is a powerful approach. Not giving them weight, not following them.

And in that act of not engaging, of ceasing to battle these patterns, a new path emerges—one of creatively seeking more virtuous responses. This means offering what one can honestly give, asking for what is genuinely needed, recognizing one’s values and talents with balanced perspective, and using them in service, neither inflating nor diminishing oneself. From this space, gratitude arises for all that life offers, in every detail, experience, and person… opening a deep connection with the divine that manifests in everything around us.

At this stage of their journey, self-preservation E2 begins to connect more fully with their essential being, resonating with the high-frequency vibration of true freedom. One simply is, without needing to do anything extraordinary, like a little bird that sings and flies freely. By simply being, in their natural simplicity, they bring joy to those around them without ulterior motives. This freedom leads them toward loving service that is selfless and given without expectation. They no longer seek reciprocation, reward, or change. They give simply because it is needed. And in doing so, they experience a profound joy, which they long to share with the world.
summary: This chunk details the challenging journey of self-preservation E2 toward humility as a counter to pride, involving continuous exposure of ego traps, detachment from manipulative patterns, and emergence of authentic, selfless service grounded in gratitude and inner freedom.

title: Victimhood, humility, and personal transformation
text:
This process of self-awareness also allows them to stop resorting to victimization as a strategy. Though it may seem opposed to superiority, it is in fact its counterpart—neither “above” nor “below.”

Part of the transformation involves confronting the inner emptiness concealed beneath false love, false abundance, and apparent availability. When speaking of humility, Naranjo always warns against confusing it with humiliation. It’s not about feeling wretched, but about recognizing oneself as just one among many, acknowledging the value and power of others. To take this step, it’s crucial to revisit childhood experiences of humiliation. This recognition is particularly difficult because Type Two personalities have responded to humiliation with egoic pride, which they use as a shield against suffering. In therapy, it’s helpful to nurture the child’s healthy sense of pride while tempering the spoiled pride of the little one who wants to feel powerful. Learning to distinguish between dignity and grandiose pride is essential.

Two things have helped me in working on my ego: becoming a mother and practicing yoga. Motherhood was a major wake-up call. It taught me to love, to put someone else before myself and my own ego-driven needs. I had to set aside my ambitions and whims, to reshape my life with greater responsibility. Cooking, keeping the house clean—simple habits of care. Pleasure has changed. It’s no longer about indulging in whatever I want, whenever I want; now, the joy of being there for my daughter, listening to her, watching her, fills my soul. It’s powerful to see how she mirrors my habits, my ways of acting and thinking—it makes me feel the need to transform them. A habit like quick anger is turning into patience. I’ve always struggled when people don’t move at my pace, and she has been my greatest teacher.
summary: This chunk explores how self-awareness ends victimization strategies, clarifies humility as distinct from humiliation, and shares personal transformation through motherhood and yoga, which foster responsibility, patience, and ego regulation by prioritizing others and embracing humble care.

title: Yoga and financial responsibility
text:
Yoga has helped me cultivate patience and be present for others, to find wonder in the power of slowness. It has also supported me in navigating situations that easily cause me anxiety or stress, through posture and breath.

I’ve had to think about the future—things like owning a home, building a stable life. As an artist, I always prioritized pleasure, and that worked for me—until my daughter arrived. Now I have to build financial independence and capitalize on the knowledge I have.
summary: Discusses how yoga supports emotional regulation and presence, and reflects on shifting priorities from artistic pleasure to financial responsibility after becoming a parent, particularly for an E2 personality type.

title: Relationship commitment and financial consequences of helping
text:
With my partner, I’ve wanted to separate since the first year, but I’ve worked to stay together for the love of my daughter. It’s very important to her that we’re both present.

I’ve gotten myself into financial and other kinds of trouble because of my need to help others, and in the end, that affects my daughter. I’m finally starting to see that people don’t need what I think they need. I’m beginning to understand that everyone does what they can with their lives.
summary: Explores the tension between personal desire to leave a relationship and commitment for the child's sake, alongside recognizing the financial and emotional costs of overextending oneself to help others, leading to greater self-awareness.

title: Self-preservation and therapeutic transformation
text:
FRIDA ISLAS SUÁREZ

Self-preservation in service of life helps this personality type learn how to truly sustain—whether in something as concrete as financial stability, taking care of one’s health, or caring for another.

The process of transformation also involves outwitting the ego. When embarking on a relationship, a project, or simply facing oneself, new challenges arise that demand greater skill and offer the opportunity to commit to deeper growth. It’s important that this kind of “deception” be part of a therapist’s strategy when guiding the process, as it allows the patient to take risks along the path of self-discovery.
summary: Highlights how self-preservation enables E2s to sustain care for self and others, and describes therapeutic transformation as involving strategic ego work to foster deeper growth and self-discovery.

title: Testimony: Long-term therapeutic commitment
text:
Here is a testimony:

When I first began therapy, in a moment of deep need and vulnerability, I found great support from a female therapist who lived two hours from my city. I took the bus every two weeks to see her. During our first session, I spent most of the time crying—just crying, without even knowing why. She sat with me patiently and told me to take all the time I needed. I kept making that journey for over a year. It wasn’t until years later that I realized how the entire process—committing to therapy with her—required effort, discipline, the courage to go alone, saving money, and maintaining consistency. All of that slowly built the structure I needed to take care of myself and look out for my own well-being.
summary: Shares a personal testimony about the long-term commitment to therapy, emphasizing the effort, discipline, and consistency required to build self-care structures over time.

title: The heroism of ordinariness
text:
CATI PRECIADO

The everyday, the ordinary—learning to live there. That is what’s heroic, what’s extraordinary. To be “normal,” to have flaws, to not be exceptional—this is the most difficult path of transformation for a personality steeped in grandiosity, always striving to be the favorite child, the most charming little girl in the house.
summary: Argues that finding value in ordinary life and embracing normality is a profound challenge for grandiose personalities, particularly E2s, and represents a heroic path of psychological transformation.

title: Autobiography: Birth trauma and rebirthing experience
text:
AUTOBIOGRAPHY

The melody of the heart
by Fernando Ramos

Birth and childhood

I was born in São Paulo, Brazil, in 1968. Today, I am fifty-one years old. Yet, I still have a youthful face and a fairly good physical condition. It is often said that self-preservation E2s have a childlike nature, and indeed, I feel a certain sense of eternal youth, as if I have never fully reached adulthood. Responsibility weighs heavily on me.

During labor, my mother recalls undergoing an emergency C-section because, according to the doctor, her uterus did not dilate enough for a natural birth. She was urged to proceed with the surgery as I was already showing signs of exhaustion, and my life was at risk.

I have a distinct bodily memory of my birth. In 2003, during a rebirthing therapy session in water, using holotropic breathing, I experienced sensations strikingly similar to my mother’s account. I distinctly recognized a feeling of abandonment that dates back to my very origin—an impersonal feeling that has become a key to my personal transformation.

Just as my mother described her labor as slow to progress, my rebirth also unfolded gradually. While everyone around me in the session had already completed their experience and their catharses were settling, I was just beginning to feel tired from breathing, doubting that anything significant would happen to me at all. People were already leaving the pool when, finally, the experience intensified for me, with tingling sensations and tetany.

At the peak of my catharsis, I was overcome by uncontrollable sobbing and deep sorrow. The person guiding me through the session later told me that I kept whispering, “I don’t want to.” I submerged even further and felt transported to a place of pain and resentment. My cries were a lament against the imposition of a forced birth—being made to submit to the logic of the material world, to the conditions of this “vale of tears” that is life itself.

It was a profoundly emotional experience, but I understood what was happening. Being born meant returning to a realm governed by suffering and pain. More than that, birth was something imposed on me against my will, despite all my resistance.

This experience allowed me to recognize an emotional framework shaped by the belief that birth is an unjust obligation. I felt, in the depths of my being, like the victim of a sadistic God who had decided it was better to pull me out of the peaceful, harmonious place where I had been. And I could see how this fundamental sense of injustice had echoed throughout my life in the form of rebellion and sadness, despite my outward appearance as a good boy—cheerful and well-behaved.

The ten years following this rebirthing experience were spent trying to integrate this foundational realization. The feeling of being abandoned by God became a recurring theme in almost all my therapeutic work. Finally, during an ayahuasca ceremony (which, in Brazil, is part of our culture and often regarded as a sacrament), I had another profound experience that added a new perspective.
summary: Details a personal autobiography covering birth trauma, a rebirthing therapy experience that reactivated early feelings of abandonment, and the long-term integration of this insight, later expanded through ayahuasca, linking early trauma to lifelong emotional patterns in an E2.

title: Видение выбора рождения и переосмысление ответственности
text:
The psychedelic tea brought me a vision of a prenatal moment when my consciousness had not yet fully merged with this body. I understood that my birth had been my own decision, that I had willingly accepted it, that I had consciously left the place I once believed I had been expelled from—driven by my ego’s inflation. I realized I had been living my personal story as a reenactment of the myth of expulsion from paradise.

Finally recognizing that my arrival in this world was the result of a choice made by me, with free will, rather than an arbitrary act of the universe, allowed me to reframe my story from a place of greater responsibility rather than victimhood. This new perspective has brought me significant healing, as it freed me from the constant need to justify my frustrations by feeling like a victim—blaming my struggles on circumstances or other people.
summary: The author describes a psychedelic experience revealing that their birth was a conscious choice driven by ego, not a victimization. This insight allowed them to shift from a victim narrative to one of personal responsibility, leading to emotional healing.

title: Семейные динамики и роль матери
text:
My family

My parents knew how to play the roles expected of a respectable Brazilian middle-class family. My father was the provider, managing the family business and assets, while my mother, a homemaker, took care of the household and daily family life.

My father was forty when he married my mother, who was only eighteen; a twenty-two-year age gap is no small thing. Coming from different generations became a source of many conflicts and frustrations, which only grew more pronounced over time. My father entered old age far earlier than my mother, and that was not easy for either of them.

I often heard my mother lament her decision to marry an older man who had already been through a lot, suffered from addictions, and was often absent. She complained of wasting her youth and beauty on a man who didn’t appreciate her and who limited her. She made it clear that the only reason she stayed in that sacrifice was us, her children. I was terrified that one day, she wouldn’t be able to bear it any longer and would leave us.

I am the youngest of three siblings, with a considerable age gap between us. I am eight years younger than the middle child and fifteen years younger than the eldest. By the time I was born, my parents had already been married for seventeen years. That meant I entered a family system with a long history before my arrival, with alliances and rivalries already well established. I was a late-born child, welcomed as the baby of the family. In fact, “Baby” was my nickname for many years. That’s what everyone called me at home.

My mother was thirty-five when she gave birth to me. Her Polish ancestry gave her a strikingly European appearance—blonde with light eyes—which made her stand out in a country as racially diverse as Brazil. She has always been a beautiful woman, not only because of her looks but also because of the energy and vitality she exudes. She likes to say she was restless and independent from a young age. Ambitious, at seventeen, she left the small farm where she lived with her peasant parents to pursue her studies in the state capital.

Blessed with a vivid imagination, every morning she would tell us about the dreams she had during the night. She amazed me with the sheer amount of detail she could recall. She believed some of these dreams were premonitions that could intuitively influence her decisions and guide her. This trust in the dream world felt like a magical gift she had been given that I always admired and tried to emulate.

However, my mother often felt overwhelmed by responsibility and underappreciated, and she never hesitated to express it with great emotional intensity. She resented the endless demands of family life and frequently complained about the little time she had for herself. She had a demanding, sometimes dramatic, and capricious side, capable of making a scene over trivial matters. Like the time she wept inconsolably in a gift shop because the wrapping on a present she bought for a friend was done poorly.

She was also a loving mother who made us feel cared for in countless ways, like when she told us bedtime stories or prepared my bed with my favorite blankets. But this tendency toward maternal overcare sometimes took on a theatrical tone. There were moments when she would hug me, kiss me, and shower me with exaggerated praise, as if to publicly showcase what a good mother she was.

When frustrated or confronted, she would become extremely irritated and could lash out aggressively at whoever was in her way. If I broke a glass or dropped a plate, she might react with crushing, invalidating remarks like “You can’t get anything right” or “You’re useless.”
summary: This section details the author's family background, focusing on the parents' age gap, generational differences, and the mother's complex emotional nature—her dreams, emotional volatility, theatrical affection, and critical outbursts, which deeply influenced the author's childhood experience.

title: Динамика зависимости и эмоционального выживания с матерью
text:
I absorbed her compulsive emotionality as part of her unhappiness and suffering, and I felt that the loyal thing to do was to suffer along with her. Like my mother, I was an emotionally unstable child, sensitive to criticism and prone to tears. But unlike her, I didn’t have her strength.

I also tried to live up to what I believed she expected of me: to be her beloved little son, never causing her any trouble. I wanted to be her source of joy and affection in the midst of all the disgust she felt toward her life. In return, I expected her to love me, care for me, and shield me from her anger.

The unspoken terms of our alliance were that I would always be close to her, protected, and treated with special favor over my siblings. I would respond to her with sweetness, and I would suffer on her behalf. To this day, my mother describes me as an incredibly sweet and affectionate child. That’s how I learned to negotiate love. Now, I can clearly see the effects of that contract with her—for example, how I can instinctively adopt a soft, smiling demeanor whenever I want someone’s approval.
summary: The author describes internalizing their mother's emotional pain as a form of loyalty, adopting a role of the sweet, obedient child to earn love and avoid her anger. This unconscious contract shaped their behavior, leading to a habitual people-pleasing demeanor aimed at gaining approval.

title: Описание отца и его происхождения
text: My father was born in the early 20th century (1911, to be exact) into a family that reflected the deep racial and cultural mixing of Brazil over generations. From what I know of his lineage, there were Portuguese whites and formerly enslaved Black people, among other backgrounds. As the eldest of seven siblings, he often said he had to take on many responsibilities from a young age.
summary: Описывается происхождение отца, его бразильское наследие с примесью португальских и африканских корней, а также его роль как eldest sibling в большой семье.

title: Отношения с отцом в детстве
text: In my childhood, I remember him as an old, tired man. In my earliest memories, he was already over sixty, weakened by a lifetime of heavy smoking. Though affectionate and never violent, he showed no real interest in my world. He simply didn’t have the energy left to meet a child’s needs. I don’t recall him ever reading a book with me, playing soccer, coming to a school event, or taking me to the park. I wasn’t intimidated by him, but there was no real closeness either. He fulfilled his role as a provider admirably, and I learned to go to him only when I needed something concrete, like money.
summary: Автор описывает отца как уставшего, курильщика, emotionally distant человека, который выполнял роль кормильца, но не был вовлечен в эмоциональную жизнь ребенка.

title: Уважение к отцу как профессионалу
text: At the same time, I admired the image he projected as a respected lawyer and intellectual. He became a lawyer in 1937, earning the title of “doctor,” which was a big deal in a mostly agrarian and illiterate Brazil. Within our family, this status commanded great admiration and pride.
summary: Несмотря на эмоциональную отстраненность, автор уважал отца за его профессиональные достижения как юриста и интеллектуала в контексте бразильской действительности того времени.

title: Конфликт с матерью и её влияние на восприятие отца
text: As he grew older, more exhausted, and less attentive, my mother’s resentment toward him intensified. She never held back her criticisms, and it didn’t seem to bother her to belittle him in front of us. Looking back, I now realize how much my mother and my bond with her shaped the image I formed of my father. When she complained about him and blamed him for her unhappiness, I internalized that resentment as if it were my own.
summary: Мать усиливала свою критику отца по мере его ослабления, а автор, будучи привязан к матери, перенял её негативное отношение к отцу как своё собственное.

title: Взросление и переосмысление отношения к отцу
text: Because of this dynamic, I entered adulthood with a deeply distorted view of my father, which was poisoned by my mother’s pain and relentless invalidations. I’ve spent years trying to exorcize these inherited wounds, rebuilding an image of him based on admiration and my own lived experience with him.
summary: Автор осознаёт, что его образ отца был искажен влиянием матери, и сейчас работает над восстановлением более объективного восприятия через личный опыт и admiration.

title: Отец как провайдер, а не как эмоциональная фигура
text: I lived with my father until I was twenty. To him, love was expressed through provision. He made sure there was always food, clothing, education, and comfort. But beyond that, he didn’t seem to know how to connect emotionally with his family. The truth is, he was more like a grandfather than a father.
summary: Автор описывает отцовскую любовь как выражавшуюся только через материальное обеспечение, отмечая эмоциональную дистанцию и сравнивая роль отца с ролью дедушки.

title: Влияние братьев и кузена на формирование идентичности
text:
It was my older brother, already a young adult, who played the biggest role in introducing me to the world from a masculine perspective. He took an interest in my games, worked on projects with me, and took me to soccer matches to watch our team play. Honestly, I found him a thousand times more interesting than my father.

My middle brother, on the other hand, was emotionally very similar to my mother—temperamental and easily irritated. He didn’t hide his jealousy and often treated me aggressively, which made our relationship much more difficult.

The picture of my family wouldn’t be complete without mentioning my cousin, my father’s nephew, who was taken in by our family. He was the same age as my oldest brother and had been living with us long before I was born.
summary: Описывается compensatory роль старшего брата как мужественного наставника, напряжённые отношения с средним братом, похожим на мать по темпераменту, и наличие кузена в семье как части семейной системы.

title: Роль ребёнка-миротворца в семье
text: The family dynamics were often turbulent. I think my arrival represented a kind of renewed hope for peace, a promise of harmony. Not long ago, one of my brothers told me, quite literally, that he believed I came into the family like an angel, sent to soften the atmosphere and reconcile people. At first, the idea seemed absurd to me, but over time, I realized how accurately it described the role I unconsciously took on. I conformed to what was expected of me: to be the joy of the household. My mother still describes me as a gentle, easy child who never gave her any trouble.
summary: Автор осознаёт, что с раннего детства несознательно выполнял роль примирителя и источника радости в напряжённой семье, что соответствовало ожиданиям окружающих, особенно матери.

title: Раннее воспоминание о конфликте родителей и чувство ответственности за гармонию
text: One of my earliest memories gives another important clue about how my character was shaped. I vaguely recall a scene from when I was a baby, lying in my crib, witnessing a fight between my parents. I didn’t understand the reasons behind it, but I could feel the heavy emotional tension in the air. And I believed, somehow, that it was my responsibility to restore their harmony.
summary: Автор вспоминает эпизод из младенчества, когда, видя ссору родителей, уже тогда ощущал свою ответственность за восстановление мира в семье, что отражает глубинную установку Е2 на угождение и заботу о других.

title: Фантазия о себе как миротворе и её связь с E2-подтипами
text:
I recently realized that this scene reflects a wild and fanciful idea I formed at a very young age, the belief that I was capable of pacifying family conflicts. Something like an extraordinary peacemaker. It’s hard to draw the line between memory and projection in this case, but it’s very possible that there was indeed an expectation for me to play the role of savior or mediator, given my alliance with my mother and the long-standing family divisions.

The image of the crib evokes feelings of anguish, helplessness, and fear of abandonment. What could a child possibly do to reconcile a divided and conflicted family? The very idea that it might be possible, and that the task might depend on me, already provides a strong clue as to how my self-preservation Two ego took shape: my reaction to the scene expresses a deep-rooted sense of pride.

I felt that sweetness and affection could be contagious and that my family could be healed through this kind of emanation from me. This is a clear expression of my egocentric “generosity,” which, as a self-preservation E2, I kept well hidden and disguised, living it out in an imaginary and fantastical storyline, without actually doing anything concrete or taking any clear initiative, as the other two subtypes might.
summary: Автор связывает раннее воспоминание с формированием фантазии о себе как спасителе семьи, что раскрывает механизм его self-preservation E2: скрытая, воображаемая щедрость, направленная на получение любви через эмоциональное исцеление других.

title: Символическое отстранение отца и привязанность к матери
text:
Looking further back, I believe my pregnancy was unplanned, and I also suspect that my birth marked the beginning of the end of my parents’ sex life. I have no confirmation of this, but the fact remains that as I grew and outgrew my crib, I began sleeping in my parents’ bed. Soon, my father was displaced and moved into a room with my middle brother.

For the first ten years of my life, I slept with my mother in her bed every night, symbolically taking my father’s place. This disruption of the emotional hierarchy played a fundamental role in shaping my character and had lasting consequences for the entire family system.

The official justification for this arrangement was that my father’s deafening snoring made sleeping in the same room with him a nightmare, and the only person who could tolerate the noise was my middle brother. There was also the concern that if I shared a room with my middle brother, I’d be in constant danger of being attacked due to the jealousy he displayed toward me. However, I suppose that my mother simply liked having her newborn, youngest child close to her and that she knew I would be her last baby. And perhaps my father wasn’t particularly thrilled about being around me. Everything suggests that by then, he wasn’t too enthusiastic about fatherhood anymore.

And I, of course, was delighted to have my mother all to myself, to bask in her affection. I loved having her physically close, resting my head on her lap or wrapping my arms around her. I clearly remember intertwining my feet with hers to keep warm.

Replacing my father as the primary source of warmth and affection may have fostered a sense of rejection in him toward me. His bond with my brothers was visibly more intimate and affectionate. Initially, I thought this was simply because of the stage of life he was in when I was born, that he was more tired, that he didn’t have the energy left for me. But now I understand that part of his coldness stemmed from resentment over that triangle dynamic I had created within their relationship, where I competed with him and took his place.
summary: Автор описывает, как с раннего детства спал с матерью в одной кровати, символически замещая отца, что нарушило эмоциональную иерархию в семье и сформировало его характер. Эта динамика привела к отчуждению отца и усилению зависимости от материнской привязанности.

title: Осознание необычности ситуации и подавление потребности в отдельности
text:
Honestly, I have no memories of any sexual abuse. However, I am unsure how the confusion between maternal and erotic love operated within me. As I grew older, I realized that something wasn’t right about sleeping in my mother’s bed for so many years. By the time I was seven, I overheard my friends at school talking about how nice their bedrooms or personal beds were, and I became aware that my situation was unusual.

I didn’t like people knowing I still slept with my mother because I could sense their judgment. I felt ashamed and kept it a secret, convinced that I shouldn’t let anyone know. I only got my own bed when my cousin moved out to get married, and at around ten years old, I finally began sharing a room with my older brother.

The prolonged symbiosis with my mother reinforced the stigma of being the baby of the family, which made my journey toward self-assertion much harder as I grew up. My mother continued calling me “Baby” in front of others for years, despite my clear verbal and nonverbal protests. When I got upset and voiced my discomfort, she manipulated me with guilt, saying I was an ungrateful son. This effectively prevented me from openly rebelling.

Ultimately, my family became accustomed to seeing me as the baby and put a great deal of pressure on me to stay in that role. I felt that growing up required much more effort for me than it did for my friends because my family, especially my mother, simply didn’t seem to want me to.
summary: По мере взросления автор осознает, что его привычка спать с матерью является социально неприемлемой, что вызывает стыд и секретность. Мать укрепляет его роль «ребенка» через эмоциональное давление и вину, что затрудняет процесс отделения и самоутверждения.

title: Открытие семейной тайны: полубрат и последствия скрытия
text:
The secret family

My mother was my father’s second wife. His first marriage, which produced a son, had been arranged between families and didn’t work out. It wasn’t until my father passed away in 1988 and his will was read that I discovered he had another family.

No one had ever told me! So, at twenty years old, I was hit with this massive surprise. I couldn’t believe that something so significant had never even been mentioned, that it had simply been kept from me. My brothers admitted they had always known but said it wasn’t talked about because it wasn’t important.

The subject was a major taboo in the family. From that moment on, everyone was impatient and reluctant to answer my questions about my father’s first family. My mother told me that my half-brother had serious psychological problems and that my father used to visit him during his childhood, but gradually stopped until he lost contact completely. The official story was that the boy had a psychotic break when he was introduced to the first child of my father’s new family and, from that moment on, refused to see him again. My brothers’ version was that they never felt any obligation to meet this “crazy” half-brother, that it was an issue concerning only my father.

I felt deeply unsettled knowing that I had a half-brother whom I was never allowed to meet, and even more so when I realized my other siblings didn’t share my concern. As I gained a better understanding of family system dynamics, I gravitated toward this issue, which became a significant focus in my therapy work.

After attending a SAT course in 2010, I decided to search for my half-brother so I could acknowledge and integrate him into my family system. I was terrified of what might come of it. I had nightmares and anxiety attacks before finally mustering up the courage to track down his number and call him. When I finally worked up the nerve, and he picked up the phone, I took my time introducing myself. He was surprised and very anxious. He told me he had no interest in any kind of contact with “that branch” of the family, made his excuses, and hung up.
summary: В возрасте 20 лет автор узнает о существовании半брата от первого брака отца, который долгие годы скрывался от семьи. Эта тайна становится источником глубокого эмоционального беспокойства, и несмотря на попытки воссоединения, полубрат отвергает контакт, усиливая чувство потери и экзистенциальной изоляции.

title: Попытки восстановить связь с братом и её последствия
text:
After that disappointment, I still sent him a letter, though I don’t know if he ever read it. I told him how much I regretted living my life without ever having the chance for us to know each other and that I completely respected his decision to keep his distance. And little by little, I let go of the matter… until recently, when I found out that he had passed away in 2016.

Even now, I still wonder what direct or indirect effects the removal of this half-brother from the family may have had on our family system. Or even what impact this could have on our descendants—mine and my siblings’. This lost brother felt the abandonment of the father we shared far more intensely than any of the three of us. I sense that his absence has affected all of us in different ways, through guilt in my father and through anger in my mother.
summary: The author describes sending a letter to his half-brother after a failed phone call, coming to terms with his rejection, and later learning of his death in 2016. He reflects on the lasting emotional impact of the brother's absence on the family system, noting guilt in the father and anger in the mother.

title: Детство без ответственности и формирование внутреннего мира
text:
Childhood and school

My childhood was free of any kind of responsibility. My family lived on a tight budget, but my parents had an agreement that we, the children, would be exempt from any obligations beyond our education. I believe that one side effect of this decision was my tendency toward comfort and ease—so much so that I was spared even the simplest tasks, like making my bed or organizing my toys. My mother or the housekeeper took care of everything.

At a SAT course in 2005, a therapist on the team told me that my life "should have been harder," suggesting that my struggles stemmed from my low tolerance for setbacks due to having been so protected and spoiled.

I grew up in an urban environment at a time when the city wasn’t nearly as dangerous as most Latin American cities are today. There was freedom to explore the streets and plazas around my home, to build my own social network based on my interests. As a child, I remember walking long distances in random directions, driven purely by curiosity. I wandered along train tracks, climbed rooftops, ventured into tunnels, attended mass at different churches, scaled rocks… Exploring the city itself was a fascinating game.

I often played alone. I was fascinated by the tiny creatures I found in the soil whenever I buried objects, imagining them as paleontological treasures. I could spend four or five hours straight swimming in the sea, lost in fantasies of encounters with mythical marine beings. I had done this since I was very young. People called me a dreamer, saying I was "off in the clouds." My attention was often submerged in an ocean of images and sensations, which shaped how I engaged with the tangible world. That inner world of images and sensations can be a wonderful channel for creativity, but it can also serve as a refuge for neurotic fantasies. And I used it as both.
summary: The author describes a sheltered childhood free from chores, marked by financial constraints but parental indulgence. He developed a rich inner life through solitary exploration, imaginative play, and deep engagement with nature and fantasy, which served both as a source of creativity and a refuge from reality.

title: Кража скульптуры и стремление к восхищению обманом
text:
Despite the freedom I enjoyed growing up, I had a deep need to be seen and admired. When I was around nine or ten, I had an experience that illustrates just how intense this need was. I visited a classmate’s house and saw a wooden sculpture. It was a human figure, and I found it breathtakingly beautiful. I longed to create something like that myself, wondering if I could earn admiration for it. I even tried carving with a piece of wood and a sharp knife, but I quickly realized I couldn’t come close to that level of craftsmanship.

That’s when I started imagining another way: I could steal the sculpture, sign my name on it, and pass it off as my own. One day, when no one was home, I climbed over the wall and took it. Just as I had planned, I painted my name over the real artist’s signature, which had been carved in low relief.

I waited for the perfect moment to present “my masterpiece,” offering it as a gift to a friend of my brother’s. Everyone was impressed and wanted to know more about how and when I had made it. I started making up explanations. At one point, I noticed my brother and his friend pointing at the real signature underneath mine. From their expressions, I knew they had uncovered my fraud.

A cascade of terrible emotions overwhelmed me: shame at being caught, guilt for stealing, and sheer astonishment at the realization of how much risk and effort I had put into this elaborate deception, all for the fleeting reward of admiration.
summary: Driven by a strong desire for admiration, the author stole a classmate's sculpture, forged his name on it, and presented it as his own work. When the fraud was exposed, he experienced intense shame, guilt, and astonishment at the lengths he went to for fleeting validation.

title: Кража наклеек и осознание зависти как мотива
text:
I remember another similar incident from that same period when I stole a classmate’s sticker album at school. But this time, the meaning hit even harder; even now, I still feel a deep remorse when I think about it. My motivation wasn’t admiration or recognition. It was pure envy. I wanted his album simply because it was more complete than mine. I maintained the lie, even as I watched how sad it made him. I knew I had done something awful, but I couldn’t find a way to undo it without exposing myself. I experienced the full weight of guilt and remember thinking there must be something fundamentally wrong with me, something that needed fixing.

Up until then, I had a certain tendency toward petty theft. I would steal chocolates from the market and take bills from my mother’s purse or my father’s wallet. I loved the adrenaline rush and the thrill of seeing if I could get away with it. Luckily, that phase ended after the sticker album incident.
summary: The author recounts stealing a classmate’s sticker album out of envy rather than desire for admiration, leading to deep remorse. He reflects on a broader pattern of petty theft driven by thrill-seeking, which ended after this incident as he began to confront his moral shortcomings.

title: Провал в учёбе и перелом в самооценке
text: I was a mediocre student until I was thirteen or fourteen when I failed a grade and had to repeat the year. It was a harsh fall. Where I came from, repeating a grade carried the stigma of being “not very smart.” My parents told me that school was my only responsibility and that I had no excuse for failing. I hit rock bottom and realized something had to change in me, that I had to reevaluate my approach. From that point on, I withdrew into an intense, high-pressure mindset, convinced that if I didn’t change, I was doomed.
summary: After years of mediocre performance, the author failed a grade and faced social stigma and parental disappointment. This experience became a turning point, prompting him to adopt a rigid, high-pressure approach to academics out of fear of failure and a need to prove his intelligence.

title: Трансформация личности и успех после провала
text:
The following year, I adopted a more disciplined and serious attitude. I started waking up earlier to organize my schoolwork, cut down on my free time outside the house to review my lessons, chose a seat in class away from the chatterboxes, and tried to avoid getting into trouble. Changing classes also helped. I found it easier to adapt to a new, more responsible group of friends.

In just two years, I transformed from one of the worst students in class to one of the top performers. The change was so drastic that it triggered a complete shift in my self-image. I started seeing myself as intelligent and attractive, and even girls began to take an interest in me.

At sixteen, I had my first girlfriend, a stunning girl from my school. Being with her made me feel worthy, capable, like I had made it. In no time, I had gone from being “the ugly duckling and half-wit” to one of the most popular guys, dating the most beautiful girl in school. It was the beginning of an unprecedented ego trip.
summary: Описывает резкое улучшение успеваемости и самооценки после провала в учебе, приводящее к популярности и первым романтическим отношениям, которые становятся началом эгоцентричного периода.

title: Разрыв и существенный кризис после первой любви
text:
Our relationship lasted about a year and a half, and its end was, at least in theory, a mutual decision. It was incredibly difficult because, despite my pride—which wouldn’t allow me to admit it—I was still deeply in love with her. Deep down, I hoped she would give in and come back to me. But that never happened.

A few months later, I took a severe blow when I found out she had started dating an older guy, who had his own car and who also played the guitar. An opponent who seemed unbeatable. I was in shock when, not long after, I learned that she was pregnant. But the final, crushing blow came when, in a twist of cruel irony, she moved in with her partner and their newborn child right across the street from my house.

I started seeing her with her new family several times a week. It shattered my self-image, threw off my internal balance, and left me mentally and emotionally unmoored. The experience of abandonment triggered my first major existential crisis. I realized I needed more than just a few adjustments to my habits and attitudes. I had to become someone different. But I had no idea where to start.
summary: Детализирует болезненный разрыв с первой девушкой, её последующие отношения и беременность, что привело к разрушению самооценки и existential кризису, заставив рассказчика осознать необходимость глубоких изменений.

title: Самодеструктивный цикл отрицания, жертвы и гнева
text:
At first, my instinct was to numb the pain of fragility and rejection through sheer denial. I started drinking, competed with my friends to see who could seduce the most girls, and indulged in other reckless behaviors, all as an expression of my rebellious and immature state. This pattern made me aware of how shocks from frustration or failure cause me to spiral into a loss of self-worth. I began to recognize the early stages of this downward cycle through symptoms of depression and apathy. It felt like an abrupt emptiness washing over me.

From that denial, I would slip into a state of melancholic victimhood, which would then morph into anger and resentment. At its most extreme, my frustration would turn into dramatic, almost theatrical demands, quickly escalating into rage, loss of control, and bursts of aggression. These reactions resembled childish tantrums; intense emotional turbulence that felt like a chaotic yet powerful force taking over.

What’s strange about this state is that I can clearly feel the wave building up inside me. It draws on my vital energy, concentrating it entirely on preparing for an explosion. I feel the intensity of its flow, and there’s something tempting about surrendering to it. Resisting it feels almost impossible. There’s a kind of pleasure in the process, a false sense of empowerment that builds artificially. And once I reach the point of no return, I can no longer hold back, and everything erupts like a bomb.

But this energy burns out just as quickly as it builds up. The forceful imposition of my will collapses, leaving me drained. The euphoria vanishes, giving way to guilt over my outburst, which in turn feeds my depression. Depending on how intense the episode was, it can take me days to regain my balance. I end up utterly exhausted.
summary: Описывает повторяющийся эмоциональный цикл: от отрицания и ухода в рискованное поведение через состояние жертвы к взрывной ярости, за которым следует истощение и вина, осознавая этот паттерн как саморазрушительный.

title: Осознание паттернов и влияние первой любви на трансформацию
text:
I lived out this same self-destructive pattern countless times throughout my life. The only thing that changed was the frequency and intensity of the falls. Fortunately, as I began to understand the mechanics of it, I learned to slow its progression. Looking back now, I can recognize the importance of that first girlfriend in my life and how the pain of her abandonment became a catalyst for many transformations. It was through this experience that I began to see just how destructive this cycle had been.

One of the major consequences of that heartbreak was the complete reshaping of how I related to women. My models for romantic relationships had been my middle brother and my cousin, who would harass their girlfriends in an aggressive, manipulative way, making them feel guilty to gain control. I unconsciously adopted the same techniques with my girlfriend, believing for a while that I could break her will and make her think she was always the one responsible for our arguments.

Luckily for me, she was neither as fragile nor as submissive as my brother’s girlfriends. By leaving me, she forced me to realize that this was an unhealthy pattern I shouldn’t be copying. It dawned on me that I had absorbed a toxic way of behaving in relationships. It wasn’t originally mine but had been ingrained in me through the example set by the male figures in my family.
summary: Рассказчик осознает повторяющийся самодеструктивный паттерн и связывает его с первым романтическим опытом, осознавая, что его агрессивное поведение в отношениях было приобретено из токсичных семейных моделей, а не являлось врожденным.

title: Проблемы с самореализацией в карьере несмотря на преимущества
text:
Work

Work, career, and professional fulfillment remain unresolved issues for me. This is one of the biggest struggles in my life, which I associate with my difficulty, as a self-preservation Two, in fully stepping into adulthood.

I have a background that qualifies me for a broad professional field that includes architecture, design, and visual arts. I hold both a master’s and a doctorate, which allow me to work in research and higher education. I see my skill set as a valuable inheritance from my parents, who encouraged us to explore, experiment, and carve out our own paths. Financially, I also have a fair amount of freedom, even if with some limitations.
summary: Несмотря на сильное образование и профессиональные возможности, автор испытывает трудности в карьерной самореализации, связывая это с его типом Enneagram — самосохраняющейся Двойкой и трудностями во взрослении.

title: Проблемы с самооценкой и профессиональная реализация
text:
And yet, several psychological factors combine in a way that prevents all these advantages from translating into real professional or financial fulfillment. A beloved psychotherapist who often participates in the SAT program once told me, when I asked for guidance on my career dilemmas, that my main issue is that I don’t believe in my own capabilities. When I asked how I could overcome this, he simply suggested: “Honor your father’s memory."

I never fully understood how my father approached work, as there was nothing particularly structured or routine about his profession. He was self-employed, and his office was in a room at home, near the street. He could go for long stretches staying at home, then suddenly disappear on a business trip. Sometimes, he’d receive generous payments for a service, and during those times, he would joyfully shower us with gifts and fill the pantry. Other times, money was tight, and he would carefully ration expenses. He valued freedom and autonomy over financial stability, preferring an unpredictable income over the constraints of a steady paycheck. When times required saving, the atmosphere at home would shift. Things became more austere, and my mother would remind us to only ask for money when absolutely necessary.

From a very young age, I remember feeling deeply anxious about whether I would ever be able to support myself, let alone a family. The adult world and its responsibilities felt overwhelming, as if I simply lacked the ability to develop the skills needed to face the challenges I saw all around me.
summary: The author discusses how despite having professional qualifications and freedom, psychological barriers prevent fulfillment. Key issues include lack of belief in one's capabilities, an unconscious pact with the mother to remain dependent, and modeling after a father who valued freedom over stability, leading to anxiety about adulthood and self-sufficiency from a young age.

title: Саботаж успеха и искаженная самооценка
text:
Recently, another therapist familiar with my story suggested that my professional struggles are also the result of an unconscious pact I made with my mother: to never grow up, to always be her Baby. The logic goes that if I don’t succeed, I’ll never have to be an adult; and if I’m not an adult, I’ll always be dependent and will never have to leave my mother. It makes a lot of sense and evokes in me the image of still needing to symbolically cut the umbilical cord.

I recognize a pattern of self-sabotage in myself. It holds back the progress of many of my projects, which I abandon just as they’re about to be completed, presented, or sold. It’s as if I have an ingrained resistance to the legitimate right to feel satisfied and nourished by the results of my work, out of some shameful sense of being a beggar for recognition. Once again, my pride at play!

Another friend (half therapist, half witch) visited my home recently and was struck by how dismissively I spoke about my own work. She recognized this self-deprecation as an expression of my self-sabotage and suggested a simple act of psychomagic: I should hang on my walls all the paintings and artwork that were scattered haphazardly on the floor and in the corners. Though it seems like a simple task, I still haven’t managed to do it.

The boundaries between my sense of self-worth and the external validation of my work are blurry. This confusion paralyzes me when it comes to action and achievement because, deep down, I feel that any rejection of my work is a rejection of me. This crazy belief follows the script that if I can’t offer something admirable, I won’t be loved. It also fuels my hedonistic tendencies, leading me to pursue too many interests at once. This expansive urge to look in all directions turns any activity requiring long-term discipline into a personal hell.
summary: The author identifies an unconscious agreement with their mother to remain emotionally dependent as a core cause of professional stagnation. This manifests as self-sabotage, where completed work is abandoned due to shame in accepting recognition, confusion between self-worth and external validation, and a belief that love is contingent on admirable output, which fuels distraction and avoidance of disciplined effort.

title: Когнитивный хаос и трудности с организацией
text:
I see all of this as a cognitive dysfunction that hinders my ability to take concrete action in the world, tied to my struggles with organization. I feel a mental chaos that makes prioritizing difficult. It’s as if I’m surrounded by tasks from all sides. Wherever I look, I see something demanding my attention, and I don’t even know where to start. This messy, exhausting mental state drains my energy without actually changing anything.

As a classic Two, I feel uncomfortable with routines and bureaucracy, which I see as threats to my sacred freedom, making it difficult for me to integrate discipline into my work. As a therapeutic approach to my professional struggles, I find that structured methodologies—with clear goals, deadlines, and tasks—help me stay on track.

Since there’s no risk of me turning my need for organization into an obsession, developing a more practical approach to planning could yield visible results in the short and medium term. In fact, cultivating a sense of practicality and operating in the tangible world is already, in itself, a healing experience for my neurosis.
summary: The author describes their professional struggles as rooted in cognitive dysfunction and disorganization, leading to paralysis despite numerous demands. As a Two, they resist routines as threats to freedom but find that structured methodologies with clear goals help them stay on track, and cultivating practicality in the tangible world serves as healing for their neurosis.

title: Эмоциональные раны от семейного унижения
text:
Wounds and scars

In my family, there was a toxic sense of humor that revolved around identifying people’s weaknesses and ridiculing them. The person being mocked didn’t even have to be present—we could be tearing someone apart over lunch, for example. The comments carried an undertone of contempt and belittlement, and the punchline always seemed to land when someone laughed, following the typical dynamic of bullying.

The episodes of emotional abuse I was exposed to are wounds that have not fully healed, and from time to time, they still trigger reactions in me. The disguise of humor made the aggression less obvious, but it wounded my self-esteem far more deeply than any physical harm ever could. I still remember the anger I felt. I couldn’t understand the reason or motivation behind those humiliations, which seemed completely gratuitous. I didn’t know how to set boundaries or express how much they hurt me, since my depression and sadness were dismissed in my family as weakness and laziness.

As a self-preservation Two, I have an extreme sensitivity that makes me susceptible to being wounded by even the smallest comment. My parents never seemed to realize the impact those taunts had on me. Not long ago, I told my mother that the memories of those abuses still hurt me, and she was genuinely surprised. In truth, I’m not entirely sure she took what I said seriously or even believed me.
summary: The author describes enduring emotional wounds from a family culture of ridicule disguised as humor, which targeted vulnerabilities and caused deep self-esteem damage. As a self-preservation Two with extreme sensitivity, they internalized these attacks, struggled to express pain due to familial dismissal of emotions as weakness, and found even confronting their mother about lingering hurt met with surprise and possible disbelief.

title: Public humiliation and emotional abuse in family dynamics
text:
I remember one particular scene, in front of some cousins and friends, when my brothers decided to have some fun at my expense. They told everyone at what embarrassingly late age I stopped using a baby bottle or how a childhood friend used to trick me into giving her money for ice cream. My brothers would seize every opportunity to publicly ridicule me. They clearly knew how much it hurt me and how humiliated I felt when everyone laughed, and I hated them for it.

For much of my life, I couldn’t understand the sheer senselessness of these aggressions. Now I realize they may have been expressions of resentment over our mother’s favoritism toward me, a way of telling me they were fully aware of my seductive strategy and maternal alliance.

My mother had a different style, but she didn’t spare me from public embarrassment either. I remember one day when I came home and found her chatting with two neighbors on the street. As I approached to greet them, she suddenly blurted out, “Look how big he is! But to me, he’s still a baby... My baby.” I felt deeply humiliated and begged her to stop, but it was useless. My discomfort wasn’t acknowledged. I understand now that she didn’t mean to humiliate me on purpose, but she also wasn’t willing to let go of the role we had unconsciously agreed upon in my early childhood. That of the eternal child.

Whenever my family was in a social setting, or in the presence of others, I lived under the tension and expectation that soon my mother’s embarrassing love performance or my brothers’ teasing would begin. It was like being caught in the bipolar dynamic of being both pampered and ridiculed for it.
summary: Describes specific instances of public humiliation by brothers and mother, highlighting the family's toxic dynamic of ridicule disguised as affection, and the narrator's ongoing sensitivity to such treatment as a self-preservation Two.

title: Internalized shame and emotional castration
text:
Over time, this constant emotional abuse created a deep sense of incompetence in me, as the narrative always revolved around proving how inept, cowardly, stupid, or weak I was, making me feel utterly ridiculous. I perceived each of these episodes as a form of emotional castration and felt that I had to push back against my mother’s attachment in order to carve out space to grow. This struggle also played out internally in the form of conflict and insecurity. What would growing up mean? Would it mean losing the privileged position I had with my mother and, by extension, within my family, despite the price I paid for it?

Even today, despite having examined it many times, I still feel a strong reactivity when I find myself exposed at the center of attention. In negative situations, this manifests as counterphobia, which can quickly escalate into resentment or explosive anger, often disproportionate to the situation.

Fortunately, I can see that, over time, these reactions have become less frequent and less intense, undoubtedly a result of my therapeutic work. I have learned to recognize certain triggers more precisely, making it harder for me to fall into the same trap.

I have also realized how I became a master at responding to toxicity with humor, yet in doing so, I was unknowingly part of a cycle that transformed me from the abused into the abuser. This chronic resentment led me, at times, to take on that same role, ultimately pushing people away.
summary: Explores the internal impact of chronic emotional abuse, including feelings of inadequacy, emotional castration, reactivity to attention, and the unconscious adoption of abusive behaviors as a defense mechanism, all processed through therapeutic awareness.

title: Acting out and behavioral expression of inner turmoil
text:
As long as I remained unaware of this cycle, blindly oscillating between feeling victimized and adopting the stance of an aggressor, I lived with a deep sense of inadequacy and isolation. Some of my friends, who are still in my life today, remember me as an aggressive child, even at home, despite my mother and other adults describing me as a “sweet and affectionate boy.” In fact, between the ages of ten and fourteen, I often got into fights, caused trouble at school, and was frequently reprimanded for my disruptive behavior. These were all echoes, outside the home, of the neurosis I was living with my family.

At home, coercion through threats became the norm, though only my middle brother would actually cross the line into physical aggression. When I reached adulthood at eighteen, my body changed rapidly through sports, and just in time, I became very strong.

Once I was physically on par with everyone else and capable of confronting them, I established a new dynamic in how I related to the adults in my home. I made it clear to each of them that from that moment on, threats would have no effect on me. The fear I had once felt was gone, and I let them know that every humiliation I received would be met with a response. The only one I still exchanged blows with was my middle brother, but only long enough for him to understand that his advantage in physical strength no longer existed.

This phase of self-assertion, which lasted until I was twenty, reshaped all my relationships. But it also coincided with crucial family events, such as my father’s death.
summary: Details the external manifestation of inner turmoil through aggression and disruptive behavior in childhood, followed by a physical and assertive shift in late adolescence that redefined family power dynamics, culminating around the time of the father's death.

title: Father's death, family fragmentation, and transition to adulthood
text:
Shortly before passing away at seventy-seven, my father no longer concealed the discomfort between us. During his last year of life, our interactions were dry, superficial, and impatient. I experienced his death with a mix of ambiguity and confusion. I felt a strange sense of guilt for not having had a closer, more intimate relationship with him, unconsciously acknowledging my own share of responsibility for the weakness of our bond. At the same time, I was deeply angry at his inability to reach out to me. After all, he was the father, and I was the son.

That same year, I was admitted to a university in another city and began to disconnect from my family of origin. My middle brother also left home to live with his girlfriend in another state. My eldest brother remained with my mother and took on my father’s role as the one responsible for managing the family property.

Entering adulthood
summary: Reflects on the complex emotions surrounding the father's death—guilt and anger—followed by physical and emotional separation from the family of origin through university and siblings' departures, marking the beginning of independent adulthood.

title: Взросление и осмысление семейной роли
text:
By the time I was twenty, coinciding with my father’s passing, I had entered the adult world. But I experienced it as if I had been the cause of my family’s fragmentation simply by growing up and attempting to separate myself from them. Though, honestly, I didn’t feel bad about it. In some way, I believed that the strength of our family ties would be enough to redefine my relationships with them. But that never really happened.

Looking back, I can see that throughout my life, I created an image of myself as a force holding my family together, preventing it from falling apart. I realized that my ego was built around this identity, the idea of being “so special” within the family, almost like a Child Jesus figure. It’s difficult to say how much of my personality was shaped as a response to their expectations and how much emerged from my own inclinations.

It’s interesting how, even today, I feel responsible for mediating between family members. Maybe this is just an echo of my childhood egocentrism, still fantasizing about a harmonious family united by my efforts—a magnetic presence, someone who brings stability and serves a higher cause of love and unity. But in a healthier, more mature version of myself, this role could also reflect a willingness to take responsibility for what I’ve come to understand about my family’s dysfunctions, including my own. This time, however, without illusions of special gifts or privileges, just with a genuine desire to contribute to ending this journey in a better place than where we started.
summary: The author reflects on entering adulthood after his father's death, recognizing his lifelong role as a stabilizing force in the family, rooted in childhood egocentrism and a self-image of being 'special' like a Child Jesus figure. He acknowledges both the unconscious motivations behind this role and his matured desire to contribute to family healing without illusions of superiority.

title: Университетские годы и поиск себя через аяваску
text:
Between the ages of twenty and twenty-five, during my university years, I experienced an unprecedented level of freedom in a semi-independent life. I still had financial support from my family to help with my studies, but I also enjoyed the autonomy to live however I wanted.

I was far more interested in spending time with other young people than in my studies. I became an average student who attended plenty of parties and social gatherings. I had my favorite professors I grew close to and even befriended. They were always the more alternative, philosophical, and abstract thinkers. One of these professors, whom I enjoyed talking with, also happened to be a teacher within an ayahuasca-based religion. He eventually invited me to participate in a session. I was twenty-two at the time and deeply interested in experiencing altered states of consciousness in a safe environment. I was born in 1968, a year of great countercultural movements around the world, and it’s possible that this left some kind of imprint on me, shaping how I engage with the world.

When I finally drank ayahuasca for the first time at a União do Vegetal session, it was as if I had found the missing proof of the spirit’s existence. The clarity of understanding and the beauty of the visions pointed me toward a deeper, subtler layer of existence, and I was eager to explore it. The brew brought me symbols, memories, feelings, sensations, expansion, and insight, but also discomfort and suffering. I believed I had found my path, and for several years, I became completely immersed in that culture and the people within it.
summary: During his university years, the author embraced freedom and explored alternative spirituality through ayahuasca in the União do Vegetal tradition. He describes profound spiritual experiences, a sense of finding his path, and deep immersion in the culture, influenced by his countercultural birth year and attraction to philosophical mentors.

title: Эволюция в аяваскной практике и встреча с будущей женой
text:
Over time, I began adapting to the profile of ayahuasca religion followers. I was seeking a more Apollonian sense of self—disciplined and devoted—because I felt these were the virtues I lacked. I assumed that my life needed more structure, and that meant adopting new attitudes and habits. That religion seemed like the ideal place to learn how to become that kind of person.

I was a regular member of União do Vegetal for about fifteen years, and I experienced many joys there. I learned the fundamentals of working with plant medicines, the energetic structure of systemic fields, and the tools to maintain balance during the intense storms their effects bring to the mind and body. However, I eventually realized that my personal growth within that group had stalled. I had become rigidly neurotic, allowing an artificial sense of order to override my more spontaneous impulses. Over time, I became interested in exploring the effects of the tea in different contexts and with other groups, and I gradually drifted away from that community.

It was during an ayahuasca ritual in 1994 that I met Ana Paula. In 1996, at the age of twenty-eight, we got married. We've now been together for twenty-four years, and in many ways, we are the complete opposite of our parents. Ana Paula is an emotionally steady and gentle woman, the exact opposite of my mother. On the other hand, the warmth and spontaneity that attracted her to me stood in stark contrast to the emotional coldness and control of her father.
summary: The author describes his fifteen-year involvement with União do Vegetal, where he sought structure and discipline but eventually grew rigid and neurotic, prompting his departure. It was during an ayahuasca ritual in 1994 that he met his future wife, Ana Paula, whose emotional steadiness contrasts with his mother, while her attraction to his warmth highlights complementary dynamics in their relationship.

title: Динамика брака и движение к зрелости
text:
She seems immune to my emotional turbulence and doesn’t get caught up in my excesses when they surface. This has helped me grow by preventing my ego from becoming inflamed and cutting off its justifications. From the start, I sensed that being with her would be a challenge, but also a valuable opportunity to learn how to manage my overwhelming emotional expressions. Besides, I had already learned from my teenage girlfriend that emotionally healthy women, sooner or later, lose interest in abusive men.

What brings us together is our shared sense of humor, spontaneity, and the fact that we have always been united in our pursuit of transformation. We became life partners even before we became husband and wife. I also believe we were drawn to each other because of our respective neuroses. On my part, the search for a woman who could replace my mother in terms of care and privileges; on hers, perhaps the need to reinforce the superiority that comes with being the caretaker. Over time, I realized that for our marriage to be more than just a meeting of two dysfunctional patterns, I needed to step out of my place of dependence and move toward greater autonomy and self-sufficiency. In other words, I needed to grow up and present myself to her as a man rather than as a child.
summary: The author reflects on how his wife Ana Paula stabilizes his emotional excesses and supports his growth, despite their shared neuroses. He recognizes their mutual attraction rooted in unconscious patterns—his search for maternal care and her need for caretaker superiority—and realizes that true marital health requires moving beyond dependence toward autonomy and mutual maturity.

title: Роль отцовства и брака в личностном росте
text:
I never had any doubts that marriage and fatherhood were part of my path to growth. I understand that this isn’t necessary for everyone, but I imagine my life would have been far less fulfilling had I spent it alone. Becoming a father shifted my perspective by forcing me to prioritize the needs of others above my own. This had never come naturally to me. I had to learn to live with the discomfort of caring for someone else instead of being taken care of, and I had to confront my own selfishness, complacency, inertia, and narcissism. I fully committed myself to sharing in the responsibilities of raising our children, which allowed me to form a deep bond with them in a way I had never experienced with my own father.

We have three children: nineteen, fifteen, and twelve years old. They are very different from one another, and we know each will face their own challenges in life. But I take great comfort in knowing that certain unhealthy patterns from my own family haven’t carried over to them. I believe I avoided passing them down not just because I recognized them (at the cost of many hours of therapy) but also because I caught them before they had a chance to contaminate my relationship with my children. Unlike the home I grew up in, ours is free from theatrical fights, loud arguments, or any form of aggression. None of my children have ever been slapped.
summary: Автор описывает, как отцовство и брак стали частью его пути роста, заставив его преодолеть эгоизм и нарциссизм, и как он осознанно разорвал семейные паттерны насилия и дисфункции в отношениях с детьми.

title: Свобода и автономия в браке
text: A key clause in our marriage contract was that staying together should always be a conscious choice. At various points, we’ve felt free to renew our vows and reassess the terms of our relationship. There is no control over one another, no jealousy forcing us to change our behavior. Most of our friends are mutual, but we also give each other the freedom to cultivate our own circles. We believe it’s important to create spaces where our marriage is not an obstacle to individual growth but rather an enhancer of our experiences.
summary: Автор подчеркивает, что их брак основан на сознательном выборе, отсутствии контроля и ревности, а также на взаимной поддержке индивидуального роста партнеров.

title: Преподавание как путь самопознания и уязвимости
text:
After completing my doctorate in 2008, I dedicated myself to teaching and research in architecture and design schools. It was a brilliant and intense twelve-year phase during which I discovered a true vocation. I felt more motivated to study than ever before, structuring my courses and lectures specifically for students aged eighteen to twenty-two. The intellectual and logical challenges of this work deeply enriched me.

In some classes, I was able to incorporate less conventional approaches beyond the rigid standards of formal education, introducing activities inspired by Gestalt techniques. In that context, I sometimes felt like a therapist, as my goal was to do more than simply deliver academic content. I aimed to create an atmosphere of unity and trust where learning could flow naturally. I encouraged students to share their personal processes and struggles.

Through this experience, I gained a deeper understanding of the power of compassionate love, which is particularly strong in the self-preservation subtype. I was genuinely interested in my students and enjoyed getting to know them on a personal level.
