After her failed marriage and miserable life in the Dutch East Indies with her husband and his family, tragedy struck: her four-year-old son, Norman, died under mysterious circumstances. Many stories have been written about the possible cause of his death, though most seem to belong to the legend rather than reality. The most plausible theory today is that Norman died from mercury poisoning while being treated for congenital syphilis. His death further strained the family, leading to their divorce in 1902.

Margaretha moved to Paris in search of work. She tried acting and posed for artists, but her only reliable source of income was pleasing men in exchange for money.

Like a phoenix rising from the ashes, Griet reinvented herself as Mata Hari in 1905 after a painful and tumultuous period. This pattern is often seen in the biographies of Enneatype 2 personalities: a glorious childhood where they are treated like royalty, followed by a period of suffering and humiliation, only to be reborn with strength and determination. A wounded pride incubates its power, waiting for the right moment to manifest. Above all, she saw herself and her own interests—this was her time for revenge.
summary: Описывает смерть сына Нормана, развод, переезд в Париж и перерождение Маргариты в Мата Хари как типичный путь E2: от унижения к возрождению через самолюбие и месть, где новая идентичность становится источником силы.

title: Создание сценического образа и эстетика танца
text:
She reemerged with a keen sense of what could bring success. She developed a series of “sacred dances” she had learned in the Dutch East Indies. Her performances were far from classical; rather, they seemed to birth a new, original style that masterfully combined an aura of extreme sensuality with an atmosphere of religious and devotional mysticism. Passion and drama blended into a performance that was both provocative and sublime. Her costumes were striking, with sheer fabrics that were more than suggestive, and Javanese jewelry that combined gold with precious stones.

Years later, Mata Hari confided in a friend:

Pretending to consider my dances very artistic and full of character, thus praising my art, they came to see nudity, and that is still the case. I act as thousands do; I speculate on sensuality; I behave coquettishly, and flirt now and again with a full house, that comes easily to me, that came always easily to me.

Mata Hari’s passion was seduction, the art of attracting and captivating, the power to conquer and enthrall. She used her entire being—her body, her movements, her gaze, her voice—to exude provocation and desire. She knew it, and she took full advantage. Her performances became wildly popular throughout Europe.
summary: Описывает создание Мата Хари уникального стиля «священных танцев», сочетающего sensuality и мистицизм, ее откровения о том, что зрители ищут наготу, а не искусство, и как она осознанно использовала свою сексуальность и артистизм для завоевания аудитории.

title: Мифотворчество как инструмент самопрезентации
text:
Margaretha invented an entirely new identity, claiming she was born into a family of Indian Brahmins. She imagined that her mother had been a glorious temple dancer at Kanda Swany, who died at the age of fourteen, on the day of her birth. According to her tale, she had been raised by temple priests, who named her Mata Hari, meaning “eye of the dawn,” and she had learned the sacred rites of dance in the temple of Shiva.

Mata Hari allowed herself to invent, create, and dream in front of those who questioned her about her past. The emotional drive behind her fabricated story dictated the version of reality she presented, shaping it on the spot according to the circumstances. Her timeline was vague, events were told enigmatically with shifting characters, and she altered settings, names, and cities, concealing key facts. This elaborate narrative helped build the mysterious and exotic aura that made her famous, ethereal, and above all, desirable.

Her truth, much like in the world of pride, is relative—dictated by the emotional reality of the moment, or rather, the instant. The impulse to please is irresistible. Details and objective facts do not matter. It is a truth molded to fit the story, serving the artistic creation of the moment, enhancing a self-crafted, fabulous, and magnificent image. Sexual instinct grants pride the power of externalization, dramatization, and theatricality like no other subtype. Both conscious and unconscious emotions find the perfect stage to capture attention and applause.
summary: Описывает выдуманную биографию Мата Хари о браминском происхождении и храмовом танце, ее способность адаптировать легенду под ситуацию, а также объясняет, как у E2 (особенно сексуального субтипа) эмоциональная истина подменяет фактическую, служа созданию великолепного образа и привлечению внимания через драматизацию.

title: Успех и признание в Париже
text:
Her first public appearance arrived, along with her success. As she began performing in salons and theaters, newspapers and magazines commented on her art, and she received glowing reviews.

By the time she had become the Hindu dancer Mata Hari in Paris, La Presse wrote on March 18, 1905: “Mata Hari is an Apsara, sister to the nymphs, the undines, the Valkyries, and the naiads, created by Indra for the downfall of men and sages.”
summary: Описывает первое публичное появление Мата Хари в Париже и восторженные отзывы прессы, сравнивающей ее с мифологическими существами (Апсара, нимфы, валькирии), созданными для соблазна и разрушения мужчин и мудрецов, что подтверждает ее образ как воплощения опасной sensuality.

title: Описание выступлений и имиджа Мата Хари
text:
Parisian Life described her as “the Indian dancer, voluptuous and tragic, who dances naked in the latest salons. She wears the costume of the bayadère [female Javanese court dancer], as much simplified as possible, and toward the end, she simplifies it even a little more.”

Her success was rooted in her ability to channel her emotions into an unparalleled performance. Mata Hari maximized her histrionic talents in both her art and her dance. Every gesture and movement of her body became a sensual expression that not only hinted but actively provoked a passionate response from her male audience. She became an icon of feline femininity, wildly erotic and mysterious, through seduction and secrecy. To avoid appearing as just another common courtesan, she crafted an improvised art form and invented a sacred origin for herself, elevating her persona to that of a goddess.
summary: Описывает сценические выступления Мата Хари, её эротический имидж и способ создания мистической личности через танец и самопрезентацию как божество.

title: Романтические отношения и финансовая зависимость от богатых любовников
text:
Her romantic life was filled with lovers—men of immense wealth and power: sovereigns, ministers, ambassadors, bankers, officers, police chiefs…

The Belle Époque—golden era of art, science, and culture in France that began in about 1890 and lasted until the beginning of the First World War—was an era of lavish spending and open luxury; successful men had beautiful mistresses who were paraded openly and received in society, sometimes even holding intellectual salons.

In Vienna, one of her lovers, Alfred Kiepert, gave her 300,000 marks upon their separation due to his family obligations—the equivalent of over a million euros today. She, who adored luxury and stayed in top-tier hotels without concern for cost, soon found a new wealthy lover: a well-off, handsome stockbroker named Xavier Rousseau. He even rented a countryside château in Esvres, where Mata Hari lived for an extended period. Rousseau, who visited her every weekend, provided her with four magnificent riding horses, a carriage, luxurious furniture, and an entourage of servants—including her loyal maid, a second housekeeper, a stableman, a coachman, a cook, and a gardener. Neither Rousseau’s wife nor his mother could persuade him to leave Mata Hari—until he declared bankruptcy, and his wife blamed Mata Hari for his financial ruin.

Her love was exchanged for great wealth. What did the irresistible lover demand from men? Everything. Possession gained meaning when one understood Mata Hari’s ability to extract from men their companionship, money, and favors.

And what did Mata Hari offer them in return? A blend of wild passion, feminine tenderness, and entertainment. That intoxicating perfume of freedom and independence, combined with her seductive prowess, bent the powerful men of her era to her will, turning them into puppets at her command.
summary: Детализирует отношения Мата Хари с богатыми любовниками, обмен её чувств на материальные блага и её способ манипулировать мужчинами через сексуальную притягательность и иллюзию свободы.

title: Попытки вербовки в разведку и сотрудничество с немцами
text:
By 1914, the Belle Époque was coming to an end. War had been declared. Foreigners were treated like outcasts, and she was arrested several times. The Germans had confiscated her bank accounts and belongings at the start of the war while she was living in Berlin. She never forgave them for this, and it fueled a deep sense of vengeance within her.

She moved to The Hague, supported by yet another lover, Colonel Van der Capellen. But wartime Holland was dull, gray, and devoid of glamour. Mata Hari longed for excitement.

While she was the official mistress of Dutch army Colonel Van der Capellen, she was also involved with Belgian Commander Marquis de Beaufort and Russian Captain Maslov, who introduced her as his fiancée—an illusion she eagerly played along with. This triple romance didn’t stop her from indulging in fleeting affairs with a Montenegrin officer, an Italian, two Irishmen, three or four Englishmen, and five French officers.

Far from being ashamed, she took pride in it:

I love officers. I have loved them all my life. I would rather be the mistress of a poor officer than a rich banker. My greatest pleasure is to go to bed with them without thinking of money, and then, I like to make comparisons among the different nationalities.

It seemed she had a fixation on uniforms. In her biography, she recalled being mesmerized by a painting of her father dressed in a military uniform, mounted on horseback.

In the autumn of 1915, Karl Kroemer, a German honorary consul who recruited spies across Europe, visited her. He tried to persuade her to join his organization, offering 20,000 francs—a considerable sum. But she scoffed at the amount and demanded more. Kroemer explained that it was just a trial period and that she could earn more in the future. He also instructed her to write in invisible ink and provided her with three bottles.

Later, she would express that she was bored, lacking entertainment, and that her lover, Colonel Van der Capellan, visited her rarely. As we mentioned before, she was also resentful toward the Germans, who had unjustly confiscated her money and her fur coats in Berlin.

To persuade her to join their espionage network, the Germans used naïve flattery, saying things like: “You, who are the only one capable of understanding...,” “You, who desire peace...,” “You, who have the greatest influence...,” “You, who could prevent so much misfortune...”

Here, we see how a master seductress falls into her own trap, seduced by flattery and manipulative appeals to her heart and her desire for peace. They inflated her ego, and, feeling worthy of all the praise, she fell into the web of espionage like one of those vain little birds in fables.
summary: Описывает начало Первой мировой войны, финансовые потери Мата Хари, её множественные романные связи и вербовку немецкой разведкой через лесть и манипуляции её желанием почувствовать себя важной и влиятельной.

title: Mata Hari's betrayal of German espionage attempt
text:
She accepted the money but never intended to work for Germany. She went to the canals and poured out the contents of the three bottles of invisible ink, along with the bottles themselves. She felt neither guilty nor obligated to do anything, despite having received 20,000 francs. All her life, she had accepted money from different men simply because she needed it and they had it; she always believed she deserved it. So why would this time be any different?

This was the tantrum of a spoiled child, used to getting her way—lying in a childish manner to a German consul who ran a spy agency.
summary: This chunk describes Mata Hari's rejection of German espionage efforts after accepting payment, highlighting her pattern of taking money without obligation and her childish deception of the German consul, reflecting a sense of entitlement and manipulative behavior.

title: Mata Hari's love for Vadime and failed espionage with France
text:
In 1916, Mata Hari fell deeply in love with a Russian officer eighteen years her junior. He was twenty-one; she was thirty-nine. She called Vladimir de Massloff "Vadime," and he called her "Marina." He was perhaps the only man she truly gave herself to, even sending him money when he was wounded on the battlefield.

During the war, Mata Hari had lovers among officers and politicians from both sides. She could cross borders with a certain degree of freedom thanks to her contacts and influence—one of the reasons she was under investigation.

The French also sought to recruit her as a spy. Once again, Mata Hari accepted—this time demanding one million francs in exchange for seducing and extracting valuable information. With this extravagant sum, she hoped to retire with Vadime. Here, love became her motivation once more—this time, the fantasy of finally surrendering to the love of her life.

The investigating judge, Pierre Bouchardon, who sentenced her for espionage, never believed that Mata Hari was truly in love with Vadime or anyone else, except herself and her sensual pleasures.
summary: This section covers Mata Hari's genuine romantic relationship with Vadime, her continued affairs during the war, her failed attempt to spy for France for a large sum to secure a future with him, and the investigator's skepticism about her capacity for authentic love, viewing her as self-absorbed and pleasure-driven.

title: Mata Hari's imprisonment, isolation, and final moments
text:
Mata Hari, who had never been faithful—to men or to the truth—who had always invented stories that suited her, was finally caught in a web of interests, a conspiracy that sealed her fate.

During interrogations, the lack of evidence became apparent, as did Mata Hari’s disinterest in the events of the war. Accused of espionage, the elegant woman who had once seduced all of Europe spent eight months in the filthy, rat-infested cells of Saint-Lazare prison, alongside prostitutes and petty criminals. Almost completely isolated, she was forced to face one of her greatest fears, one she had managed to avoid all her life: loneliness.

Under extreme circumstances, she teetered on the edge of madness, descending into a cold, painful hell that stripped her of her pride. She begged for any improvement in her conditions—no longer demanding, but pleading. She reached out for help from the lovers and contacts who had once adored her, but few spoke in her defense; given the political climate in France, defending a spy was too risky. At last, she came face to face with abandonment, the very thing she had spent her life running from.

Mata Hari’s ultimate paradox was that the queen of love, for once in her life, had found love—and barely got to enjoy it. The letters she exchanged with Vadime ("possibly the only love of my life") were intercepted and never reached him.

She had lived at the extremes of manipulation and boundless ambition until she finally surrendered her pride and understood the deeper meaning of the word "love"—a word she had played with so often.

Then came the dawn of October 15, 1917. She prepared to die as she had lived—with elegance and courage. She refused the blindfold offered by an officer and declined to be tied to the post. She waved to the two tearful nuns who had cared for her in her final months, blew a kiss to the priest—an irrepressible playful gesture—and another to her lawyer.

She died as Mata Hari—the woman who, through seduction, had everything and lost it all.

In the year 2000, the Museum of Anatomy in Paris announced that Mata Hari’s head, which had been part of its collection since her death in 1917, had been stolen—presumably by an admirer. The passion lives on.
summary: This chunk details Mata Hari's arrest, imprisonment in harsh conditions, her psychological torment from isolation and abandonment, the tragic interception of her letters to Vadime, her belated understanding of love, and her dignified execution, followed by the posthumous notoriety of her stolen head as a symbol of enduring fascination.

title: Introduction to Isadora Duncan and the multiplicity of self-perception
text:
***

Isadora Duncan

by Erika Marchetti

How can we write the truth about ourselves? Do we even know it? There is the vision our friends have of us; the vision we have of ourselves; and the vision our lover has of us. Also the vision our enemies have of us. And all these visions are different. [...] It seems to me there was not one, but hundreds—and my soul soaring aloft, not really affected by any of them.

Isadora Duncan is remembered in history as a dancer who made a significant contribution to the birth of modern dance. A visionary, she rebelled against the social norms of her time, subverting rigid conventions both in art and in her private life. She dedicated her entire existence to fighting for her "art" in the name of love and freedom. She provoked either harsh criticism or absolute devotion. Some called her the Divine Isadora, a bold, captivating, and visionary woman; others condemned her for her nonconformity. She herself cultivated her mythical image: enamored with an exalted self-image, she never missed an opportunity to adopt provocative and exuberant attitudes, presenting herself as unique and incomparable.
summary: This section introduces Isadora Duncan through a reflective preface on the fragmented nature of identity and self-perception, then outlines her legacy as a revolutionary modern dancer who defied social norms, embraced artistic freedom, and cultivated a powerful, mythic self-image through boldness and nonconformity.

title: Isadora Duncan's unconventional childhood and early independence
text:
Childhood

Dora Angela Duncan, known artistically as Isadora Duncan, was born on May 27, 1877, in San Francisco. During her difficult gestation, her mother, in the midst of a deep spiritual crisis, was said to take no food except iced oysters and iced champagne. While pregnant, she often repeated, "This child that will be born will surely not be normal." After the birth, commenting on Isadora’s vitality, she would say, "You see, I was quite right; the child is a maniac!" Isadora later reflected on how her mother’s distress had shaped her destiny, claiming that she began dancing while still in the womb.

Her mother was a pianist who gave private lessons, spending long hours away from home, both during the day and at night. As a result, after school, Isadora and her siblings could wander for hours. Discipline did not exist for them, not even in their mother’s presence. Immersed in her music, she was largely oblivious to the world around her. Constantly struggling financially, the family moved countless times, unable to pay rent. Yet poverty did not trouble Isadora. On the contrary, when there was no food at home, she saw it as an opportunity to showcase her charm and resourcefulness, taking on the role of a miniature mother:

Of all the family I was the most courageous, and, when there was absolutely nothing to eat in the house, I was the volunteer who went to the butcher and through my wiles induced him to give me mutton chops without payment. I was the one sent to the baker to entice him to continue credit. I took a real adventurous pleasure in these excursions, especially when I was successful, as I generally was.

Her parents divorced when she was three. Her mother, heartbroken, decided that all sentimentality was nonsense: "There is no Santa Claus and there is no God, only your own spirit to help you," she would tell young Isadora.

Her first memory of her father was at the age of seven. Until then, she had imagined him as a demon in a picture book, with horns and a tail—a mysterious figure no one wanted to talk about, the man who had "ruined her mother’s life." In realit
summary: This chunk describes Isadora Duncan's prenatal and early childhood environment, marked by her mother's spiritual crisis and financial instability, which fostered Isadora's early independence, boldness, and resourcefulness—such as securing food through charm—while shaping her perception of her father as a demonic figure due to maternal narratives, contributing to her later rebellious and mythic self-formation.

title: Детство Изадоры: самостоятельность и семейные трудности
text:
Her mother was a pianist who gave private lessons, spending long hours away from home, both during the day and at night. As a result, after school, Isadora and her siblings could wander for hours. Discipline did not exist for them, not even in their mother’s presence. Immersed in her music, she was largely oblivious to the world around her. Constantly struggling financially, the family moved countless times, unable to pay rent. Yet poverty did not trouble Isadora. On the contrary, when there was no food at home, she saw it as an opportunity to showcase her charm and resourcefulness, taking on the role of a miniature mother:

Of all the family I was the most courageous, and, when there was absolutely nothing to eat in the house, I was the volunteer who went to the butcher and through my wiles induced him to give me mutton chops without payment. I was the one sent to the baker to entice him to continue credit. I took a real adventurous pleasure in these excursions, especially when I was successful, as I generally was.

Her parents divorced when she was three. Her mother, heartbroken, decided that all sentimentality was nonsense: “There is no Santa Claus and there is no God, only your own spirit to help you,” she would tell young Isadora.

Her first memory of her father was at the age of seven. Until then, she had imagined him as a demon in a picture book, with horns and a tail—a mysterious figure no one wanted to talk about, the man who had “ruined her mother’s life.” In reality, he was an artist and poet who had built and lost fortunes multiple times. One day, he appeared at their doorstep. Unlike the rest of the family, Isadora welcomed him with excitement. She was thrilled to finally have, like other children, a father—especially one who paid attention to her: “He is a perfectly charming man, and he is coming tomorrow to give me more ice-cream.”

That “tomorrow” arrived years later when her father regained financial stability, allowing his ex-wife and children to live with fewer hardships. However, his return—and their newfound security—was short-lived. He soon abandoned them again, moving to Los Angeles with his new family. This fleeting paternal presence left Isadora with a lifelong aversion to marriage. Rather than blaming her father, she resented the narrow-mindedness of a society that forced women into marriage to maintain their rights and honor. Her rejection of marriage was not just about her desire for an unrestricted life where anything was possible, but above all, it was about avoiding the humiliation of potential abandonment.
summary: Описывается детство Изадоры Дункан: финансовая нестабильность семьи, отсутствие дисциплины, ранняя самостоятельность в обеспечении себя, развод родителей, сложные отношения с отцом и формирование aversion к браку из-за страха abbandона.

title: Ранние предпринимательские попытки и стремление к свободе
text:
She was a confident and enterprising child. At just six years old, she “opened” her first dance school, gathering a dozen neighborhood children to whom she taught arm movements. By ten, pretending to be sixteen, she promoted her method—what she called the “new system” of dancing—to San Francisco’s wealthiest families, with the help of her sister and her mother’s musical accompaniment. In reality, as she later admitted: “In reality there was no system. I followed my fantasy and improvised, teaching any pretty thing that came into my head.” Her popularity grew, and the venture became quite profitable. Alongside her siblings, she performed in theatrical productions with moderate success. But that wasn’t enough for her. The desire that would define her entire life had already begun to take root—she longed to escape in search of a bigger world.

In search of pleasure

I was never able to understand, then or later on, why, if one wanted to do a thing, one should not do it. For I have never waited to do as I wished. This has frequently brought me to disaster and calamity, but at least I have had the satisfaction of getting my own way.

Chicago, New York, London, Paris, Budapest, Florence, Moscow... Her life was an endless series of moves and new beginnings. With incredible ease, she reinvented herself over and over again. Her extraordinary energy allowed her to navigate between excuses and impulsive initiatives: she led a carefree life, disregarding practical matters, completely focused on her desires. One day, she lived in extravagant luxury; the next, she was in ruins. At first, she felt physical repulsion for the pianist accompanying her, yet in an instant—bored of domestic life—she discovered in him an irresistible genius and surrendered to his arms.

Her obsessive pursuit of pleasure—especially her escape from frustration when she was not receiving the attention she craved or when stimulation ran out—kept her from settling anywhere or maintaining stable relationships. In a perpetual state of excitement, she rushed impatiently toward life: “I used to run on dirt, skip on pavement, and walk on wood to make the way seem shorter. I had all sorts of systems for that.”

Men, students, artists, works of art—all those who admired her (succumbing to the charm of her seduction), as well as the cities she lived in, were to her marvelous and unforgettable.

Ah, Budapest! It was the month of April. It was the springtime of the year... Ah, gypsy music! This was the first call to the awakening of my youthful senses. With such music what wonder that my budding emotions were beginning to flower. Is there any music like this—the gypsy music springing from the soil of Hungary? [...]

We alighted from the train at Florence and spent several weeks in ecstatic wanderings through the galleries, gardens, olive-orchards. At that time it was Botticelli who attracted my youthful imagination. I sat for days before the “Primavera.”
summary: Описывается ранняя предпринимательская деятельность Изадоры в танце, её импульсивное стремление к удовольствию и новизне, постоянные переезды, романтические увлечения и глубокие эмоциональные отклики на искусство и музыку, особенно в Будапеште и Флоренции.

title: Impulsivity and the illusion of safety
text: But it was, above all, the lack of stimulation and attention, as we said, that drove her to reshape reality with her imagination and give free rein to impulsivity and excess. Her life was a grand adventure, with the illusion of searching for a safe harbor that, deep down, she never truly wanted to find. “Pim brought me pleasure—just pure delightful pleasure—and at a moment when I most needed it, for without his ministrations I might have sunk into a hopeless neurasthenic. [...] I forgot my chagrin, and lived in the moment and was careless and happy.”
summary: Describes how the subject's need for stimulation led to impulsive behavior and a cycle of seeking pleasure without true desire for stability, using a personal anecdote about Pim to illustrate temporary relief from distress.

title: Isadora’s dance philosophy and practice
text:
Dance

Isadora discovered the expressive power of her body at a very young age. As a child, she would stand on the table and entertain family and friends by dancing to every melody she heard. Tumbling around her mother, who was lost in her music, was merely a way to capture her attention. And it was precisely by performing her dances that she continued, throughout her life, to draw the gaze of others.

She appeared on stage barefoot, dressed in a simple white tunic that revealed the contours of her body. Without ballet shoes or tutus, she decorated the backdrop with drapes, eliminating any element that might distract the audience’s attention from her presence. For Isadora, it was enough to give free rein to her emotions, practicing a dance that was spontaneous and self-expressive. She sought to exalt the female body through natural movement, rejecting the artificial positions of academic ballet. “With my ideals it was impossible for me to have anything to do with the ballet, whose every movement shocked my sense of beauty, and whose expression seemed to me mechanical and vulgar.”

Her goal was to elevate dance to the same status as the other arts: a means through which the artist expresses their spirit and creativity, and which has the power to shape future generations of women—free in their spirit, their movements, and their sexuality. “Man must speak, then sing, then dance. But the speaking is the brain, the thinking man. The singing is the emotion. The dancing is the Dionysian ecstasy which carries away all.”

She founded schools in Germany, England, and the Soviet Union, not without opposition. She felt it was her duty to offer the world her revolutionary ideas, believing them to be essential to society’s transformation: “At the end of each performance, I made an appeal to the public for help to find some way of giving to others, from my own life, the discovery I had made, and which might liberate and illumine the lives of thousands.”
summary: Details Isadora Duncan’s early life, her revolutionary approach to dance as a natural and expressive art form, her rejection of ballet, and her efforts to establish dance schools abroad as a means of social transformation.

title: Sacrifice and struggle in Soviet Russia
text: She always longed to feel indispensable to someone and was willing to make any sacrifice to satisfy those who flattered her by seeking her help. In 1921, the Soviet government sent her a telegram inviting her to open a school: “The Russian Government alone can understand you. Come to us; we will make your school.” In reality, they only provided a building; they seized the furniture and cut off the hot water supply. These were hard times, and misery was widespread. Isadora was surrounded by desperate parents pleading with her to take in their little ones, hoping at least they would have shelter and a warm meal. She was able to offer refuge to only fifty children. It pained her to recognize her own limits, to know she could not save them all, and she exhausted herself caring for those unfortunate souls.
summary: Recounts Isadora Duncan’s difficult experience in the Soviet Union, where despite official invitations, she faced material hardships and emotional strain while trying to care for refugee children beyond her capacity.

title: Love as validation and self-erasure
text:
Love

The intense need to feel special and desirable found its ultimate satisfaction in the experience of love. To conquer, to seduce, to give herself fully to another without limits—this was the only way she knew to quell her sense of personal insignificance. Sweeping passions, tempestuous affairs, fateful encounters—Isadora devoted herself entirely to relationships, with no half-measures. She had countless lovers for whom she was willing to do anything: leave suddenly, embark on romantic escapades with men she barely knew, make sacrifices, even endure humiliation. Beneath her appearance as an independent, exuberant, and confident woman lay a deep desperation, a dependence on validation from her beloved: “To live with him was to renounce my Art, my personality, nay, perhaps my life, my reason itself. But to live without him was to be in a continual state of depression, and tortured by jealousy.”

Theatrical designer Gordon Craig, the father of her daughter, saw in Isadora the living embodiment of his dreams. He would repeatedly tell her, “You belong to my scenery.” And she, flattered by such adoration, endured his sudden mood swings, aggression, and fits of jealousy: “Why do you want to go on the stage and wave your arms about? Why don’t you stay at home and sharpen my lead pencils?”

It was a stormy, symbiotic passion, often ending in dramatic arguments and scenes of jealousy. “He would go out, slamming the door. Only the noise of the slammed door would awaken me to the terrible catastrophe. I would await his return and, when he didn’t return, spend the night in stormy and tragic weeping.”

Her encounter with Paris Singer, heir to the sewing machine empire and father of her first son, came at a time when she had decided to pursue a relationship with a millionaire who could help her establish her school. “I realised that this was my millionaire, for whom I had sent my brain-waves seeking.”

Singer, too, wanted her entirely for himself. He had fallen for the bold, fearless woman but could not tolerate her freedom. He used various tactics to tie her down, showering her with wealth and allowing her to open a school. Yet his suffocating presence became unbearable for Isadora, who soon surrendered to a new love that gave her the courage to escape.
summary: Explores Isadora Duncan’s pattern of intense, dependent relationships where love served as a source of validation and escape from inner emptiness, illustrated through her tumultuous bonds with Gordon Craig and Paris Singer.

title: Последняя великая любовь и сердце разбито
text:
Her last great love was the Russian poet Sergei Yesenin, twenty years her junior. He was the only man she ever married, forced by Soviet law. She barely knew a handful of Russian words, and he spoke no other language, yet their passion was overwhelming: intertwined bodies dashing across the world amid feasts, drugs, alcohol, and furious fights. But after fifteen months of marriage, when the passion had burned out, they had nothing left to say to each other.

Heartbreak could plunge her into states of emotional and physical distress. She wouldn’t eat, couldn’t sleep, suffered nervous breakdowns that kept her from dancing. The only remedy was to quickly find a new love to devote herself to, hoping it would be reciprocated.

I could not work, I could not dance. I did not care at all whether the public liked it or not. I realised that this state of things must cease. [...] And, as everything that we wish for very much comes, the remedy came. He entered one afternoon: fair, debonair, young, blond, perfectly dressed.
summary: This chunk describes Isadora Duncan's intense but short-lived marriage to Sergei Yesenin, the emotional devastation she experienced after their separation, and her pattern of seeking new love to alleviate heartbreak and emotional distress.

title: Материнство и потеря детей
text:
Children

Isadora, a firm believer in free love and voluntary motherhood outside of marriage, had three children with three different men: Gordon Craig, Paris Singer, and a young Italian artist. She lost all three prematurely: the eldest two in a tragic car accident while under the care of their nanny, and the third, whom she had hoped would ease the pain of the first loss, died of natural causes just hours after birth.

Pregnancy was difficult for her. The gestation period made her feel “ill” and hindered her ambitions, her art, and her life. She no longer recognized her changing body, felt a different energy, and was overcome with the urge to isolate herself from the public eye.

I had a great longing to be alone, and to retire far from the gaze of human beings. [...] I struggled with an overwhelming desire to escape, escape. Where? Perhaps even into the midst of the sullen waves. [...] More and more my lovely body bulged under my astonished gaze [...] Where [was] my ambition? My fame? Often, in spite of myself, I felt very miserable and defeated.

Motherhood, however, was a radically different experience. The birth of her children filled Isadora with overwhelming energy and complete fulfillment. It restored all the confidence and strength she felt she had lost during pregnancy, compensating for her sacrifices and suffering. She felt invincible again.

Oh, women, what is the good of us learning to become lawyers, painters, or sculptors, when this miracle exists? Now I knew this tremendous love, surpassing the love of a man. [...] Life, life, life! Give me life! Oh, where was my Art? My Art or any Art? What did I care for Art? I felt I was a God, superior to any artist.

She was a loving mother, deeply attached to her children. However, she often left them in the care of their aunt and nanny to travel with new lovers or perform her shows.

The loss of all three children left an indelible mark on her life. The searing pain of their deaths, the deep sense of abandonment, created a wound she could never heal. Strikingly, in her autobiography, she repeatedly references clairvoyant episodes, premonitory dreams, and visions linking the birth of her children to their eventual deaths, as if searching for a reason that would allow her to believe she had controlled even that tragic ending she had never chosen.
summary: This chunk explores Isadora Duncan's experience of motherhood, her complex emotional journey through pregnancy and childbirth, the profound joy she felt as a mother, and the lasting trauma caused by the loss of all three children, including her spiritual reflections on their deaths.

title: Смерть и наследие
text:
Death

On September 14, 1927, Isadora Duncan died in Nice in a bizarre accident: her long silk scarf became entangled in the wheel of the Bugatti she was riding in, breaking her neck. She had been happy that evening, escaping a party in the company of her latest conquest—a young Parisian in his twenties.

Her best friend, Mary Desti, claimed that Isadora’s final words were, “Farewell my friends. I go to glory.” Years later, however, she retracted this version. According to the new account, Isadora’s actual last words were: “I am off to love!” (“Je vais à l’amour!”)

It was a spectacular death, dramatically true to her story. For it was in the pursuit of love—in the relentless quest to satisfy that insatiable need—that Isadora lived without pause, always searching for someone or something to fulfill her dreams and, in doing so, to save herself from her own sorrow.

Literary and cinematic examples

A literary example

Nana

From the novel of the same name by Émile Zola

by Alba Chartroux

Nana serves as a clear literary example of character study, particularly in how the author vividly portrays the defining traits of the sexual subtype of Enneatype 2, especially in their most extreme expressions.

Born in the impoverished outskirts of Paris during the imperial reign of Napoleon III, Nana is the daughter of a laborer who, after a workplace accident, drowns his sorrows in alcohol, and a laundress who, in a desperate attempt to escape poverty, turns to prostitution. As a young teenager, the beautiful Nana runs away from her family, drawn to the dazzling excitement of the social scene. With her irresistible beauty fueling an insatiable hunger for luxury and indulgence, she swiftly embarks on a chaotic rise through society—first in the demi-monde of dandies, and later in the grand-monde of Parisian finance and aristocracy.

The novel is steeped in destruction. Nana thrives in a disintegrating social landscape, one that provides fertile ground for her schemes as a femme fatale. Through her seductive promises of love and sensual allure (predatory in nature and ultimately false, revoked just when they seem to offer fulfillment) she ignites uncontrollable passions. These passions spiral beyond all limits, inevitably transforming Eros into Thanatos. Though she appears as a goddess of love, Nana is incapable of truly loving, for to her, “love was stupid, it got you nowhere.
summary: This chunk covers Isadora Duncan's dramatic death, the conflicting accounts of her final words, and how her life embodied a relentless pursuit of love. It then introduces Nana from Émile Zola's novel as a literary example of the sexual subtype of Enneatype 2, highlighting her destructive, seductive nature and inability to truly love despite her allure.

title: Nana's sexual compulsion and self-destructive path
text:
This is the story of a mesmerizing seductress—angelic and demonic in equal measure—who devours men and fortunes, consumed by an insatiable and compulsive sexuality that is anything but truly free. The novel opens in a decadent operetta theater, a setting that is both real and symbolic. Through this obsession, Nana ultimately self-destructs.

The atmosphere of the novel is not one of simple romantic longing or pleasure that finds satisfaction in its fulfillment. Instead, it is one of sexual seduction as a means of manipulation—an insatiable thirst that grows ever more destructive and contagious. This reaches its peak at the novel’s end, as Nana dies of smallpox while the ominous cries of war fill the streets of France, foreshadowing the collapse of society itself.
summary: This chunk describes Nana as a sexually compulsive and manipulative figure whose insatiable desires lead to her self-destruction and mirror societal decay, emphasizing the destructive nature of her sexuality as a tool of control rather than fulfillment.

title: Nana's early rise and theatrical debut
text:
The novel begins with Nana’s first steps in her ascent through society. At just eighteen, she is cast in the lead role of The Blonde Venus at the Théâtre des Variétés by a theater manager who had first encountered her in a brothel. He does not choose her for her artistic talent, but for the raw sensuality she exudes, her mesmerizing allure. Nana sings and acts terribly, but “this strapping young wench who kept slapping her thighs and cackling like a hen, exuded an exuberant, overpowering sex-appeal that intoxicated the audience. […] all she needed to do was to turn round and laugh and people would cheer.”

Her public debut coincides with a period in which she is being “kept” by two different men who take turns in her bed, alongside various occasional lovers. She has a two-year-old son, initially left with a nurse and later with an aunt. Delicate and silent, he is a mere shadow in contrast to his mother’s overwhelming presence. Yet he is the only being for whom Nana feels something akin to tenderness, a sentiment that her own harrowing childhood has otherwise stripped from her.

Nana enjoys a life of frivolous luxury, aided by her loyal maid Zoe, who arranges her romantic encounters and shields her from creditors. Yet despite her growing wealth, debts constantly pile up, as she squanders every fortune laid at her feet. She takes and wastes it all in a breath, mocking those who provide for her, for “she was delighted to be keeping these men waiting.”
summary: This chunk details Nana's early rise through society via her sensuality rather than talent, her theatrical debut, her relationships with multiple lovers, her neglect of her son, and her extravagant yet self-sabotaging lifestyle fueled by a desire to maintain power over those who support her.

title: The dinner party as revelation of Nana's core nature
text:
One particularly significant scene is a lavish dinner party Nana hosts after a night at the theater, with the aim of ensnaring the wealthy Count Muffat. This scene is crucial as it lays bare the essence of her character and the environment that enables her.

As the dinner stretches into the early morning, waves of guests arrive, drawn by Nana’s libertine reputation. As the night wears on, filled with indulgent feasting and endless wine, the behavior of those present grows increasingly depraved. Here, the novel’s central theme emerges: raw, unscrupulous sensuality—incapable of transforming into love—is isolated from the rest of life and worshipped as pure lust. In a society rife with hypocritical puritanism, Nana becomes an idol, the living embodiment of a fractured condition to which her victims willingly sacrifice themselves.

Her relationship with the austere Count Muffat, chamberlain to the Emperor and Empress and a key figure of the Parisian aristocracy, serves as the ultimate example of this fatal form of submission. His piety—proud in its social standing yet laced with fear and guilt—offers no protection from the destruction Nana represents.
summary: This chunk analyzes the dinner party scene as a pivotal moment revealing Nana's character: her sensuality is portrayed as a destructive, loveless force that corrupts others, with her relationship with Count Muffat exemplifying how even the pious are unable to resist her manipulative allure.

title: Psychological defenses and emotional theatricality in E2s
text:
Beneath the ostentatious debauchery, which is merely a tragic parody of true freedom, sexual E2s hide repression, suppressing powerful emotions. To avoid the sting of envy, they glorify themselves as the axis mundi. To stave off fear and pain, they mock them. To evade guilt, they reject commitments and responsibility. To keep from being consumed by true anger, they become hypersensitive. To numb the thirst for love, they devour and dissipate. And to escape the powerlessness that comes from acknowledging authentic needs and desires, they perform an elaborate illusion of emotional self-sufficiency. The ultimate result is theatricality—emotions and feelings are not truly experienced but merely dramatized, just enough to be performed on the social stage, as if by a second-rate actor.

Returning to Zola’s novel, the dinner party scene encapsulates this personality type, both in their personal traits and in the collective setting that allows them to prosper.
summary: This chunk explains the psychological mechanisms behind the sexual Enneatype 2, detailing how they use repression, grandiosity, mockery, avoidance of responsibility, hypersensitivity, indulgence, and emotional performance to defend against inner pain, resulting in a theatrical presentation of self rather than authentic emotional experience.

title: Nana's mood swings and intolerance of neglect or responsibility
text:
During the dinner—officially celebrating her theatrical and social debut as the Blonde Venus—Nana exhibits a seemingly minor yet recurring personality trait that is worth noting: the sudden volatility of her mood. From cheerfulness, spontaneity, and flattery, she abruptly shifts to anger, indignation, or even tears. These dramatic mood swings seem to arise in response to two particular triggers: first, when she loses the center of attention; second, when she is confronted with responsibility. This personality type cannot tolerate either. One leads to an unbearable sense of annihilation, the other to a crushing feeling of inadequacy—both emotionally intolerable. Yet, as soon as a comforting word is offered or a reproach withdrawn, her good mood miraculously recovers, restored with a self-satisfied, magnanimous flourish.

These paragraphs vividly illustrate her arrogant haughtiness:

Then, as people were again starting to forget Nana, Vandeuvres caught sight of Daguenet poking his head through a doorway and making signs to him. Vandeuvres went in and saw Nana, tense and pale, sitting on her bed. Daguenet and Georges were standing watching her in consternation.

“What on earth’s the matter?” he enquired in surprise. She made no reply, and continued to stare in the other direction. He repeated his question.

“The matter is that I won’t have people making a fool of me!” she cried in the end.
summary: This chunk highlights Nana's extreme mood volatility triggered by loss of attention or confrontation with responsibility, revealing her deep fear of insignificance and inadequacy, and her rapid emotional recovery when ego is soothed, illustrating the fragile, performance-based nature of her self-worth.

title: Гнев и разочарование Наны
text: And she started to pour out everything that came to her lips. Oh, she wasn’t all that stupid, she could see all right. All through the meal, they’d been saying horrible things to show how much they despised her. A bunch of dirty bitches who weren’t fit to clean her shoes! It’d be a long time before she took all that trouble again, just so people could pull her to pieces afterwards! She didn’t know why she didn’t kick the whole bloody lot out on their arses! She was choking with anger and her voice was breaking into sobs.
summary: Nana expresses intense anger and hurt after overhearing insults during dinner, revealing her sensitivity to rejection and tendency toward emotional outbursts when feeling disrespected or abandoned.

title: Театральность как метафора лицемерия
text: One of the most remarkable aspects of the first part of the novel is how the author uses the theatrical setting as a metaphorical counterpoint to the inauthenticity and egotistical illusions of the characters who take the stage. In the incisive introduction of Count Muffat, for instance, Zola portrays his terror at being overwhelmed by Nana’s sensual magnetism, his inability to resist her. The novel conveys his growing turmoil through his unsteady steps onstage, his anxiety at the open trapdoors leading to the dark underbelly of the theater, the stifling heat in the corridors leading to the dressing rooms, the heavy air thick with perfume and breath, the carnal temptation in the sounds of women rinsing their bodies, the laughter and idle chatter. It is the vertigo of his once-pious self-restraint, the whirlwind of ruin that will consume him. Yet the count will be just one of Nana’s many victims, marked for downfall by his wealth and his high status in Parisian aristocracy.
summary: The theatrical setting reflects the characters' inauthenticity, illustrated by Count Muffat’s downfall due to Nana’s overwhelming sensual power, symbolizing the destructive allure of illusion and desire in a performative world.

title: Нана и Жорж: невинность и обман
text:
As a counterpoint to this, Nana has young Georges, a bourgeois teenager without wealth of his own, but full of youthful innocence and naive adoration for her. To Nana, Georges is a sweet plaything—she affectionately calls him Zizi—allowing her to slip into the role of an experienced, indulgent woman, protecting him from everything but herself, while basking in the illusion of virgin fantasies, feeling pure and sentimental, like a young girl in love for the first time.

In the boy’s arms Nana felt like a 15-year-old girl again. She was used to being with men, who disgusted her; but now love was rekindled by the caresses of a child. She would suddenly blush, shivers would run down her back; she felt a need to laugh and cry, an uneasy, new-born innocence and bursts of sensuality which left her ashamed. Never had she had such feelings before.

Nana plays with her Zizi in a tender, mutual game of childish murmurs that lasts only a breath, interspersed with other, far more lucrative encounters—such as with Count Muffat or the banker Steiner, who had gifted her a lavish country house.

What follows is a scene of seduction between Nana and Georges, in which she, manipulatively, assumes the role of the seduced.

Meanwhile Georges was depositing gentle little kisses on her neck which tickled and flustered her even more. Timidly, she pushed him away, like an over-affectionate child, insisting that he must go now. [...] A bird sang and then stopped. [...] As she listened to the robin and the boy snuggled up to her, Nana was thinking: yes, she’d seen this sort of thing happening in romances. In the old days, she’d have given her heart to have all this, the moon, robins, and a young fellow full of love. Heavens, wasn’t everything so nice, so good! She could have cried. Obviously she was born to live a sensible, respectable life. Georges was growing bolder and she was holding him off.

“No, leave me alone, I don’t want to, it’d be very wrong at your age… Look, I want to be just a mother to you, that’s all…”

She was blushing with embarrassment and modesty. [...] Never before had she felt bashful like this. Little by little, in spite of her embarrassment and reluctance, she was beginning to weaken. [...]

“Oh, it’s not right, it’s not right,” she faltered.

It was her final effort; surrounded by the beauty of the night, she fell into the boy’s arms; she felt like a girl losing her virginity.
summary: Nana’s relationship with Georges rekindles her fantasies of pure love and innocence, allowing her to regress emotionally and playfully manipulate his affection while maintaining control, despite her genuine emotional turmoil and modesty.

title: Самообожание и нарциссизм Наны
text:
Her relationship with young Georges fuels Nana’s fantasies of pure love, far removed from the violent misery of her childhood home, where she had lived surrounded by her father’s alcoholism and her mother’s prostitution.

This seduction scene is preceded by another, in which Nana dresses Georges in one of her own nightgowns, emasculating him. In truth, Nana holds a deep contempt for men, which she uses to justify humiliating them.

Even as she indulges in sentimental daydreams, she skillfully employs deception and lies to maintain a stable of wealthy lovers who can guarantee her life of luxury and excess—an obsessive, defensive pursuit of abundance that defines her.

Through fevered imagination, Nana theatrically shifts between different identities without ever integrating them, a trait emblematic of this character: the love-struck adolescent intoxicated by pure romance, the femme fatale who devours men and fortunes, the impulsive mother, the devoted lover, the cynical schemer, the loyal friend, and so on. Yet despite the illusion of giving love, her desires lack true pleasure. They have nothing to do with love but are instead driven by the triumph of her narcissistic pride.

Nana is not in love with anyone—except herself.

Nana enjoyed undressing in front of her wardrobe so that she could see her whole body in the mirror. She took off everything, even her chemise, and stood there naked, lost in contemplation of herself. She adored her own body, her satin-smooth skin, the flowing curves of her waist and she would stand there sunk in thought, completely absorbed in her self-adoration.

Her love affairs last only as long as it takes to financially drain and psychologically destroy each man who falls for her charms. But the fire that drives Nana does not seem to stem from a hunger for material wealth—she squanders it carelessly—but rather from an obsession with asserting her superiority, proving her dominance over men and women alike, indulging in an unchecked narcissistic delirium.
summary: Nana’s behavior is driven by deep narcissism and self-adoration, using relationships to affirm her superiority rather than seeking genuine connection; her shifting identities and sensual self-focus reveal a personality rooted in illusion, control, and emotional self-absorption.

title: Nana's masochistic devotion to Fontan
text:
And the moment she encounters a man who, despite enjoying her favors, refuses to submit to her, she becomes a willing slave to his pleasure, intoxicated by equally narcissistic fantasies of an all-consuming, self-annihilating love. There must always be destruction—either of the other or of herself.

Chapter VIII opens with Nana in the role of the devoted lover. With the impulsive recklessness of an arrogant queen, she ruthlessly discards her two wealthiest lovers and suddenly rekindles “her old dream of becoming a florist,” swept up in an unforeseen and intense infatuation with Fontan, a comic actor at the Variétés. She hastily sells whatever she can, vanishes from her creditors and former lovers, and moves in with Fontan to cramped, modestly furnished living-quarters, basking in the glow of love—full of tender coquetry, affected simplicity, and false modesty.

However, Fontan soon reveals the crude violence that defines him. The arguments begin, followed by slaps, reconciliations, and an unchecked crescendo of brutality. But the abuse only fuels Nana’s increasingly passionate self-sacrifice. When Fontan, beyond humiliating her in every possible way, steals her last penny and still expects to find dinner ready every night, she prefers—rather than lose him—to secretly return to the streets.

And the more he [Fontan] ridiculed her, the more she gritted her teeth, taking a bitter enjoyment in her crazy, heroic infatuation which made her, in her eyes, a very noble woman, capable of great love. Ever since she’d been going with other men in order to provide for Fontan, she loved him all the more because of the disgust and hardships she suffered for his sake. He was her private vice which she couldn’t do without and for which she was prepared to pay the price; his thrashings added zest.
summary: This chunk describes Nana's intense, self-sacrificing relationship with Fontan, where she endures abuse and humiliation out of a narcissistic need to feel noble and indispensable, framing her devotion as a form of heroic love rooted in pride rather than genuine affection.

title: Nana's vengeful return to high society
text:
But one day, Nana sees Fontan with another woman—and she does not tolerate rivals. Her love vanishes in an instant, leaving no trace. She abandons Fontan and coldly calculates a cunning strategy to rekindle the passion of Count Muffat, whom she had once rejected, after insulting and humiliating him by revealing his wife’s adultery. She succeeds and returns to her life as a high-class courtesan, admired by women and desired by men.

So Nana became the toast of Paris, the queen of first-class tarts, battening on the stupidity and beastliness of males [...].

Her rise to fame was meteoric; and she immediately joined the ranks of the most expensive. Her photo was on display in every shop-window; her name featured in the newspapers. When she drove along the boulevards in her carriage, everyone turned to look and breathed her name like subjects greeting their monarch while she, in her loose dress with her tiny blonde curls tumbling down over her blue-rimmed eyes, would sprawl back giving a cheerful, friendly smile with her red, painted lips.

And miraculously, this big, sturdy girl, so awkward on the stage and so ludicrous when she tried to play the part of a respectable woman, became, off-stage, an effortless public charmer, looking as lithe as a snake in her skilfully low-cut dresses, exquisitely elegant, which offered, as though by accident, revealing glimpses of her body, as refined and supple as a pedigree cat. She represented the aristocracy of vice, magnificent and untamed, holding Paris to ransom under her all-powerful heel.
summary: After being spurned by Fontan, Nana vengefully returns to her former life as a high-class courtesan, regaining fame and power through manipulation and allure, using her sexuality and charm to dominate Parisian society while masking her inner emptiness with outward splendor.

title: The hollowness beneath Nana's luxury
text:
In exchange for a guarantee of boundless luxury, Count Muffat extracts from Nana a promise of fidelity—she must belong to him alone. A promise, of course, that is entirely false. She loves excess and pleasure far too much. She takes many lovers, playing the part of the outraged woman whenever anyone dares question her loyalty.

But in spite of being surrounded by her admirers and in spite of all her luxury, Nana was bored to death. She had men to fill every minute of her nights and money even tucked away with her brushes and combs in the drawers of her dressing table, but still she wasn’t satisfied. She felt a vacuum, a hole in her life which left her yawning.

Throughout the novel, Zola repeatedly highlights this feeling of emptiness that grips Nana—a fundamental void that material wealth can never fill. It reflects the emotional deprivation of her miserable childhood, a wound only deepened by her immersion in the even more sordid world of a high society corrupted by power and hypocrisy.
summary: Despite her wealth, luxury, and numerous lovers, Nana remains chronically bored and unfulfilled, driven by a deep emotional void rooted in childhood deprivation, which no external validation or material excess can heal.

title: Nana's destructive entanglements and sadomasochistic dynamics
text:
Restless and craving ever-stronger sensations, Nana adds to her affairs a stormy homosexual relationship with a friend from the brothels and streets. She subjugates the woman with lavish gifts, demanding, in return, infinite gratitude.

With her lovers, she invades their personal lives, drawing out their confessions with an indulgent, receptive air. Here emerges a typical trait of this personality type: involving themselves in others’ affairs with an attitude that seems impartial and benevolent but is, in reality, another way to feed their narcissistic sense of importance. Through these confidences, Nana grants herself the right to weave intrigues—arranging marriages, breaking up relationships, squandering fortunes, and corrupting prestigious positions—all in her insatiable urge to “possess everything in order to destroy everything.”

But the destructiveness of both Nana and the aristocratic society that fosters her—each a reflection of the other—begins to eclipse the glory. The novel’s later pages depict this escalating devastation. Among Nana’s lovers, some commit suicide, others end up in prison, many are ruined, and some destroy their families, all victims of the passions she stirs with the lofty indifference of her voracity.
summary: Nana escalates her pattern of manipulation by engaging in a homosexual relationship and exploiting others' confessions to fuel her narcissism, ultimately causing widespread ruin among her lovers as her need to control and destroy intensifies, mirroring the corruption of the society that enables her.

title: Nana’s relationship with Count Muffat and her psychological denial
text:
Yet the true target of Nana’s punitive rage against high society is Count Muffat. He is not only the greatest financier of her extravagant whims—he is more than an aristocrat; he is the Emperor’s chamberlain. Though she drains him dry, leaving both him and his family in utter ruin, Nana acts as if she is the one giving everything, receiving nothing in return but trouble and ingratitude. She subjects him to increasingly humiliating degradations, which, in Muffat, intertwine with his guilty conscience. His obsessive desire for Nana leads him into the depths of his own shadow—the dark counterpart to his prestigious, austere, and self-controlled image. Their relationship spirals ever downward, and on a sexual level, it devolves into sadomasochism (a disintegration of sexual E2 into E8, and Enneatype 1 into E4).

At a certain point, Nana realizes that everything around her is falling apart. But she immediately smothers this flicker of awareness, reinforcing her belief that she gives endlessly and receives only ingratitude, refusing to take any responsibility.

All the unhappiness surrounding her, the harm she’d caused, were drowning her in emotional self-pity; she was uttering faint moans, like a little girl.

“Oh, I feel dreadful, so dreadful! … Oh, it’s unbearable, I can’t breathe! It’s so hard to be misunderstood, to see everybody against you because they’re stronger than you … And yet you’ve done nothing wrong, you’ve got a clear conscience … No! No! It’s not right! [...] No, they can say what they damn well like! It’s not my fault! Am I unkind? I give away everything I’ve got, I wouldn’t hurt a fly. It’s them, it’s always them! … I didn’t ever want to be unkind to them. And they were forever sniffing round my skirts and now they’ve kicked the bucket or they’re begging or pretending to be desperate… [...] Look, I can tell you one thing now: Whenever I went with them, you know, well, I never enjoyed it, I got absolutely no pleasure out of it at all, it was just a chore, I tell you honestly… [...] Yes, they bored me stiff! But for them, my dear man, but for what they made me do, I’d be a nun praying to God, because I’ve always been religious… And if they lose their money or their lives, it’s their own fault, they can go to hell … It’s nothing to do with me!”
summary: This section analyzes Nana’s destructive relationship with Count Muffat, her psychological denial of responsibility, and her self-pitying monologue where she portrays herself as a victim despite her harmful actions. It references Enneagram type disintegrations (E2 to E8, E1 to E4) in a sexual context and highlights her narcissistic justification of behavior.

title: Nana’s final years, decline, and death
text:
With one of her impulsive yet calculated gestures—and realizing that there is nothing left in Paris for her to devour—she sells everything. Laden with treasures and legendary fame, she departs for exotic lands. It is known that she lived in Cairo, then later in Russia.

After a long absence, she unexpectedly returns to Paris and finds her son, who has been living with his aunt and is dying of smallpox. When he dies, she flies into a rage, accusing the aunt of neglect and abandonment.

But her reckless fury does not last long—she contracts the disease herself and dies, disfigured within days, in a room at the Grand Hotel. Outside, the first cries of war ring out—the war that will mark the fall of Napoleon III’s empire. She perishes in the decay of her own flesh, amid the murmurs of a crowd unable to believe the end of a legend. Her unopened suitcases, still brimming with her last riches, remain untouched.
summary: This chunk describes Nana’s departure from Paris after exhausting her resources, her life in exile in Cairo and Russia, her return to Paris upon her son’s illness, her brief rage at the aunt, her contraction of smallpox, and her solitary death amidst the looming war, symbolizing the end of an era and her tragic legacy.

title: Introduction to Lyubov Ranevskaya and The Cherry Orchard analysis
text:
***

A cinematic example

Lyubov Andreyevna Ranevskaya

From The Cherry Orchard by Anton Chekhov

by Consuelo Trujillo

Almost three years ago, I had the opportunity to perform this play in a small theater in Madrid. Since the run lasted six months, I had the chance to delve deep into the intricacies of the character and explore the root of her suffering. When you play a character, your job is to empty yourself in order to become even more yourself within the character—so that the character can emerge through the tangled layers of ego and express itself freely and purely. The more you detach from yourself, the better you come to know the character; the more you open your perception of life, the deeper you can enter its light and darkness, unravel its pain and desires, and dare to embody it with lightness, humor, and compassion.

This was the journey I was on as I searched for Lyubov Ranevskaya—daughter of landowners and owner of The Cherry Orchard—wondering what the essential trait of her character might be. What passion ruled her, what inner conflict tormented her existence, and what caused so much suffering around her? In this piece, I will attempt to express what I discovered through rehearsals and performances—about her inner motivation, her madness, her hunger for love, and how her pride kept her from receiving it, distancing her from herself and everything that could have helped her reclaim her home, her essence, her orchard.

Chekhov wrote this character with his wife, Olga Knipper—leading actress of the Moscow Art Theatre—in mind, and she did, in fact, play the role. From what I’ve read about her and the letters they exchanged, I suspect that many of her personality traits (such as her expressive freedom, histrionics, cheerful and egocentric nature, and an unconscious yet enveloping femininity that so captivated Chekhov) served as inspiration for Ranevskaya’s character.

Chekhov drew inspiration for his play from the spirit of the 19th-century Russian landowning nobility—a fading way of life, people living in their now-impoverished estates, refusing to accept the decline of an era.

He originally intended The Cherry Orchard to be a comedy, a farce—perhaps as a way to distance himself from the sadness of his own life. But somehow, along the way, the play became a tragedy. Everything in it carries the scent of death. Chekhov stages ruined aristocrats, a once-admirable estate doomed to destruction, and at its center, the fascinating, alluring, and proud owner of the orchard—a once-admired landowner—who has already been battered by life’s blows, abandoned by a younger lover, and left bankrupt, on the verge of losing the most beautiful estate in the region.
summary: This section introduces the analysis of Lyubov Ranevskaya from Chekhov’s The Cherry Orchard, describing the author’s personal experience performing the role, the character’s background, Chekhov’s inspiration from his wife Olga Knipper and the declining Russian aristocracy, and the play’s evolution from intended comedy to tragedy centered on loss and decay.

title: Точность названия и исторические детали постановки
text: The play’s title in Spanish [jardin] is not an entirely accurate translation, as the estate is not a garden famous for its cherry trees but rather an orchard spanning a thousand hectares, as Lopakhin’s character notes in the first act. Moreover, these are not cherry trees (which would not withstand Russia’s harsh climate) but sour cherry trees. Chekhov wrote the play in the summer of 1902, and it premiered at the Moscow Art Theatre on January 17, 1904, with Olga Knipper playing Lyubov Ranevskaya, the orchard’s owner, and the great master Konstantin Stanislavski playing Lopakhin—the former muzhik (a Russian peasant who owned no land and lived as a serf), now rising in wealth and social status.
summary: This chunk clarifies the inaccuracy of the Spanish translation of the play's title, describes the actual nature of the orchard (sour cherry trees over a large area), and provides historical context about the writing and premiere of the play, including the casting of Olga Knipper and Konstantin Stanislavski in key roles.

title: Возвращение Раневской и её эмоциональное состояние
text:
The play opens with Ranevskaya returning to her estate in the early hours of a spring morning, just as the cherry trees begin to bloom, after spending five years in Paris. There, she has led a reckless life, supporting a lover who squandered all her money, leaving her penniless and stripped of her property. Now, she returns home with her youngest daughter, Anya, who has traveled to retrieve her, bringing the grim news that they will lose their estate if they fail to pay the interest on their debts.

From the very first act, as Lyubov reenters her home, we witness the emotional and histrionic nature of her character. Everyone looks at her with both admiration and apprehension, fearing her excessive reactions in the face of the looming tragedy—the potential loss of the house. The house where she was born, where she spent her childhood and youth, where she married, had children, lost her youngest son to drowning, and ultimately fled—to reunite with her lover in Paris, abandoning her mourning, her daughters, Anya and Varya, and her responsibilities as a landowner. She left everything behind for love and the intoxicating intensity of a forbidden passion.

Here is one of her first monologues upon arriving home—filled with such deep and shifting emotions, moving effortlessly from one feeling to another, in a tone that is seductive yet falsely affectionate. Though, of course, she fully believes in the sincerity of her own emotions:

LYUBOV: Am I really here? Is this me? (laughs) I feel like dancing about and swinging my arms around. (covers her face with her hands) Perhaps it’s all a dream. God knows I love my country, I love it so dearly. I couldn’t see out of the train window, I was crying so much. (on the brink of tears) Well, I must drink my coffee. Thank you, Firs, thank you, you dear old man, I’m so glad you didn’t die. [...] I can’t sit still—my body won’t let me. (Lyubov leaps up and walks up and down, in a great agitation.) I could die with happiness, I’m silly with it and you can laugh at me. Here’s my little book cupboard!—(kissing the book cupboard) and my little table . . .
summary: This chunk describes Lyubov Ranevskaya's return to her estate after five years in Paris, her financial and emotional ruin due to a destructive relationship, and her overwhelming, fluctuating emotions upon reuniting with her home, illustrated through a vivid monologue that reveals her histrionic, passionate, and self-deceiving nature.

title: Конфликт мировоззрений: Раневская против Лопаткина
text:
Her brother, Leonid Gayev, abruptly interrupts this moment of emotional exaltation, telling her that the housekeeper passed away while she was gone. Lyubov responds without a trace of empathy: “I know, God rest her. They wrote to me.” Then, without dwelling on it, she immediately continues her effusive expressions of love for the house, its objects, and her memories.

This first act revolves around Lyubov Ranevskaya’s reunion with her home, her brother, her adoptive daughter Varya (who manages the house and servants), her youngest daughter Anya (who traveled to Paris to bring her back), close friends, and the people who work for her and, by extension—given the time period—are under her care.

She soon learns that the estate’s interest payments remain unpaid. Lopakhin—a former muzhik with a close bond to Lyubov, and Varya’s suitor, now a wealthy merchant (representing the rise of a new social class in Russia, the small landowners)—proposes a solution to prevent her from losing the property: dividing the orchard into parcels to build summer cottages for rent, generating enough income to cover the debt and much more.

Lopakhin embodies the new, modern, business-minded mentality—the rise of speculative land development and all it entails: the promise of quick wealth at the cost of nature’s destruction. Here, two entirely opposing worldviews collide.

LOPAKHIN: All you have to do is clear the ground, tidy it up, get rid of the old buildings, like this house, which won’t have any use now, and cut down the cherry orchard!

LYUBOV: Cut it down? My dear, I’m sorry but you don’t understand. If there’s one thing of any interest—one remarkable feature—in this whole district, it’s our cherry orchard.

LOPAKHIN: The only remarkable thing about your cherry orchard is it’s big. But it only gives a crop every other year, and then you don’t know what to do with all the cherries, no one wants to buy them.

Two opposing worlds, two contrasting characters:

Lopakhin is a self-made man, having built himself up from nothing. He trusts neither life nor those around him. Hard work and earning everything through his own effort have shaped his character; he knows how to invest and run businesses. To achieve his goals, he has no qualms about destroying beauty—he doesn’t even stop to consider it.
summary: This chunk highlights the emotional detachment of Lyubov in the face of tragedy, her reunion with family and servants, the financial crisis threatening the estate, and the fundamental clash between Lyubov’s idealized, emotion-driven attachment to the orchard and Lopakhin’s pragmatic, profit-oriented vision that sees the land only as a commodity.

title: Образ Любови Раневской как представителя уходящего класса
text:
Lyubov Ranevskaya comes from the lineage of old Russian landowners. Her pride is that of her class—privilege flows through her blood; there is nothing to be done to earn it, only to be who she is. She lives to charm others, to feel, to exalt love for her way of life, her home, her memories, her loves, her losses, her orchard… She is a soul accustomed to contemplating beauty, never having had to work for a living. In Lyubov’s way of seeing the world, there is no common sense—only sensitivity, emotions, and devotion to an idealized love for her parents, her children, her lovers… She feels protected by her status, her place in the world, by simply being who she is. She doesn’t feel at risk; she cannot conceive that anyone could take the orchard from her—just as she never believed her son would die so tragically, that her lover would abandon her, that she would be ruined, and that her entire world would collapse.

The entire play recounts her downfall—the downfall of an entire Russian social class embodied in this warm, captivating, loving woman, admired by all, seductive and powerful. It is the fall of a human being who never imagined she could lose what she held most dear: her love, her greatest treasure, her orchard. In truth, the orchard symbolizes an intimate, idealized paradise—one that pride claims ownership over, one she clings to as proof of her uniqueness. A deeply personal place no one can take from her. A place likely incomprehensible to others—emotional, sacred, untouchable, beyond violation, beyond the axe that fells trees, tramples flowers, and strips the privileged of their untouchable birthright.

There is, in Lyubov’s behavior, a detachment from reality, an absence of survival instinct. She cannot conceive that her life—like the orchard—could be cut down. The mad thought persists: “If I love this orchard with such intensity, no one will be able to take it from me.”
summary: Описывается характер Любови Раневской как представителя уходящего аристократического класса: её эмоциональность, привязанность к прошлому, идеализация прошлого счастья, непринятие реальности и убеждённость в том, что любовь и чувства защищают её от потерь, что приводит к её параличу перед лицом надвигающейся катастрофы.

title: Воспоминания как escape от реальности и предчувствие неизбежного
text:
LYUBOV: Oh, it’s my childhood come back!—innocent days!—when I slept in the nursery and woke with happiness every morning and looked out at the garden. It was just the same, nothing has changed. (laughs with joy) White everywhere… my orchard!—young again after the gloomy darkness of autumn and the winter cold, and happy again, the angels in heaven haven’t forsaken you! Oh, if only I could lose the weight of this stone I carry in my breast. If only I could forget everything up to now!

She clings to memories, to the idealized fantasy of past happiness, as a way to escape suffering—the pain of loss, the limits of life. And yet, the weight is there. Her descent into reality is becoming inevitable—the reckoning with loss, with decay, with the end of youth.

While I played Lyubov in that small theater, I sensed, and longed for, the peace that comes after surrender—the acceptance of reality, the relief of ceasing to battle giants. And I felt that, deep down, Lyubov longed for it too, even if she didn’t know it.
summary: Любовь использует воспоминания о детстве и идеализированном прошлом как психологическую защиту от боли реальности, но чувствует внутренний груз вины и усталости; автор отмечает, что глубине она, возможно, стремится к принятию реальности, несмотря на своё сопротивление.

title: Диалог о великанах и метафора внутренней борьбы
text:
