LOPAKHIN: [...] Sometimes when I can’t sleep, I think, “Dear Lord, you have given us these vast forests and boundless plains to the wide horizon—living here we should really be giants!”

LYUBOV: How would it help being giants? Giants are all very well in fairy tales but anywhere else they’d just frighten everybody.

We are in the second act. The scene unfolds outdoors, among the cherry trees, just before nightfall. The air is heavy—by now, a decision should have been made, yet nothing has been done. With each passing day, the auction draws closer. Lyubov knows she is going to lose the orchard, yet she remains paralyzed, incapable of action. In her mind, the same mad hope lingers—that in the end, a miracle will happen, because it is simply impossible to lose her beloved orchard, because life cannot be so cruel to her, because this cannot happen to her.
summary: В диалоге Лопахин выражает желание действовать смело и масштабно, словно гигант, тогда как Любовь отвергает такую позицию как непрактичную и пугающую, подчеркивая свой внутренний паралич и надежду на чудо apesar надвигающейся потери имения.

title: Исповедь Любови: признание вины и мольба о прощении
text:
And while Lopakhin, frustrated, tries to offer her a solution to save the estate, she opens her heart to him instead:

LYUBOV: Please, please stay! You cheer me up somehow, despite yourself. (pause) I keep expecting something to happen, as though the house were to fall around our ears. [...] We must be paying for our sins… so many sins…

LOPAKHIN: Oh, yes? And what sins would they be?

LYUBOV: Oh, my sins! I’ve always squandered money without a thought like some madwoman, and then I married a man who did nothing but run up debts. My husband died of champagne, he was a terrible drinker. Then I had the misfortune to fall in love and take up with someone else just at the moment when… and this was my first punishment, like a blow to the head—it was here—here in this river, my little boy drowned, and I went abroad, I didn’t pause—I meant never to return, to see this river ever again. I shut my eyes and fled, not knowing where I was going, and he came after me, he wouldn’t give up, he was merciless. I bought a little house near Menton when he fell ill there, and for the next three years I had no rest day or night, he wore me out, my soul dried up. Then last year when the house had to go to pay the debts, I went to Paris, and there he robbed me of everything. He threw me over and went off with another woman, and I tried to poison myself. It was all so stupid and humiliating. And all of a sudden I knew I had to come back to Russia, to my home, to my daughter. (wipes away tears) Oh God forgive me, forgive my sins! Don’t punish me any more! (takes a telegram from her pocket). I got this from Paris this morning. He asks me to forgive him, and implores me to go back. (tears up the telegram) Isn’t that music I can hear? (listens)
summary: Любовь раскаивается в своих прошлых действиях: расточительность, неправильный выбор мужей и любовников, бегство от горя, эмоциональная зависимость от любви как наказания и спасения одновременно, получает телеграмму от бывшего любовника и разрывает её, демонстрируя внутренний конфликт между виной, болью и привязанностью.

title: Анализ характера Любовь Раневской: вина и манипуляция
text: This confession lays bare the essential traits of her character. She feels sinful and longs to be understood in her darkness. And yet, at the same time, she is manipulating—casting herself as a victim before Lopakhin, the strongest and most powerful man near her. She admits her guilt—squandering her family’s fortune, abandoning her daughters, not being there when her son drowned because she was with her lover. But there is always an excuse: she was trapped, driven mad, devoured by love. She sees herself as a victim of love—something beyond her control, something that brings out both the best and the worst in her. She confesses herself addicted to it. And at the same time, she presents herself as a martyr—the devoted nurse, the self-sacrificing caregiver, only to be discarded in the end.
summary: The passage analyzes Lyubov Ranevskaya's character, highlighting her mix of guilt, self-victimization, and manipulation. She admits fault but frames her actions as beyond her control due to love, positioning herself as both sinner and martyr.

title: Любовь как逃 от реальности и символ упадка имения
text:
In this act, a pivotal moment unfolds—one that affects the entire family and everyone working on the estate. The auction is now less than two weeks away. Yet what truly consumes Lyubov is the telegram from her lover.

Love, too, is an escape from reality. A way of not seeing that she is on the verge of losing everything, that she has no money, that she is no longer a grand lady, that she is growing older, that her time has come… It is a reckless flight forward, an attempt to outrun what she cannot accept about herself—the frustration, the helplessness, the limits, the fall… And despite this speech, in which she speaks of her downfall, of how she allowed herself to be stripped of dignity by this man, there remains, deep inside, a defiance—a refusal to fall, to taste the dust of defeat.

The central theme of the play, as we have discussed, is the loss of the estate—the protagonist’s downfall due to poor financial management and a lifestyle beyond her means. Lyubov Ranevskaya’s personal struggle serves as a symbol of the Russian aristocracy, which always considered itself untouchable and is now on the brink of extinction.
summary: This section explores how Lyubov uses love to escape impending financial and emotional ruin, framing her personal decline as symbolic of the fading Russian aristocracy. Despite her awareness of doom, she clings to defiance and denial.

title: Компульсивная щедрость как защита от пустоты
text:
“I’ve always squandered money without a thought like some madwoman…” This carelessness with money—which she mistakes for generosity—reflects a sense of arrogance and superiority (the overabundance characteristic of sexual E2), manifesting as: “I don’t need anything.” She feels most alive when she feels full, while those around her live in need and lack—needs she will eagerly fulfill. Her generosity is both egocentric and narcissistic, yet at the same time, a lifeline to avoid feeling her own emptiness. It is grotesque, even comical, to see how—despite the obvious financial ruin of both herself and her family—she continues to spend, give away, and lend money she doesn’t have. There is more pleasure in spending and giving than in saving and possessing.

For example, in the first act, her youngest daughter, Anya, recounts to her adopted sister, Varya, how difficult the journey from Paris to the Russian countryside was due to their mother’s extravagance, despite her dire financial situation: “The villa near Menton is already sold. She has nothing left, nothing at all. I haven’t got a kopek, we barely made it to Paris. And Mama simply doesn’t take it in. At the station restaurant she ordered the most expensive things on the menu and tipped the waiters a rouble each.”

Later (when it is already clear that they are about to lose the estate), Pishchik, a fellow landowner also on the verge of ruin, asks her for a loan:

PISHCHIK: Two hundred and forty roubles to pay the interest …?

LYUBOV: I have no money, my sweet.

PISHCHIK: I’ll give it back, my dear. It’s a trifling sum.

LYUBOV: Oh, all right—ask Leonid for it—go on, Leonid—give it to him.

GAYEV: I give it to him?—he’ll be lucky.

LYUBOV: What else can one do? He has to have it. He’ll pay it back. (She goes out.)

GAYEV: My sister’s still in the habit of throwing her money away.

This brief scene clearly illustrates her compulsive need to give, her inability to face her own lack. As long as she gives, she can avoid acknowledging that she has nothing. She tells the young Peter Trofimov: “Why have you lost your looks? How did you get so old? You’ve aged too, Leonid!” She can see decline in others, but not in herself.

She resists limits, refuses to acknowledge scarcity. At the same time, there’s a guilt that manifests in a histrionic way, excused by a sense of helplessness, a “I can’t help it,” a refusal to take responsibility for her actions and their consequences—and therefore, for her ability to change, to wake up, to become aware and own her mistakes:

LYUBOV: There was lots of money in here yesterday, and now there’s hardly any. Poor Varya’s economising, feeding us on slops, and the old ones in the kitchen only get dried peas… and here am I spending money without a thought, I don’t know where it goes… And why ever did I go out for lunch? That frightful restaurant of yours…
summary: Lyubov's compulsive giving is analyzed as a defense against inner emptiness and lack. Her generosity stems from narcissistic pride and avoidance of scarcity, allowing her to feel superior while denying her own financial and emotional depletion.

title: Символизм денег и предзнаменования: разорванная струна и нищий
text:
Money is a constant presence in the play, but in the second act, it takes on a more mysterious dimension. Chekhov conveys it symbolically, through other senses and meanings. Night falls, and the atmosphere becomes eerie. “Suddenly a distant sound breaks the silence, as though from the sky: the sound of a breaking string, dying away, a sense of melancholy.” Upon hearing it, Lyubov shudders, feeling a deep unease, a bad omen. The old servant, Firs, says the same sound was heard before a past tragedy. He is interrupted before finishing his thought, but we understand that he is referring to the day Lyubov’s young son drowned. Anya begins to cry, though we do not know why—we sense the raw sensitivity of a young soul who feels both the beauty and fragility of life. And then, a passerby appears—a beggar, slightly drunk…

PASSER-BY: Excuse me, can I get to the station through here?

GAYEV: You can. Follow the track.
summary: This section describes symbolic omens— the breaking string and the appearance of a beggar—that foreshadow tragedy and reflect Lyubov's inner turmoil. Money and loss are framed through sensory and spiritual cues tied to past trauma and impending ruin.

title: Пассер-бай просит милостыню, Любовь отдаёт последние деньги
text:
PASSER-BY: Much obliged. (with a cough) What wonderful weather… (recites) “To the Volga! The sounds that call us to Russia’s great river belong to the groans and cries of the haulers! Pity the land that calls it a song!” (to Varya) Mademoiselle, spare thirty kopecks for a hungry fellow-countryman.

(Varya takes fright, and shrieks.)

LOPAKHIN (angrily): Hey, you!—watch your step!

LYUBOV (panicky): Here take this… (searching in her purse) I have no silver—never mind, here’s ten roubles.

PASSER-BY: Deeply grateful to you!

(The Passer-by goes on his way and the others laugh.)

VARYA (frightened): I’m going in. Honestly, Mama, we can’t feed the servants and you gave him a gold piece.

LYUBOV: I know, I’m such a fool. What’s to be done with me? I’ll give you all I’ve got left when we get home. Yermolai Alexeievitch, you’ll lend me some more, won’t you?

LOPAKHIN: Your humble servant.
summary: В этом фрагменте просят милостыню Пasser-by, Любовь в панике отдаёт ему свои последние деньги, несмотря на протесты дочери Вари, демонстрируя свою неспособность отказать в помощи даже в ущерб себе, что типично для Enneatype 2.

title: Анализ поведения Любови: страх бедности и компульсивная жертвенность
text: Faced with fear and omens, confronted by the beggar—the physical embodiment of poverty, the dark tunnel she knows awaits her and which she fights so desperately to escape—Lyubov cannot bear to be in the presence of lack, of need, of the shadow that haunts her. She cannot endure it. And so, compulsively, she gives away what she does not have, only to then apologize: “I’m such a fool…” She cannot bear the moment when she and the beggar are one and the same. She pulls out a coin she cannot afford to part with; in that instant, she must admit to Varya that she has made a mistake and then immediately asks Lopakhin for another loan. And beneath it all, there’s the unspoken premonition of disaster—the memory of her lost son. Soon, she will lose the house, she will lose herself. She has received a telegram from her lover, and once again, she begins to think of running away—because he needs her.
summary: Автор анализирует поведение Любови, объясняя её компульсивную жертвенность страхом перед бедностью и нужду, которую она ассоциирует с собственной тенью; её действия движимы потребностью быть нужной, несмотря на осознанную самопожертвование и предчувствие катастрофы.

title: Третий акт: аукцион, вечеринка и признание в любви
text:
And so, we enter the third act: the day of the auction. Rather than confronting reality, Lyubov throws a party, hiring musicians she has no money to pay. Everyone dances and drinks; there are magic tricks; it feels like a celebration—a farewell to a life of splendor.

In a fleeting moment of awareness, she remarks: “It wasn’t the best moment to have a band and throw a party. Well, let’s not worry about that.”

The moment has arrived—she knows it. She voices her fear and turns to Peter Trofimov, the young tutor, to pour out her heart, to let the volcano of her emotions erupt. That volcano that has been waiting, waiting—because she still needs to be a good person, a good mother, sister, friend…

LYUBOV: It’s a telegram from Paris. I get one every day. One yesterday, another today. That wild man is in a bad way again, he’s ill. He asks to be forgiven, begs me to come back, and I really should go to Paris to be near him for a while. Don’t look like that, Petya, what else can I do?—he’s sick and all on his own, and unhappy—who’s going to look after him there, who’s going to stop him getting into a pickle again, and make sure he takes his medicine? Why bother to deny it, I love him, that much I know. I love him. Love!—it’s the millstone round my neck and I’ll go to the bottom with it, but I love love and I won’t live without it. (squeezes Trofimov’s hand) Don’t think badly of me, Petya… don’t say anything.

TROFIMOV (on the brink of tears): Please… please God forgive my bluntness but that man stole everything you had, he robbed you!

LYUBOV (covering her ears): No, no, you mustn’t say that.
summary: В третьем акте Любовь избегает реальности, устраивая праздник несмотря на предстоящий аукцион, а затем открывается перед Трофимовым, признаваясь в своей зависимой, саморазрушающей любви к мужчине, который её эксплуатирует, демонстрируя классическую паттерн E2: жертвенность ради любви и страх быть ненужной.

title: Потеря имения и символика падения
text: At the end of this act, Lopakhin—the former serf—arrives with the news that the estate has been sold, and he is the one who has bought the cherry orchard. The servant is now the master. The loss of the orchard symbolizes the fall of pride, privilege, and superiority. It is also a farewell to beauty—the kind only those with a certain sensitivity could ever truly appreciate. Now, the cherry trees will be cut down, replaced by summer cottages that will turn a profit for their new owner. This possibility never even crossed Lyubov’s mind—she never truly believed she could lose something that had always belonged to her, something that felt like an extension of her own proud, beautiful essence.
summary: Любовь теряет своё имение, купленное бывшим крепостным Лопахиным, что символизирует конец её привилегированного мира и невозможность принять реальность упадка; потеря сада становится метафорой утраты идентичности, связанной с красотой и гордостью.

title: Четвёртый акт: отъезд в Париж и жертва ради любви
text:
If the third act represents our protagonist’s downfall, the fourth act shows how pride—though battered—can rise again and adapt to new circumstances. Lyubov prepares to leave for Paris, returning to her lover. “I’m sleeping well. Bring my things, Yasha. It’s time. (to Anya) Darling, we’ll see each other again before long. Paris here I come, with great-aunt’s money she sent to buy the estate. Here’s to her! Well, it won’t last long.”

This detail is often overlooked, but the money she’s taking belongs to her daughter, Anya—her grandmother sent it for her. So, while her mother spends it in Paris with a lover, Anya—innocent and kind—speaks hopefully about the future: “But you’ll come back soon, won’t you, Mama? You will, won’t you? I’ll study hard and pass my exams and then I’ll go to work, so I’ll be able to help you… So come back, Mama.”

Lyubov loves her daughter, but she cannot sacrifice herself for her. She knows this trip to Paris and this relationship are doomed to fail, that she will return penniless once again, seeking refuge with Anya. But she can’t help it—she needs to feel desired, loved, needed. She needs to experience the intensity of passion that keeps her alive. And she knows this will be the last time. She is growing older. She will come back, and life will have lost all meaning. And then—like the orchard—she will wither and die.
summary: В четвёртом акте Любовь уезжает в Париж на деньги, предназначенные для дочери, предпочитая свою страстную, обречённую отношения заботе о ребёнке; она осознаёт порочность своего выбора, но не может изменить паттерн поиска любви любой ценой, что ведёт к её духовному упадку.

title: Proщание с домом и садом
text: Now, all that’s left is to say goodbye to the house where she was born, to her beloved orchard. In the distance, the sound of axes and machinery echoes—soon, the house will be torn down, the trees felled. “Goodbye, old house, old grandfather house. Come the spring, you won’t be here anymore…” She is speaking of herself. And she continues her farewell: “I never took the slightest notice of the walls and ceilings before… and now I want to look at them forever, they break my heart… [...] Oh, my poor, sweet, lovely orchard! My life, my childhood, my happiness, goodbye! Goodbye!
summary: This chunk describes Lyubov's emotional farewell to her childhood home and orchard, symbolizing the end of her past life and identity, as she prepares to leave for Paris despite knowing the relationship is doomed.

title: Юмористические vignettes о сексуальной E2
text:
It is a farewell to the life she once dreamed of, to the love she believed in, to the illusion of eternity…

Goodbye! Goodbye! Goodbye!

Jokes and vignettes

“It’s just that I’ve already been given a ton of hearts… What else are you offering?”

Illustration by Juan Pablo Compaired

“Nice try!”

The apron: “Kiss me a lot”

Illustrations by Jordi Díaz

In these two panels, we see the seductive trap set by a very attractive cannibal who, with her provocative gestures, manages to lure the three explorers into the pot. At the same time, her apron reads “Kiss me a lot,” almost hinting that it’s the only, and last, chance for salvation. But the cannibalistic sexual Two demands more from her victims… though in doing so, she guarantees her share of contact and passion.

Illustrations by Jordi Díaz

The secret of the sexual E2 woman is that she enchants and provokes strong, confident men simply by dancing. And in the end, she manages to turn her attractive suitors into lapdogs, completely under her control. Her hidden desire is to create pocket-sized Goliaths.
summary: This section uses illustrative vignettes to depict the sexual E2 woman's seductive power—using dance and provocation to control strong men, turning them into compliant partners while seeking to create 'pocket-sized Goliaths' as a reflection of her need for dominance and passion.

title: Процесс трансформации и терапевтические рекомендации
text:
Transformation process and therapeutic recommendations

by Alba Chartroux

According to the Enneagram psychology model, personality is structured through fairly specific and describable traits, shaped by a combination of social, relational, and intrapsychic dynamics. As we grow, every aspect of life—how we think, express ourselves, feel, suffer, love—is conditioned rather than freely chosen. The process of self-knowledge, which exposes these unconscious patterns, inevitably leads to change by activating new choices about how to be and how to relate to others.

This change is a journey longer than life itself, unfolding as a person gradually disidentifies from their most ego-driven and limiting traits. It is also a path with setbacks. Often, we return to the same point, the same existential knot, but with a broadened perspective that expands each time we reengage with the process.

Personal transformation is, at its core, a journey of self-awareness. It begins when a person starts to recognize that they themselves are the primary cause of their difficulties, even though they have been influenced by social, cultural, and familial pressures. This process is not about striving to become a better version of oneself—creating an idealized self that meets internal and external expectations—but rather about becoming who one truly is.

This means progressively dissolving the gap between one’s authentic self and the artificial, defensive personality that was constructed as a means of coping. The person begins to prefer simply being who they are, moving toward an ego-transcendence that is not about self-annihilation but rather about stripping away the manipulations that obscure their real identity.

This requires a conscious and voluntary commitment. One stops believing they are either entirely free and fully formed or entirely conditioned by their environment, as if they were a mere product of external forces. Instead, they take responsibility for what they are, including their conditioning, and begin peeling away the layers of false identity, shedding everything that no longer belongs to them.

As one testimony describes:

Trying to change my behavior was deeply frustrating because, rather than transforming into something else, what I actually experienced was a descent into the real world… a painful journey toward discovering who I truly was. Two quotes by Guillermo Borja helped me a lot: “Pathology is the denial of what one is” and “Guilt is a child who refuses to take responsibility.”

I spent a year working with the mantra: “I am what I do, not what I feel or think I am,” and my self-image crumbled in the face of my own avoidances and denials.

I couldn’t even take refuge in the inconsolable feeling of being nothing, because that, too, was a negative narcissistic defense: being “the worst of the worst”—a kind of noble title. In the end, I had to accept the hardest truth of all: being ordinary… Having my ups and downs. And, above all, embracing this middle ground that, in its anonymity, had always been the very thing I rejected in my life.
summary: This chunk outlines the Enneagram-based transformation process, emphasizing self-awareness, responsibility, and the dissolution of false identity. It includes a personal testimony about moving beyond narcissistic defenses to embrace ordinariness and authenticity as the path to genuine self-discovery.

title: Осознанные изменения в поведении E2 при работе над собой
text:
TONI AGUILAR

Enneatype 2s often mistake their dysfunctional traits for virtues. When they become aware of their suffering, they try to escape it as quickly as possible—through bursts of enthusiasm, fleeting emotional highs, and a generally optimistic attitude that is more about denial than genuine confidence or acceptance.

But as self-revelation progresses, the person starts to see what lies behind their facade of warmth and apparent self-sufficiency. This is when the more immature aspects of their narcissism begin to collapse. It becomes harder to keep believing in their own specialness and desirability. At this point, a conscious shift in how they relate to others begins. Where the E2 once threw themselves forward in a dramatic, even intrusive way—trying to capture or corner the other—they begin to take a step back. They start to feel a sense of modesty. They begin to abstain. If self-awareness is combined with meditation practice, this ability to refrain from imposing themselves on others can grow, allowing people to be truly free from their invasive energy.
summary: This section describes how E2s, upon developing self-awareness, shift from denying their dysfunctional traits to recognizing the narcissistic roots of their behavior. It highlights their progression from intrusive giving to modesty and self-restraint, especially when supported by mindfulness practices, leading to healthier relationships.

title: Compulsive giving as disguised superiority in sexual E2
text:
Taking steps away from their inflated self-image (that swings between excessive self-satisfaction and dramatic self-denigration) helps them recognize their own vulnerability. In the sexual and social subtypes, this vulnerability is particularly well-masked by a belief in their own indispensability and magnificence. It manifests as a compulsive urge to give—offering help, advice, gifts, smothering maternal care—providing an excess of love that can feel more like emotional vampirism. Outwardly, this may seem altruistic, but at its core, it maintains their sense of superiority and control, keeping them on a pedestal from which they can bestow their presence upon others.

Even the sexual E2’s occasional air of haughty disdain, making the other person feel indebted, can be understood as a form of giving. In this case, they offer their withdrawal as a gift: “I want nothing more to do with you; you don’t deserve me.”
summary: This chunk explains how sexual Enneatype 2 individuals mask vulnerability through compulsive giving or withdrawal, framing these behaviors as forms of control and superiority disguised as generosity or rejection.

title: Rebellion and ego fuel in sexual E2 relationships
text:
The rebellion of the sexual E2 is directly tied to this disguised sense of superiority. “You don’t deserve me” is also “You limit me.” This dynamic fuels many of their relationship breakdowns. Though the sexual E2 may appear indulgent, they are, in reality, extremely demanding. What they demand is a constant supply of fuel for their ego and inflated self-image.

To sincerely unmask themselves as a calculatedly generous person, someone who gives with unspoken expectations, shatters their pedestal. It forces them to recognize their vulnerability and the personal ugliness of having exploited others’ needs. It brings them down to the same level as everyone else.
summary: This section describes how the sexual E2's rebellion stems from egoic demands in relationships, and how confronting their exploitative giving patterns leads to humility by dismantling their false sense of superiority.

title: The paradox of E2’s pseudo-independence and true freedom
text:
It is as if the E2, despite their deep longing for freedom, locks themselves inside their own infatuation with themselves, clinging to an ideal of personal independence that serves more as an ego defense than a path to true liberation. In truth, they are unwilling to pay the price of real freedom.

And yet, they do pay a toll: an overestimation of their own autonomy, or at least a distorted version of it. Their idea of independence is rooted in a fantasy of being able to stand up to the other person, though often through seduction rather than direct confrontation. In this way, the E2’s rebellion is not so much against authority as it is against submission. And for the sexual subtype, the primary arena where this battle plays out is in intimate relationships.
summary: This chunk explores how the E2's pursuit of independence is actually a defense mechanism rooted in ego, particularly in the sexual subtype, where it manifests in intimate relationships as resistance to submission rather than true autonomy.

title: Humility as the virtue of E2 transformation
text:
Just as we can trace the compulsive and destructive traits of character, we can also begin to outline some aspects of transformation—those that, in the psychology of the Enneatypes, are expressions of what is called virtue. For Enneatype 2, this virtue is humility.

For real change to happen, the wounds to the ego that the sexual E2 fears most are precisely the ones that can become the most powerful tools for transformation—because they crack the pride open. When arrogance gives way, humiliation is no longer met with the usual defensive and self-important reaction but instead makes space for humility to emerge.

For that to happen, the person needs to embrace the small, everyday opportunities life offers to take responsibility—even in the simplest tasks—with a learning mindset and a capacity for delayed gratification. In this Enneatype, humility can show up as an ability to step down a notch compared to how they’ve always been. At the same time, however, they may retain a certain degree of pride—not arrogance, but a sense of personal dignity, critical thinking, and self-respect that is fundamentally different from self-indulgence.
summary: This section defines humility as the core virtue for E2 growth, explaining how ego wounds can lead to transformation when faced with honesty, responsibility, and a shift from arrogance to genuine self-respect.

title: Ego collapse and secondary defenses in E2 awakening
text:
As E2 peels away the layers of their ego defenses, they start to see the hidden traps of their personality and the deep sense of lack that lies beneath their apparent self-giving. They become aware of the exhaustion and harm caused by certain relational and survival strategies and begin to take responsibility for their own character traits.

In the early stages of awakening, Enneatype 2 collapses into the sadness of self-disillusionment, coming face-to-face with their most intimate sense of deprivation. This is a delicate phase of transformation because, time and again, they fall back into self-deception—unmasked through the ego’s angry outbursts, which only serve to reinforce their armor.

At this stage, they may even swing in the opposite direction, embracing their flaws with the same arrogance they once used to hide behind their powerful defenses. The sexual E2 might become noticeably less affectionate, tapping into their cynicism, worsening their behavior, and displaying a more crude or provocative attitude. Their pursuit of pleasure may become more self-serving, no longer driven by the compulsive need to give pleasure to others. They might not feel “okay” anymore. But they also might not care.

They begin to recognize the link between their need for love and tenderness and the pride that has served as a defense against the frustration of that need. That same frustration, instead of softening their defenses, has often reinforced them. They see their envy of love and the deep emptiness beneath it. As a result, they might take on egoic traits similar to Enneatype 8. But if they remain conscious of these secondary defenses, this phase can represent the final struggle of their old, dying persona.
summary: This chunk describes the painful early stages of E2 self-awareness, including ego collapse, defensive swings, and the potential emergence of E8-like traits as secondary defenses during the disintegration of the false persona.

title: Integration and authentic connection in transformed sexual E2
text:
At this point, the sexual E2 fully engages with their dominant instinct (connection) while beginning to separate it from their passionate distortion (pride). They seek a clearer confrontation with the underlying aggression in their impulsiveness—honestly and without disguise. They may stop chasing conquest, stop needing to feel “special” and desired, and let go of the exhausting effort to appear altruistic just to feel superior to others. Their mood swings also start to level out, a natural result of greater inner coherence.

They begin to see themselves for what they are: either a fool caught up in their own delusion or the small, insignificant being they’ve spent their whole life trying not to be.
summary: This section outlines the progress toward integration in the sexual E2, where they begin to separate healthy connection from pride-driven impulses, leading to greater self-honesty and emotional balance.

title: Работа с разочарованием и иллюзиями
text:
They face disillusionment with themselves, but without clinging to the grandiosity of guilt or the desperate hunger for forgiveness, both of which would only reignite the illusions of compensation, driving them toward the egoic traits of Enneatype 4: over-identifying with lack, comparing their worth to others, and sinking into self-pity.

If they manage to navigate this dangerous regression, the sexual E2 begins to accept their limitations without pretending to be something they’re not. They see others and the world more clearly, without exaggeration or idealization. As a result, they take on responsibilities with honesty, meeting their commitments without making grandiose promises they won’t keep. They become less eager to please and, therefore, more sincere. Their excessiveness fades, and in its place, a more measured and grounded presence emerges. They accept that they have simple needs, just like everyone else. In the end, they realize they’ve been living life as an image, a constructed persona, rather than as an expression of their true self. And all they need to do is allow that self to surface.
summary: Describes how the sexual E2 confronts self-disillusionment without falling into guilt or self-pity, moves toward authenticity by accepting limitations, and begins to live from their true self rather than a constructed persona, integrating modest traits of Enneatype 4.

title: Преображение любви и отношений
text:
Love remains a crucial part of life for this subtype, but they no longer put it on display. Instead, they experience it in a more intimate and authentic way, with a real interest in the other person—not as a means to elevate themselves, nor as an object for their compulsive pseudo-altruism. They no longer view love as a grand romantic adventure but as a deep, equal connection. In this new state of transformation, even monogamy is no longer something to resist or escape. It becomes an expression of the joy of being with someone. The fear of abandonment in love and friendship also lessens, as their relationships become less based on indulgence and people-pleasing and more rooted in real, honest connection.

Ultimately, love remains just as important for the sexual subtype of E2, but what changes is how they understand and express it. They don’t love less. They love more authentically, with less drama and intensity. Love is no longer tied to the fantasy of an ideal, eternal, and unshakable romance but instead is grounded in the reality of a flawed human being, someone whose limitations reflect their own. And in the end, this is what true compassion is all about.
summary: Explains how the sexual E2 transforms their experience of love—from performative and idealized to authentic, grounded, and compassionate—based on mutual reality rather than fantasy or self-validation.

title: Интеграция потребностей и простоты бытия
text:
When it comes to themselves, the sexual E2 becomes more capable of expressing their being with simplicity, including their needs, which allows them to accept their limits without self-pity or shame. They remain naturally self-interested but less focused on their image, learning to ask without demanding and to accept a “no” without resentment. At the same time, they come to understand that their compulsive search for approval has nothing to do with the fundamental human need for love—something that does not depend on putting oneself on display. As a result, they also learn to say no, without being controlled by the fear of humiliation or disapproval, and therefore, of being unloved. The romantic idealization of love transforms into true intimacy—something simpler and more humble. Sensuality is no longer confined to sexual conquest but expands into the pleasure of contemplating a leaf, a stone, a ray of light, or listening to the murmur of water or the roar of a storm. No longer enslaved by the pursuit of intensity and pleasure, they begin to discover small and simple joys.

The desire to be at the center of others’ admiration and longing gives way to a new perception of themselves: they’re simply “nothing special.” This shift also brings the ability to slow down, replacing the voracious craving for ever-new and intense stimuli with the enjoyment of smaller pleasures.
summary: Details how the sexual E2 learns to express their needs honestly, releases attachment to image and approval, finds value in simplicity and presence, and redefines self-worth as 'nothing special'—leading to greater inner peace and authentic engagement with life.

title: Преодоление дезориентации и интеграция ответственности
text:
This transformative process of self-awareness, which involves the crumbling of pride, often leads to phases of disorientation and passivity that, from a clinical perspective, might resemble depression. But from the viewpoint of Enneagram psychology, these are signs of integrating the more introverted and modest traits of Enneatype 4.

The disorientation also comes from the fact that others notice the change, and don’t always appreciate it. These subtle or not-so-subtle shifts don’t necessarily make life easier for the sexual E2, but they do make it more transparent. A sense of identity is always the result of an ongoing negotiation with those whose recognition they seek, but now this negotiation no longer comes at the cost of their authenticity. They are no longer attached to external validation.

The need for connection remains, but the way they relate to others changes. The flattery and indulgence that once shaped their interactions start to fall away, along with the inevitable trace of hidden hypocrisy that came with them. They begin to express themselves in a more direct and honest way, no longer needing the same level of approval and admiration. In this process, they integrate certain qualities of Enneatype 8, which can create some distance from people they previously related to in a more accommodating manner. This is understandable, as love (broadly speaking, not just romantic relationships) is no longer governed by seduction and indulgence but instead unfolds with clarity and without pretense. However, this doesn’t mean they reject vulnerability or deny their own and others’ limitations.
summary: Addresses the disorienting but transformative phase of pride dissolution, where integrating E4 and E8 traits leads to greater authenticity, honesty in relationships, and freedom from external validation—despite social discomfort.

title: Жизнь в полноте настоящего с осознанием времени
text:
There’s one final aspect in the transformation of the sexual Two. On the surface, they appear to live fully in the here and now, but this is often in a more superficial, pleasure-seeking, and non-committal way. Eventually, they realize that the here and now also contains a there and then and a what comes next, which they can set aside temporarily if needed but cannot completely erase.

At that point, they have no choice but to stop living day-to-day with the same old dose of irresponsibility. Instead, they begin to live each day as it truly is—with all its implications—without overdramatizing or falling into nihilism.
summary: Describes the final stage of transformation where the sexual E2 moves beyond superficial present-moment pleasure to embrace responsibility and the full implications of living in time—balancing presence with awareness of past and future.

title: Автобиография Консуэло Трухильо: детство и семейные отношения
text:
by Consuelo Trujillo

I came into the world at noon on August 2nd, with the sun in Leo, in the small town of La Línea de la Concepción in Cádiz. I’m the eldest of four siblings, born at the dawn of the sixties.

I felt loved and valued in my childhood. From the very start, I was my father’s daughter. “You’re just like your daddy” was a phrase my mother, grandmothers, and aunts repeated constantly. Since I was little, I admired him deeply. He was my love, my passion. I craved being around him and cherished his world, his ideas, his virtues... which seemed far greater in number than those of my mother’s. When he came home from work, he’d whistle from the gate, and I’d run into his arms. He would greet me by saying “You’re the one who loves me the most.” I could feel him comparing me to my mother, and I knew I came out on top.

My mother, with her sexual Three character, presented herself to the world as the perfect wife and mother, but behind closed doors, she often lost her temper. There were times when she felt weak, overwhelmed. She’d get dizzy, anxious, unwell. I remember my father’s voice before leaving for work: “Take care of your mother.” And I took it to heart. Not so much in the sense of handling household chores, but in an emotional responsibility that carried an underlying sense of superiority. I felt capable of taking care of my siblings, of holding everything together: “I can handle this,” “I’m stronger,” “I have more than enough to give.”

With his gaze, my father made me feel bigger than I was: more responsible, more mature, special. And this feeling intensified around my mother, because she acted like a child in front of my father and me. I could sense her weakness, her nervousness, her mood swings, her dependence on him. She made herself small, needy, and by her side, I learned not to need, not to ask, to feel abundant in my own resources, in my self-sufficiency, in my superiority. A superiority that was physical, emotional, and intellectual, and it grew under my father’s gaze. I remember myself as a happy girl, carefree, who did things on her own, who never missed home, who could be fine anywhere.
summary: The author describes her childhood in Cádiz, her deep admiration for her father, and her mother’s sexual Three traits—outwardly perfect but inwardly volatile. She internalized a sense of emotional superiority and self-sufficiency, learning to care for others while suppressing her own needs, shaped by her father’s affirmations and her mother’s fragility.

title: Образование и ранняя самостоятельность: поступление в Терцианскую школу
text:
When I was six, my teacher told my parents that I had a lot of academic potential, and that they needed to give me the chance to go to a better school. So, they enrolled me in a Teresian school, which at the time had a reputation for using innovative, modern teaching methods. It was something rare in Franco’s Spain, especially in the deep South.

At seven, my father took me to my new school, far from home, so I could learn the way and eventually go on my own. It was the first day, and my mother was supposed to pick me up. The time came, but she didn’t appear. I waited, feeling scared and anxious but I didn’t let it show. Other mothers and girls asked about her, and I told them it was fine, that she would come. I waited, but she never did. Without saying anything to anyone, I set off on my own, trying to remember the way I had walked with my father. When I got home, everyone cheered: “Look at her, so grown-up! She made it home alone!” “This girl is one of a kind!” “There’s nothing she can’t do…” My mother told me she had simply forgotten. But all the praise drowned out my fear, my anger, my sadness. Abundance masked lack; my smallness, my need, my rage. How could I be upset? How could I cry in the face of so much admiration? From that day on, I walked to school alone. And later, I would take my sister Lorena and my cousins, all under my care. I became the leader, the guide, the eldest sister.
summary: At age six, the author was identified as academically gifted and enrolled in a progressive Teresian school. At seven, she walked to school alone after her mother failed to pick her up, suppressing her fear and anger beneath praise. This experience reinforced her self-reliance and leadership role, establishing a pattern of emotional self-sufficiency that masked inner vulnerability.

title: Поиск любви и признания вне семьи: привязанность к бабушке и тете
text:
Since I was little, I loved going up to my grandmother’s house to be with her and my aunt. They would teach me things and have me memorize them. I gladly accepted, and they would tell me how smart I was, shower me with affection, spoil me, and laugh with me... Even then, I was already starting to look for a place where I could stand out, where I could feel loved outside my immediate family.

At that time, between the ages of three and five, my father was working in Gibraltar, and we wouldn’t see him for months. My mother was very depressed. My brother Fale, born when I was just seventeen months old, cried a lot, and my mother was constantly worried about him because he was born with an umbilical hernia. I didn’t demand attention; instead, I learned to do what would become a pattern throughout my teenage years—leaving, searching elsewhere for what I wasn’t getting at home. And I was happy upstairs with my grandmother and aunt. They taught me new things—like the capitals of every country in the world—and once again, they applauded my achievements, gave me love, and made me feel seen.
summary: The author found emotional nourishment and recognition at her grandmother’s house, where her intellect was praised and she felt seen. During her parents’ absence and her mother’s depression, she withdrew inward, developing a lifelong pattern of seeking validation and love outside the home when her emotional needs went unmet within the family.

title: Ранний сексуальный опыт и его психологические корни
text:
When I was five years old, there was a girl of about fourteen or fifteen who helped my mother at home with the chores. Once, in secret, I sneaked with her into the green room, where nobody usually entered and I kissed her and hugged her passionately. My memory is made up of these sensations, but now I wonder: How is it possible that a five-year-old girl would take the lead in sexual games with a fourteen-year-old? I don’t know how it really happened, but that’s how I remember it. I see myself taking control, making the first move in those childhood games. Deep down, there was probably a desperate need for my mother’s love, for her attention. I think I took on my father’s role with her, trying to do what he did to win her love.

I remember my father’s loving and lustful treatment of my mother, and how she resisted. It was something subtly present in the way they interacted. It was clear to me that my father desired my mother very much and that my mother was more passive. This has deeply impacted me and has strongly influenced my sexuality, both in my sexual preference for women and in the way I approach it. I tend to take a more active rather than passive role, taking the initiative and seeking sex as a substitute for love. Or rather, as a way to feel love.
summary: At age five, the author engaged in a passionate encounter with an older girl, which she interprets as an attempt to gain her mother’s love by imitating her father’s affectionate behavior. She links this early experience to her adult sexuality—characterized by initiative, a preference for women, and using sex as a means to feel loved, rooted in childhood emotional deprivation.

title: Финансовый крах и эмоциональная трагедия семьи
text: A little later, we had to move after one of the many financial collapses that have followed my father throughout his life. We had no money, but we were still living in the grand, stately house my grandfather had built… and now we had lost it. There was so much sadness in the new house. My great-grandmother was dying of grief, and my mother, sinking into depression, never recovered from her passing. To her, she had been more than a mother. My mother had a deeply fractured childhood. She grew up without her own mother, who had to leave for Gibraltar to make a living, and without ever meeting her father, who died in the war before he could even marry. Later, my grandmother married a man who was an alcoholic and a freeloader, typical of that era. He never took care of my mother, quite the opposite. The only role model she had, the only person she felt had loved her unconditionally, was my great-grandmother. And when she died, my mother wanted to die too. She clung to my little sister, Lorena, who was still just a child. That experience would leave a deep mark on my sister’s childhood and her life.
summary: Описание последовательных финансовых кризисов семьи, потери дома, смерти прабабушки и глубокой депрессии матери, которая потеряла смысл жизни после её ухода, а также влияние этой травмы на сестру рассказчика.

title: Бегство от дома и ранняя независимость
text: I was eight years old, and I ran away from it all. I escaped to the streets, to school. The last thing I wanted was to be at home. My father came home late; he worked all day to get the family business back on its feet and had another job on top of that because otherwise, we wouldn’t make it to the end of the month. It was a sad time, and I drifted away, distancing myself. I couldn’t bear my mother’s sorrow, and at the same time, I felt so responsible for her…
summary: Восемнадцатилетний рассказчик убегает от эмоционально тяжёлой атмосферы дома, ищет refuge в школе и на улицах, не вынося печали матери, но чувствуя за неё ответственность.

title: Пубертатный опыт: первое сексуальное пробуждение и телесное self-acceptance
text:
When I was eleven or twelve years old, we moved again, this time to my grandmother’s house—a very small one, where I could hear my parents making love—the sensations, the sounds, the words... I got aroused, then afraid. I hid it, but I’ll never forget it.

At that age, I had a good relationship with my body. I felt pretty, well-balanced, tall, slim, cute. At a pool, I flirted with a friend; he looked at me, and the feeling was pleasant. I got tingles, I blushed, there was a sense of seduction. I swam, feeling the water caress my skin. I was on vacation with my parents; it was our first vacation ever. My little brother was still very young. We played in the waves, and I felt something akin to happiness… though I’m not sure if it was happiness or euphoria.
summary: В возрасте 11-12 лет рассказчик сталкивается с несознательным восприятием сексуальных действий родителей, что вызывает возбуждение и страх, одновременно развивая положительное отношение к своему телу через плавание, флирт и ощущение собственной привлекательности.

title: Море как источник духовной и эмоциональной свободы
text: The sea has shaped my life; I also carry within me my father’s seafaring legacy: his experience of freedom, his longing for vastness, his courage, his drive to go beyond, to dive into the intangible, to find pleasure, renewal, and a return to myself. I swim down as deep as I can, until I feel a hint of danger. And when I do, I keep going. I realize nothing happens, that the feeling is even better, and I just want to keep swimming, to never stop… Out there, I didn’t mind being alone. Quite the opposite. The sensation was sublime. It’s where I first encountered the feeling of infinity, a spiritual yearning, the sense of being part of something immense. I’ve always been an excellent swimmer. I learned from my father. I would have loved to compete, but at the time, affording travel and training wasn’t easy. So instead, I became the champion among friends and cousins. One day, my father organized a race at the beach. I was the only girl competing against all the boys. I swam until I was completely exhausted but I finished first. The joy of beating them all! Of standing on that podium, being the best—the best for him, for my father. These small victories in childhood gave me strength, a rush, a euphoria that masked a deeper sense of lack—the absence of maternal support, the smallness of being little among the grown-ups.
summary: Морей символизирует свободу и духовную глубину, наследуемую от отца; плавание становится метафорой поиска бесконечности и самовосстановления, а детские победы в плавании дают ощущение силы и эйфории, компенсируя эмоциональную нехватку.

title: Подростковый кризис идентичности и отторжение материнского идеала
text:
Then came winter, always so bleak. And at home, growing up felt impossible. I felt different. I wasn’t like my mother. I didn’t dream of becoming a proper young lady who would find a good boyfriend and get married. I didn’t know who I was, but I always knew that wasn’t what I wanted. Maybe my only defense was my rebellion against her. I wanted to leave, to go far away, to be a journalist, a teacher, a historian... I felt trapped there, desperate to escape, but I knew nothing about the world beyond the borders of my small town.

I was thirteen then, already 5’6”, lanky and awkward, slouching because I didn’t know what to do with this body that suddenly felt too long, too strange. I felt ugly, out of place, unsure of what being a woman even meant. My father pulled away from me. I was no longer his little girl, no longer the chosen one. And my mother saw me as so different from her that she didn’t know what to do with me. Since I was little, she’d poured hydrogen peroxide into my hair to bleach it, to make me blonde like her. She made me walk up and down the hallway with books balanced on my head so I’d stand straighter. She signed me up for children’s fashion shows so I could learn to walk like a model... But I knew I disappointed her. I’d tried, but I didn’t fit the mold. I would never be the delicate, graceful, fair-haired young woman she once was—polished, well-mannered, effortlessly charming to men. I didn’t measure up. Next to my mother, I felt monstrous, ugly. But I had my pride. I never showed her my pain, my longing for her to accept me, to embrace me as I was. Instead, I turned my back on her. I rejected her. I convinced myself I was above her.
summary: В тринадцать лет рассказчик переживает глубокий идентичный кризис: отторжение женственного идеала матери, чувство неполноценности и уродливости по сравнению с ней, попытки соответствовать её ожиданиям через внешние изменения, и最终 отвержение и эмоциональное дистанцирование как форма самосохранения.

title: Школьные годы и духовное пробуждение
text: The best part of my life was school. There, I learned, I felt valued, I was loved. And it also gave me the chance to travel, to leave La Línea. I took part in summer retreats where I met people from other places, people different from me. I became involved with the Teresian sisters, fell in love with my teacher, and through my love for her, I discovered my love for God, for faith, for prayer. I sublimated my sexual awakening into religious experience. I began reading St. John of the Cross and St. Teresa, memorizing the poems that moved me the most. I saw myself in mystical ecstasy—a love that, even then, carried strong sexual undertones, though I didn’t yet know what my sexuality was. Now I realize I was attracted to women, but no one had ever spoken to me about such things. So I sought deep intimacy with certain teachers and with friends, exchanging letters—love letters, though I never told myself that’s what they were.
summary: Автор описывает школьный период как время духовного и эмоционального роста, где она влюбилась в учительницу, что привело к открытию своей веры и подавленной гомосексуальной привязанности, выраженной через религиозный опыт и тайные письма.

title: Пробуждение внутреннего мира и одиночество
text: I can now see how, during that time, my passion for intimacy began to awaken—the deep need to form an intense bond with someone I choose, to be utterly special to them. I felt unacknowledged jealousy that tormented me. I wrote poetry, started my diary, and began crafting a private world of fantasy, sadness, and solitude. In my room, I daydreamed about my life, telling myself I was different, that my parents and family didn’t understand me. I wandered through imagined cities, picturing myself as the protagonist of a special life—one unlike my family’s, unlike the people around me—something extraordinary. But the adolescent in me felt lonely, sad, unmoored, filled with a restless longing I didn’t know where to place, trapped in a body I struggled to accept. There was no one to talk to about what I felt, no role models to look up to.
summary: Автор осознает растущую потребность в глубокой эмоциональной близости, выражает её через поэзию и дневник, живет в мире фантазий из-за чувства чужачности и одиночества, не находя понимания у сверстников и взрослых.

title: Разочарование в сверстниках и вопросы идентичности
text: My friends were starting to like boys, but to me, they seemed crude, rough, aggressive. I couldn’t share my inner world with them. I was thirteen, and I was trying. I went to parties, I danced, I let them touch me, I hung out in groups… but I didn’t feel anything. I wasn’t myself. Questions started plaguing me: Who am I? What do I need? What do I want? What do I desire? Where do I belong?
summary: Подросток чувствует отчуждение от сверстников, интересующихся мальчиками, не находит отклика в типичных подростковых активностях и начинает задавать себе фундаментальные вопросы о своей идентичности и месте в мире.

title: Духовный конфликт и подавление sexuality
text: A teacher at school once told me I was like the rich young man from the Gospel who had all the qualities to be called, but when chosen by God, did not follow Him. That comment struck me deeply and stayed with me. One day, we were scolded harshly for staying out late with boys. That was when the stigma around sexuality took hold—the feelings of guilt, the sin… It all settled into my imagination, lodged itself in my memory, unattended, because I didn’t know how to process it. All I could do was bury it and move on.
summary: Комментарий учителя и публичное порицание за отношения с мальчиками усилили внутренний конфликт между религиозными идеалами и подавленной сексуальностью, приведя к чувству вины и вытеснению переживаний.

title: Поиск смысла через служение и отношения
text: So, until I turned twenty, I juggled my religious commitment, my involvement with Christian communities, and my dedication to helping the less fortunate with my deep need to form strong bonds, to build intense, special relationships—the search for union.
summary: До двадцати лет автор пытается совместить религиозную преданность, общественную деятельность и жажду глубоких эмоциональных связей, видя в них путь к духовной и эмоциональной целостности.

title: Средняя школа: отчуждение и самозащита
text: The atmosphere grew harsher. I was in secondary school now, and relationships there were much more difficult. There were so many boys, the teachers were more detached, nothing like the dedicated Teresian nuns, and the environment was tense... It was a jungle. Toughness mattered more than intelligence, dominating others more than studying… At fifteen, I had gained weight, cut my hair short like a boy, and didn’t feel good in my body… but I didn’t really connect with that feeling. Instead, I rejected what I didn’t have and clung even more to my own way of understanding life: I wasn’t feminine, but I had ideas, strong emotions. I wanted something that no one in that lost corner of the world seemed able to understand.
summary: В средней школе автор сталкивается с враждебной, гипермаскулинной средой, отвергает традиционную женственность, опираясь на свой интеллект и эмоциональную глубину как на источники самоуважения и отличия от окружающих.

title: Друзья, наставники и первые шаги к самовыражению
text: I had always had friends, people who loved me, groups where I took the lead. They liked me for being a bit of a clown, bold, daring, affectionate. I had a special intuition for seeking out people who were good for me, who helped me grow, like my friend Pepe Luis, who helped me with Latin and Greek because I hadn’t studied them in my earlier curriculum. I found good teachers who became my lifeline, like Inmaculada, who had me recite Lorca for the first time. That was when I started reading poetry, making the words of poets my own, living through their emotions, their worlds.
summary: Несмотря на трудности, автор находит поддержку в друзьях и наставниках, особенно в Пепе Луисе и Инмакуладе, которые помогают ей развить интеллектуально и эмоционально через язык, литературу и поэзию.

title: Сложные отношения с мужчинами и тайна веры
text: At fifteen, I was in high school. It was a gray building battered by the Levante winds, where storm surges sometimes flooded the place. I tried hard to adapt to both schoolwork and relationships with men. But I didn’t feel like boys my age were really interested in me. My relationship with them was strange. Now I can see that I had been hiding my sexuality because it was different, but back then, I didn’t understand myself. I kept my religious calling a secret. None of my friends knew, nor did my family, though my mother sensed it, and her critical gaze made me pull away from her even more, feeling rejected.
summary: В пятнадцать лет автор чувствует отсутствие взаимного интереса со стороны сверстников-мужчин, осознает позже, что скрывала свою гомосексуальность, и держит в тайне своё религиозное призвание, усугубляя отчуждение от матери.

title: Конфликт и одиночество в роли лидера
text: In my final year of high school, I was class representative. We had to make a decision about a subject, and I made a proposal. The vice-representative disagreed, an argument broke out, and he slapped me in front of everyone. I felt hurt and humiliated; against brute force, there was nothing I could do. No one defended me. I despised him and tried to rise above it, hiding my pain and fear. And so, the divide between me and the male world grew even wider.
summary: Как классовый представитель, автор сталкивается с публичным насилием со стороны мужчины, оставаясь без защиты, что усиливает её отчуждение от мужского мира и укрепляет ощущение одиночества и несправедливости.

title: Прибежище в вере и ощущение принадлежности
text: As a child, I had identified with my father and with masculinity. But by then, the world of men didn’t see me as an equal, and I didn’t feel like the other girls either. I didn’t share their concerns, I wasn’t part of the game of sexuality with men. Where did I belong in that jungle? I kept seeking refuge in my religious calling. There, I was seen, valued. I could talk about my feelings, be among women, connect deeply with others. I wasn’t strange there. I belonged. And I enjoyed a sense of leadership.
summary: Автор описывает, как религиозное сообщество стало для неё единственным местом, где она чувствовала себя понятой, принятой и способной к глубоким отношениям и лидерству, в противоположность отчуждению в светской школе и семье.

title: Подростковые годы: подавленность и бунт
text: Throughout my adolescence, I felt suffocated, repressed. I couldn’t meet society’s expectations of a “proper young lady,” a little woman-in-the-making. My mother’s demands on how I should behave in public made me feel weird, insecure, powerless, and terribly alone. I masked all of this with rebellion, defiance against my parents, their rules, their way of life. Inside me, a completely ego-driven thought took root: I am better than them. But at the same time, I had a real thirst to explore other aspects of life.
summary: The narrator describes feeling suffocated by societal expectations of femininity during adolescence, responding with rebellion and a sense of superiority, while also harboring a genuine curiosity about life beyond imposed roles.

title: Пробуждение социальной и политической осознанности
text:
As I was about to start university, my social and political awareness began to awaken. I founded a Christian social action group in a working-class fishing neighborhood, where we worked with the people and celebrated the Eucharist like the first Christians. In this group, I finally felt comfortable with boys and formed my first male friendships, many of which still last today. Pepe Luis was one of them, and our friendship later deepened through political activism in the Andalusian Socialist Party. Eventually, we became a couple.

Three new teachers crossed my path. Vicky, my Contemporary History professor, opened my eyes to a new way of seeing history and understanding what had happened in my country during the 20th century. Juan, my Contemporary Literature professor, introduced me to an incredible number of writers and playwrights. I discovered the intellectual and artistic brilliance of Republican Spain, and the cultural devastation the Francoist dictatorship had brought upon the country. Franco had been dead for only two years, and I had grown up with a very distorted version of the Civil War and its aftermath. Another Juan, my Philosophy professor, led me to reflect on a worldview that wasn’t based on religious dogma: Kant, Hume, Nietzsche…
summary: As university approached, the narrator's social and political consciousness awakened through founding a Christian activist group and forming meaningful relationships, while three professors expanded her intellectual horizons by revealing suppressed historical and philosophical truths.

title: Интеллектуальное увлечение и эмоциональная зависимость
text: The year before university, my eyes began to open. I loved my classes, I excelled in my studies. Learning has always been a pleasure for me, and it still is. I think my grandmother and aunt instilled that passion in me when I was little, teaching me the world’s capitals upstairs in their apartment. I absorbed knowledge easily, showed interest, and was praised for it. That made me feel loved; it was a pleasant sensation of achievement, growth, and capability. My father also loved teaching me things. He taught me to swim and helped me with school projects, and through that, I felt like his daughter. Later, I had teachers who believed in me and supported me in pursuing a better education. All of this built my ego, but in a way, it also saved me. My experience of life was completely emotional. I was blinded by the need to feel loved. And in a place where intellectual development was scarce, my love of learning gave me structure, a lifeline for the emotional storms that would soon take over my youth.
summary: Before university, the narrator's love of learning—nurtured by family and teachers—became both an ego-building achievement and an emotional lifeline, providing structure amid emotional deprivation and a deep craving for love and validation.

title: Университет: лидерство в общежитии и дискомфорт в аудиториях
text:
Finally, the moment arrived to leave for university—the long-awaited chance to get away from my parents, from my hometown, from the small-minded society that, I felt, looked at me with suspicion, not knowing where to place me. I needed space. I needed to fly, to get away in order to find myself. I chose to study Philosophy and Education Sciences at the University of Seville.

In my first years, the focus of my life was the university residence. There, I could recreate the happy environment of my childhood school. I thrived in a position of leadership, enjoyed the sympathy of my peers, and was well-regarded by the tutors. I felt completely at ease and poured all my energy into maintaining that privileged position.

In university classrooms, however, I didn’t feel as comfortable. Academically, I had no problems, but the world was bigger now, and I couldn’t quite grasp it. And men? They were still strangers to me, whom I distrusted and with whom I competed. I hadn’t yet learned how to engage with them in a seductive way, and I sensed they weren’t interested in me. If they don’t show interest in me, I won’t show interest in them. And so, they remained outside my world, beyond my sphere of concern.
summary: At university, the narrator found leadership and belonging in the residence but remained emotionally and socially disconnected in classrooms, particularly with men, whom she viewed as rivals and strangers due to lingering distrust and insecurity.

title: Первая глубокая романтическая связь и ее трагический конец
text:
During this time, I had my first intense romantic experience. I fell for a classmate. I loved her with the passion of a first forbidden love. I needed to be close to her, to share intimacy, and when I couldn’t, I felt a deep frustration, a sadness that drained my will to live. In our moments together, we shared physical affection, had deep conversations, and talked about our ideals. But we never spoke about what it meant to be two women in a relationship. In that environment, it was a massive taboo. And we weren’t ready to face it.

And for the first time, I experienced the pain of heartbreak. She left me for another friend, and that was how I fell into the first great crisis of my life, burning in the hell of abandonment. I vomited, lost my appetite, dropped twenty kilos, failed my classes for the first time, shut myself away, and cried alone… I couldn’t tell anyone what was happening to me because I couldn’t even admit to myself what I felt for her. But it hit me like a violent blow, like a vice tightening around my heart, and, above all, with a deep sense of confusion over what was happening. Trapped by my youthful pride and my overabundance, I couldn’t accept that she could love someone else more than me… It just didn’t make sense. If I loved her with passion, devotion, and unwavering loyalty, if my love was unique and complete, then she had to love me back.
summary: The narrator recounts her first intense romantic relationship with a woman, marked by passion and idealism but shadowed by societal taboo and silence; when her partner left her, she suffered a devastating emotional collapse fueled by pride, confusion, and an unconscious belief that love must be reciprocated.

title: Прятки за равнодушием и первая буря любви
text: I never showed her my pain. In front of her, I acted indifferent, as if I were handling the situation with ease. I believed that by doing so, she would return to me, that my strength would win her over. I was convinced I must never show her my anger or heartbreak. My irrational belief was that if I humbled myself, if I revealed my need for her, she would reject me… she would see my smallness, my incompleteness. This was the first great love storm of my adult life. I lived my own private hell, sharing it with no one. My pride kept my heart locked shut, unable to express my suffering. I couldn’t bear the idea of others seeing me wounded, lacking, or desperate. Life struck me down and forced me to step off my pedestal, at least a few steps. I was twenty years old, still deeply unaware of myself, of my own neurotic patterns, of how unbearable it was for me to accept frustration. But whether I understood it or not, frustration won; I had no choice but to endure it. That made me more human, more real. Many more blows still awaited me before I would start to understand that pain is an inescapable part of the journey.
summary: Автор описывает подавление боли после разрыва, веря, что равнодушие вернёт любовь, и переживание внутренней бури, которая заставляет смириться с разочарованием и вырасти через боль.

title: Крушение идеала и бегство в завоевание мужчин
text: If my mother had been my first ideal woman and had abandoned me—if she didn’t recognize my worth, if I understood that she had withdrawn her love—now, once again, a woman to whom I had given all my love was leaving me. With that, something inside me broke, and the idea that if I loved, I would always be loved in return began to crumble. And in that moment, the animal emerged—the beast crawled out of its cave, claiming its place in the world. I broke off my religious commitment, left behind the female-only enclosure that was the university residence, and threw myself into the conquest of men. I wanted to prove to myself and to the world that I could seduce them, love them, be desired by them, and find among them the great love I had always longed for. My first man was my friend’s brother. If I couldn’t have her, I would have her brother. I tried to be the perfect girlfriend, to follow my mother’s example. But it didn’t work. Then came Pepe Luis, who has always been a part of my life. I started doing theater at university, my world was expanding, my experiences multiplying.
summary: После второго предательства любовным идеалом рушится вера в взаимную любовь, автор отказывается от религии и женской среды, начинает искать подтверждение через завоевание мужчин, вступая в отношения с другом друга и Пепе Луисом.

title: Предательство без вины и погоня за интенсивностью
text: Pepe was the first person I betrayed and hurt without remorse, without conscience. I didn’t know what I wanted—I was pure impulse, desire, and an endless search for satisfaction. I loved him as a friend, but we became a couple because he wanted it, and I let myself be swept along. I had no idea how to navigate relationships, and he was kind and generous with me. Together, we dove headfirst into the adventure of youth—going to concerts, hitchhiking, traveling in the old car he had inherited from his father. We camped in remote places, got involved in politics… Pepe craved the intensity of life and love as much as I did, but he wanted it with me—I was his center. For me, he was my escape from confinement, the key to experiment. He gave me security because he loved me and took care of me. In return, I cheated on him in the worst possible way, without a hint of guilt. In an instant, our relationship came to an end, and I moved on to something else. I had fallen in love with my acting professor, who was older than me and in a stable relationship with another woman. But I didn’t care. By then, nothing and no one could stop me.
summary: Автор описывает первые отношения с Пепе, построенные на импульсе и стремлении к интенсивности, измену без вины, переход к запретной любви с профессором и полное поглощение желанием быть желанной.

title: Театр как новая религия и погружение в гедонизм
text: From that moment on, theater became my god and my calling, replacing my former religious beliefs. I broke away from the life I had known and plunged into the darkest labyrinths of bohemia—into the night, the wild abandon, the hedonism, the sex, the independence. Dedicating myself to theater meant defying my father’s wishes for the first time, and in response, he withdrew both his moral and financial support. I was shattering the image of the ideal daughter. I felt the sting of his rejection, but by then, I had already been swept up in the whirlwind of a new life, a storm pulling me further away, pushing me to lose myself, to go mad… and I needed that. At the time, I wanted to be the best at the theater school where I had begun my training—the most admired by my teachers, the most beloved by my classmates, especially by the most exclusive group. And I succeeded. I was one of the best, and I was also one of the most adored. I had a deep need to stand out socially, though I wasn’t fully aware of it. I was too proud to admit my competitiveness. That attitude sapped my energy and strength, holding me back from my goals. I distracted myself by avoiding direct confrontation because, deep down, what I craved most was to be loved by everyone, to have them all under my spell. And, as I would later come to understand through the words of Hugo, my therapist: “…sometimes, to be true to yourself, you have to betray others.”
summary: Театр заменяет религию, автор погружается в богемный образ жизни, ищет признания и власти через успех в театре, избегая прямых конфликтов, стремясь быть обожаемой всеми, даже ценой предательства других.

title: Секс как завоевание и разрушение чистоты
text: My experience with sex also escalated rapidly and intensely. I was focused on conquest, not pleasure… on feeling desired, not surrendering to my own desire. During those years, my sexual experiences were deeply self-destructive, and my body became a temple desecrated by my need to have every man who crossed my path. It was as if I erased in one fell swoop my twenty years of virginity and belief in the purity of love.
summary: Секс становится инструментом завоевания и подтверждения желанности, а не источником удовольствия, prowadя к саморазрушению и потере прежних идеалов чистоты и невинности.

title: Запретная любовь и жизнь в компульсивной интенсивности
text: I continued my relationship with my professor, even though he had a partner and had no intention of leaving her for me. But all of that only made him more enticing to me. Once again, I was caught up in the thrill of a forbidden love story, intoxicated by the excitement of chasing what was hardest to obtain, what was out of reach. During those years, I had boyfriends, I was unfaithful, I learned what it meant to be “the other woman”—the secrecy of love, doing whatever I pleased. And not once did I feel guilty for any of it. I was alive; I could only feel alive through compulsion and intensity. It was the era of drugs, alcohol, unprotected sex, and endless nights. I pulled out the plug, and the monster inside me demanded its freedom—wild, relentless. It wanted everything.
summary: Отношения с женатым教授 усиливают влечение к запретному, автор живёт в цикле компульсивных связей, измен и самодеструкции, находя живость только в интенсивности, без чувства вины.

title: Конфликт с матерью и внутренняя стыдливость
text:
Once, when I was twenty-two years old, I was at my parents’ house, taking a shower. My mother walked in and showed me a paper she had found in my room, an appointment slip for my IUD check-up. I stood there, naked, and she called me a “whore.” Once again, I felt her rejection. I didn’t defend myself; I just told her she knew nothing about my life. I started coming home less and less, keeping my distance. Those moments became imprinted in my body, feeding my guilt, the stigma around my sexuality, and the way I experienced it.

Now I realize how much my relationship with my mother has made me suffer, how much it pushed me away from her, how hard I worked to not need her—to place myself above her, as if that could ease the pain of not having her acceptance. As a child, I wasn’t the daughter she had wanted. As a teenager, I began turning into a woman unlike her. My commitment to the Teresian nuns wasn’t what she wanted for me either. Later, when I started being with men, in her eyes, I became a whore. When I chose theater as my profession and way of life, she disapproved again. And when she eventually found out I liked women, that was the final blow. How could she have a daughter so different from her?

My mother’s rejection wasn’t obvious. There were arguments, fights, and quarrels, but it wasn’t overt. It was buried: a silent criticism, a look of disapproval, of disdain, of disappointment. And her rejection chipped away at my self-esteem, my strength; it made me feel wrong, ashamed. That’s the word: I felt ashamed of myself. And so, when I went back to my hometown, I hid the way I lived, changed how I dressed, and tried to lead a social life that, in my mind, aligned more with what I thought my parents wanted for me. This didn’t make me happy. It caused me a lot of anguish, so I distanced myself from them. So much so that, in important moments for them, times when a daughter would normally have been there, I wasn’t: my mother’s surgery, my father’s surgery, moving…
