Coming into contact with our own vulnerability is wisdom, it is a guide, a light, bringing us closer to our essence—to love.

How is my life now, at fifty-six? How is it to work, to travel, to move through the world with this body, this soul, this age? How is it to accept exhaustion, to take pleasure in small things, in simply observing life? I always wanted to be present, but my presence used to get lost in the need to please, to prove my worth, to do. It got lost in the gaze of others, in self-aggrandizement, in running from how small I sometimes felt. My life once drew meaning from intensity.

Now, as I finish this account of my life, I find myself in a faraway place, across the sea. The journey has worn me down; I’ve fallen ill. I’ve felt small and unsteady, and more than anything, I just want to go home—to sit in my room, unmoving. I remember Claudio’s story about the seasoned seeker who no longer needs to leave his room to find the longed-for bluebird, the metaphor for wisdom—because everything he seeks is already there, in that still center, in that simplicity. And as this realization settles in, so does the fear—the fear of losing my strength, of staring into the abyss. And yet, alongside it, there is also a great hunger to live, to devour life.
summary: The narrator reflects on embracing fragility as a source of strength, reevaluating presence and purpose in midlife, and finding wisdom in stillness while balancing fear of decline with a renewed hunger for life.

title: Возвращение к жизни после болезни
text: After my illness, I spent years in a kind of Heaven, with no desire to return to the world. It was a time of departure, the most spiritual period of my journey. But after turning fifty, it was as if life took me back again, devouring me with an insatiable thirst to experience it all, to drink it in. It’s beautiful to feel this, to know that my way of experiencing life has deepened. But now and then, I grow tired. I want to stop, to be still, to simply be—to listen to the pulse of my existence and prepare myself for letting go.
summary: The author reflects on their spiritual withdrawal after illness and the subsequent return to a deepened, insatiable engagement with life after turning fifty, balanced by a growing need for stillness and presence.

title: Осознанное наблюдение за умом
text: I now understand more deeply the practice Claudio taught us: Observe the mind. Be the witness, watching one thought after another. I’m not used to this—I’ve always observed emotions more than thoughts. But now, I watch my thoughts, and I realize how heavy they are, how enslaving the mind can be. Everything is in my mind, even if I’m not fully conscious of it, shaping my life from the shadows. My path now is to become more aware of my mind—to see its darkness and its light. Because that unseen part of me shapes my actions, my emotions, my very way of being.
summary: The author describes their growing practice of observing thoughts as a witness, recognizing the mind's powerful influence on life and emotions, and commits to becoming more conscious of its patterns and shadows.

title: Освобождение через осознанность мыслей
text: During a therapeutic exercise, I felt the overwhelming presence of my mind like never before—the frenzied movement of my thoughts, amplified as if under a magnifying glass. I could hear them, their voices, their noise, their chaos… And I realized that awareness is what creates space, what liberates. If I can become more conscious of my mind’s movements each day, more space will open up—through meditation, through breath, through watching the mind itself. And in those spaces between thoughts, there is freedom. There is happiness.
summary: Through a therapeutic exercise, the author experiences the chaotic nature of their thoughts and discovers that mindful awareness creates mental space, leading to freedom and happiness between thoughts.

title: Критика поверхностной медитации и поиск глубины
text: I also see now that when I meditate, my focus has been on calming my mind, soothing it—but not truly observing it. My attention is drawn to the body, to sensations, to emotions, to moments of insight. But I haven’t intentionally studied my mind itself—its weight, its restlessness, its light and shadow. And yet, little by little, humor and awareness bring relief. I see now: the relentless noise of the mind is an unbearable torment, one that pulls me away from true life, from the peace I long for…
summary: The author reflects that their meditation practice has focused on calming the mind rather than observing it, realizing that the mind's relentless noise is a source of torment that distracts from true peace and presence.

title: Питание духа в упадке тела
text: When the body begins to decline, the mind must be illuminated to grasp the Mystery. It is time to nourish the spirit, to let it guide me. The soul is needed to walk through this life. May I never lose my soul; may I feel it in every step. Why try to decipher the ocean, when the waves return it to you effortlessly?
summary: As the body declines, the author emphasizes the need to illuminate the mind and nourish the spirit to grasp life's mystery, trusting the soul's guidance and the natural return of wisdom like waves to the shore.

title: Слова учителя как исцеляющая мантры
text: And so, I close this account of my life, carrying with me the words of my teacher, Claudio Naranjo: “No one can perceive the bluebird except through the eyes of an experienced seeker. It takes the trials of the journey, the pain of experience, to truly penetrate the invisible that was always there.”
summary: The author concludes their life account by carrying forward Claudio Naranjo's teaching about the bluebird metaphor, which represents wisdom accessible only through lived experience and inner seeking.

title: Кризис в отношениях и разлука
text:
Four years later, I write an epilogue

I hesitated to write this epilogue.

I still resist it, but the delay in publishing this book—these four years that have passed since I finished my story—have given me both the opportunity and the push to do it.

In October 2018, I returned from a trip to Amsterdam with Susi. Our relationship was in shambles—it was as if we no longer understood each other at the core, as if we were speaking different languages. It was painful yet necessary to accept that love isn’t always enough, that sometimes paths diverge, and the needs of two people who love each other no longer align.

Susi had sensed it for a long time, and deep down, I knew it too, even though I refused to name it, to give it space among the realities my mind allowed in. There was nothing left to say or do—she told me she was leaving, and when I returned from teaching a SAT Program course in Russia, she was gone. I came home to find the house empty of her, half the furniture missing. A home stripped bare, mirroring my own existence in that moment. The greatest fear of my life had taken form—it was now something I could speak of, though it pained me to do so.
summary: The author describes the painful realization and acceptance of the end of their 27-year relationship with Susi, reflecting on misaligned needs, emotional avoidance, and the profound loneliness of returning to an empty home after her departure.

title: Поддержка учителя в боли разлуки
text:
On January 1, 2019, I wrote to Claudio to tell him everything. This was his reply:

Dear Consuelo,

I am still in Italy, and I no longer even use my phone since my last hospitalization here. I’m focused entirely on finishing my writings before I lose this body, which fails me more each day. I deeply regret your suffering after separating from Susi after twenty-seven years, and I hope you do not shy away from it, so that it may serve you fully—since, it seems, nothing gives us as much as what we lose.

A big hug until we meet again...

Claudio.

His words became a healing mantra for me: “Do not shy away from pain so that it may serve you fully,” and “Nothing gives us as much as what we lose.”
summary: After contacting Claudio Naranjo about her separation from Susi, the author receives a compassionate reply that becomes a healing mantra, urging her not to avoid pain so it can serve her growth and emphasizing that loss offers profound gifts.

title: Постоянная любовь и поиск свидетеля жизни
text:
More than a year has passed, and I still haven’t separated from her inside me. I haven’t stopped loving, nor have I detached.

In July 2019, our teacher died. And once again, the same question I had asked Claudio when my father died resurfaced: Who sees me now? Who bears witness to my life? No father, no teacher, no beloved. Who sees me, then? Who do I live for? Just yesterday, I told a friend: for God, for myself, for that essence that has been with me since I existed, for my soul.

But in this experience, there is a deep solitude. Almost every night, I wake up to an enormous, unbearable void that aches, that devours, that pulls me into the abyss. I feel a fear of dying alone, and despair overtakes me. Everything is gone, everyone is gone—the dreams, the person I thought was the love of my life, the future I had imagined. And still, I keep asking myself: Who do I live for?
summary: Over a year after separation, the author still feels internally connected to Susi, and after Claudio's death, confronts deep existential questions about who witnesses their life and for whom they live, overwhelmed by solitude and the void of loss.

title: Смирение и сдача судьбе
text: Of course, I know that the meaning of life is life itself—surrendering unconditionally to fate without demanding explanations. And I keep in mind the path of heroes, though I wish there were more heroines to look to, though there are fewer stories of them. I think of Oedipus, who did not truly see until he tore out his own eyes, and I remember Claudio’s words when I fell ill: “Have you taken this as a punishment or as an opportunity?”
summary: The author affirms that life's meaning lies in unconditional surrender to fate, draws inspiration from heroic paths (while noting the lack of heroine narratives), and reflects on Claudio's reframing of illness as either punishment or opportunity for growth.

title: Эго и страдание в горе
text:
I know that what hurts is ego—the sting of love failing when I believed love was everything, the weight of that word: separation, the wound of being left, abandoned, of watching everything collapse. It’s ego because I assumed I had control, that I was the cause, that I could have prevented it. If I could embrace true humility, there would still be pain, still sadness, but not anguish—not suffering.

I wrote these words after an intense therapeutic experience in Brindisi last year:

I realize that all of life is dying, that to live is to die continuously.

I recall the dream I had when Claudio left, where I asked myself why I hadn’t accompanied him on his passing. And the answer was in the experience: I stayed behind to learn how to die.

Everything is dying, and we don’t know how to do it—or at least, I don’t.

And living is that constant dying—dying to each bond, each attachment, each experience. It’s releasing, ceasing to grasp, to possess. Simply letting go, allowing things to leave, and welcoming what comes next—only to let go once more.
summary: The author reflects on how ego amplifies suffering in grief, framing life as a continuous process of dying and letting go, inspired by a therapeutic experience and a dream about Claudio’s departure.

title: Освобождение и одиночество как путь к себе
text:
I am still discovering what love looks like after letting go, after releasing, after detaching. Because the bond doesn’t disappear—only the attachment, the chain, the knot.

Grief.

Releasing.

Letting go.

Walking alone.

Being alone—without romantic love.

At times, a quiet joy emerges—the feeling of truly being alone with myself,

for the first time in my life.

Of listening to myself. Of allowing myself to be me.

At times, a newfound sense of freedom—a deep spontaneity.

Just me, with myself—alone.

And enjoying it.

But suddenly, anguish creeps in, dragging loneliness, death, illness—making me feel unbearably fragile. And I force myself to push through—to go to the theater, to study, to talk to my mother on the phone, to walk outside, to take a flight, to teach a course, to return home, to go to bed, to cook, to buy clothes, to see people.

Everything feels strange, and at times, unbearably hard.
summary: The author describes the duality of solitude—initially painful, then liberating and self-affirming—but still interrupted by waves of anguish that require active coping through daily engagement and creative expression.

title: Творчество как исцеление и преобразование боли
text:
Inside me, there is an ongoing battle—a pull to let go completely, to disappear, to cry and never stop.

And then, suddenly—life. The sun. The balcony and the park.

The dogs and the theater—the theater is saving me.

Being able to channel despair, rage, frustration, powerlessness, desolation—and also love—into art.

Because I still feel love.

And I feel deeply sensitive to even the smallest gestures of love from others—and I cherish them more than ever.

The little things.

And feeling what I am: a small being. That, perhaps, is the cure. To let go of grandiosity.

And yet, I keep reflecting—delving deeper into this holy freedom, into this essence of the warrior, the rebel, the wild, the untamed.

How do I transform sin into virtue, passion into gift, mistake into talent? How do I honor my essence—the jewel that the child I once was dreamed of, full of innocence? To be. To simply be what I am. To embrace my destiny without shame and without arrogance, with humility and gratitude. To take my gifts and create with them. To find the joy of being.

And poetry helps me—reading it, reciting it, working with it, writing it. “A single word, and everything is illuminated,” says Wajdi Mouawad.
summary: The author finds salvation in theater and art, using creativity to transform despair into expression, while seeking humility, authenticity, and joy in being through poetry and self-acceptance.

title: Поэтическое завершение: metamorphosis как жизнь и молчание
text:
I want to end this story with words that inspire me, illuminate me, heal me—words that give meaning to this journey where I feel utterly out of control, flung into the abyss, held up only by poetry and theater, which is also poetry.

I usually write from texts that pierce through me; I like to make them my own, to weave my words into them. That’s how I merge with Sophocles, Lorca, Gioconda Belli, Virginia Woolf… They are all in this final poem, and I am there with them:

Make way for the woman who never feared the tides of love or the hurricanes of scorn…

I need strength, energy, the leap, the resistance—

to feel sovereign, mistress of my own life, to recognize myself in the face I’ve worn at two, at thirty, at forty, at fifty.

Now I am Orlanda, living the gift of having existed in the twentieth century, the twenty-first, and why not—the twenty-second.

I move through history; I am an actress in Greece, standing in the great Dionysian festivals. I give voice to Antigone and say to this patriarchal civilization:

“It is you who draws the margins

that distort the truth

of what has always been just.

Must one obey

a law that is inhumane?

I do not know, nor does it matter now,

whether divine forces,

living nature,

or the power of the universe

created the unchanging,

unwritten laws—

timeless and eternal,

born with the first

spark of consciousness,

the laws that separate us from beasts,

that bind us and compel us,

echoing in the deepest

chambers of the soul.

I will not obey you

by betraying my own nature.”

But I tell Antigone this: Beasts are far more merciful than the laws of our civilization—freer and wiser.

I wish I could be a beast, to recognize myself in my animal self, to surrender to the limits of my body, my age, my ailments—to make peace with watching, with saying goodbye, with embracing myself and retreating, ceasing to fight, like the elder creature that I am.

And yet… oh, and yet… “Hope bites me like a dying wolf.”

I resist, I rebel,

“I dance, I stomp, I strip, I wrap you in me, you wrap me in you…”

You asked me, What comes next?

I don’t know, because I am still in this passage.

Awed by the metamorphosis of my body, my flesh, my blood, my bones.

I fear and tremble at what is yet to come.

And you answer: Love.

And I say: Not even that—silence.

The metamorphosis will be silence itself—the freedom of silence, the stillness, the end of striving, the sunbeam that simply warms, the deep listening to all my secrets, the embrace without demand, love that loves itself, love that loves you without needing you to love me, the joyful heartbeat, the anchored acceptance, the effortless dance, the surrender to becoming, without conditions. The metamorphosis will be life—life, life, life, the soul’s time in life!
summary: The author concludes with a powerful poetic invocation of sovereignty, mythic identification (Antigone, Orlanda), and a redefinition of metamorphosis as silent, self-sufficient life—beyond love, embracing stillness and self-embrace as ultimate freedom.

title: Journey to Final Metamorphosis
text:
And then, we will journey there—to where Antigone and Orlando have gone, where Oedipus and Tiresias have gone, where Juan, my father, and Claudio, my teacher, have gone. To where we all go—to the final metamorphosis.

I fly toward death.

Without wings.

Without eyes.

Without a body.
Lady of the stars with burning breath,
mistress of nocturnal songs,
possess me with your frenzy,
show me the light in the darkness.

Mother?
Father?
Love of my life!
Help me!

“Silence coils upon itself.
I am flesh of stone.
Soon, only dust.
Perhaps this is what must be—
between being and not being
until all is nothing.”

“To live without yesterday,
to live without tomorrow.”

I dissolve into you,
Lady of Souls.
A part of the whole,
which is everything and nothing.
Scattered in the wind.
Free.
Make me dance.
Make me dance.
Make me dance.
summary: A poetic and spiritual passage describing the journey toward death and final metamorphosis, invoking imagery of dissolution, silence, and unity with the Lady of Souls, culminating in a plea to be made to dance repeatedly.

title: Social E2 Subtype: The Empress/Emperor
text:
BOOK THREE: THE SOCIAL SUBTYPE

Passion in the sphere of instinct: How pride works in the social

A sense of belonging (whether to family, a group, or a tribe) is a core and often conflicted issue for all social subtypes. Social E2s are no exception. These ambitious individuals are like orphans searching for the necessary and legitimate place they were denied as children. Struggling to develop a positive, identifying bond with a secure parental figure, they transform their fear and anger into resentment. Lacking a role model to admire and someone to make them feel valued, they instead take on that role themselves. Thus, the “child of no one” strives to become the “parent of all.”

They cannot form a positive connection with any “parental” figure because, for them, opening up to recognize goodness in someone else (and therefore admiring them) is inextricably linked to feeling humiliated by that very person, whom they will inevitably come to resent.

Social E2s are generous and benevolent as long as they don’t feel challenged. But they are extremely sensitive, and any sign that they lack absolute control over others makes them feel insecure, triggering insecurity, authoritarian outbursts, and a domineering, invasive response.

With a strong sense of vengeance, they spend their lives striving to claim what they see as their rightful place at the top of the social hierarchy. Their ambition is fueled by a competitive and destructive drive, directed at the source of their own feelings of inadequacy and self-contempt. They swallowed the disappointment of an authoritarian father or an unsatisfied mother and now “vomit” that frustration onto others.

The term that defines this subtype (“Empress” or “Emperor”) evokes power, territoriality, leadership, and protection. But it also brings to mind tyranny, abuse, absolutism, and excess. These various aspects together paint a social dynamic marked by a strongly hierarchical view of relationships.

Among the proud, social E2s stand out by taking up space—physically, vocally, and through expressive gestures. Their presence exudes confidence and conviction. They are histrionic performers, adding a serious, almost worried expression to their demeanor, as if constantly preoccupied and committed to a greater cause; it’s the attitude of someone very mature, who knows what they are doing and what needs to be done. At times, their intensity can give them an air of clairvoyance, as if they see what others cannot. They often appear to carry a heavy weight, yet they do so with a sense of self-sacrifice and selflessness.

The social E2 replicates the roles and relational patterns they developed in childhood within their social interactions. They don’t just want their family and friends to see them as important. They want everyone to recognize them as a central, indispensable figure in their lives.

From a young age, social E2s were placed near adults, regarded as important within the family dynamic—but not as children. They missed out on the experience of simply being a child. Stepping into oversized shoes too soon, they received admiration from their parents for what they did rather than for who they were. Deprived of sibling-like peer connections, they struggle to relate to equals in any way other than through competition or dominance. They extend the triangulated dynamics of their early family system into all relationships, dividing people into allies or enemies, “with me or against me.”

This early confusion of roles carries into adulthood, shaping how they perceive relationships through a hierarchical lens. Social E2s categorize people based on influence and power, making it difficult for them to form emotional bonds that aren’t strategic or practical. They value others based on their position within a real or imagined institutional hierarchy—what might be a CEO or board member in a company, they apply to friendships, social groups, or family dynamics.

They equate a person’s status with their personal worth. They don’t truly see others or themselves. For them, doing is being, and only what they can outwardly display gives them a sense of identity. It could be said that among all Twos, social E2s are the least empathetic, relying heavily on strategy and organization. They have greater access to functions associated with the frontal and prefrontal lobes: planning, problem-solving, error detection, decision-making, social cognition, and working memory.

All are equal, but some more than others

The emperor expresses pride in the social realm, convinced they are far more capable than others when it comes to leading, planning, or executing any given task. Like all proud individuals, social E2s crave recognition—specifically, the validation of groups. Paradoxically, deep down, they struggle with intense self-doubt and a profound sense of loneliness.
summary: An in-depth analysis of the social subtype of Enneagram Type 2 (the Empress/Emperor), detailing its psychological roots, behavioral patterns, emotional dynamics, cognitive tendencies, and social perceptions, including their compensatory strategies for childhood neglect and their hierarchical worldview.

title: Самооценка и потребность во внимании
text: They believe they have much to contribute and often fantasize about their social impact and place in the world, imagining that their actions and opinions leave a lasting impression on others. They like to see themselves as extremely important and central to everything. Their narcissism demands that they remain at the center of attention: it doesn’t matter if they are disliked; what matters is that they’re never ignored.
summary: Описывает завышенную самооценку социальных E2, их стремление быть в центре внимания и нарциссическую потребность в признании, независимо от того, нравятся они другим или нет.

title: Сходство с E1 и эмоциональная отстраненность
text: In some ways, they resemble E1s, projecting an air of certainty, speaking with such passion and confidence that they easily persuade others, even if their knowledge is only superficial. Their anger can flare up suddenly when challenged or contradicted, and they seem immune to shame, since they remain disconnected from feelings of fear, lack, or insecurity.
summary: Сравнивает социальных E2 с E1 по проявлению уверенности и persuasive коммуникации, отмечая их внезапный гнев при противоречии и эмоциональную отстраненность от страха и стыда.

title: Самообраз и трудности с границами
text: Social E2s tend to have a self-image that is quite close to reality: they see themselves as capable, competent, committed, and hardworking. However, their struggle with boundaries prevents them from knowing when to stop, often pushing themselves to the limit. They are incredibly demanding of themselves. So much so that even illness won’t slow them down unless they end up in the hospital. They need someone in a position of authority to firmly enforce and convincingly justify the importance of self-care, as their deep-seated belief in limitless capability makes it hard for them to recognize when they’ve reached their limit.
summary: Описывает реалистичную самооценку социальных E2 как компетентных и трудолюбивых, но их невозможность устанавливать границы приводит к переутомлению и пренебрежению заботой о себе без внешнего вмешательства.

title: Лидерство и конфликт ролей
text: At the same time, they believe they are well-suited for leadership, though they often experience cycles of failure they seldom acknowledge. Their confusion around roles leads them to take an ambiguous stance toward their subordinates, treating them as equals and aligning themselves with a fraternal system. However, when they must exert authority, they take on a paternalistic role. And no one likes to be bossed around by a “brother acting like a father.” In their false sense of abundance, they try to please everyone, but their inability to delegate and follow through on all their commitments eventually forces them to step down or be removed.
summary: Анализирует склонность социальных E2 к лидерству, их рольную неопределенность (смещение между дружеским и отцовским поведением), склонность угождать всем и последующее выгорание из-за невозможности делегировать и выполнить все обязательства.

title: Личный опыт перегрузки и поиска одобрения
text: When I held a leadership position in a healthcare company, I tried to balance strong leadership with an indulgent approach, putting in a lot of effort to listen and accommodate everyone on my team. I exhausted myself seeking consensus, making promises I couldn’t keep, and overvaluing every request that came my way. I wanted to be the most beloved “boss,” despite working in a power structure that left little room for flexibility. At the same time, I sought the approval of higher-ups, without burning out. In short, I wanted to be loved by everyone, to please everyone, but in the end, I just felt incredibly alone.
summary: Персональный пример illustrates, как социальный E2 выгорает, пытаясь угодить всем, искать одобрение сверху и снизу, жертвуя своими границами и в итоге чувствуя глубокое одиночество malgré усилия.

title: Самоугождение как стратегия совладания
text: Social E2s are deeply committed and meticulous in every project they take on. However, they struggle with teamwork: they can be despotic toward both others and themselves. The self-indulgence that is common among prideful personalities manifests in social E2s through behaviors that serve as emotional relief, such as sex, food, media consumption, or exercise. These distractions help them disconnect from their own self-imposed pressures.
summary: Описывает приверженность социальных E2 проектам, их деспотизм в командной работе и использование самоугождения (секс, еда, медиа, спорт) как способа снять давление от самокритики и перфекционизма.

title: Оправдание самоугождения и прокрастинация
text: I expect so much from myself—doing many things, doing them well, knowing everything, being everywhere, never missing a thing… and with such passion that when something doesn’t go as I’d hoped, instead of engaging in self-criticism or analyzing the reasons why (“Those who try to do too much end up doing little… am I taking on too much?”), I become self-indulgent. I tell myself it’s fine, I give myself a pat on the back. I struggle to see my mistakes, and before I can even acknowledge that I might have made one, I’ve already forgiven myself.
summary: ПерSONальное отражение показывает, как социальный E2 избегает самокритики через немедленное самоугождение и прощение, не позволяя себе осознать ошибки из-за страха перед собственной несостоятельностью.

title: Прокрастинация как контроль и avoidance
text: Social E2s justify this self-indulgence by believing they “deserve” it because of everything they give to others. But, as we’ve pointed out, it’s also their only way of surrendering; of escaping their own internal control and relentless self-demands. If I have to wake up at five in the morning for a meeting, I do it without hesitation. But if I have to wake up at eight for something related to my personal well-being, I’ll find a thousand excuses to postpone it.
summary: Объясняет, как социальные E2 оправдывают самоугождение как заслуженное за обслуживание других, но на самом деле используют его как побег от самоконтроля, exemplified через прокрастинацию заботы о себе несмотря на дисциплину в работе.

title: Прокрастинация как утверждение власти и избегание ответственности
text: Another form of self-indulgence in social E2s is procrastination. It helps them avoid unpleasant or unrewarding tasks. It can also be a way of asserting dominance, since they decide when things get done. If a task is invisible, routine, or mundane, they either avoid it or delegate it to someone else. They might also procrastinate out of fear of success, fear of public failure, or fear of being called out for not delivering on their promises. In general, they struggle with time management because they take on more than they can realistically handle. Their difficulties with authority also contribute to their procrastination. For instance, if they have to report to a superior they don’t respect, they may delay completing a task just to avoid being accountable. Even when they do acknowledge an authority figure, they might still be slow to deliver, believing their work is flawless and doesn’t require review. Because, in their mind, there’s no room for error.
summary: Анализирует прокрастинацию у социальных E2 как многогранную стратегию: избегание рутины, утверждение контроля над временем, страх перед успехом/неудачей и сопротивление авторитету — все из-за перфекционизма и невозможности принять собственную уязвимость.

title: Реакция на неудачу и внешнее винивание
text: Social E2s have a low tolerance for frustration and feel powerless when their projects or ambitions don’t succeed. If they fail, they can feel anything from irritated to furious, blaming others or external circumstances rather than recognizing their own role or the unrealistic nature of their goals. They can be ruthless with subordinates, even though they see themselves as understanding, fair, and well-liked leaders. I was coordinating a team of seven people. The work environment and my relationships with them were becoming increasingly difficult, but I was convinced the problem was the team. Not me. I felt misunderstood despite all the effort I put in for them.
summary: Описывает низкую толерантность к фрустрации у социальных E2, склонность винить других в неудачах, жестокость по отношению к подчиненным несмотря на самообраз как справедливого лидера, и личный пример проекции вины на команду вместо самокритики.

title: Поведение социальной Э2 в конфликтной ситуации
text: One day, during a meeting, an educator whom I considered lazy was sharing an approach she had used that didn’t align with my instructions. I looked at her angrily and, raising my voice, I said, “Next time, I’ll smash your head in.” And I felt nothing about it. It was only when I glanced at my colleagues’ faces (they were horrified, angry) that I became somewhat aware of what I’d done. But I still didn’t think it was a big deal. I didn’t see any problem with it.
summary: Описывается эпизод проявления гнева и агрессии со стороны социальной Э2, который она не осознает как проблему, несмотря на реакцию коллег.

title: Манипулятивные навыки и стиль руководства социальной Э2
text:
ANA BAZA

One of their greatest skills is using empathy to mirror others, adopting their gestures, speech, and mannerisms to win them over. They can be manipulative, getting others to take on tasks they themselves don’t want to do. They surround themselves with the best people, selling them on an idea and showering them with praise and incentives. Those individuals, believing it’s a privilege to take on the task, end up doing the work, while the social E2 focuses on the creative aspects, organization, networking, or developing new projects.

They usually work long hours, becoming so deeply involved that they end up pushing themselves (and those around them) to exhaustion. They expect absolute loyalty and dedication from subordinates and collaborators, demanding the same level of availability that they give. This results in an intense, high-paced work environment that not everyone can or wants to keep up with. They are intolerant of other people’s limitations, seeing them as obstacles. As a result, they constantly try to “fix” and “improve” those around them. They tend to treat people as mere tools for achieving their goals, reducing interactions to transactional exchanges. They see family, partners, subordinates, and others as extensions of themselves, expecting them to be just as competent and brilliant.
summary: Описывается, как социальная Э2 использует эмпатию для манипуляции, создает высоконапряженную рабочую среду и рассматривает людей как инструменты для достижения целей.

title: Отношения с иерархией и peers у социальной Э2
text:
They are highly skilled at assessing the importance and capabilities of individuals within a social or work hierarchy. They often disregard those they perceive as being at the bottom, unless they see some advantage in forming a connection with them. For example, they may cultivate strong relationships with administrative staff or building personnel.

With those few they recognize as authority figures, they adopt a strategic charm. If they receive recognition from them, they see it as something rightfully owed to them for their hard work and talent. They easily view themselves as the key contributor to successes—even when achievements result from teamwork. If they don’t receive recognition, they downplay its importance, attributing it to mediocrity or jealousy on the part of their superiors.

And among peers, since they never fully integrate into a fraternal system, they establish competitive relationships, maintaining a self-appointed superiority that can come across as condescending and paternalistic. This often leads to isolation.
summary: Анализируется поведение социальной Э2 по отношению к подчиненным, авторитетам и коллегам: стратегическое очарование, конкуренция и изоляция из-за ощущения собственного превосходства.

title: Глубинная мотивация и внутренний конфликт социальной Э2
text: In the end, following an infantile pattern, E2s seek proximity to authority figures, to “adults,” whom they see as their natural reference points. However, while they neurotically pursue power and even aim to replace leaders, they ultimately find that achieving this does not satisfy their deeper longing. What they truly crave is a family where they will be recognized, loved, and accepted unconditionally. Beneath their dominant and fiercely independent exterior, they are essentially searching for someone who will finally protect them and take care of them.
summary: Раскрывается, что за стремлением к власти и доминированию социальная Э2 скрывает глубокую потребность в безусловной любви и защите, как в детстве.

title: Концепция долгов и манипуляции в отношениях у социальной Э2
text:
Debts

A social E2 shows no scruples when it comes to getting what they want. To that end, they form strategic alliances based on complicity—this can include bribery, blackmail, mutual assistance for personal gain, or temporary partnerships. Naturally, aside from outright illegal maneuvers, this might seem logical and reasonable in the pursuit of one’s own desires. However, for a social E2, the motivation is purely selfish, devoid of genuine compassion or solidarity—though they might convince themselves it’s for the greater good. In reality, the ambitious social E2 serves only themselves. Their generosity is part of a calculated charm, a seductive tool for influence. And in the end, they always take far more than they give. Besides, any “debts” owed to them are rarely forgiven, and the “favors” they bestow come with a steep price.

On the other hand, when a social E2 experiences rejection, failure, or being ignored, they take it as a deep humiliation, an assault on their dignity. These wounds don’t fade; they are stored as long-lasting resentment.

Being a creditor puts a social E2 in a position of power, allowing them to wield influence over others and use them in their plans. They have a vested interest in keeping debts alive for two main reasons: first, it allows them to appear above the need for repayment, reinforcing their false sense of abundance; second, it serves as a tool of control and dominance.

When I forgive someone, I do it from above, as if I were a high priestess granting absolution. I do this because I dislike people apologizing to me. I just need an explanation to ease the discomfort of not knowing where the mistake was. One day, an old friend came to apologize for something from the past. I didn’t let her fully apologize. Later, I realized that this way, I could keep her in debt to me forever.
summary: Описывается, как социальная Э2 использует концепцию долгов как инструмент контроля и власти, превращая прощение в способ удержания других в зависимости.

title: Неустанная потребность в признании и страх уязвимости у социальной Э2
text:
ANA BAZA

A deeply ambitious social E2 has an acute sensitivity for detecting when someone does not regard them with the high esteem they believe they deserve. It is not enough to have been recognized once; they demand continuous reaffirmation of their excellence and superiority. Naturally, this is a thin veneer covering their deep insecurity and inner sense of lack.

Their relentless pursuit of power, influence, and capability can be seen as an attempt to break free from the constraints that threaten to suffocate them.
summary: Подчеркивается, что потребность социальной Э2 в постоянном признании маскирует глубокую неуверенность, а стремление к власти является попыткой избежать ощущения уязвимости и слабости.

title: Fear of being small and the need for dominance
text: The mere feeling of being small—smaller than others, insignificant, weak, dependent, in need—triggers an overwhelming anxiety. This leaves them with only two options: either they are on top, which provides them with a sense of security, or they are below, which means submission, exploitation, and ultimately, erasure. A social E2 learns early on that survival depends on always maintaining the upper hand.
summary: Describes how a social E2 experiences intense anxiety when feeling insignificant, leading to a compulsive need to maintain superiority as a survival strategy rooted in early childhood experiences of conditional love and vulnerability.

title: Difficulty receiving and transactional mindset
text: They struggle to receive; they don’t know how. Gifts, in particular, are difficult for them. If they receive something, they assume it’s a form of payment for a favor they’ve done or that a request will soon follow. If they haven’t done anything yet, they grow suspicious or assume it’s a transaction disguised as generosity. Their mindset operates like a meticulous accounting system—tracking favors, payments, debts, and credits in an internal ledger where even the smallest “good deeds” are recorded, including those that were never asked of them.
summary: Explains the social E2's inability to accept gifts or help without suspicion, interpreting all receiving as part of a debt-based transaction due to their deep-seated fear of obligation and weakness.

title: Debt as servitude and distrust of authority
text:
For a social E2, needing something is synonymous with weakness and danger. The fear of being small is deeply rooted in their childhood, where they were never truly loved or recognized in their vulnerability. Except when they were being used or exploited.

Being indebted to someone is intolerable because it contradicts their self-image of being above obligations or ties to others. To them, debt equals servitude. And if there’s one thing they love, it’s believing they are free and untethered. They instinctively distrust and reject anyone they perceive—even in the slightest way—as a superior or authority figure, whether emotionally, sexually, professionally, or spiritually. They carry lifelong trauma from feeling overpowered by “the elders” and, at some point, may have genuinely feared for their survival.
summary: Details the social E2's aversion to dependency and debt, viewing it as humiliation and servitude, rooted in childhood experiences where love was conditional and vulnerability led to exploitation, resulting in lifelong resistance to authority.

title: Isolation during depression and self-reliance
text:
To an emperor or empress, asking for help is a public admission of incompetence. Being helped is humiliating. And being helped without having asked (an already unlikely scenario) is outright insulting. When they are feeling low, defeated, depressed, or withdrawn, they retreat into their home, hiding their struggles until they have fully recovered and are ready to return to the stage.

I was lying on the couch in my house with a severe depression; only my closest family knew. I wasn’t going out or talking to anyone. Who was I supposed to call? I didn’t think anyone could possibly know how to help me.
summary: Illustrates the social E2's tendency to isolate during emotional distress, viewing help-seeking as shameful and incompetent, preferring to suffer in silence until they can return to a position of strength.

title: Distrust in relationships and emotional isolation
text:
ANA BAZA

A social E2 harbors an irrational belief that putting themselves in someone else’s hands will lead to betrayal and emotional ruin. This distrust originates from their relationship with their mother and extends to the rest of their life. It explains their skepticism toward receiving without reciprocating, as well as their constant arrogance in the face of their own vulnerability. To maintain their self-sufficiency, they operate under the premise that they need no one. A social E2 is highly skilled at dismissing and looking down on those who don’t serve their ambitions. This ensures that few people truly get close to them, reinforcing their sense of independence but also their underlying loneliness. Ironically, when a crisis arises, people often turn to them, which feeds their narcissistic need to feel indispensable while masking the solitude they have built around themselves.
summary: Describes the social E2's deep distrust of others rooted in early maternal relationships, leading to emotional isolation, self-reliance as a defense, and a pattern of pushing people away while secretly needing to be needed.

title: Ambition as compensation and rejection of tenderness
text:
The characteristic neurotic need

Ambition is the last refuge of the failure.

OSCAR WILDE

Ambition and love are the wings to great deeds.

J.W. GOETHE

Being a point of reference within what they consider their territory is the driving desire that makes a social E2 come alive. To achieve this, they have developed a strategic mind, the ability to influence, and a sharp, opportunistic intelligence that is always on high alert. But to maintain this position, they have also had to suppress certain inherently human traits—compassion, tenderness, the ability to make mistakes, and above all, the thing they fear most: love. Love unsettles them, yet it is also the one thing that could truly heal them. One could say that the social E2 buried (or rather, banished) their heart, their childhood, and their humanity when they took on the responsibility of adulthood far too early.

Tenderness and compassion are for others, for the weak, for those who lack the sacred mission of helping or saving others. I was chosen to be strong among my peers.

ROSA USELETI

I feel tenderness inside, but it never manifests externally. In my interactions with others, my expression is harsh, direct, and cold. Even when I feel compassion, I struggle to show it; I sense it within me, but it never reaches the other person. I suppose it has to do with self-image. When someone speaks too sweetly or softly, I get nervous.
summary: Explores how social E2s channel ambition to compensate for inner emptiness, suppress vulnerability and tenderness to maintain strength, and struggle to express compassion due to self-image fears, despite feeling it internally.

title: The proud pursuit of grandeur and historical archetypes
text:
ANA GONZÁLEZ TEJERA

One could say that the social subtype is the proudest of the proud. They don’t fantasize about reclaiming the warmth of a mother or father, even if they once learned to feel like “the chosen one” in their parents’ eyes. Nor do they settle for captivating just a handful of people. A social E2 aspires to conquer territories, groups, and, if they lose themselves in the pursuit, the entire world. Historical figures like Cleopatra, Napoleon, Eva Perón, Alexander the Great, and even Lucifer embody this charismatic, seductive, and manipulative subtype. As Karen Horney describes in her definition of expansive personalities: “They are bent on self-glorification, on ambitious pursuits, on vindictive triumph, with the mastery of life through intelligence and will power as the means to actualize their idealized self.”
summary: Defines the social E2 as driven by an insatiable need for grandeur and recognition, rejecting familial warmth in favor of global influence, citing historical and archetypal figures who embody their expansive, self-glorifying personality structure.

title: Детская травма и формирование гордости как защиты у социального E2
text:
As a child, the social E2 felt worthy of being loved. However, when they were no longer useful to their mother or father—whether for practical reasons or sheer convenience—they were cast aside with gestures and body language laced with contempt. This left them feeling deeply humiliated. It was in this moment of downfall that pride and ambition emerged as mechanisms to reclaim their lost dignity, seeking recognition and striving to once again become that admired and “unconditionally loved” reference figure in every setting.

Praise, feeling special, and being “the chosen one” coexisted with disdain and humiliation. I had to do my utmost to remain in that position within my family. Pride became my shield against humiliation, my way of pulling myself out of the abyss—giving everything I had to win back my parents’ approval. It was as if humiliation threw me into a deep pit, and pride was the force that drove me to climb out
summary: Описывает, как социальный E2 в детстве пережил отвержение родителей, когда перестал быть им полезным, что привело к унижению, а в ответ развилась гордость и амбиции как защита и способ вернуть любовь и одобрение.

title: Интеллектуальная защита и подавление эмоций у социального E2
text:
ROSA USELETI

Claudio Naranjo describes the social E2 as the most intellectual of all Twos. Like the other subtypes, they use emotionalization as their primary defense mechanism. However, unlike the others, they repress their emotions and lean toward discipline, prioritizing the strategic ambition of conquest. Only illness or a significant professional failure forces them to confront their physical limits and experience even a fleeting sense of vulnerability.

Only when I end up in a hospital do I feel justified in being cared for. […]

When I was diagnosed with cancer, it felt like just another inconvenience, another challenge to overcome. It was only when I saw my friends’ expressions after telling them that I had a fleeting realization that maybe what was happening to me was actually serious
summary: Рассматривает социального E2 как наиболее интеллектуального из подтипов двойки, который подавляет эмоции в пользу дисциплины и стратегических целей, сталкиваясь с уязвимостью только в кризисах здоровья или профессиональной неудачи.

title: Амбиции как компенсация утраченного детства и места в семье
text:
ANA BAZA

This relentless drive, this passionate pursuit of goals, is masked as ambition and focused on securing achievements, territories, or groups. At its core, it is a desperate attempt to carve out a place in the world, compensating for the fact that they were never given one by right within their family. It is also a way to escape the chilling void they would inevitably encounter if they ever stopped moving. The social E2 was not seen for who they were but rather for how useful they were in supporting and fulfilling the needs of one or both parents.

They often played the role of confidant, exposed to information beyond their emotional maturity. They sometimes filled the role of a parental partner, competing early on with the actual parent of the same gender. For women, adolescence often brings a direct confrontation with the father figure—who may have been idolized—leading them to symbolically take over his role as the “head” of the family.

They were their mother’s unconditional support, the vessel through which one parent sought to shine, the one expected to “save” the family. It is common for them to have been used as a tool for manipulation and conflict between adults. However, there is one role they were never allowed to play: that of a child. This experience connects them with E1 and E8, the two power-driven types within the action triad of the Enneagram. For them, childhood effectively ended by the age of seven or eight.

Faced with a lack of boundaries, emotional protection, or support from one or both parents, they survived by growing up too soon, claiming an important role within the family system. They were often isolated from their siblings, either because they were denied that bond or because they rejected it themselves. The absence of a true place of belonging, the mandate of self-sufficiency, and a persistent undercurrent of loneliness accompany them throughout life, driving them toward the pursuit of glory.

I was seven years old, and my brother was two and a half. The day my father left home, his last words to me were: “Take care of your mother.” […]

My mother and I were in the kitchen. I was crying because my father was gone. She wiped the tears from my face and said, “Don’t cry. If you do, I’ll cry too. You’re already big, you’re smart, and you can handle this. Be strong; we have to take care of your brother, he’s so little.”

I learned that my needs didn’t matter. My pain had to be hidden. Besides, I could handle everything. I was big enough. Big enough to carry my mother’s pain and meet my brother’s needs.
summary: Объясняет, как социальный E2 был вынужден рано взрослеть, выполняя родительские функции, будучи инструментом родительских амбиций, но никогда не имея права быть ребёнком, что привело к хронической одиночке и стремлению к славе как способу обрести ценность.

title: Страх уязвимости и избегание помощи как следствие детской эмоциональной брошенности
text:
ANA BAZA

What unsettles the social E2 the most is coming into contact (on the rare occasions they allow it) with the underlying deprivation and depression within them. The fear that if they fall, they might never recover lingers in their subconscious, surfacing in recurring nightmares. This fear stems from never having been protected or emotionally supported as a child during their lowest moments. The feeling has stayed with them—the belief that they could perish unnoticed, with no one there to catch them. In adulthood, they are deeply suspicious when someone offers care. Taken to the extreme, they might even let themselves collapse before ever asking for help. To avoid facing this sense of abandonment and to soothe their anxiety, they have placed their mind and body in service of strategy and action—banishing their inconvenient heart, which they see as just as disruptive as tending to their most basic needs or believing in love without an ulterior motive.
summary: Описывает глубинный страх социального E2 перед уязвимостью и падением, коренящийся в отсутствии эмоциональной поддержки в детстве, что приводит к избеганию помощи и экстремальной самодостаточности даже в кризисных ситуациях.

title: Внешняя уверенность и социальная доминирующая наличность амбициозного социального E2
text:
The image of the ambitious

The ambitious social E2 is easy to spot—boastful even without speaking. When they do speak, their voice rises, gestures become animated, and they captivate those around them. They smile often, and while they don’t laugh much, their voice carries across the room.

Walking down the street, people naturally make way for them. Their stride is firm yet graceful, exuding an air of authority, as if they own the very ground they walk on. Like a peacock, they project an image of importance, regardless of the context they find themselves in.
summary: Описывает характерную внешнюю уверенность, авторитетность и притягательность социального E2, который производит впечатление важности и доминирования через осанку, голос и жесты, даже без слов.

title: Социальная E2 в колледже: пример ANA BAZA
text:
I was in college when I once walked into the computer lab. There, I saw a friend of my brother’s. Later, when I greeted them, they looked surprised and said, “I thought you were a professor, just by the way you moved around here.”

ANA BAZA
summary: Короткий анекдот из жизни АNA BAZA, иллюстрирующий, как социальная E2 производит впечатление авторитетного человека по манере движения и поведению, даже будучи студенткой.

title: Оскар Уайльд как пример социальной E2: образ как инструмент
text:
Oscar Wilde is a fitting example of this subtype: a modern figure, akin to a Renaissance man in his curious, poetic openness, and somewhat baroque in his expression. A true contemporary of his time, he had an eye for art and beauty in all its forms. An intellectual, well-connected, and surrounded by the influential figures of his era, he was witty, sharp, and always informed. His personal appearance was carefully curated, adapting seamlessly to suit his goals.

As chameleonic as E3, social E2s use their appearance more as a tool to achieve their objectives rather than as part of an image. With strategic adaptability and keen empathy, they identify the subtle cues that define different social circles. They adjust their presence accordingly, never losing their identity or desire to stand out, integrating themselves into the groups that interest them. Their mere presence adds value, making them both visible and admired.

They are opportunists, drawing inspiration from various sources and making ideas or projects their own. But they don’t settle for mere imitation. Instead, they take what they need and combine it with other elements in a creative way, producing something innovative. Masters of patchwork, they weave together disparate influences, giving them a unique brilliance that makes even the most improbable ventures seem achievable.
summary: Описание социальной E2 через пример Оскара Уайльда: использование внешности и адаптации как стратегического инструмента для достижения целей, творческая интеграция влияний и способность добавлять ценность в социальные группы за счёт харизмы и гибкости.

title: Наполеон как архетип завоевателя и амбициозной E2
text:
Take Napoleon, the last great conqueror. Only someone as audacious as him, a narcissist consumed by an insatiable hunger for “more and more,” could dare to claim nearly impossible territories. Eleven countries, including half of Russia, conquered at a time when the available resources were far from sufficient for such an undertaking.

Social E2s often feel like frauds on the inside, yet they carry themselves with remarkable confidence, compulsively seeking opportunities to captivate the masses. Figures like Elvis Presley, Truman Capote, or Eva Perón exemplify how a social E2 can sublimate their ambition into a cause: “everything for the people.”
summary: Анализ Наполеона как прототипа социальной E2: гипер амбициозность, стремление к невозможному, внутреннее ощущение фальшивии при внешней уверенности, а также примеры знаменитостей, которые направили свою амбицию на служение делу или народу.

title: Философия завоевания: Юлий Цезарь, Ева Перон и Наполеон как образцы социальной E2
text:
The great ambition. The conquest

Cleopatra, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, and Alexander the Great all share a defining trait: they were conquerors—of people, of territories, of history. They built empires whose legacies have endured despite the centuries that separate us from them.

Reading their biographies, we see common threads—characteristics that align with this subtype:

The social E2 believes they can do things better than anyone else. They do not take orders, especially in areas they consider their own domain. If authority stands in their way, they rebel against it, claiming it’s for the greater good. Napoleon and Caesar both declared themselves emperors, convinced that only they knew what the people needed. Ironically, they fought against absolute power—only to seize it for themselves, echoing the childhood impulse of usurping the father’s role.

If a rule is inconvenient or obstructs their goals, the social E2 bends it, ignores it, or even creates new ones, believing their version should be universal. They don’t see their actions as wrong but as necessary. The end justifies the means. They embody the phrase “the road to hell is paved with good intentions,” as they can rationalize anything in the name of the greater good.

A true visionary always wants to change the world and make it a better place for the less fortunate:

I am prepared to resort to anything, to submit to anything, for the sake of the commonwealth. ~ JULIUS CAESAR

I don’t ask or want anything for myself. My glory is and always will be to be Perón’s shield and the flag of my people, and though I leave shreds of my life along the road, I know that you will pick up my name and will carry it to victory as a banner. […] If this people asked me for my life I would joyfully give it, for the happiness of one descamisado is worth more than my entire life. ~ EVA PERÓN

I have a tender heart — but it is the heart of a sovereign. The tears of a duchess move me to no pity whatsoever, but I am touched by the woes of peoples. ~ NAPOLEON

They are convinced they can achieve anything they set their sights on. Their ambition fuels grand projects—not just for themselves, but for the world. This confidence, coupled with their visionary mindset, makes them incredibly persuasive when they are passionate about something. Risk-takers, great strategists, and pioneers in their fields—whether in music, literature, or war—they also possess the discipline and tenacity to accomplish what others wouldn’t even dare attempt.
summary: Глубокий анализ завоевательного аспекта социальной E2 через примеры Цезаря, Наполеона и Евы Перон: вера в собственное превосходство, оправдание средств целями, видение блага для народа, готовность к самоотверженности и убеждённость в своей способности изменить мир.

title: Тирания успеха: завоевание как зависимость и невозможность удержания власти
text:
To get what they want, they will do whatever it takes, regardless of the cost or consequences for themselves or others. Their vision is expansive, and they seize every opportunity to create something new or rise from failure. However, they are conquerors, and they need the group, both for support and for the social recognition of their achievements.

When striving for victory, they are ruthless. But once they’ve won, they show magnanimity. Like Julius Caesar, who respected the beliefs and customs of conquered peoples. This was both a display of tolerance and a strategic move to maintain control over them. Social E2s need control to the point that they can become tyrannical, sometimes even turning their own groups against them.

Conquest fuels their adrenaline. They are addicted to the rush of power, influence, and status. What they cannot do is settle down and maintain what they’ve conquered. That would require caretaking, consistency, and routine—things they struggle to sustain. Instead, they move from one conquest to the next, leaving others to manage what they’ve acquired.
summary: Описание паттерна поведения социальной E2: ruthless pursuit of victory, post-victory magnanimity as инструмент контроля, зависимость от адреналина завоеваний и inability to sustain achievements due to aversion to routine и caretaking, ведущее к постоянному поиску новых вызовов.

title: Insatiable ambition and inevitable downfall
text: They are insatiable, rarely satisfied for long. Their ambition drives them ceaselessly toward the impossible. But their inability to acknowledge limits (both their own and those of others) inevitably leads to failure. Like Julius Caesar or Napoleon, they push themselves so far, in their desire to become God, that they meet the same fate as Lucifer—falling from the heights of power.
summary: This chunk describes how social E2s are driven by insatiable ambition that pushes them toward impossible goals, ignoring limits, which ultimately leads to failure and downfall, using historical figures as parallels.

title: Reclaiming lost dignity
text:
Reclaiming lost dignity

The word that best defines the neurotic need of the social E2 is ambition. Etymologically, it is interesting to trace related words that might explain the genesis of this subtype: dignity and humiliation.
summary: This chunk introduces the central theme of reclaiming lost dignity for social E2s, linking their neurotic need of ambition to the concepts of dignity and humiliation.

title: Ambition as drive for validation and meaning
text:
According to dictionaries, ambition has two meanings, both of which convey a strong desire to achieve something with vehemence. This immediately connects us to the proactive and intense nature of this character, whose vital movement is one of “going toward,” as Claudio Naranjo, following Karen Horney, points out: “The so-called E2 is a striking example of an expansive type, meaning they approach conflict by pleasing and yielding […], and we could say that the social subtype is the most powerful and antagonistic.”

I don’t concern myself with the home… I’m not receptive; I don’t stay to receive, I “go toward” things, which is a more masculine trait. What matters is out there, in the world. Life happens outside. Domesticity robs me of time for what’s truly important. I don’t wait for things, people, or opportunities to come to me… I go out and find them.

ANA GONZÁLEZ TEJERA

For the social E2, ambition is not primarily about wealth or image (as it is for the social E3), but about an insatiable drive to be more, experience more, do more. This drive for more gives their life meaning. If they were to stop, they would have to confront their own inner lack—an absence of self, an unbearable emptiness. They would also lose the hope of being loved and valued. To be just one among many would feel like not existing at all, like having no place in the world.

When I was a lawyer, I didn’t make much money, but just being able to say I was a lawyer gave me a status that money couldn’t buy.

MÓNICA ANGULO

At its core, this is the passion for being someone important that people turn to, a point of reference. Looking deeper, what they truly seek is dignity: to be worthy of love, to deserve love. However, they do not pursue this search inward, toward the intrinsic value of human dignity. Instead, they divert it outward, believing dignity lies in being validated by the world through their great achievements.
summary: This chunk explores how social E2s channel their ambition into seeking external validation and dignity through achievements, driven by an inner lack and fear of being insignificant, with personal testimonies illustrating their need to be important and seen as a reference point.

title: Humiliation as formative experience
text:
Following this thread, we encounter two meanings of the word “humiliate”: “to wound someone’s self-esteem or dignity” and “to go through a situation in which a person suffers a loss of status.” This experience is what will shape the development of this personality.

I went through repeated humiliating experiences with three different groups of friends at school, and I clearly remember the day I decided to put an end to it—that I would never again suffer or feel pain over something like that. I practiced looking tough, unyielding, commanding respect… And yes, I succeeded. That’s how I survived.

MÓNICA ANGULO
summary: This chunk discusses how experiences of humiliation—defined as wounds to self-esteem or loss of status—shape the social E2's personality, using a personal account of overcoming school humiliation through adopting a tough, commanding persona.

title: Early validation and maternal withdrawal
text:
When a human being is born, they are whole and fully capable of loving and being loved. The social E2’s environment reaffirms to the child that they are worthy of being looked at with love, that they are special, that they are meant to do something important. This, in turn, sustains their self-concept and self-esteem.

However, something disrupts this nirvana. The mother, primarily, “withdraws” or averts her gaze in some way. Perhaps simply because, upon ceasing to be a child, that unconditional gaze is no longer there. But what the social E2 experiences is the beginning of a perverse game where they become the repository of high expectations and responsibilities beyond their developmental capacity. This grants them an overwhelming confidence in their potential but, at the same time, drains their energy and cyclically leads to states of stress or depression. In return, they obtain something they will never stop craving: a position of power within the system.

My mother says to me: “Ask your father for this. He doesn’t yell at you.” I go to ask him, and he yells at me like he does at everyone else. He gets angry, tells me I have no right to ask him that, that I have no idea who I think I am—an insolent little brat—and then punishes me by locking me in my room.

Filled with rage, I scream at my mother to let me out, because she was the one who asked me to do it. She doesn’t show up, and after quite a while, she finally tells me I can come out, but only if I apologize to my father, because it was just a momentary outburst… None of it makes sense to me. Not a single mention of the fact that she sent me to do it in the first place, nor of the shouting and punishment I endured. Only a focus on my pride, my anger at my father, and my mother’s indulgence toward his rage.

In those moments, I feel hatred toward both of them and deep contempt for my mother… for being weak, for being a liar, for not daring to set boundaries against my father’s violence. I start to build the belief that I can’t trust them, that I am above them, that I am alone, and that no one can help me.

ROSA USELETI
summary: This chunk describes how social E2 children initially receive validation and a sense of importance, but experience maternal withdrawal and paternal rejection, leading to humiliation, rage, and the development of a belief in their own superiority and isolation as they seek power to compensate.

title: Expulsion from importance and original humiliation
text: At the same time, another family dynamic feeds the child’s uncertainty about where they truly belong. In the future, this will drive them to claim a place of their own within groups. From the position of recognition and equality that was once granted to them, they now feel humiliated when they are treated like the child they still are, as if they have been “demoted,” deceived, betrayed. This expulsion from a position of importance, this ambivalence about where they stand in the eyes of significant adults, is perceived as the original humiliation.
summary: This chunk explains how social E2s experience original humiliation when they are demoted from a former position of recognition and equality, creating uncertainty about their belonging and driving them to seek a rightful place in groups later in life.

title: Динамика власти в семье: роль ребёнка как спасителя
text: My mother confessed to me that she was unhappy with the decision they made to move houses. She sought my alliance; she was the one giving me that power. Since I was always there to help and save her, I stepped into the role of her rescuer and entered into battle against my father. I placed myself above him, but he did not grant me that power because I was the youngest in the household. One parent gave me power, while the other tried to strip it away with absurd rules and restrictions, which he imposed solely to dominate me and assert his authority over me. That was the ambivalence I felt.
summary: Автор описывает конфликт между родителями, где мать наделила его властью и привлекла в союз против отца, но отец, видя в нём лишь младшего ребёнка, пытался лишить этой власти через контроль и ограничения, создавая ощущение двусмысленности и внутренней борьбы за признание.

title: Первые переживания стыда и отвержения
text:
ANA GONZÁLEZ TEJERA

When the little girl confidently strides toward her mother in high heels, proud and self-assured, the mother, who has no need for her in that moment, dismisses her with disdain, as if she were nothing more than a nuisance. These are the first experiences of shame, humiliation, and the feeling of being a fraud.

My mother was always busy, rushing around the house. If I approached her seeking attention, comfort, or support, she wouldn’t even look at me. She just hurried from one task to another, telling me she didn’t have time.

And yet, she relied on me for various household matters or things related to my brother. But if I made a mistake, if I did something wrong, she would get incredibly angry, and I can still remember the look on her face and the word I still can’t bear to hear: “Disgusting. Disgusting!” It was a mix of pain, worthlessness, rejection, and humiliation. I felt like my body was being torn in half.
summary: Ребёнок сталкивается с противоречивым отношением матери: потребность в помощи сочетается с полным игнорированием эмоциональных потребностей и резкой критикой за малейшие ошибки, что приводит к глубокому чувству стыда, отвержения и внутреннему разрыву.

title: Объектivирование ребёнка в отношениях с матерью
text:
ANA BAZA

There are some differences between boys and girls, but what truly matters is how the child is used—first being elevated, only to be “dethroned” later.

In a boy’s relationship with his mother, we see a similar objectification to what happens with girls:

To my mother, I was her toy. She played with me. But only up to a point. When she got bored or it was time to feed or bathe me, she would hand me off to the nanny and disappear. It was like a little girl who, after growing tired of a toy, tosses it aside and looks for another distraction. In fact, she still does this now that I’m an adult. I always had the feeling that she was less of a mother and more of a spoiled child, throwing tantrums, and using money as a way to exert authority or to compensate me.
summary: Ребёнок, независимо от пола, часто становится объектом использования родителями: сначала его ценят и вовлекают в свои нужды, а затем отвергают, когда он перестаёт быть удобным или интересным, что особенно проявляется в отношениях с матерью, которая traktирует ребёнка как игрушку, которую можно бросить.

title: Одиночество и тревога в условиях эмоционального abbandона
text:
MARIO MEDALION SERRANO

For both boys and girls, though not in every case, one parent positions themselves as a partner or comrade in life and struggles. Yet, even here, the child will eventually be abandoned when they become a burden or a nuisance—without consideration for the fear, anger, or sadness inflicted upon them.

I remember being in Pattaya (Thailand) on vacation for New Year’s Eve. My father decided that we should go to the hotel’s gala dinner. During the cocktail hour, a man he knew approached him and whispered something in his ear. My father looked at me and said, “I’ll be right back. Chai wants to introduce me to a friend.” At ten and a half years old, I already knew that “friend” was most likely a prostitute. So there I stayed, alone, at a table with ten strangers, celebrating the New Year, wishing my father would come back soon.

Minutes passed, and my anxiety turned into anger, and then back into anxiety. I looked around, keeping my expression neutral, acting as if everything was normal, because I was terrified that when my father returned, someone might call him out on leaving me alone and he would feel betrayed by me.

Five minutes before the clock struck midnight and the waiters started pouring champagne, my father reappeared as if nothing had happened. And just like that, my anxiety and anger gave way to simple relief. He was back.
summary: Автор recounts опыт эмоционального abbandона в детстве: отец оставил его одного в чужой ситуации, вызвав тревогу и гнев, но вернувшись, как будто ничего не произошло, что оставило глубокий след чувства незащищённости и гипервигилантности в ожидании betrayal.

title: Стратегии защиты социального E2: от гиперкомпенсации до девальвации любви
text:
When faced with their own inadequacy, the future social E2 counters it by raising their chin and setting personal goals to prove their self-sufficiency and skill in everything they undertake. As an adult, they will seek to reclaim that “unconditional” love within the groups they try to conquer, confusing territory with love.

Paradoxically, when love does come their way, the social E2 distrusts it and cannot surrender to it, as that would mean exposing what they see as their greatest weakness: their vulnerability and need for others. If they feel they are not loved or that the love they receive does not meet their expectations, they feel betrayed and metaphorically “behead” the person, the authority, or the entire group. Alternatively, they may simply walk away without explaining or asking what really happened.

The exit of the ambitious

Like all narcissists, social E2s carefully and secretly hide (if they are even aware of it) their shortcomings, failures, and, above all, the emptiness that accompanies them. They end up trapped in a cycle between success and failure, anxiety and depression. As will be discussed in the chapter on childhood, social E2s may have experienced anaclitic depression as children and introjective depression as adults.

The dreaded scenario is being abandoned, not being enough... not being able to fix other people’s lives. I sell myself as something bigger than I am, creating expectations that later become a burden because deep down, I feel there isn’t much inside me. It hurts to see how I disregard what I do have, how I devalue myself for not always being sharp and quick-witted. I look at the colorful cellophane I’ve wrapped myself in. It’s worn, like an old plastic bottle. Beneath it, there’s barely anything visible: something small and square… a bar of soap.

ANA BAZA

The social E2 constantly struggles with the tension between their narcissistic aspirations and reality. On top of that, they have little tolerance for frustration, leading to a collapse in their sense of omnipotence. In response to this imbalance, they have two possible reactions: either rage (directed at others or turned inward as self-aggression, both rooted, as Kohut states, in experiences of humiliation) or depression.
summary: Социальный E2 компенсирует чувство неполноценности через гиперкомпенсацию и стремление к успеху, но отвергает искреннюю любовь из страха перед уязвимостью. Их защита построена на скрытии пустоты за фасадом компетентности, что приводит к циклу успеха и падения, а фрустрация вызывает либо гнев, либо депрессию, rooted в детской травме humiliation.

title: Introjective depression in social E2s
text:
According to Blatt, narcissists subject themselves to constant scrutiny and live in perpetual fear of criticism. As a result, their depression in adulthood tends to be introjective, characterized by feelings of worthlessness, inferiority, failure, and shame, all accompanied by harsh self-criticism. Most notably, these depressions are difficult to detect, as their speech rarely conveys just how defeated they feel. It is common for them to be unaware that they have gone through depressive episodes or to isolate themselves until they have recovered.

The social E2 disconnects from their needs and self-care because they associate reconnecting with their inner child with being humiliated and unsupported.

I have felt a lot of sadness, though I never thought of it as “depression.” Among other things, because I never allowed myself to feel pain and sadness until I was well into my personal growth journey. I could feel sad, but I would immediately transform it into anger or withdrawal, disconnecting in some way.
summary: This chunk describes the introjective depression experienced by social E2s, including their self-criticism, emotional avoidance, and difficulty recognizing their own depressive states, as illustrated by personal testimonies.

title: Childhood origins of the narcissistic voice in social E2s
text:
MONICA ANGULO

I became ill with childhood stress because I couldn’t keep up with the self-imposed demands I believed were necessary: to be the best at school, in sports... to win back my parents’ love, which I thought I had lost due to punishments and situations I perceived as humiliating. I think depression would have been a healthier way out—to surrender, to give up on being the best. Instead, I accumulated stress and anger.

ROSA USELETI

One of the central aspects of narcissism is the severe self-critical conscience. And one of the driving forces behind this ambitious personality is precisely an internalized, severe, and persecutory parental voice that torments them, whispering that they are not enough, that they can take on more goals, more commitments. This voice stems from a relentless pursuit of recognition that was ingrained in them as a child.

As a child, the social E2 received an incoherent message that kept them in a state of anxious vigilance: they could be praised or reprimanded for the very same behavior or attitude.

On this subject, Horney states:
