A blind adoration may inflate his feeling of significance. He may feel wanted, liked, and appreciated not for what he is but merely for satisfying his parents’ needs for adoration, prestige, or power.

At the same time, a rigid regime of perfectionist standards may evoke in him a feeling of inferiority for not measuring up to such demands. Misdemeanors or bad marks at school may be severely reprimanded, while good behavior or good marks are taken for granted.

Another contradiction they were subjected to, which adds a social dimension to their experiences of humiliation, is that in private, their mother would show disappointment if they failed to meet the lofty expectations placed upon them—an essential factor in the formation of their narcissistic character. However, in the presence of “witnesses,” whether at home or in public, the message was one of exaggerated praise and blind confidence in their abilities. The child would feel ashamed of how they were being flaunted—humiliation turned public.

I felt like I was being put on display, like an object, a product of my parents. I think that’s why seduction comes so easily to me. It’s a way of “prostituting” myself, and at the same time, of reliving what my parents did to me by imitating their behavior. Always searching for that lost love. By “prostitution” I mean a betrayal of myself, a dishonesty. I align myself with anyone as long as they admire me, and if I feel aggression, I invalidate my own feelings and let myself become a punching bag. Because, after all, I neither feel nor suffer…
summary: This chunk explores how contradictory parental messages in childhood—combining conditional praise with harsh criticism—form the internalized persecutory voice and narcissistic defenses in social E2s, leading to chronic stress, self-betrayal, and emotional disconnection.

title: Adult struggles with recognition and intimacy in social E2s
text:
MARIO MEDALION SERRANO

As an adult, the social E2 pays a high price for this family pattern, distrusting anyone who speaks well of them. Ironically, although they crave public recognition, they struggle to accept it, interpreting it as something artificial or false, just as they did in childhood. This is compounded by their fear of being exposed as a fraud or of failing to meet the expectations built around them. This fear forms one of the pillars of their difficulties with intimacy and the poor quality of the relationships they establish.

The term recognition, so prevalent in the social E2’s world, carries a dual yet not mutually exclusive meaning. On the one hand, it implies gratitude and appreciation, which ties into their arrogant act—believing they deserve special consideration as repayment for a debt incurred toward them in childhood.

On the other hand, to recognize also means to accept someone as legitimate, which is linked to their fear of being exposed as a fraud and, in losing their position, reliving their original humiliation. The social E2 pushes themselves to exhaustion to fulfill the “promises” that will keep them in their desired place or status. However, both their own expectations and those they have generated in others are so high that they often fear (deeply and secretly) that they will be found out as incapable.

In reality, they’re tired of maintaining the image they have built of themselves. What they truly need, in order to be recognized as legitimate, is simply to show themselves fully—with their shortcomings, their limits, their vulnerabilities, and their fears—just like anyone else.
summary: This chunk examines the adult social E2’s conflicted relationship with recognition—simultaneously craving and distrusting it—due to fears of exposure as a fraud, and highlights their exhaustion from maintaining a false image, emphasizing the need for authentic self-presentation.

title: Fixation and the false abundance of the social E2
text:
Interpersonal strategy and associated irrational ideas

Fixation represents the core cognitive distortion that shapes personality. It is a coherent interpretation of reality that a child constructs throughout their upbringing, adapting to family expectations and social messages. Over time, this interpretation solidifies into an “objective” truth that reinforces their passion. This creates a vicious cycle where their convictions and perceptions of reality strengthen behavioral strategies consistent with these interpretations. As a result, they become increasingly attached to this way of being, losing sight of the broader context.

The false abundance of the social E2
summary: This chunk introduces the concept of fixation as a core cognitive distortion in personality development and begins to define the false abundance of the social E2 as a narcissistic belief in having more than others, despite inner feelings of lack.

title: False abundance as cognitive fixation of Type Two
text:
False abundance is the cognitive fixation of Type Two. It is the distorted belief that one has more than others, that they have an excess—when in reality, they have no more than anyone else.

Pride causes them to suppress their needs, convincing themselves they don’t have any. The abandonment they experienced is not consciously acknowledged, yet it shapes their behavior. They present themselves as abundant precisely because, deep down, they feel like they are lacking. This mirrors the condition of E4, with the key difference being that E2 copes by repressing their sense of lack and identifying with an idealized, grandiose self-image.

The false abundance of an ambitious social E2 is, unsurprisingly, focused on the social realm. It is a narcissistic response in which they need to be seen as they ideally see themselves. This self-idealization disconnects them from the deep-seated feeling that they are, in fact, a fraud. As a reactive defense, they reinterpret all their actions and behaviors as part of a grand mission and a benevolent attitude toward others. They seek situations where they believe they will be perceived in the way they desire, craving recognition while avoiding failure and emptiness. Thus, they become trapped in their own character’s vicious cycle.
summary: This chunk defines false abundance as the core cognitive distortion of Type Two, explaining how pride and repressed lack lead to an inflated self-image and narcissistic self-presentation, particularly in the social realm, trapping them in a cycle of validation-seeking and self-deception.

title: Self-perception and internal beliefs of the social E2
text:
Their self-perception

The social E2 sees themselves as someone who, in the future, will achieve their goals and be praised by those around them for their qualities. They project onto others the gaze that confirms their ideal self-image because their internal gaze is not enough.

They constantly deceive themselves by fantasizing about actions that will place them in the position they believe they deserve. Ultimately, they hold the belief that they are superior to others and that, sooner or later, this will be acknowledged. Their narcissistic layer serves as an overcompensation for their shadow self, where they actually devalue themselves. In other words, they need to fantasize about having superior abilities because, deep down, they don’t truly value the ones they already possess; they don’t recognize or appreciate them.

The irrational, or crazy, beliefs that social E2s hold about themselves revolve around themes of grandiosity, omnipotence, messianic purpose, and the illusion that their love is unique. They see themselves as possessing a universal love that sets them apart from the rest of the world, powerful enough to bring about change.

Despite appearing constantly engaged with people—available, attentive, and kind—they feel profoundly alone. They isolate themselves because they struggle to tolerate others' flaws and become frustrated when their idealized self-image goes unrecognized. Both this isolation and their tendency to overemotionalize their experiences serve as defenses against confronting their limitations and “flaws”—especially when faced with physical, psychological, or emotional challenges such as illness, romantic failures, or career setbacks. This is their way of escaping depression.

Additionally, they push themselves relentlessly because their willpower alone is not enough to reach the constant goals they pursue. This often turns them into workaholics, engaged in a relentless effort to earn recognition.
summary: This chunk explores the social E2’s inflated self-perception, grandiose fantasies, and irrational beliefs about superiority and unique love, which mask deep insecurity and lead to isolation, workaholism, and emotional defenses against perceived failure.

title: View of others and interpersonal dynamics
text:
Their view of others

The social E2 sees others as means to achieve their goals. These goals are usually strategic: having friends to feel supported, a partner to fulfill their sexual needs, influential connections to climb the social ladder, and maintaining good relations to avoid conflict. There is very little room for the other as an individual because their ambition blinds them to the fact that they are dealing with a person. In actuality, despite projecting the image of having many friendships, the social E2 is prone to abandoning them, especially when they believe there is nothing left to gain from the relationship.

In group settings, the ambitious social E2 is an expert at capturing attention. Their emotionally charged speech ensures they are never boring; they know exactly where to place emphasis to hold the external gaze. In fleeting encounters, this makes them captivating. However, over time, it becomes a drawback. People begin to see them as over-the-top and manipulative, always needing to add the final flourish to every interaction.

Their keen social intuition allows them to gauge relationships and offer just enough to keep things running smoothly. However, due to their own emotional numbness, they struggle to maintain authentic connections. They are overly demanding of others and find it difficult to admire people, often confusing admiration with envy. They tend to view them as slow, incompetent, clumsy, or dull.

In relationships, they offer care in a superficial way while subtly disparaging the other person and gradually placing them in a lower position so they can feel superior, secretly taking control.
summary: This chunk describes how the social E2 views others instrumentally—using relationships for status, validation, and personal gain—while struggling with authentic connection due to emotional numbness, envy masked as admiration, and a tendency to manipulate and devalue others to maintain superiority.

title: Worldview and quest for immortality through deeds
text:
Their view of the world

When it comes to the world, the social E2 presents themselves as generous, adopting behaviors designed to leave a lasting impact. At its core, this is a quest for immortality through good deeds that will echo in society.
summary: This chunk outlines the social E2’s worldview, in which they seek lasting significance and immortality through generous, impactful actions, framing their benevolence as a means to achieve enduring recognition and legacy.

title: Worldview as a staircase to climb
text: For this ambitious personality, the world is a grand staircase to climb, a vast terrain to conquer. They believe there are always more social circles to infiltrate, more people to impress, and they thrive on being part of these spaces—so long as they can occupy a prominent position. If they are not in a leadership role, they believe they could do better than the actual boss, often devaluing them despite not shouldering their responsibilities. They prefer to be the right-hand person, the one in a position to receive recognition and validation. However, when their actual abilities are measured against those of others in the groups they join—or when they are assigned a role that accurately reflects their capabilities—they perceive it as an insult or humiliation and look for an escape. Once their personal charm and persuasive skills give way to a more realistic assessment of their competence, they feel exposed as frauds and become consumed by shame.
summary: Describes the ambitious social E2's worldview as a competitive hierarchy where they seek prominent roles, feel humbled by accurate assessments of their abilities, and experience shame when their charm fails to mask perceived inadequacy.

title: Naïve messianic love and neurotic mechanisms
text:
The ambitious social E2 believes that love must triumph in the world. Their worldview is both naïve and messianic, convinced that human suffering would end if only people loved the way they believe they do. This is a profound challenge, stemming from their refusal to acknowledge their own shadow self. To silence this internal void, they cling to the belief that one day, ultimate recognition will come—the grand validation that will justify all their efforts. They also overestimate the strength of their relationships, relying on them as a shield against their own dissatisfaction and emptiness, despite the fact that they often neglect to nurture these bonds in a meaningful way.

Neurotic mechanisms

Emotionalization is the typical defense mechanism of E2s, through which they “produce” an emotion or exaggerate it to the point of dramatization. (Type Two is associated with histrionic personality disorder, although the social subtype is more closely linked to narcissistic personality disorder). The goal is to shield themselves from the real emotions they are experiencing, such as pain, fear, or frustration.

Additionally, they tend to prioritize emotions that appear pleasant, like joy or enthusiasm. Instead of expressing the emotion they actually need to process, they transmute it into something seemingly positive, sometimes to the extent that they forget what they truly needed to express. This is reinforced by an interpretation shaped by false abundance: by feeling so full of pleasurable, beautiful, joyful, and vibrant emotions, they infer that they must possess special qualities. In this state, they feel like the Sun King, radiating happiness everywhere they go.

This further deepens their disconnection from themselves, making them unaware of what they are actually experiencing and how to express it. For E2, understanding what they are going through is secondary to the ego-driven need for external validation. They lack confidence in the truth of their own emotions, as they either exaggerate or alter their primary emotional quality.

This is the foundation of their dependence on external perception, characteristic of emotionally-driven personalities: they need others to affirm the illusion they live in because they cannot sustain it on their own, given their limited real understanding of their deeper feelings.

What happens to E2 is obviously the same as what happens to everyone else. However, their narrow perspective and self-absorption lead them to believe that their experiences are more significant and fundamentally different from those of the rest of the world. The self-reflection necessary to resolve issues through sound judgment is disrupted by their tendency to emotionalize their thoughts, making them less precise in their reasoning. By failing to see themselves as just one among many, they self-exclude. In that space—where they lack a sense of being on equal footing with others—social E2s feel profoundly alone and empty, like a fraud.
summary: Explores the social E2's messianic belief in love as salvation, their reliance on relationships for validation, and the neurotic mechanism of emotionalization—where they dramatize or transmute emotions to avoid inner pain, leading to disconnection and dependence on external approval.

title: The illusion of greatness
text:
One of the most significant ideas these shameless characters shield themselves with is greatness.

A sense of greatness

Greatness, in this context, refers to a fundamental cognitive distortion: the belief that “bigger is better”—that the great triumphs over the small. Instead of seeing themselves in terms of their own qualities and experiences, social E2s evaluate themselves in comparison to others. Greatness, for them, turns into the idea that “one must be more than others to be included” since, internally, they only accept what they deem truly superior. There is no room for what is not “great.” Anything that does not meet this standard is pushed into the shadows, which is why they often appear arrogant toward those who, unconsciously, remind them of the parts of themselves they are trying to suppress.

This narcissistic response creates a grandiose façade, concealing the inner fear of not measuring up that threatens their inflated self-image. These unsettling perceptions occasionally break through their emotional state, especially when they face criticism, leading to a cyclical pattern of behavior alternating between euphoric highs and semi-depressive lows.

This idea of greatness also reflects their social worldview. The ambitious social E2 sees their environment as stratified; everyone belongs to a social rank. And “since bigger beats smaller, it’s better to be on the upper rungs of the social ladder.” This irrational belief is obviously formed in childhood. A “grandiose child” often gravitates toward older individuals. In adulthood, “older” no longer refers to age, but to people who hold prominent positions in the social hierarchy. In short, those with authority.
summary: Defines the social E2's core distortion of greatness as a narcissistic defense mechanism rooted in childhood, where superiority over others is equated with worth, leading to arrogance, fear of exposure, and a hierarchical social worldview driven by the need to occupy positions of authority.

title: Сложности восхищения у социального E2
text: With this idea of greatness, it’s difficult for them to experience what Claudio Naranjo calls admiring love, which is the way we relate to something greater than ourselves, such as the divine, authority figures, or even the qualities in others that we value. Social E2s struggle immensely with admiration, and they experience it in two distinct ways. One is by exaggerating the abilities of others in alignment with their own idealized self-image. That is, seeing in others the skills they fantasize about possessing or hope to develop. The other, darker form of admiration is repressed envy. They secretly desire what others have but do not show it. As a result, they cannot truly admire others, relating to what they value in an ambivalent manner—projecting arrogance onto what they secretly admire.
summary: Описывает два типа восхищения у социального E2: преувеличение способностей других в соответствии с идеализированным образом себя и подавленную зависть, из-за чего истинное восхищение невозможно.

title: Вертикальное мышление и стремление к статусу
text: This subtype has a vertical concept of social structure, where there is always a “top” and a “bottom.” The ambitious social E2 wants to be on top and believes they currently occupy a lower position than they deserve. This is precisely what drives them to pursue a status that, in reality, they can never fully embody, despite seeing it as their ideal self. Excessive work is a crucial tool for achieving this. It’s difficult for them to attain the position that aligns with their perceived abilities unless they exaggerate those abilities, which leads to extreme self-demand that can turn into self-exploitation.
summary: Объясняет, как социальный E2 воспринимает социальную иерархию вертикально, стремится к верхней позиции через чрезмерную работу и преувеличение способностей, что приводит к самовыпасу.

title: Источники чувства исключительности и давление ожиданий
text:
This self-demand results in an overvaluation of their status, linked to a sense of inherent greatness. As we’ve discussed, it often originates from parents or role models who instilled in them the idea that they were destined for something extraordinary, perhaps due to their own unfulfilled ambitions.

When I was little, I found studying easy and loved learning. I was passionate about medicine: I watched medical TV shows, documentaries, and even live surgeries. I always said I wanted to be a doctor. My parents supported me every step of the way, telling me I would be a great doctor, that I would discover the cure for cancer. I felt proud when I heard them say that. They bragged about me everywhere. I was always “the girl who would become a doctor and cure cancer.”

Years passed, and my whole family knew I was going to be an oncologist. But when it came time to choose a career, and decide on my college major, I didn’t even list Medicine as an option. Not even as a backup. I felt so much pressure from my family’s expectations that I couldn’t bring myself to do it. Instead, I chose a completely different field.
summary: Описывает происхождение чувства исключительности у E2 от родительских ожиданий и личный пример ROSA USELETI, которая отказалась от медицины из-за давления семьи.

title: Цена величия и безумные убеждения социального E2
text:
ROSA USELETI

What is the price they pay for their sense of greatness? Living by standards that are not truly their own. They are always ahead of their current stage in life, skipping over the present because they are already fixated on the next. And once they reach adulthood, they continue wanting more: they must be in a different place, be more aware, more accomplished… In short, more.

Some of the “crazy” beliefs related to greatness include:

“I am the most important; you cannot do without me.”

“Others are always behind me.”

“I am better than everyone else.”

“I am the pillar of my household; everyone’s happiness depends on me.”

“Only I can support my parents.”

“I am the prettiest, the most intelligent, the nicest child. I am the best at everything…”

“I see the world as my subjects.”

“I’ve done so much, I’m so fast and efficient that others cannot keep up; it’s better if I do the thinking and they just follow my orders…”

“Others are on a different level than me.”

“I am the most special.”

“If I am not great, I am nothing.”

“If I am not great, I disappear; I am invisible, unloved, worthless.”

“One day, my greatness will be recognized, and then they will praise me.”

“My thirst for greatness is necessary to fulfill my mission.”
summary: Перечисляет последствия стремления к величию у социального E2: жизнь по чужим стандартам, постоянное незадовлетворенность и список грандиозных убеждений о своей исключительности.

title: Иллюзия всемогущества у социального E2
text:
The illusion of omnipotence

Omnipotence is a belief that fuels the near-manic behavior of the social E2—the belief that they can do anything. This is similar to the social E3 ideal, in the sense that they buy into the idea that, in a competitive society, a person can shape themselves and rise through sheer effort, without acknowledging external obstacles, personal limitations, or the costs—both their own and others’. The difference between the Two and the Three is that the social E2 already believes they possess all the necessary skills; they just need others to recognize them. In contrast, the social E3 understands that they must “work” hard to achieve success and strategically leverage the strengths of those around them.

Social E2s assume that because they have felt intelligent at some point, they must truly be so. They believe in their own omnipresence. They overestimate themselves, exaggerating or multiplying their abilities in their own mind.

Believing in their own omnipotence is one of the most harmful illusions they carry. They become deeply attached to work, as it provides them with the resources to feel abundant and superior. It becomes their measuring stick. The self-imposed pressure to perform gives them certain benefits, reinforcing the belief that they are all-powerful. This is the self-imposed servitude of the ambitious social E2.

Their omnipotence finds ultimate satisfaction in planning acts of conquest, whether of people, status, or territory. The mere thought of achieving a goal makes them feel as if they already have it in their grasp: “If I want it and think about it, it is already mine.” (Let’s not forget that this is the most intellectual of the three subtypes). Many times, these conquests require little actual effort, as social E2s excel at claiming the victories of others, usually after convincing them of how much they have helped or how indispensable they are due to their “incredible” skills.
summary: Описывает иллюзию всемогущества у социального E2: преувеличение своих способностей, зависимость от работы как меры самооценки, и тенденцию присваивать чужие успехи через манипуляции.

title: Социальный E2 как создатель зависимости
text: In these cases, they unleash their false generosity by showing how they can be helpful and service-oriented or how they can “save” you from countless difficulties: “I’ll do it, I’ll take care of it; don’t worry.” But at the same time, they ensure that you become dependent on them, even indebted to them… essentially becoming their subject. It is very common to see how, in relationships, social E2s create an environment where the other person remains in a state of almost childlike dependence, caught up in the idealization of an authority figure who is both immensely powerful and endlessly loving.
summary: Описывает, как социальные E2 используют мнимую щедрость и помощь для создания зависимости и контроля над другими, превращая их в зависимых субъектов через идеализацию своей власти и любви.

title: Потребность в признании и страх среднего
text:
All E2s have a radar that allows them to detect others’ needs better than anyone else. However, this can sometimes backfire. When the social E2 realizes they cannot meet the excessive demands they place on themselves, they fall into a depressive state, even belittling the abilities they do possess. One way or another, they avoid truly engaging with who they are.

Their primary goal is to stand out and be recognized—at any cost, whether by rising above or sinking below. The important thing is not to go unnoticed. Like the E4, they struggle with being moderate, average, neutral. The social E2 rejects mediocrity, and if they cannot achieve omnipotent excellence, they prefer to exaggerate their shortcomings instead.
summary: Рассматривает повышенную чувствительность социальных E2 к потребностям других, их склонность к депрессии при неудаче и навязчивое стремление выделиться, избегая посредственности любой ценой, даже через преувеличение недостатков.

title: История из упражнения «лодка»
text: Once, in a group setting, we were asked to participate in the “boat” exercise (where, at each turn, one person must be thrown out of an imaginary boat). Six people could be saved, while six had to be cast off. One person saved me, and five voted me out. Later, as I sat in my room reflecting on it, a thought crossed my mind, bringing a smile to my face: “Well, they don’t like me, but at least they’re not indifferent to me.”
summary: Личный anecdote о групповом упражнении, где автор 반друет, что даже негативная оценка лучше indifference, иллюстрируя потребность E2 в любом виде признания.

title: Фантазии и обесценивание как защита omnipotence
text:
ANA BAZA

One way social E2s maintain their sense of omnipotence is by disregarding their actual abilities and instead indulging in fantasies about themselves and others. They imagine other people’s capabilities without truly being aware of them. There is a certain disdain for intellectual pursuits that might actually help them understand these abilities. Most of all, they struggle to intellectually and concretely accept that others may possess something they lack.

Another way social E2s uphold their illusion of omnipotence is by simply belittling what others do. The ambitious E2 focuses on seeing the inept side of others, which they effortlessly detect in those around them, especially the idealistic social E1 and the highly efficient social E3. By looking down on others, they clear the way for themselves to stand out, which is ultimately a form of repressed envy. Their bombastic language is filled with absolutes and delivered with such vehemence that it can make others doubt themselves, eventually accepting the social E2’s perspective. Their speech doesn’t need to be deeply thought out; at times, they rely too much on their ability to improvise, resulting in words that may be passionate but ultimately lack substance.
summary: Объясняет, как социальные E2 поддерживают иллюю omnipotence через фантазии о собственных и чужих способностях и через активное обесценивание других — особенно E1 и E3 — как форму подавленной зависти и способа утвердить своё превосходство.

title: Стратегии избеганияLimit: прокрастинация и циклическая работа
text:
Speed and emotional numbness serve as ways to disconnect from feelings. As the most mental among the emotional types, the social E2 is not particularly tearful. Only when they confront failure or see through the illusion of their own invincibility do they allow themselves to step into a warmer, more vulnerable space.

One method they use to avoid facing their own limits is procrastination. The immense pressure they place on themselves to meet their own high standards leads them to delay tasks until the last possible moment. This forces them to complete things in a rush, relaxing their own strictness just enough to convince themselves that they can do it all. After all, they manage to finish in less time than others. What they overlook is that this approach keeps them in a constant state of stress, and prevents them from enjoying what they do.

The social E2’s work often happens in bursts. A period of intense effort is followed by a break (or rather, a necessary period of detachment) during which they withdraw from the task, exhausted by the intensity with which they started it. Then, once they regain energy, usually just as the deadline approaches, they re-engage with another titanic push. This serves a dual purpose: completing the task on time and reinforcing their belief that they can achieve anything they set their mind to, feeding their sense of omnipotence.
summary: Описывает, как социальные E2 избегают столкновения со своими пределами через эмоциональную оторванность, прокрастинацию и циклические вспышки интенсивной работы, которые служат для подтверждения веры в собственную всемогущественность.

title: Мантрa omnipotence
text:
“Crazy” ideas related to omnipotence:

“I don’t need anyone; I can handle everything myself.”

“I achieve everything I set my mind to.”

“I know what the world needs.”

“I can excel at anything I choose.”

“Nothing can resist me if I focus on it. There’s nothing I can’t do.”

“I know everything, and I can solve all problems.”

“No one will ever be as complete as I am.”

“I can do it all effortlessly.”
summary: Перечисляет характерные утверждения, отражающие иллюю omnipotence социальных E2: вера в полную самодостаточность, всезнание, неуязвимость и способность достичь чего угодно без усилий.

title: Ложная любовь и внешняя валидация
text:
False good love

Although the social E2 may appear to love themselves, it is merely a facade. They long to regain the unconditional love they once felt and believe they can achieve this by creating an exchange in which they play the role of the generous giver, ensuring that the other person will need them forever—thus securing an important place for themselves. By demanding so much of themselves, constantly positioning themselves as the giver, they avoid confronting their own emotional voids. In doing so, they neglect self-love and search for it externally.

They don’t just crave romantic love—though they often dismiss it—but rather the validation of the group, which serves as their emotional fuel and reinforces their irrational belief in being indispensable. They often forgo romantic relationships, as they require effort without social reward, only turning to them when feeling defeated. Social adoration, being worshipped by the masses, is what truly inflates their sense of abundance.
summary: Анализирует, как социальные E2 маскируют отсутствие самоуважения ложной щедростью и служебностью, стремясь к групповым похвалам как источнику чувства значимости, избегая при этом глубоких личных связей, которые требуют взаимности.

title: Social E2 as conqueror of crowds and creator of dependency
text:
Social E2s are conquerors of crowds. They seduce groups one by one, seeking collective admiration. This fosters an attitude we could call counter-dependent, because in order not to feel dependent on others’ love, they secretly work to make others dependent on them. They achieve this by infantilizing others—providing everything they believe the other person needs during the “conquest” phase. It’s as if they’re creating a debt-based system, where the other person “owes” them love, much like owing money. And once someone is in their debt, how could they possibly be ungrateful or unloving toward their “benefactor”?

Thus, love becomes currency. Once the social E2 has put the other person in their debt—and manipulated them into dependency—they move on to the next conquest, neglecting the relationship they worked so hard to build and have already tipped in their favor. From that point on, they will only return when they need something, either out of self-interest or to increase the debt. However, a healthy relationship, in which the social E2 reveals their vulnerability and admits their manipulation, is unlikely. Instead, they will always justify their actions by believing the other person needs them. Moreover, they will convince themselves that this is proof of their immense love, expecting to be valued for all they have “given.”
summary: Describes how social E2s treat love as a transactional currency by making others dependent through over-giving, then abandoning relationships until they need something, justifying manipulation as love.

title: Origins of conditional love and belief in superior love
text:
Parental love was perceived as conditional. The social E2 was projected as grand and omnipotent, raised without clear boundaries. As a result, they developed the irrational belief that “if someone sets limits for me, it means they don’t love or understand me.” Since they were loved based on their actions—whether they were good, bad, loving, or not—they learned that love had to be earned, that it’s a transaction.

The social E2 also believes that “my love is superior” to the love of others. This previously mentioned sense of grandiosity reinforces their idea of good love, meaning: “I am loved because I am great.” Or even: “If I’m not omnipotent, no one will love me.” And another step further: The social E2 will only love you if you feed their sense of greatness, if you shower them with praise.
summary: Explains how conditional parental love leads social E2s to believe love must be earned and that their love is superior, reinforcing grandiosity and dependency on admiration.

title: Irrational beliefs about false 'good love'
text:
Some irrational beliefs related to false “good love”:

“I will save you.”

“If I don’t earn everyone’s approval, I have failed.”

“If I don’t have the attention of the person I desire, I don’t exist or I am not enough.”

“If I win you over, you will always think highly of me.”

“I am loved because I am great.”

“If I am not omnipotent, you won’t love me.”

“If you fall in love with me, you will love me forever.”

“Once you experience my love, you won’t want to try any other.”
summary: Lists specific irrational beliefs that reflect the social E2’s distorted view of love as something earned through performance, rescue, and omnipotence.

title: Do-goodism as a disguise for egoic ambition
text: A special form of false good love is what we might call do-goodism. To climb the social ladder, a person must not only possess the omnipotence previously described but also demonstrate good intentions. Do-goodism serves as a way to disguise hidden egoic interests and push them into the shadows. Consciously, it manifests as a way for social E2s to spiritualize themselves. It’s a shortcut to enlightenment—presenting themselves as someone who has already attained such generosity and virtue, using displays of kindness as a means to sublimate ambition and turn it into something transcendent.
summary: Defines do-goodism as a spiritualized facade used by social E2s to mask ego-driven ambitions and present kindness as virtue while seeking status and control.

title: Personal anecdote revealing self-deception in generosity
text:
One evening, I was walking home from work on a rainy night. The streets were nearly empty. Suddenly, I heard music. It was a violinist, an elderly man from the East, accompanied by his grandson. I stopped and stood there in the rain, listening for a while. I even sat down on a wet bench, as if to show him how much I appreciated his music despite the rain, despite the cold. I was the only one who recognized something so beautiful... As I approached him, I kept mentally increasing the amount of money I was going to give, caught up in my own grand generosity.

As I walked home, I thought to myself, “I must be the most sensitive person in the world.” And just as my pride began to swell—bam!—the realization hit me: I didn’t even need an audience. I was my own most loyal spectator.
summary: Shares a personal story illustrating how the narrator’s apparent generosity was actually self-aggrandizing, revealing the hidden need for internal validation behind altruistic acts.

title: The burden of aspired status and the façade of virtue
text:
ANA BAZA

What social E2s aspire to become, or the status they seek, is often something that, once achieved, they despise and refuse to fully inhabit. Deep down, they know they lack the real capacity to uphold it—or that they don’t truly deserve it—because, along the way, they have taken advantage of others, their ideas, and their efforts, presenting them as their own. Even as the most disciplined of Twos, power eventually becomes a burden to them.

Do-goodism means attributing virtue to actions that are disconnected from genuine desire. It’s a cover-up, a façade. True kindness is different from naively walking through life. Failing to recognize the hidden selfishness behind seemingly altruistic actions only reinforces the egotistical generosity of the social E2s. From this place, they may harm others and themselves, as they remain unaware that their seemingly benevolent actions actually serve a secret purpose: to control others through dependency.

Throughout my training, I took extremely detailed notes. Others found out and started asking me for them. I always shared them, but in return, they owed me loyalty. And when I needed them, I would not take “no” for an answer.
summary: Describes how social E2s seek elevated status they feel unworthy of, use do-goodism to mask control-seeking behavior, and exploit generosity to create dependency, illustrated by the example of sharing notes as currency.

title: Осознание ошибок и внутренний конфликт у социальных E2
text: When a social E2 becomes aware that they have done something wrong, they often experience a sense of bewilderment—an almost dissociative numbness. For them, it’s as if a saint had sinned—an almost unthinkable notion. The guilt and shame that follow are immense, mixed with the shock of uncovering hidden intentions they had been denying. In some cases, they adopt a false humility, believing this will allow them to escape the consequences of their actions. At other times, they are able to truly connect with others, realizing that their perceived superiority is merely a defense mechanism. In those rare moments, they can release its weight and relate to others, and to themselves, as simply human.
summary: Описывает реакцию социальных E2 на осознание собственных ошибок: смешение замешательства, вины и стыда, попытки избежать ответственности через ложную скромность или, реже, настоящее соединение с собой и другими как равные.

title: Иррациональные убеждения социальных E2 о своей роли и ценности
text:
Let’s take a look at some more irrational ideas that can serve as examples of this:

“I am the best support anyone could ever have.”

“I am one of the kindest people you will ever meet.”

“I will save you.”

“My gift is spontaneity, and through it, people will love me.”

“I do so much for you…”

“No one will ever listen to you like I do.”

“I sacrifice myself for others.”
summary: Перечисляет типичные иррациональные убеждения социальных E2, связанные с гиперболизированной самооценкой в роли поддержки, доброты и спасения других, которые служат защитой от внутренней незащищенности.

title: Мессианский бред и fantasy «Избранного» у социальных E2
text:
The chosen one

To lead groups (or to believe they are fit to do so) social E2s embrace the grandiose, messianic fantasy that they possess abilities far superior to others, making them fundamentally different. This idea of being The Chosen One—the divine child of God, the appointed successor, or the one seated at the right hand of the Father—borders on delusional. It is so narcissistic that it becomes almost embarrassing, especially given how little foundation it actually has.

At the beginning of the Introductory Course to the Psychology of Enneatypes I took in Burgos, I introduced myself by saying that I wished for everyone to kneel before me and praise me as the savior, the beloved one. I had no real basis for saying that; it was more of a theatrical exaggeration, a humorously delusional, almost psychotic statement. I wasn’t psychotic; I knew how absurd the thought was. But still, I felt it deeply.

Years later, the first time I had a private conversation with Claudio, I confessed this thought to him. I told him that I had since realized I didn’t need to be like his beloved disciple. I simply wanted to learn from him and his students, and I was willing to be of service. He didn’t seem to react much at the time, and when I left the conversation, I felt as if he had dismissed me the way my father used to, as though he saw me as just a child.

The next day, I found out that Claudio had invited me to assist with the introductory workshops. I had been chosen. Not as the beloved disciple, but chosen nonetheless. And it was precisely because I had told him I didn’t need to be chosen. It was incredibly difficult for me to receive something I had long desired without believing it made me “The Chosen One.” Every time I achieve something I’ve aspired to, I struggle to accept that it comes from my own natural growth, not because I’m inherently different from others.
summary: Описывает мессианскую фантазию социальных E2 о себе как о «Избранном», иллюстрируя её личным опытом автора и внутренним конфликтом между欲望 быть замеченным и страхом быть увиденным как особенный.

title: Исторические примеры мессианского бреда и его корни в детстве
text:
Someone who sees the world as a social hierarchy, who believes themselves capable of everything, who views themselves as inherently good, and who thinks their love is uniquely special, will naturally assume they are meant to lead others… or even proclaim themselves the new Jesus Christ, the savior of the masses. Figures like Napoleon, Julius Caesar, Alexander the Great, Eva Perón, and Cleopatra are fitting examples. They all believed it was their destiny to guide their people to victory, convinced that under their leadership, the empire would become wiser and stronger.

The messianic delusion of being The Chosen One is often rooted in having actually been treated that way during childhood. Social E2s possess an instinctive ability to win favor with authority figures, even when they come into conflict with them. This skill was developed through having served as an emotional reference point for their parents.
summary: Приводит исторические примеры фигур с мессианским бредом и объясняет, как у социальных E2 такая фантазия часто формируется в детстве через опыт быть эмоциональной опорой для родителей и получения особого отношения со стороны власти.

title: Эмоциональная холодность и отстраненность у социальных E2 как защитная реакция
text:
Other characteristic features and psychodynamic considerations

Cold

Among E2, which is the most emotional enneatype, social E2s are the least emotional of the three subtypes. If the core defense mechanism of an E2 is repression—making unacceptable thoughts, desires, or needs unconscious—then, for social E2s, this strategy manifests as an almost complete emotional detachment. At times, when faced with a significantly painful event, they “freeze” and lose touch with parts of their emotional world.

I was at my grandmother’s funeral. She had played a major role in my upbringing, and I was very fond of her (I was even named after her). My cousins were visibly affected, each in their own way. I, on the other hand, moved around, criticizing the priest and various aspects of the funeral, but without showing the slightest sign of pain or sadness; I don’t think I shed a single tear.

In less than a year, I had lost three of my grandparents. Fifteen years later, I realized that I hadn’t cried since then. How could I have been so disconnected from myself?

ANA BAZA

A social E2 can remain impassive, elevated beyond question or doubt. To be seen as incapable, lacking knowledge, or unworthy would be catastrophic, because a role model must never fail. At the same time, this coldness and hardness serve as protection, helping them conceal their deep fear of being betrayed once again, of falling without a safety net. “To protect themselves, they sometimes mock their own feelings, ironizing them, attempting to evade them, or trivializing them altogether.”
summary: Описывает эмоциональную отстраненность социальных E2 как форму психологической защиты: подавление боли через интеллектуализацию и критику, страх показаться слабым и использование холодности как щита от страха предательства и уязвимости.

title: Осознание личной отстраненности через работу и отношения
text: I have lost track of time, always prioritizing work, projects, or clients over rest. My last partner told me that I always left them for last. That moment snapped me out of the autopilot mode I so easily fall into and made me realize just how much I invest in my profession.
summary: Автор описывает, как погруженность в работу и пренебрежение личными отношениями led to осознание своей эмоциональной отстраненности, что стало поворотным моментом в понимании собственного поведения.

title: Контраст в эмоциональной вовлеченности социальной E2
text: Yet, when in pursuit of someone, a social E2 can be immensely empathetic and emotionally expressive—only to become emotionally indifferent once their interest fades or when they move on to another conquest.
summary: Социальные E2 проявляют высокую эмпатию и эмоциональную вовлеченность в начале отношений, но быстро становятся равнодушными, когда интерес исчезает, демонстрируя цикличность привязанности и detachment.

title: Избегание уязвимости через поверхностное представление себя
text:
From a deeply subjective perspective, social E2s may transgress boundaries with ease, detaching themselves from responsibility, suppressing emotions, justifying unacceptable actions, and channeling all their energy into their desired goal—placing it above moral codes or social norms.

To avoid confronting their own deficiencies and vulnerability, they present only a surface-level version of themselves, keeping others at arm’s length and preventing anyone from truly seeing their more shadowed, needy, or flawed side. They may also cover up their mistakes with lies and arrogance, defending themselves with intense conviction and an air of innocence that can overwhelm or alienate those around them.
summary: Социальные E2 избегают контакта со своей уязвимостью, подавляя эмоции, оправдывая поступки и демонстрируя лишь идеализированную версию себя, используя ложь и высокомерие как защиту от страха быть увиденными недостаточными.

title: Жажда внимания как защита от одиночества и недостаточности
text:
Egocentric

A social E2’s craving to be at the center of attention—giving, organizing, doing, or speaking—is another way they try to soothe their feelings of loneliness and inadequacy while reinforcing their conviction that they are the center of the universe. They believe that from this position, they are indispensable and beyond questioning, protected from being brought down from their pedestal, where they receive fleeting admiration they mistake for love.

In the end, they are in love with themselves; their most fascinating conquest is their own persona. From this perspective, they interpret others’ behaviors as always being about them, whether in a positive or negative light. They also show great skill in ensnaring others to fulfill their own needs.
summary: Социальные E2 стремятся быть в центре внимания, чтобы компенсировать чувство одиночества и inadequacy, воспринимая восхищение как любовь, а свою персону — как главный объект привязанности, интерпретируя все события через призму собственного значения.

title: Внутренний критик и самоподавление как путь к истощению
text:
Demanding and hypercritical

Within a social E2 exists a relentless, insatiable inner critic that is demanding, cold, and ruthless both outwardly and inwardly, manifesting as two parallel internal forces. One refuses to let anything or anyone divert them from their ambitions and predefined ideals. Only when they achieve these goals will they allow themselves a brief moment of self-validation… before quickly moving on to the next objective or conquest. The second force is an undercurrent of aggression, a hidden and often unconscious anger that they usually direct at themselves, neglecting their own well-being, health, rest, and the ability to receive affection or care.

It may sound shocking or painful, but sometimes, contemplating death seems like the only escape from a life that is overwhelming, demanding, suffocating, burdensome, excessively sacrificial, or so full of “shoulds” that no other way out appears possible.
summary: У социальных E2 присутствует жесткий внутренний критик, который подталкивает к бесконечному достижению целей, сопровождаемый самонаправленной агрессией и пренебрежением собственными потребностями, что ведет к экзистенциальному истощению и мыслям о смерти как об избавлении.

title: Самонаказание и компенсация через самоизобилие
text:
ANA BAZA

Here, social E2s are following the deeply ingrained parental message: “No matter what you do, it will never be enough.” This is why they sometimes turn to self-indulgence—to ease their own persecutory anxiety or the harsh self-judgments they see reflected in the eyes of those they have deemed authoritative.

At times, they may stage a withdrawal, but only as a strategic move to prove that things cannot function without them.

This self-directed anger also finds an outlet in their interactions with others, taking the form of competition or contempt.

As Karen Horney points out, these are two sides of the same coin:

The proud person develops a set of values that define what they accept in themselves, what is to be glorified, and what is to be proud of. But this value system must also dictate what must be rejected, scorned, and hated—one cannot exist without the other. Pride and self-hatred are two expressions of the same process.
summary: Социальные E2 внутренне верят, что их усилий никогда недостаточно, что приводит к самонаказанию и периодическому самоизобилию как способу справиться с тревогой; их гордость и самоненависть являются двумя сторонами одного внутреннего конфликта.

title: Презрение к несовершенству как наследие родительской поляризации
text:
Contemptuous

Like E1s, social E2s have, in some way, invalidated their parents and developed (though this often remains hidden) a deep contempt for mistakes, imperfection, slowness, stupidity, pessimism, and fragility, both in themselves and in others.

This devaluation begins in the Oedipal stage, when they polarize their parental figures, idealizing one and despising the other, only to later discredit both. This inevitably places them in a relational position that does not belong to them, either as equals to or above their parents. By devaluing both figures, they are left without parental role models to idealize and identify with. This, in turn, sows the seeds for their inability, in adulthood, to recognize authority figures, viewing themselves as the only reliable source of power.

My father was a symbol of power and strength to me, while my mother remained silent. But as a child, and especially as a teenager, I hated him for the way he treated us. I saw it as an abuse of power.
summary: Социальные E2 развивают скрытое презрение к imperfection и fragility, начиная с поляризации родительских образов в Эдиповой стадии, что приводит к отвержению родительских авторитетов и вере в собственную непогрешимость как единственный источник власти.

title: Бунтарство и тирания как проявление потребности в власти и превосходстве
text:
Rebellious and tyrannical

Ever since they were little, social E2s realized that being close to authority granted them special treatment and certain benefits over their peers. They’ve learned that having privileged information or being involved in decision-making, in certain matters, comes with power.

Therefore in adulthood, social E2s are characterized by believing they know more or are more efficient than others, and by dismissing, as envious individuals, others’ attributes. It’s truly difficult for them to grant authority to anyone, beyond themselves and their own convictions.

Many biographies of social E2s include stories of intense and unstable life experiences. These, combined with their grandiose and important ideas, make them believe they have certain privileges above others. They might resemble self-preservation E2s in this way; however, they do it with open anger and a demanding, arrogant, and despotic attitude.
summary: Социальные E2 стремятся к власти с раннего возраста, связывая близость к авторитету с привилегиями; во взрослом возрасте они считают себя превосходными, отвергают чужой авторитет и проявляют деспотизм, открытую arrogance и гнев, оправдывая свое доминирование через личный опыт и grandiose идеи.

title: Этический код и отказ от правил
text:
They have their own ethical code, deciding which rules should be respected and which should not. This code can change over time, as they see fit, with total disregard for ethical or other implications. They use and abuse selective memory when it comes to their responsibilities in their affairs.

The rules are made by common men for common men. These men only legislate. I’ve had experiences that have given me a deeper understanding of life, far beyond that of the lawmakers; therefore, their rules don’t apply to me. Common people need authority to feel protected; I’ve always been alone, with no one to help or protect me. Therefore, I don’t need the others, nor do I need their rules.
summary: Описывает, как социальные E2 создают собственный этический код, игнорируя общественные правила, считая себя выше закона и не нуждающимися в внешней власти или правилах.

title: Ролевые границы и авторитет
text:
ROSA USELETI

The lack of clarity about roles and the absence of boundaries between the family subsystems are the greatest obstacles for a social E2 in managing the responsibilities that come with assuming authority. This individual wants to be both a sibling (peer) and a parent (leader) to the group at the same time.

With their critical, sharp, and disdainful thinking, and their narcissistic fantasy of omnipotence, they are distrustful of anyone who might try to lead them. Deep down, they remember a time when they naively surrendered to the will of their parents, only to be used and betrayed. This experience is the source of their suspicion toward authority.

If my boss doesn’t recognize me, I start questioning what I’m doing wrong and push myself even harder. It’s this mindset of “I have to be the best for him (or her), the favorite, the most special, the indispensable one…” because, in fact, I am that. It’s about maintaining that status, not failing, so I can keep being that way and continue climbing.
summary: Обсуждает трудности социальных E2 в определении ролей и границ, их стремление совмещать роли друга и лидера, недоверие к авторитету из-за детской травмы и зависимость от внешнего признания.

title: Невозможность терпеть границы и критику
text:
MÓNICA ANGULO

Intolerant of limits

The social E2 cannot conceive of external limits when it comes to achieving what they want, nor any limits on their own possibilities. Ironically, despite their aggressive and confrontational nature, they also don’t know how to set boundaries with others (though they do know how to humiliate them). They often fail to recognize abuse or aggression as such, and may even humiliate themselves to avoid losing a relationship. However, the pain they feel at the thought of potential loss is less about the bond at risk and more about the fear of confronting the idea of being worthless, leading to abandonment—a humiliation far greater than anything else.

Intolerant of criticism

Without confronting their own frustrations, their ego grows exponentially, making it very difficult for people of this subtype to accept the possibility of failing, making mistakes, or being seen as flawed in the eyes of others. The idea of receiving any form of criticism feels unbearable to them.

What emotions and thoughts arise when I receive criticism? The first thing I feel is that it’s a humiliation. Immediately, confusion, surprise, and anger appear, but underneath, there’s sadness and the fear of rejection, of not being worthy of love, of that love (which is really admiration, not love) disappearing. And I believe it’s the only thing that feeds me because I equated admiration with love...

The thing is, to be worthy, you need to have some merit. When I was little, it was given to me without question, but later, if I didn’t “earn” it, I didn’t get it, and even then, it wasn’t enough because for my mother, it was never enough. I want to clarify that

title: Критерий достоинства и сравнение с другими
text:
not enough.” It’s not just about how you behave, but about who you are: You must be smart, good, interesting, have conversation, be dynamic, be an atheist and a leftist, have no shame, have no fear; understand and comprehend the world and what happens in it; know about politics, religion, economics, philosophy... and become a modern, educated, proactive, brave woman. And you’re encouraged and reinforced to be fun... to be the life of the party.

ANA BAZA

I was expected to be religious and charitable. In my household, the reference figure for kindness and generosity was Mother Teresa of Calcutta. My family looked favorably upon my helping many girls with their homework; I even stayed at school with them. They would have loved for me to become a missionary and encouraged me to do so. What they didn’t know was that my motivations were driven by the attention I received from the teachers and nuns at the school, and the opportunity to prove to all my classmates that I was better than they were.
summary: Продолжение темы критики и самооценки: социальные E2 привязывают свою ценность к достижениям и внешнему одобрению, описывая строгие внутренние критерии достоинства и пример воспитания, где доброта использовалась как способ доказать превосходство.

title: Реакция на критику и страх отвержения
text:
ROSA USELETI

If someone criticizes me, I feel like I’ve failed. I no longer have all the social recognition, I’m no longer the best or the most special for the whole group. And if this happened in a group where the feedback was public, I saw it as a humiliation. There’s a fear of rejection or being no longer loved if I “don’t measure up.”
summary: Описывает острое переживание критики как унижения и потери статуса, связывая страх отрицательной оценки с потерей любви и признания.

title: Отрицание конкуренции и скрытое соперничество
text:
MÓNICA ANGULO

Competitive

For that inflated self-image, there is no possible competition. If you ask a social E2 if they’re competitive, they will firmly deny it.

I am competent, not competitive. I don’t need to compete. That would be... vulgar.

ANA BAZA

They “know” they’re the best and want the position they deserve. While they often maintain an air of composure, security, and confidence, it doesn’t always work out. Entering into competition means wanting something they don’t have, which would bring them face-to-face with a feeling of lack or envy, both of which lie beneath their character; or even more terrifying, with the emptiness that comes from feeling powerless.

I would never have called myself competitive because, honestly, when I was little, I saw all the other girls as so inferior to me that there was no competition.
summary: Обсуждает парадоксальное отношение социальных E2 к конкуренции: они отрицают свою конкурентоспособность из-за убеждённости в собственном превосходстве, но на самом деле избегают competition, чтобы не столкнуться с чувством недостаточности или envy.

title: Hidden competitiveness and fear of inadequacy
text:
Until I started getting sick, because a brilliant girl appeared in my class, and I couldn’t stand it. I subjected myself to stress and effort that kept me sick for a year, with headaches and severe dizziness. I never admitted this, but what I do remember is that when I had to repeat a year due to my absences from going to doctor after doctor, the first thing I thought was, “If I did well before, now I’ll have no competition.”

At work, I’ve also struggled with this hidden competitiveness within myself when a potential rival appeared. I’ve suffered a lot when I’ve seen someone more capable than me in some way, near my significant other. That’s when I saw my shortcomings, and I broke down, feeling I wasn’t up to the level.
summary: The speaker describes experiencing physical illness due to hidden competitiveness triggered by a superior peer, and later recognizing similar feelings at work when a rival appeared near their partner, leading to emotional breakdown and self-doubt about adequacy.

title: E2 ego and childhood origins of competitiveness
text:
ROSA USELETI

Their ego cannot conceive of a worthy competitor to take seriously. They’ve already defeated the toughest and most powerful competitor in their childhood: mom or dad. That’s why they enjoy conquering the giant only to then despise or abandon it. The underlying fear is that if they don’t succeed, they will become what they fear most: useless. Then comes the contempt and expulsion, being abandoned, just like in their childhood, to a chaotic emotional world and loneliness.

I am usually chosen, but when I’m not, it’s because they haven’t noticed me or because they are fools, not because there is someone better.

ANA GONZÁLEZ TEJERA

I can compete with women, but from above. It also depends on where I place the other woman in my hierarchy: in a position of admiration or indifference…

ROSA USELETI
summary: This chunk explains how E2s develop an inflated self-image by having 'defeated' parental figures in childhood, leading them to dismiss real competitors, interpret lack of recognition as others' failure, and rank others in hierarchical terms to maintain superiority.

title: E2 self-esteem tied to usefulness and fear of abandonment
text: A person with this character has built their self-esteem around being valuable and useful to others. If they fail to achieve this, the threat of being useless arises, leading to the inevitable feeling of abandonment. “Everyone either leaves, or I push them away,” they often say, but it’s just a way to reinforce their narrative of orphanhood and the duty to be self-sufficient. In the face of this downfall, the social E2 recomposes themselves, isolates the fear, shrinks their heart, freezes their emotions, and swears they won’t need anyone.
summary: The social E2's self-worth is contingent on being useful to others; failure triggers fears of uselessness and abandonment, prompting emotional withdrawal and self-reliance as a defense against perceived rejection.

title: Hungry for success and blind to failure
text:
From an early age, the social E2 has internalized the high expectations placed upon them, driving them to succeed in whatever they pursue. However, they are entirely unprepared for failure. Through a mix of fantasy, defense mechanisms like repression and sublimation, and an inflated self-image, they skillfully mask failure—so much so that they fail to see it at all.

From a young age, they speak eloquently about themselves as someone who does many things—which is true—and that they do “all” of them flawlessly—which is not quite as true. The key lies in how easily adults believe them and encourage them to keep going, fueling their sense of admiration and power. They grow confident in their ability to persuade others, even of their lies. Over time, they internalize an image of themselves as someone destined for greatness, expected to achieve success in whatever they undertake.

As an adult, the social E2 tries to recreate the same dynamic by imagining numerous projects and speaking about them as they did in childhood. They channel nearly all their energy into their professional life, mistaking the pursuit of achievements for the experience of love. By constantly seeking new challenges and goals, they reinforce their self-image as competent and admirable.

They are an expert at reframing setbacks, making it seem effortless to others—even under pressure. They collect achievements across their personal and professional endeavors, reinforcing the belief that they always accomplish their goals. However, while they do reach significant milestones, they often sell an image of success that surpasses their actual results. In this pursuit, they remain blind to the collateral damage left behind—something they never acknowledge—further validating their own neurosis.

Failure in the workplace is one of the rare moments when a social E2 may become aware of the extent of their self-sabotage and the harm they cause to others.

When I was a mid-level manager at a human resources consultancy, I pushed my team so hard to meet results that they eventually burned out—and I ended up changing companies. I constantly shifted between being an authoritarian leader and the most fun, easygoing colleague. I truly believed everyone could match my relentless pace, my intense dedication of time and energy. I justified it all as being necessary for the company’s success. I convinced myself I was so competent that I could handle anything better than anyone else. It wasn’t that I refused to acknowledge others’ skills or contributions—I simply didn’t see them. My ambition was so blinding that, at times, I couldn’t even see the people around me, and I lacked the slightest empathy.
summary: Social E2s are driven by early internalized expectations to succeed, using denial and grandiosity to avoid failure, conflating achievement with love, and becoming blind to their impact on others due to relentless ambition and self-deception.

title: Neglect of personal life and health in pursuit of success
text:
MÓNICA ANGULO

All the energy, creativity, effort, and passion that social E2s pour into their work come at the expense of their personal lives. They push aside anything related to love, family, friendships, or even their own physical and mental health, leaving these aspects in a barren landscape they rarely visit. They have forgotten how to play, how to enjoy love and affection—all to avoid connecting with their own vulnerability.

Taken to the extreme, social E2s neglect their diet, health, and even their most basic and urgent needs, which they see as inconvenient compared to the more “important” tasks that truly deserve their attention.

I would work on my computer for hours without stopping to eat, sometimes five or six hours straight. If I felt the need to go to the bathroom—well, by the time I actually noticed I had to go—I would look down at myself and scold myself: “Can you stop being a nuisance? Don’t be inconvenient, I’m doing something important right now.”
summary: Social E2s sacrifice personal well-being, relationships, and basic health needs for work, viewing self-care as inconvenient and using overwork to avoid vulnerability, often to the point of self-neglect.

title: Perfectionism and self-worth in social E2s
text:
I can’t comprehend mistakes, nor do I tolerate them in others—I project the same high standards onto those around me. Any mistake, no matter how big or small, feels like a failure—something unacceptable that must never happen again.

Because of my perfectionism, if even one student or participant in a group is dissatisfied, I take it personally. I feel like I must have done something wrong, and that my success within the group is at risk because of it. As if everything depended on me, as if it were all about me.

MÓNICA ANGULO
summary: This chunk describes the perfectionist tendencies of social E2s, their intolerance of mistakes in themselves and others, and their tendency to internalize group dissatisfaction as personal failure, rooted in an inflated sense of responsibility.

title: Coping mechanisms and workaholism in social E2s
text:
When social E2s experience failure, they tend to withdraw, hiding at home or seeking drastic changes in their lives—switching social circles, ending relationships, changing jobs, or even moving to another country. They may also seek refuge in addictions, such as sex, drugs, extreme sports… or, most commonly, work, which remains their top priority. Among all Enneagram types, social E2s can most accurately be described as workaholics.

If they are not in a romantic relationship, they throw themselves into friendships to fill the void. Likewise, if they experience professional failure, they redirect their energy into their partner, increasing their demands and expectations—planning trips, trying to “fix” their partner’s life, and attempting to “improve” them, as if they held the ultimate guide to being the perfect partner. In doing so, they project their own ambition onto the other person.

This obsessive drive for success often manifests as the belief that “it’s never enough.” It echoes the message they internalized from their mother figure: “It’s never enough, and you are never enough.” Each achievement becomes nothing more than a fragile confirmation of their own greatness and indispensability—but the void remains insatiable, demanding constant new conquests and extraordinary feats.

Whenever I showed something to my mom, she would always respond with, “Very good, but…” So, that “not enough” became deeply ingrained in me. The message I internalized from that “but” from my mom is: “You can still improve it, you can do better, you can perfect it even more, you can achieve a better result.” That’s how I can spend hours working, especially when I’m passionate about my job—I lose track of how much time I’ve been working. My social side also comes into play because I always have time for a glass of wine or a beer with friends. The tendency is to have my schedule overloaded with work.

MÓNICA ANGULO
summary: This chunk explores how social E2s respond to failure through withdrawal, addictive behaviors (especially workaholism), and redirecting ambition onto others. It highlights the internalized 'not enough' message from childhood that fuels relentless striving and emotional void.

title: Envy as a motivator in social E2s
text:
Envious

Envy is the hidden monster of social E2s. Admitting to envy would mean acknowledging their own lack, confronting the fact that something is missing—and that would lead them to feelings of inadequacy and emotional emptiness. Unlike E4, social E2s use envy as a fuel for self-improvement, a springboard to acquire what others have.

But let’s be clear: their focus is always on others—what power they hold, what talents they possess, what gifts they have that the social E2 does not. Of course, unlike Fours, they know that openly showing envy is not practical. To be admired, one must be useful.
summary: This chunk examines envy in social E2s as a concealed emotion that drives self-improvement rather than being expressed directly. Unlike E4s, social E2s channel envy into useful achievements while maintaining a focus on what others possess that they lack.

title: Fantasy and emotional regulation in social E2s
text:
Emotionality and fantasy

Social E2s turn to fantasy for two main reasons: first, as a defense mechanism to avoid real contact with their more depressive emotions and the underlying sense of lack; and second, as an escape from the monotony of everyday life or the discomfort of their own reality.

Their intense emotionality becomes a tool when it drives their ambition, allowing them to imagine the fulfillment they’ll feel upon achieving their goals. It also helps them spark enthusiasm and excitement in others, drawing them into the vision.

They grew up with the unspoken rule that they must control their emotions. Many individuals of this subtype experienced anaclitic depression in childhood but learned to mask it. Because hidden depressive episodes often resurface cyclically in adulthood, fantasy offers an easy way out.

Their imagination is often nurtured through reading, which, in childhood, served as a refuge, a way to disconnect from their own experiences and the vast emotional world they were never taught to understand or regulate.

The drive to actively explore the world was never encouraged in my family, especially for us daughters. My only escape came from exploring imaginary worlds through books, often beyond what was permitted. I would pretend to study or read while hiding in the bathroom, fully immersing myself in the stories, concealing the emotions they stirred in me. I kept my distance from the risk of being knocked off the pedestal of the “model daughter”—the role my parents expected me to play and the identity I clung to because, for me, it was the only way to exist.

Suicidal thoughts were a constant presence in my life until I became pregnant with my daughter.

ALBA ARENA
summary: This chunk describes how social E2s use fantasy to manage depressive emotions and emotional neglect from childhood. It highlights reading and imagination as refuges, the suppression of genuine emotions, and the long-term impact of unmet emotional needs, including suicidal ideation alleviated by pregnancy.

title: Emotional control and distorted perception in social E2s
text:
Despite being an emotional type, social E2s exercise strict control over their feelings, allowing only a few to surface—mainly aversion and anger. Other emotions, though expressed, aren’t entirely genuine, as their emotional responses don’t always flow naturally with their thoughts and actions. Instead, it’s their imagination that generates emotions, adjusting their intensity based on what’s needed in the moment. Their perception of reality is shaped by exaggeration and reinterpretation, keeping the fantasy alive.

By relying on obvious stereotypes, social E2s reshape reality, tending toward overly abstract, generalized thinking filled with absolutes. These generalizations help maintain the illusion that they understand reality, even as they completely distort it. The aim is to avoid questioning their sense of omnipotence. The reality they perceive is partly based on facts, but it’s also built on a carefully crafted personal fantasy. In this imagined world, they see themselves as special, fortunate, and important, while everyone around them seems to exist in relation to them. This self-created narrative helps uphold their idealized self-image.
summary: This chunk explains how social E2s regulate emotions through imagination rather than authentic expression, relying on fantasies and stereotypical thinking to maintain an idealized self-image and avoid confronting limitations or negative realities.

title: Использование воображения и фантазий для создания идеализированной реальности
text:
Their histrionics can also be understood as a kind of lived imagination, where they replace present reality with an idealized version of life. Social E2s are constantly creating and recreating grand scenarios in their minds that could happen. It’s similar to the daydreaming of an E7 or the fable of the milkmaid dreaming of riches from The Milkmaid and Her Pail. Being fundamentally optimistic characters, they struggle to acknowledge negative aspects or the price they may have to pay to achieve their goals.

One day, during a SAT session, they were about to play a video of Claudio for morning meditation. For some reason, I ended up without a partner (which happened often because I was so “selective”). So, I sat alone on my bench, and when I opened my eyes, of course—there was no one there. But who was in front of me? None other than Claudio Naranjo himself, looking straight at me, addressing only me. And so, I meditated with the Maestro, one-on-one. I felt incredibly lucky.

(When it was over, I laughed so hard at how I had just sublimated the fact that I had been left without a partner again.)
summary: Описывает, как социальные E2 используют живое воображение и фантазии для замены реальности идеализированными сценариями, сравнивая их с мечтательностью E7 и приводя личный пример медитации с Клаудио Наранхо как проявление их внутреннего мира.

title: Фантазия как инструмент самовозвышения и давления на реальность
text:
ANA BAZA

Social E2s tend to think in images; they vividly see what they imagine. Since they believe they can accomplish anything they set their minds to, they convince themselves that their fantasies are real. They create an idealized vision of how things should unfold and try to shape reality accordingly, sometimes even forcing circumstances, people, and themselves into alignment. Yet, they remain largely unaware of their own forcefulness or the extent to which they pressure others. Their skill lies in “inflating” reality, much like a peacock fanning its feathers—magnificent, attention-grabbing, and designed to impress. They are master tailors of a prêt-à-porter reality, crafted perfectly to fit their narrative and always in their favor. As Napoleon famously said after his early victories in Egypt: “I already see myself following in the footsteps of Alexander the Great. I imagine myself founding a new religion, marching into Asia atop an elephant, a new Quran in my hand.”

In their escape into fantasy, they see themselves as the Sun—radiating warmth, beloved by all, yet never to be approached too closely. They are like the tiny flames in Eduardo Galeano’s writing: “Some foolish flames neither burn nor shed light, but others blaze with life so fiercely that you can’t look at them without blinking, and if you approach you shine in the fire.”

I was the eldest of several siblings, burdened with the weight of responsibility my parents naturally placed on me. I had no choice but to adapt to being “the grown-up one.” Yet, whenever I realized I wasn’t truly as capable as I was expected to be, an unbearable anxiety took over—an intense fear of being exposed and humiliated. So, I took refuge in fantasies of omnipotence, which slowly became part of my personality.
