title: Реформы и стратегическое видение E2: от календаря до гражданства галлов
text:
Thus began a series of reforms that would transform the city and government. Many in Rome were unemployed, so Caesar initiated the construction of temples, libraries, and a port—seeking to benefit not only the nobility but also the common people. To address the chaos caused by an inaccurate calendar, which had led to recurring problems, he introduced a new system based on the solar year—one that would apply across the empire and endure to this day. Another bold, unexpected move was granting Roman citizenship to the peoples of Gaul. While this was meant to prevent uprisings, it also reflected a broader vision of the conquered territories. The Senate saw this as an attack on Rome, but in reality, it was a masterful strategy to keep the Gauls under control.

He was a visionary—a mix of idealist and braggart—who sometimes achieved the impossible. Everything about him was pure strategy, designed to control and pull the strings, to enrich himself and increase his glory. But at the same time, he was a revolutionary, a patriarch who delighted in pleasing his people and improving the common good. A tyrant disguised as a lamb, he wanted to dominate other nations while also being accepted and loved by them.

Something sudden was about to alter Caesar’s fate once again: the unexpected arrival of Cleopatra in Rome, bringing with her Caesarion, their son. This would strengthen Caesar’s dream of founding a dynasty, crush Brutus’s hopes of becoming his successor, and ultimately seal his fate.
summary: This chunk outlines Caesar’s reforms—calendar reform, public works, granting citizenship to Gauls—and his dual strategy of benevolent leadership and hidden control, all typical of a social E2’s visionary yet self-serving ambition.

title: Деградация E2: от самообожествления к неизбежному падению
text:
Social E2s also idealize themselves in their goals. They are relentless and don’t know when to stop, pushing beyond their limits and what the system can tolerate. This passionate pursuit inevitably leads to increasingly delusional ambitions.

In 45 BCE, Julius Caesar began fantasizing about Rome being ruled by a single family—his own. His delusions of grandeur had become boundless and unstoppable. He started commissioning statues of himself to be placed alongside those of the gods, constructing buildings in his family’s name, wearing the royal purple toga once reserved for kings, and even declaring his birthday an official holiday. Everything he did was steeped in arrogance and self-deification. The Senate was outraged when he attempted to declare himself dictator for life.
summary: This chunk describes the culmination of the social E2’s ambition—self-deification, delusional grandeur, and the move toward lifelong dictatorship—which provoked senatorial outrage and foreshadowed his assassination.

title: Убийство Цезаря и его последствия
text:
That was when some senators began plotting how to eliminate him. In a desperate yet bold move, Caesar decided to conquer Parthia. Another victory would not only bring wealth to the Roman people but also satisfy his insatiable thirst for conquest. His war plans, however, provoked an immediate and decisive reaction. Fearing that he would succeed and crown himself King of Rome, his enemies conspired to put an end to him.

A few days before his planned departure, they summoned him to a meeting. As soon as Caesar stepped into the Senate, several friends and allies suddenly surrounded him, striking him with twenty-three stab wounds. Among his assassins was Brutus. Shakespeare would later immortalize Caesar’s famous last words upon seeing him: “Et tu, Brute?”

Rome was shaken to its core. The people mourned him and avenged his killers. Chaos erupted in the city, splitting it into two factions: one led by Mark Antony and the other by Brutus. Brutus was ultimately defeated and took his own life on the battlefield. Mark Antony fled to Egypt and married Cleopatra, with whom he would later die by suicide. Caesarion was murdered at seventeen. With Caesar’s death and years of ensuing violence, his nephew Octavian eventually emerged as Rome’s first emperor, ruling for forty years. In the end, Caesar had succeeded in toppling the Republic and establishing the Julio-Claudian dynasty.

This architect of the modern world, obsessed with power and domination, failed to realize that perhaps not everyone shared his vision. That his changes were happening too fast for some. That his so-called good intentions were more a product of personal ambition than the ideals he sold to himself. But after him, nothing was ever the same again.
summary: Описывает заговор сенаторов против Цезаря, его убийство в Сенате, последствия для Рима и историческую оценку его наследия как ambitious leader, чьи действия были driven by personal ambition despite claims of public good.

title: Цитаты Цезаря, отражающие социальный E2 тип
text:
Quotes attributed to Julius Caesar that reflect the social E2 personality:

“I had rather be first in a village than second at Rome.”

“It’s only hubris if I fail.”

“Bid me run, and I will strive with things impossible.”

“If I fail it is only because I have too much pride and ambition.”

“Men in general are quick to believe that which they wish to be true.”

“I came, I saw, I conquered.”

“If you must break the law, do it to seize power; in all other cases observe it.”

“Men willingly believe when they want to.”

“War gives the right to the conquerors to impose any condition they please upon the vanquished.”

“Cowards die many times before their deaths; the valiant never taste of death but once.”

“There is nothing so difficult that it cannot be overcome.”
summary: Собрание афоризмов, приписываемых Цезарю, которые иллюстрируют черты социального E2 типа: стремление к первенству, гордость, амбициозность, манипулятивность и вера в силу воли и завоеваний.

title: Литературный пример: Люсьен де Рубемпре из «Иллюзий потерянных»
text:
Literary and cinematic examples

A literary example

Lucien de Rubempé

From Lost Illusions by Honoré de Balzac

Lost Illusions is a novel by Honoré de Balzac, published in three parts between 1837 and 1843. In it, Balzac explores a theme deeply tied to his own personal experience: his fraught relationship with the bourgeois society of his time. Blending autobiography with a sociological study, philosophy with an analysis of human passions, realism with visionary imagination, he tells the story of Lucien, a provincial poet with grand literary ambitions.

Description

The titular “lost illusions” are those of Lucien—a young man struggling to assert himself as he enters the literary world in search of a future. They are also the illusions his family once had about him.

Lucien is admired for his beauty and talent, yet he lacks willpower. He is indolent, weak, selfish, and unaware. A witness to his time, he lacks the resolve to stand against the all-consuming and ruthless Parisian society of pleasure and appearances.

A would-be writer in constant pursuit of love and happiness, he is a romantic incapable of seeing the darkness in people and society. Unknowingly, he becomes a sacrificial victim in the art of oppression. The novel chronicles his existential failure—the inevitable shattering of illusions—and the weaknesses of a provincial man who proves to be an antihero. Lucien’s disillusionment is magnified by two mirrors, two “virtuous circles”: his family and the cenacle of truly great men, the intellectuals of his time, a world to which he belongs, at least in the early stages of his life.

Plot summary

Introduced into the high society of Angoulême, Lucien, with his charm and affability, quickly wins everyone over. Men and women alike are captivated by his beauty and talent. Still young, he sets off for Paris with his mentor—an older, married woman—chasing success. This platonic love marks the beginning of many illusions that will ultimately lead to Lucien’s downfall. When he arrives in the capital, he tries to publish his poetry but fails, forcing him to turn to journalism.

The young duke watched the signs of Lucien’s meditation, and was not mistaken as to the cause of it; he had revealed to that ambitious mind, a mind without fixed will but not without desire, a whole political horizon; just as the journalists, like Satan on the pinnacle of the temple, had shown him the literary world and its riches at his feet.

Lucien meets d’Arthèz, a liberal philosopher who introduces him to the cenacle, a group of young men with different political views, professions, and social backgrounds, but bound by a deep friendship and devoted to an ascetic life in service of art or science. For a time, Lucien frequents the cenacle, but he is too impatient to compose a great literary work. His true desire is to make money—to redeem himself in the eyes of his family. Above all, he seeks easy success. He wants glory, to feel like a hero, and caught in the whirlwind of high society, he abandons all ethical principles and succumbs to ruthless competition.

It is to be remarked that certain truly poetic natures with weak wills, absorbed in sentiment and in rendering their sensations by images, are essentially deficient in the moral sense which ought to accompany all observation. Poets prefer to receive impressions themselves rather than enter into the souls of others and study the mechanism of their feelings. [...]
summary: Описывает литературный пример социального E2 типа — Люсьена де Рубемпре из романа Бальзака «Иллюзии потерянные»: его амбиции, тщеславие, отсутствие силы воли, погоня за успехом и славой, моральный компромисс и конечное разочарование в свете жестоких реалий общества.

title: Люсьен осознает силу прессы и вступает в журналистику
text:
His soul, his heart, his mind were, one and all, metamorphosed; he thought no more of doubting methods in presence of such glorious results.

He realizes that “the Press and intellect were really the means which moved society.” Entering journalism, he convinces himself that he can navigate this intriguing and profitable world, seeing it as a far easier path than poetry. He buys into the competitive mechanisms that define it, the strategic ways of networking. He believes this is his chance to stand out for his intellect and supposed cleverness. But his grand ambitions of wealth and lasting fame will ultimately lead to his ruin.

Let’s have a look at this conversation with his editor:

“Yes,” answered Dauriat. “I’ve read his article; and it is for his own sake that I refuse to publish his ‘Daisies.’ Yes, monsieur, I shall give you more money during the next six months for the articles I shall ask you to write for me than you could ever earn by unsalable poems.”

“But fame?” cried Lucien.

Lucien sees himself as the master of his destiny, when in reality, he is merely a pawn of the system. He begins signing his articles under the pseudonym “Rubempré,” using his mother’s aristocratic name, driven by a deep desire to obtain a noble title.

The consciousness of power and his own strength shone from a face now enlightened by love and experience. He had come front to front with the literary world and society, and he believed he could walk through both a conqueror.
summary: Люсьен осознает, что пресса и интеллект движут обществом, вступает в журналистику, используя псевдоним Rubempré, чтобы вернуть дворянский титул, верит в свою силу и удачу, но на самом деле становится пешкой системы.

title: Люсьен меняет allegiance ради славы и титула
text:
He falls in love with a young actress named Coralie and adopts a life of luxury. His ambition pushes him toward politics, leading him to switch from the liberal newspaper where he once wrote to an openly monarchist publication.

Lucien never allowed himself to think of the morrow. He saw his so-called friends behaving just as he did, — spending their money as they got it, and careless of the future. Once admitted into journalism and literature on a footing of equality, Lucien perceived the enormous difficulties he would have to conquer if he endeavored to rise. All were willing to have him as an equal; no one would consent to his becoming their superior. Insensibly, therefore, he renounced the desire for literary fame, and contented himself with thinking that political good fortune was easier to acquire.

Sensitive to flattery, Lucien switches sides and begins writing articles in support of the government. His ultimate goal is to reclaim the noble title of Rubempré, which once belonged to his mother.

The Countess de Montcornet flatters him while explaining the rules of the game:

“They have told her you are as handsome as you are witty, and she is dying to see you.”

[...]

“There is not one man in a thousand who unites a great talent with so marvellous an aptitude for social adaptation as you have shown.”

[...]

“Louise wished to obtain a decree from the king giving you the right to bear the name and title of de Rubempré. She wished to bury Chardon. [...] You treat these ideas as flimsy and frivolous; but we know life; we know how solid are the advantages of a title when borne by a handsome and elegant young man. Present to an English beauty, or indeed to any heiress, ‘Monsieur Chardon,’ or ‘Monsieur le Comte de Rubempré,’ and you will see the difference in the welcome. The count may be deep in debt, but all hearts are open to him; his beauty, set in the light of his title, is like a diamond well mounted. ‘Monsieur Chardon’ would not even be noticed.
summary: Люсьен переходит в монархистскую прессу, поддается лести, стремится вернуть титул Rubempré через политическую лояльность, веря, что аристократическое имя откроет двери в высшее общество, несмотря на долги и иллюзии.

title: Журналистская среда использует Люсьена, лестью подталкивая к самопогублению
text:
The competitive and sycophantic world of journalism quickly recognizes Lucien’s weakness for flattery and praises him insincerely for his supposed strategic genius. They compare his ability to conquer to that of Napoleon, all while using him for financial and political gain.

“Our friend,” resumed Finot, patting Lucien’s hand, “has made a brilliant record in this last respect. Lucien has greater means, more talent, more wit, than all his detractors put together, — and beauty to boot. His old friends can’t forgive him his successes; they ascribe them to luck.”

“Such luck,” said des Lupeaulx, “doesn’t come to fools or weaklings. Can Bonaparte’s career be called luck? There were twenty generals above him wanting to command the army of Italy, just as there are a hundred young men at this moment who long to visit Mademoiselle des Touches, whom I hear, my dear fellow,” — he added, tapping Lucien on the shoulder, — “the world gives you for a wife.”

Lucien falls into the trap set by his fellow journalists, soon revealing all the traits of a naive and ambitious man—chief among them, false modesty.

“Are you free in it?” asked Michel.

“As free as a man can be when he is indispensable,” replied Lucien with feigned humility.

Convinced of his own importance in the world of journalism, he digs his own grave.
summary: Журналисты льстят Люсьену, сравнивая его с Наполеоном, используя его тщеславие и стремление к признанию,而他沉溺 на ложной скромности и вере в свою незаменимость, не замечая, как роет свою могилу.

title: Иллюзии Люсьена разбиваются: падение и разочарование
text:
The poet saw, not without some reason, a great fortune in his beauty and his talents when supported by the name and title of Comte de Rubempré. Madame d‘Espard, Madame de Bargeton, and Madame de Montcornet held him by that thread as a child holds a cockchafer. Lucien was flying in a given circle.

Lucien’s downfall, along with his illusions, is hastened by his naivety and his fatalistic view of life. His change of allegiance is seen as disgraceful in the journalistic circles he belongs to. His old friends and acquaintances attack him without restraint, while his new colleagues quickly grow to despise him.

Before long, Lucien is entirely discredited in his profession, completely penniless, and a source of shame to his family.

Lucien adopted Blondet’s axioms as the rule of his future: “All things come out right;” “Nothing can injure those who have nothing;” “We have nothing to lose but what we seek;” “Swim with the current and it must take you somewhere;” “A man of intellect who has a footing in society can make his fortune when he will.
summary: Люсьен верит, что красота, талант и титул принесут fortune, но его легкомыслие и перемена взглядов приводят к полному краху: потеря репутации, денег и уважения, хотя он сохраняет веру в афоризмы Blondet о судьбе и успехе.

title: Падение Люсьена и его попытки восстановления
text: Lucien’s decline accelerates: his companion dies, he is left destitute, and he loses the esteem of his peers, whether in the literary cenacle, the liberal press, or the government-affiliated newspapers. He oscillates between remorse and new illusions, trying to recover from each disappointment with fresh hopes. Eventually, he returns to Angoulême, where he reunites with his family, repents repeatedly, and contemplates suicide.
summary: Describes Lucien’s continued downfall, emotional instability, return to family, repeated repentance, and suicidal thoughts as he struggles with failure and illusion.

title: Анализ характера Люсьена через призму его друга д’Артеза
text:
When his friend d’Arthèz writes to Lucien’s sister, Eve, asking about him, she replies:

Will is lacking to him; he is without strength against the allurements of pleasure, or against the satisfaction of his minor ambitions. Lazy, like all poetic natures, he thinks himself clever in shirking difficulties instead of facing them. He might have courage at one moment, at the next he would be a coward; and he deserves as little praise for his courage as blame for his cowardice. Lucien is a harp, the strings of which tighten or stretch according to the variations of his atmosphere. He might write a fine book in a phase of happiness or anger, and not be conscious afterwards of its success, much as he desired it.

D’Arthèz sees Lucien’s world for what it truly is—a construction of his own mind, built from illusions, disappointments, and regrets.

“I consider periodical repentance a great hypocrisy,” said d’Arthèz, solemnly; “repentance then becomes a premium given to wrong-doing. Repentance is a virgin act due from our souls to God; a man who repents again and again becomes a sycophant. I fear that you see only absolutions in your repentance.”
summary: Lucien’s sister and friend d’Arthèz describe his lack of will, emotional volatility, self-deception, and hypocritical repentance, portraying him as driven by mood and illusion rather than genuine integrity.

title: Truman Capote как пример социального Энеаграмма типа 2
text:
***

A cinematic example

Truman Capote

Capote (2005)

Director: Bennett Miller

As a true social E2, he presents himself as a well-groomed, elegant, modern man with a touch of effortless charm. He looks people straight in the eye, scanning those who listen to him. We first meet him at a party, surrounded by his entourage, in an open, intellectual, avant-garde atmosphere. The resemblance to Oscar Wilde is undeniable, though they belong to different eras. With his lively conversation, sharp wit, and quick, biting humor, he becomes the center of attention. Brutally honest in his words, yet so warm and playful that one feels privileged to be within his circle of friends. Here’s how he introduces himself: “I’m honest. I am honest about what I write about. I’ll let you know if it’s autobiographical, or if it’s about me, or if it’s not. And I find autobiographical stories at this juncture of my life to be quite boring.”

Then, suddenly, he shifts to another topic, revealing his direct and cutting style:

I had lunch with Jimmy Baldwin the other day. And he told me the plot of his new book. And he said to me: “the writing’s going well, but I just want to make sure it’s not one of those problem novels.” And I said: “Jimmy, your novel’s about a Negro homosexual who’s in love with a Jew. Wouldn’t you call that a problem?”

One day, while reading the newspaper, he comes across a story about a family brutally murdered in a small town in Kansas. Truman, opportunistic and astute, immediately recognizes the story’s potential. At that moment, though he doesn’t yet realize it, he is pioneering a new literary style: the non-fiction novel.

Capote rushes to cover the story, accompanied by his best friend, Nelle Harper Lee—who will later write To Kill a Mockingbird. Thus begins an epic five-year journey that will culminate in his masterpiece, In Cold Blood, making him the most famous writer in the United States.

On the train to Kansas, Truman meets with Nelle. A young Black conductor recognizes him and praises his latest book. Noticing how affected Capote is by the compliment, Nelle realizes that he has paid the man to say it. Rather than deny it, Truman simply smiles, amused by his friend’s perceptiveness. This scene reveals the relentless need for validation typical of an excessive social E2—even if it means resorting to tricks.

Upon arriving in the small town where the murders took place, Capote heads straight to the lead investigator, expecting special treatment. But he quickly realizes that neither his fame nor his refined appearance will win him sympathy or information. He is at a loss. It is Nelle who earns the trust of the locals.

Truman has no qualms about sneaking into the funeral home and secretly opening the caskets to see the victims’ bodies. Thanks to Nelle, he manages to speak with the girl who discovered the murdered family. From this point on, Truman begins to build alliances using his charm, familiarity, and emotional appeal to gain trust. What starts as a casual conversation turns into a steady stream of confessions, which he meticulously records. The girl even hands over the diary of the murdered family’s daughter.

Once Truman sets his sights on uncovering the story, he, as a social E2, detaches from emotion—his own and others’—treating people as instruments to serve his purpose.

One night, returning to the hotel, he tells Nelle that he can retain 94% of what he hears. This is a hallmark of control characteristic of the social E2 (as well as a classic boast).

That same night, Truman speaks with his partner, Jack, over the phone. He sounds despondent, admitting that he’s struggling to make progress. “Normal life falls away. But then, I was never much for normal life. People here won’t talk to me. They want someone like you, like Nelle. Me, they hate.”

His usual seductive tactics don’t work here. He doesn’t understand the townspeople, nor can he empathize with them. His carefully curated appearance is of no use in this environment. He feels out of place and powerless. Aware that he is, in some way, failing, he copes by dismissing the locals as unbearably ordinary.
summary: Analyzes Truman Capote as a classic social Enneagram Type 2, highlighting his charm, need for validation, manipulative use of relationships, emotional detachment in pursuit of goals, and reliance on image and performance to gain trust and control.

title: Truman's social E2 manipulation at the investigator's dinner
text: One evening, Nelle and Truman have dinner at the lead investigator’s home, seizing the opportunity since the detective’s wife admires Capote as a writer. He puts on his usual performance—witty and entertaining, sharing Hollywood gossip before shifting to a poignant personal story about his mother’s death and how his father once told him: “Talk. Talk about anything. I mean, any subject in the world. Don’t worry whether it’ll interest me or not. Just talk… so I won’t break down.” Most social E2s have heard something similar in childhood—when their parents deny their emotions while simultaneously asking them to take responsibility for theirs.
summary: This chunk describes Truman using a personal, emotional story to gain the investigator's trust during dinner, a tactic typical of social E2s who learned early to perform emotional labor for approval.

title: Truman's calculated social E2 behavior in investigation and relationships
text: The moment he finishes his story, he coldly and methodically transitions back to discussing the murder case. He gains another step in his investigation: the detective shows him the crime scene photos. Throughout the movie, we see Truman’s social E2 nature on full display. His demeanor is polished and seemingly effortless. His gestures and storytelling are theatrical, carefully weaving in emotional elements—enough to make an impact without overindulging in sentimentality. He knows exactly what to say to make others open up, creating a false sense of intimacy. This is how the social E2 betrays others—just as they were once betrayed. In one scene, Capote is on the phone with his partner, who complains that he hasn’t seen him in a long time. Truman promises a romantic getaway to the Costa Brava. It’s common for this personality type to sideline their partner in favor of their professional world, making grand, extravagant promises they rarely fulfill.
summary: This chunk illustrates Truman's shift from emotional performance to investigative focus, highlighting his theatrical social E2 tendencies, emotional manipulation, and pattern of neglecting personal relationships for professional ambition.

title: Truman's exploitation of Perry Smith through false intimacy
text: The two murderers are finally arrested. By the time they are brought to the county courthouse, Truman has already won the sheriff’s wife over with gifts and flattery, securing access to the jail cell of Perry Smith, one of the killers. He immediately senses that this story is bigger than a single article. Without hesitation, he calls the editor of The New York Times and persuades him to let him stay longer. Perry and his accomplice are found guilty and sentenced to death, so they are transferred to Kansas. By this point, Truman has already formed a friendship with Perry and asks to be added to his visitor list, promising to find him a lawyer for his appeal. In doing so, he subtly creates a debt that he will collect sooner or later.
summary: This chunk details Truman's strategic manipulation of Perry Smith by building a false bond of friendship and creating emotional debt through promises of legal help, typical of social E2 exploitative dynamics.

title: Truman's moral erosion and identification with the killer
text: In New York, Truman tells a journalist about his new book: “Two worlds exist in this country. The quiet, conservative life, and the life of those two men. The underbelly. The criminally violent. And those worlds converged that bloody night.” It’s as if he were describing the two opposing forces within himself. Gradually, Truman begins to realize how much he has in common with the murderer and that, sometimes, the only thing separating one world from the other is sheer coincidence. At a party, Nelle and Jack joke about their friend: “Truman in love with Truman,” as they watch him strut from one conversation to the next. At one point, his thirst for greatness resurfaces, along with his cold detachment: “It’s the book I was always meant to write… And I’d also like to see them alive… I need to hear their stories…” Jack warns him with a telling remark: “Just be careful what you do to get what you want,” cautioning him about the lines he tends to cross in pursuit of his ambition.
summary: This chunk explores Truman's growing self-awareness of his dark parallels with Perry Smith, his narcissistic drive for legacy, and the warnings from friends about his ruthless ambition, reflecting the shadow side of social E2.

title: Truman's manipulative care and emotional blackmail toward Perry
text: Truman bribes the prison warden to gain unrestricted access to Smith and his accomplice, Hickock. When he finds out Perry is on a hunger strike, he appears to show concern—though it’s likely just another ploy, using false generosity to deepen Perry’s sense of debt. He tends to him with affectionate care, feeding him baby food. Through this relationship, Truman starts to uncover the person behind the killer. He continues to manipulate Perry, sharing a painful childhood memory to gain his trust. He even tells him that, deep down, they’re not so different—trying to establish a bond of “brotherhood,” a theme that often appears in social E2 dynamics. Before leaving Perry’s cell, Truman tightens his grip, setting the first price on their “friendship.” He wants to take Perry’s notebooks and justifies his request with emotional blackmail: “If I leave here without understanding you… the world will see you as a monster… always. I don’t want that.” He disguises his true intentions, making it seem as if he is Perry’s only hope for redemption.
summary: This chunk describes Truman's exploitative caregiving, false empathy, and use of shared trauma and emotional blackmail to manipulate Perry into compliance, framing his actions as benevolent while advancing his own agenda.

title: Truman's cyclic manipulation and Perry's fading hope
text: Later, Truman talks with Nelle, who expresses concern about how he is using Perry. She tells him he’s not respecting Perry as a person. But Truman dismisses her words entirely—he can’t see past his goal and the recognition it will bring him: “Sometimes when I think how good my book can be, I can hardly breathe.” Truman returns to Perry’s cell to tell him he’ll be gone for a while. Perry, still holding on to hope, says he trusts the book will help reduce his sentence. Seizing this moment, Capote once again pressures him to reveal what happened on the night of the murders. He exerts his dominance, making Perry feel indebted: “I have invitations to be in Morocco, Greece… and I prefer to be here with you.” He lies effortlessly and, before leaving without further explanation, seduces him once more with a hollow display of affection: “I miss you already. Write me every five minutes.”
summary: This chunk captures Truman's disregard for ethical concerns, his manipulative return to Perry leveraging hope and false affection, and his persistent pressure for information through emotional domination and deceit.

title: Truman's prioritization of work over Perry and their shared origins
text: Truman heads to Costa Brava, where he and Jack have rented a house. Shawn, the New York Times editor, calls him, thrilled by the drafts of In Cold Blood he’s received. Truman laments that he can’t finish the book until Perry tells him exactly what happened on the night of the murders. Nelle visits with a letter from Perry. She and Jack silently witness Truman’s chilling indifference toward Perry’s pleas and desperation. At one point, Truman verbalizes something he has long sensed—that he and the murderer are two sides of the same coin: “It’s as if Perry and I grew up in the same house, and one day he stood up and went out the back door… while I went out the front.”
summary: This chunk highlights Truman's obsession with completing his book over Perry's emotional needs, and his profound, albeit self-serving, recognition of their shared psychological origins, reflecting the social E2's capacity for deep insight twisted by ambition.

title: Truman's deceptive manipulation and Perry's reluctant confession
text:
Back in Kansas, Truman continues lying. When Perry asks to see the book, he insists he hasn’t written anything yet—when, in truth, all that’s missing is the ending. It’s a masterclass in one of social E2’s signature betrayals: deception.

Truman returns to New York for the premiere of In Cold Blood. The packed theater listens, spellbound, as he recounts two chapters filled with hauntingly realistic imagery. When he finishes, he receives a standing ovation. Shawn tells him the book will not only change how people see his work but also how literature itself is written. Social E2 personalities, thanks to their deep self-assurance, often take bold creative risks by being innovative and transgressive, which makes them stand out as unique and creative in their fields.

Perry informs Truman that, thanks to him, their execution has been temporarily suspended. But when Perry still refuses to talk about the crime, Capote finally drops the mask. His true intentions surface, along with his cruelty: “There’s not a word or a sentence, or a concept that you can illuminate for me. There is one singular reason I keep coming here. November 14, 1959. That’s all I want to hear from you. And when you want to tell me what I need to hear, you let me know. Until then, I won’t be back.”

Desperate, Perry calls Truman back. He’s furious after reading about In Cold Blood’s release in the newspaper. Truman, without a shred of guilt, lies to his face, claiming the Times article is false. Then, once again, he leans into their so-called friendship—though it’s impossible to tell whether it’s genuine or just another manipulation: “I couldn’t pretend to be your friend… cause the truth is, I can’t help wanting to be.”

Truman gives Perry some childhood photos that his sister provided when he visited her—deceiving him once again, this time about her feelings toward him. At last, Perry softens and recounts what happened on that fateful night. Initially, they had no intention of killing anyone, but that’s how it turned out, and he was the only one who fired the gun, killing every member of the family. He admits he is deeply ashamed but also acknowledges that he acted without the slightest mercy. Just like Truman.
summary: This chunk details Truman Capote's continued deception of Perry Smith, including false claims about the book's progress and manipulative displays of affection, culminating in Perry's confession of the murders. It highlights Truman's social E2 traits of manipulation, self-justification, and creative boldness, while Perry admits to the killings without mercy, mirroring Truman's emotional detachment.

title: Truman's emotional isolation and Perry's execution
text:
The novel is finally finished, but Truman needs the sentence to be carried out, which continues to be delayed. We see him on the phone, speaking in an utterly tragic and self-absorbed manner: “It’s harrowing. All I want to do is write the ending and there’s no end in sight.”

Meanwhile, Perry keeps reaching out to the man he considers a friend. Truman, however, responds with brief, dismissive letters, distancing himself from him.

Nelle has grown apart from Capote due to his coldness regarding the case. She, in turn, has published her own book, and the film adaptation of To Kill a Mockingbird is receiving great acclaim. At the premiere party, she spots Truman standing off to the side, alone, dejected, drunkenly sipping another drink. He doesn’t congratulate her on her success. Instead, he mutters dismissively under his breath that it’s nothing special and fixates on his own misery. He is his own universe, and nothing else matters. “I may never recover from this... They’re torturing me.”

Truman sinks deeper into depression until Perry calls to inform him that their appeal has been rejected. Capote is left speechless. From that moment, he seems to be in shock, refusing to see Perry for a final goodbye, speak to anyone, or even get out of bed. It isn’t until Nelle brings him a letter from Perry that he finally decides to visit one last time. His interaction with suffering and emptiness visibly unsettles him. As a true social E2, he hides from others’ eyes, withdrawing until the situation shifts or his feelings pass.

He enters the room where the two condemned men await him, already dressed for the gallows, his posture a mix of guilt and defensiveness. They laugh, telling him they understand why he wouldn’t visit. Truman appears genuinely affected and tries to justify his behavior: “I did everything I could. I truly did.” Perry asks him to attend the execution so he can see a friendly face, and Truman agrees. But soon, he returns to his own grievances, without even alluding to his “friend’s” fate: “It was a terrible experience… And I will never get over it.”

When he tries to absolve himself—“There wasn’t anything I could have done to save them”—Nelle responds, “Maybe not… but the fact is, you didn’t want to.”

Truman Capote never finished another book.
summary: This chunk portrays Truman's deepening isolation and self-absorption after completing In Cold Blood, his emotional withdrawal from Perry and others, and his eventual visit to the condemned men before their execution. Despite Perry's plea for companionship, Truman remains fixated on his own suffering, ultimately admitting his lack of desire to save them, confirming Nelle's accusation. His creative output ceases afterward.

title: Jokes and vignettes illustrating E2 dynamics
text:
Jokes and vignettes

“Why such a tight hug? Afraid I’ll slip away?

“No. I’m just trying to deflate your ego.”

Illustration by Francisco J. Olea

“Next, the master will attempt to break an object with the power of his indifference.”

Illustration by Francisco J. Olea
summary: This chunk presents two illustrative vignettes that metaphorically capture social E2 dynamics: one depicting a hug as an ego-deflating maneuver rather than affection, and another framing indifference as a powerful, almost violent force. These highlight the manipulative and emotionally controlling tendencies of E2 personalities under the guise of care.

title: Therapeutic transformation of social E2: overcoming grandiosity
text:
Transformation process and therapeutic recommendations

The therapeutic transformation of the social E2 follows a path of humanization, which could be described as learning to feel like “just one among many.”

My first awareness of the compensatory nature of my drive to support others—and the hidden harm within it—came during the SAT program. Claudio Naranjo often used type-specific group meetings. I remember the profound impact of recognizing myself in others of my type.

On one hand, I felt an immense emotional relief, like I had finally found my long-lost herd. On the other, there was a subtle sense of distress, wrapped in the eerie precision of the Enneagram’s character descriptions and the confirmation of their accuracy in what people shared.
summary: This chunk describes the therapeutic journey for social E2 individuals, emphasizing the shift from feeling special and superior to recognizing shared neurotic patterns with others of the same type. The narrator recounts personal relief at finding solidarity, coupled with distress at confronting the accuracy of Enneagram descriptions, marking a crack in their inflated self-image.

title: Осознание типичности черт социальной двойки
text: When I finally met other social Twos, I realized that the traits I had taken pride in, the ones I believed made me unique, were actually character patterns present in all my fellow neurotics. Until that moment, I had managed to see myself as superior to every other Two, maintaining the illusion of being one of a kind. That was when a crack formed in my personality structure—the moment I saw its conditioned, automatic nature. From then on, I could no longer identify with it in the same way.
summary: Автор описывает момент осознания, что его личностные черты, считавшиеся уникальными, на самом деле типичны для социальной двойки, что привело к трещине в его самовосприятии и переосмыслению идентичности.

title: Сопротивление терапии и потребность в контроле у социальной двойки
text:
PAOLO BAIOCCHI

One of the biggest challenges for a social E2 in therapy is asking for help. Their identity is built on the belief that they don’t need it, and that they can’t afford to show any weakness or imperfection. If they do enter therapy, their greatest struggle will be admitting their problems. They may ask for help and simultaneously deny that they have, or they may approach it from a position of superiority, acting as if they already understand their patterns and know exactly how to fix them. In doing so, they block the therapist from accessing the areas they fear the most and maintain a tight grip on control.

Their resistance to authority—and their deep desire to be the authority—makes it difficult for them to acknowledge the therapist as someone who can guide them. Instead, they will instinctively position themselves as the understanding one, expressing empathy for the therapist’s workload, exhaustion, or personal struggles, which the social Two will intuitively pick up on. Above all, they will be highly seductive.

This mirrors their role in their family: taking on the parental function while losing their place as a child. Their mistrust of authority and their need to prove their superiority will shape the therapeutic relationship. Their neurotic need for acceptance will resurface through a desire to impress, making it difficult for them to believe the therapist values them unless they maintain an image of greatness.

Another characteristic of the social E2 is their tendency to place themselves on equal footing with the therapist, trying to build a friendship by discussing social, professional, or intellectual topics. The therapist’s challenge will be to cut through this rationalization and guide the conversation toward deeper, more intimate matters.

In the early stages, it is crucial to welcome the person of this character without directly challenging their need for superiority. With patience, the therapist must create a bond where the social E2 can experience that needing or asking for help does not diminish their worth. They must allow space for the E2 to accept care and guidance in a way that respects their dignity.

At the same time, therapists must be cautious of their own narcissistic need to feel indispensable or to create dependency. If they fall into this trap, they risk engaging in a power struggle with the social Two patient.
summary: Описывается сопротивление социальной двойки терапии из-за потребности контролировать, быть superior и избегать уязвимости, включая их тенденцию позиционировать себя как равного терапевту и выражать ловно вести беседу на интеллектуальном уровне, избегая глубины.

title: Нарциссическая компенсация и травма детства у социальной двойки
text:
Another area that requires in-depth work for the social E2 is their obsession with territorial conquest. Their primary form of satisfaction is being seen and feeding their grandiose self-image. The narcissistic games of proving they are the best, the most knowledgeable, or the leader mask a deep lack of maternal love. They have never experienced being seen for their true self, never known the security of a relationship that reassured them love exists. These same narcissistic games keep them disconnected from the profound loneliness they experienced as children.

They are also unaware of how their family’s high expectations—pushing them to be a trophy child, the great winner—exposed them to social pressures that were inappropriate for their age. They do not realize that they were, in fact, exploited.

Many social E2s deceive themselves with stories of a happy family life where they were deeply loved. And yes, they were loved, but under conditions far too demanding for a child.

They do not recognize that their parents—whether father or mother—competed with them, pushing them into a battle for superiority where they lost the emotional containment and protection they needed. Today, anyone who tries to offer them protection is met with distrust and defiance—including the therapist. The therapist must have the patience to accept them as a stubborn child wearing adult shoes.

Their relationship with authority is marked by the same ambivalence they felt toward their parents: on one hand, they were praised and encouraged to be great; on the other, they were humiliated whenever they expressed natural needs or emotions. To fill the void left by a lack of true intimacy and care, they built a grandiose self-image. Acknowledging the child who lost their childhood too soon feels humiliating to them. Asking for help or receiving affection puts them in a position of inferiority—something they cannot tolerate. Their response has been to suppress emotions, create distance, and look down on those they cannot win over or those who set boundaries.
summary: Обсуждается, как социальная двойка использует нарциссические стратегии (территориальное завоевание, доказательство превосходства) для компенсации незавершенной потребности в любви и безопасности в детстве, что приводит к эксплуатации, ложным нарративам о счастливом детстве и враждебному отношению к опеке.

title: Преодоление грандиозности и воссоздание связи с внутренним ребенком
text: A fundamental stage in therapy is recognizing the falseness of their grandiosity. The social Two cannot tolerate confrontation because no one has ever successfully set limits for them. There is a real risk that they will flee from the process of growth and self-awareness if they sense, even from a distance, a threat to their delusion of being the best. That is why any challenge to their narcissism must go hand in hand with a recognition of their inner child—the one who worked so hard to be seen but never was. The child whose healthy sense of pride was wounded, who had to construct an inflated self-image to avoid feeling criticized and humiliated simply for being a child.
summary: Подчеркивается, что ключевым этапом терапии является признание ложности грандиозного自我 и одновременное воссоединение с раненным внутренним ребенком, чья потребность в признании была подавлена, что привело к конструкции ложного превосходства как защиты от унижения.

title: Различие между унижением и смирением в работе с социальной двойкой
text: A key lesson will be differentiating between humiliation and humility—something Claudio Naranjo often described as the virtue of the E2. For the social Two, being small has always felt humiliating. Having emotions or being sick has felt humiliating. Even acknowledging that someone else might be greater than them can feel humiliating. To avoid this feeling, they fail to recognize others’ worth, to see and appreciate someone else’s gifts or talents.
summary: This chunk discusses how social Twos experience humility as humiliation and avoid recognizing others' worth to protect their grandiose self-image. It emphasizes the therapeutic need to distinguish humiliation from true humility as a key virtue for E2 growth.

title: Надежда на терапевтический прогресс через принятие и сострадание
text: There is hope for the social E2 “patient” to stay in therapy if the therapist can accept, with compassion, this child-emperor—recognizing the incredible effort they have made to survive and succeed in life. Over time, they may come to see the value of emotional depth and the emptiness of their worldly successes. Most importantly, they may finally recognize that their grandiose narcissism is not freedom, but a prison—a sentence to loneliness and emotional coldness. And they may, at last, become aware of what they have truly been missing: their own freedom.
summary: This section expresses hope that social Twos can remain in therapy when met with compassion, leading them to recognize their narcissism as a prison and rediscover their lost freedom through emotional depth and self-awareness.

title: Работа с инстинктами и сексуальностью у социальной двойки
text:
Another area to work on is reclaiming their natural instinct. Type Two is a seducer, appearing sexually liberated, but their seduction (especially in the social subtype) is primarily a means of possessing and controlling the other person. They know how to manufacture attraction and love, but they don’t truly understand emotional intimacy; in the end, they don’t know how to love. This also affects their children, as described in the section on love. We see how difficult it is for this personality to engage in warm, physical contact. Above all, they don’t know how to have fun. Having fun feels like a waste of time and, even more threateningly, requires being on equal footing with others and relinquishing the control of their inner Napoleonic general.

Playfulness, with the natural joy of the inner child, could also help them experience a more fulfilling sex life—one rooted in deep enjoyment rather than an exhibition of sexuality, unchecked sexual consumption, or using sex as a tool to gain admiration.

To cultivate a freer, more natural connection to their instincts, bodywork practices such as massage or dance can be helpful, allowing them to let go and develop a more subtle awareness of their body.
summary: This chunk explores how social Twos use seduction for control rather than intimacy, struggle with playfulness and fun, and can benefit from bodywork and reclaiming their inner child to develop authentic sexuality and emotional connection.

title: Личный опыт поиска сексуальной валидации и его пустота
text:
The search for sexual validation defined a part of my life. I actively sought out any form of training that could enhance my ability to seduce and fascinate. To succeed in my conquests, I subjected myself to countless small personal challenges, forcing myself to overcome every trace of shame, discomfort, fear of rejection and humiliation, the pain of loss…

Over time, I pushed past many limits and became quite skilled at relationships, enough to maintain an extremely rich and varied sex life. However, little by little, the superficiality of these encounters led me to a profound sense of emptiness and disorientation. I was disoriented by the collapse of my naïve belief that fulfillment could come from the complete liberation of Eros and libido.

PAOLO BAIOCCHI
summary: This first-person account describes the pursuit of sexual validation through mastery of seduction, which ultimately led to emptiness and disillusionment when the superficial nature of these encounters failed to provide lasting fulfillment.

title: Осознание вреда и развитие эмпатии как путь к исцелению
text:
Because they struggle to put themselves in others’ shoes and feel genuine empathy, an important step is becoming aware of the ways in which they cause harm. Recognizing how they use others as instruments for their own success can open the door to understanding true friendship, whether as a loving companionship or as an admiration that values the other as they are.

This personality must cultivate sincere, empathetic fraternity, reconnect with their sense of humanity, and learn to navigate solitude.

It’s crucial for them to see the selfishness behind their false generosity and the lack of ethics in their relentless pursuit of glory.

I turned to therapy in search of the causes of suffering, trying to increase my well-being and strength. But when I discovered the harm my personality caused others, my focus shifted. I began to care more about what I was doing to those around me.

My new goal became increasing the well-being and strength of others rather than just my own and developing empathy rather than self-awareness alone. Self-analysis was no longer about identifying my weaknesses but rather recognizing the places where I acted unconsciously, exploitatively, and without integrity.

PAOLO BAIOCCHI
summary: This section emphasizes the importance of recognizing harmful behaviors, developing genuine empathy, and shifting focus from self-validation to the well-being of others as a crucial step in the healing process for social Twos.

title: Техники терапии для развития осознанности и связи с другими
text:
What’s most essential is that they grasp the impact of their actions—when they exploit others in their thirst for adoration, when they manipulate them in their conquest of success, when they take from them to appropriate their qualities. In therapy, the hot seat technique is particularly effective, where the patient is guided to step into the other person’s shoes and truly feel their emotions. This also helps them learn how to listen and receive feedback without justifying themselves or immediately retreating behind their mask of indifference.

Group work is especially useful in the self-discovery process, as peers can mirror back how distant, hard to reach, and emotionally cold they seem—how difficult it is to connect with them in intimacy and equal companionship.

It’s important for them to cultivate genuine belonging within a group—without fleeing when they are not the most special or important person, without running away when their pride is wounded.

I used to paint over my urge to dominate the weak in a color that was seemingly warm—altruistic love. I deceived myself, disguising my selfish exploitation of people’s fragility as parental devotion, justifying within my own conscience what was, in truth, a ruthless act in service of my own narcissistic validation.

PAOLO BAIOCCHI
summary: This chunk highlights therapeutic techniques like the hot seat and group work to help social Twos develop empathy, recognize their exploitative patterns, and break through defenses by experiencing others' emotions and receiving honest feedback.

title: Освобождение от иллюзии успеха как замены настоящего бытия
text: Through this process of self-awareness, this personality type comes to realize how success is merely a substitute for true being—how it masks their deep-seated emptiness and low self-esteem.
summary: This brief but profound statement concludes that social Twos must understand that their pursuit of success masks inner emptiness and low self-worth, and true healing begins when they see success as a substitute for authentic being.

title: Преображение социальной Двойки: от иллюзии изобилия к признанию боли
text:
This is a particularly difficult dynamic to work through because, for someone who feels “abundant,” stepping down from the throne—letting go of their supposed plenitude—seems pointless. As is well known, it’s easier for someone who feels lacking to want to escape that inner hell. But for the social Two, it’s as if they must leave paradise.

This is the slowest transformation, achieved only by recognizing the prison they live in—the ways they destroy themselves and, ultimately, how alone and unloved they truly are.

If they open themselves to their pain, they may learn to love. If they face their loneliness, they may realize they are not immortal—and begin to find meaning and sacredness in the small gestures, the everyday actions of life. If they learn that they are just one among many, perhaps they will finally value life and make it sacred.
summary: Describes the difficult transformation of the social Enneagram Type Two, who must relinquish their illusion of abundance and confront their inner emptiness and loneliness to find genuine love and meaning in ordinary life.

title: Медитация и духовность как ловушка или путь к смирению для Двойки
text:
Their relationship with meditation is ambivalent. A social Two may use meditation and spiritual practice as yet another tool for perfecting their narcissistic self-image. Their grandiose self can leverage spiritual achievements as proof of their superiority over others. With this personality, there is a real risk of what Chögyam Trungpa described as spiritual materialism. It’s easy for them to slip into the role of a charlatan, a charismatic guru, promising salvation to the world (which is their primary delusion).

On the other hand, they may find it incredibly difficult to meditate because stilling the mind and pausing their relentless action forces them to confront a void they interpret as a deficiency. Likewise, they may resist engaging with a spiritual teacher, as true discipleship requires deep devotion and surrender—an attitude of humility and reverence toward higher spiritual values.

The redemptive act for a Two is to kneel, head bowed. To learn how to fall—and how to rise again, humbly, and without hiding.
summary: Explores the ambivalent relationship of the social Two with meditation and spiritual practice—both as a potential tool for narcissistic inflation and as a confrontation with inner void that can lead to humility if approached with sincerity.

title: Автобиография: наследство величия и поиск идентичности
text:
AUTOBIOGRAPHY

The gift of a simple life

by Fresia Nora Robledo Poma

Once, during a therapy session, I was asked where my strength came from. At first, I didn’t know what to say, but then I started talking about the illustrious ancestors who had inspired me since childhood, when my uncles would tell stories I longed to be part of. Deep down, I wanted them to talk about me with the same passion, enthusiasm, and admiration they had for our forebears.

Looking back on my childhood, I’m not surprised by this air of superiority I carry, considering my lineage includes General Poma, who accompanied Napoleon Bonaparte on his campaign to Egypt, and a great-great-grandfather named Napoleón, who arrived with his father in Metán (Salta, Argentina) to colonize the New World in the late 19th century. Add to that a lineage of great artists, members of the Vatican Swiss Guard, a president of the Swiss canton of Ticino, and even a cardinal of Venice who was a papal candidate. Growing up surrounded by tales of these family legends, in intellectual and cultural settings, it’s no wonder I gradually absorbed the belief that having a mission, achieving recognition, gaining fame—and even power—was of utmost importance.

Our family, the Pomas (which translates to “apple” in Italian), has its own coat of arms, featuring two rampant lions and an apple tree. My maternal great-great-grandfather, Napoleón Poma, was an architect from a wealthy family of professionals—something that, in the late 19th century, signified not only economic standing but also cultural and political influence, and therefore, a certain social power. He arrived in Argentina with his father, Paolo Poma, who had helped finance and build part of the Trans-Siberian Railway.

A more recent ancestor, who was a frequent subject of conversation at our family gatherings, was my mother’s grandfather, Carlos Poma Fantoni. Along with his brothers, he held key positions in Metán’s society. He rallied other wealthy families to secure for Metán a running water system, electric streetlights, the first telephone line, the creation of a hospital, the founding of the public library, road construction, new neighborhoods, and more schools. Through various business ventures, he also multiplied the family fortune.

How could my young mind remain indifferent to such wealth, expansion, generosity, and influence? I always wanted to hear more. I remember lingering at the table with the adults, listening intently, while my cousins ran off to play.

My father and mother embodied the union of two cultures—Argentinian and Chilean—and two social classes: aristocracy and the working class. Two economic realities: wealth and poverty. Two levels of education: nearly illiterate and university honors. It sounds like the plot of a Latin American telenovela (and as a child, I was a voracious reader of Corín Tellado’s romance novels)... except without the happy ending. That’s how my life feels—in extremis. All or nothing, black or white, with little room for middle ground. I either idealize people or disregard them entirely.

My mother dedicated her life to studying and caring for others. She became a lawyer and, from a young age, worked as a juvenile defender in the courts. Perhaps because she had polio as a child, she was driven to study and went on to build a highly respected career, first in Metán and later in Salta—this, in the 1950s, when most women were housewives or, at most, schoolteachers. Maybe due to her lack of experience with men, she was drawn to a charming, smooth-talking suitor who pursued her boldly and publicly. That man was my father. Practically illiterate, he relied on my mother to help him study and complete his education. My mother earned a good income and saved diligently; she owned multiple properties and homes. She had also inherited a highly coveted property in front of the Córdoba City Hall from the unmarried aunts she had cared for while studying law. A woman ahead of her time, at 30 and still single, she adopted my sister Natalia.
summary: An autobiographical account detailing the author's upbringing in a prestigious family with notable ancestors, which instilled a deep belief in the importance of mission, recognition, fame, and power, while also highlighting the cultural and class contrasts between her parents and her tendency toward idealization or devaluation of others.

title: Отцы, матери и ранняя семейная динамика
text: Thanks to my mother’s status, my father gained access to a world completely foreign to him—one filled with wealthy, educated elites with political and economic power. He was Chilean, of Indigenous descent, the only illegitimate son in his family, forced to step into his absent father’s role in more ways than one. He had worked as a miner, with no formal education, and came to Salta searching for a fresh start. At the time, he was already married—something my mother didn’t know when she wed him—and had two children. I only learned of their existence through Facebook after my father passed away in 2012.
summary: Описывает контраст между образованной матерью и неграмотным отцом чужого социального происхождения, их брак, скрытое прошлое отца и позднее открытие существования его других детей.

title: Детство в тени насилия и потери
text:
My childhood: a hell for me, an even greater hell for others

Even as a little girl, I showed signs of who I’d become. My aunt S. says that by the time I was two, I had a vocabulary and command of language that turned heads wherever I went. A doctor once told my parents he had never seen a child my age communicate the way I did. That had all sorts of consequences in my life—like when, at six years old, the school principal called my aunts to complain that the teacher couldn’t do her job because I wouldn’t stop whistling and singing. Clearly, I was born to stand out.

But it seems things weren’t all that normal, happy, or cheerful. My family had—and still has—many secrets, some carefully kept, others impossible to hide. My mother spent a lot of time away from home, while my father stayed with us and abused the young girls who took care of me as a baby. Only recently did my family tell me that he also mistreated and abused the minors my mother legally took in while they waited to be placed with foster families.

Finally, when I was two, my father was sent to prison for abusing another minor in the family (a second cousin of mine). But my mother got him out of jail by convincing the girl’s mother and grandmother to drop the charges. That was the moment my mother finally saw him for who he was. It was also the beginning of her own downfall.

In November 1973, she had gallbladder removal surgery, and at the age of forty-one, developed a post-op infection that my uncles—her brothers, both doctors—still can’t explain. My aunts always said she couldn’t take any more of the life she was living with my father. I lost her when I was three, and soon after, I lost my father too. He disappeared from the family picture, and I wouldn’t see him again for many years.
summary: Рассказывает о раннем осознании своей исключительности, скрытом насилии в семье, тюремном заключении отца за abuse несовершеннолетнего, освобождении через давление матери и последующей смерти родителей в раннем детстве рассказчика.

title: Жизнь у родственников и поиск принадлежности
text:
That’s how, while still very little, I left my home, my aunts and uncles, my cousins, my city, and everything I knew. I was taken 900 kilometers away to live with other relatives who would care for me: a seventy-year-old widowed grandmother and a forty-five-year-old unmarried aunt—my mother’s eldest sister. In the house next door lived my mother’s other sister, married with two kids. Now, I was part of a family of four adults and four children.

By the time I was five, I was already wandering the streets alone. I’d go to my neighbor’s house, ring the doorbell, and call for my friend L., who was three. The neighborhood was my home; the shopkeepers were my friends—the butcher, the baker, the florist, the hairdresser, the vegetable vendor, the seamstress, the man at the newsstand, the supermarket clerks, the shoemaker, the dentist, the pharmacist... It was my territory, and I roamed it like I owned the place, chatting with everyone. I even remember running the florist’s shop when I was ten! I loved putting together bouquets while the owner took her afternoon nap, leaving me in charge.

All that interaction with so many people, moving through such a big space, gave me a sense of belonging—but it also kept me from facing what was inside me and what was happening at home. I looked outside for what I couldn’t find within. Because at home, I felt like I had no place. At first, I slept in my grandmother’s room with my sister. My grandmother was a quiet woman with sad eyes. She had lost her husband young and was left to raise five children alone. She had also recently lost one of her daughters.

From the ages of three to twelve, I spent March to November in Córdoba with my sister, my aunt, and my grandmother. From December to February, I stayed at another uncle’s house with his four kids, or at Uncle C. and Aunt L.’s house, with four other children. During those three months, it was common for twenty-two of us to gather for meals—lunch, dinner, afternoon snacks... I think this is why my concept of family is so expansive.

I grew up with my cousins as if they were my siblings and with my aunts and uncles as if they were my parents. But no one actually took on a parental role. I did whatever I wanted—I’d bark and bite at anyone who got in my way. There was no real authority figure, no adult with the courage or patience to set boundaries for me. In the end, I felt like our dog, Peggy, was the only one in the family who gave me unconditional love. She was the only being I hugged and kissed. I didn’t want anyone to know how much I craved affection. Sometimes, I’d pretend to be asleep when my grandmother came near, just so she would tuck me in and gently brush my bangs out of my face, like a caress.
summary: Описывает переезд к родственникам после потери родителей, автономное детство на улице, сильную привязанность к соседям и локальным торговцам, сезонные переезды между домами родственников, отсутствие родительской фигуры и компенсаторная привязанность к собаке.

title: Потребность контролировать и доминировать с ранних лет
text:
Leading and conquering from childhood

I had to be the center of every situation; it didn’t matter whether it was for better or worse—what mattered was not being indifferent to anyone. My specialty was leading the neighborhood gang. I told everyone what to do, what to play, and what role each person had... They would always ask me, “So, what do we do now?” Even C., who was the oldest of us all. It was important for me to have control over my peers, but I took even more pleasure in challenging the adults, who were harder to dominate.
summary: Описывает раннюю потребность быть в центре внимания, лидерство среди сверстников, удовольствие от вызова взрослым и необходимость контроля над ситуациями как основную черту личности с детства.

title: Без режима и без границ
text:
I had absolutely no routine. Brushing my teeth, taking a bath, tidying my room? No one was there to teach me those habits. I didn’t have to do any chores either—everything was always clean, my room was neat, and food was served to me. So I never took responsibility for any of it. My aunt S. at least tried to get me to clean my room once a week, but I rebelled every chance I got.

My personal hygiene was neglected. I stuffed myself with candy so much that they called me The Kiosk. At first, my grandmother gave me money to buy sweets. Then, when it wasn’t enough, I started stealing from her. This complete lack of boundaries, combined with the neglect I was living in, led to all my baby teeth rotting. They had to drag me to the dentist across the street, who pulled out the remains of my decayed teeth without anesthesia. Two adults held down my hands and feet in the chair because my strength and defiance made me hard to restrain.
summary: Описывает хаотичное детство без режима, гигиены и границ: отсутствие ответственности, переедание сладостями, разрушение зубов и сопротивление любой попытке дисциплины со стороны взрослых.

title: Борьба за внимание в большой семье
text:
I learned from a very young age that standing out was difficult. I was the sixth of twelve cousins, growing up in an environment of constant competition that shaped all of my relationships from the start. We competed for recognition, attention, and the love of the adults around us. But being a niece didn’t hold the same weight as being a daughter, so I felt I had to make an extra effort whenever I was staying with one of the families I lived with throughout the year.

Then my grandmother was diagnosed with colon cancer, and my uncle bought a house in the neighborhood, close to the one we already had. My aunt S. moved in with her husband and two kids to take care of my grandmother—and of course, I was part of the package deal. My sister and my single aunt, N., stayed in the house where the five of us had been living. The separation eased the everyday friction with my sister, but I think it also turned us into strangers. Days or even weeks could go by without us seeing each other. She had a very close bond with our cousin C., who was her age, and I felt a deep envy of their connection.
summary: Рассказывает о напряженной конкуренции за внимание среди многочисленных родственников, чувстве недостаточности как племянницы и эмоциональном отдалении от сестры после разделения household.

title: Собственные правила и образ для общества
text:
Me, my own rules and public image

Between the complete indulgence of my grandmother and the relentless policing from my single aunt N., I came to the conclusion that I had to be my own authority, my own role model. I started playing an imaginary game: I had a father and a mother. Whenever I went to a friend’s birthday party or got picked up by her parents, I would tell them I had to be home early because my family was waiting for me. (In reality, my aunts often had no idea where I was.) This little lie helped me avoid the humiliation of not having a normal family—parents who cared about me. I was beginning to realize how important public image was.

At six years old, I started going to the most glamorous hairdresser in the neighborhood—the one all the wealthy women went to, even those from the city center. At first, my aunts would take me and instruct the hairdresser on how to cut my hair. This made me resent the bangs they insisted I keep. When I looked in the mirror, all I could see was an old-fashioned motorcycle helmet stuck permanently to my head. But then, one day—I think I was around nine—I started going to the hairdresser on my own and had them cut off that mop that covered half my face and forced me to tilt my head. It was my way of asserting myself.

Every year at school, we had full health check-ups, including eye exams. Mine always came back with the same results: nearsightedness and astigmatism. But the reports never made it to my family—because I was not going to wear glasses! No way. I wasn’t about to be the “four-eyes” in a co-ed school, where there were boys I liked! It was crucial not to seem weak, not to be pitied, not to come across as pathetic. In that sense, taking care of my outward appearance became a priority for me. But I never cared about fashion—just whatever suited me best.
summary: Описывает формирование собственного внутреннего авторитета, ложь о наличии родителей для сохранения имиджа, акцент на внешности (прически, отказ от очков) как способ избежать ощущения слабости и жалости.

title: Юридическая особенность и её романтизация
text:
Another big issue was my legal situation. My father lost custody of me when my mother died—probably due to his history as a pedophile and the embezzlement of my mother’s inheritance. Until I turned eighteen, my legal guardian was one of my aunts, along with the children’s court guardian, whom I had to visit at the courthouse. In my group of friends, this made me feel special—after all, I was the only one with such a distinguished legal guardian. Looking back, I now understand the horrified and pitying looks my friends gave me. They were appalled that I was proud of having a court-appointed guardian instead of parents like everyone else. From a young age, I had decided to tell my life story as if it were a grand, fantastical tale—and having that guardian was just another dramatic twist.

I had to visit him regularly. Thankfully, he was a kind man. He would receive me in the tallest building in the city, a very luxurious place with wood-paneled walls and bookshelves lined with gilded volumes. He always wore the same elegant three-piece suit, smelled of cologne, and would walk to his massive desk before sitting down. The whole experience made me feel grown-up. I was the only one among my friends who traveled alone by bus over such long distances—and not just for any reason, but to go to court! I made sure they saw my life as something exciting and glamorous—a habit I still find myself indulging in today.
summary: Рассказывает о сложной юридической ситуации (опека через суд из-за отца-педофила), но трансформирует её в источник гордости и glamour-наслаждения, романтизируя посещения суда как признак зрелости и исключительности.

title: Тайные встречи с отцом и их двойственность
text:
A covert kidnapping

From the time I was three until I was nine, I only saw my father for a few days each summer when I visited Metán. Every year, he showed up with a different woman. He’d sit me on his lap in the car and let me steer down dirt roads. There was something in the way he looked at me that made me uncomfortable, even though he pretended that I was in charge—that I was the one deciding where we went because I was “driving.”
summary: Описывает редкие, но тревожные встречи с отцом в детстве, где он создавал иллюзию контроля со стороны ребёнка, несмотря на неприятное ощущение от его взгляда и меняющихся партнёрш.

title: Похищение и попытка создать семью
text:
But the summer I turned ten, things changed. My father came to pick me up as usual, but this time, he didn’t take me back to my grandmother’s. He had planned my kidnapping. Hours passed, and no one knew where we were. I suppose covert kidnapping would be a more accurate term, because in hindsight, I see it as my father’s misguided attempt to give me a family—though his concept of family was certainly questionable.

The time I spent with my father and his partner felt like an intense and prolonged cohabitation with a man I had only seen sporadically for a day or two each summer. It was the only time since my mother’s death that I spent an extended period with him. He took me to live with a woman and her daughter, who was my age. Luckily, I liked her right away.

At first, everything seemed normal. But as time went on, things started to unravel. It was the beginning of summer, which meant the start of vacation—three months stretched out ahead of us. When I asked when I’d be going back home, he would say, “This is your home now. We’re going to be a family, and I’m going to settle down. I have a business now…” He had rented a shop where he sold candy and gifts. The name of the store was Fresi-Nor—a combination of the first syllables of my two names. That caught me off guard. Suddenly, I felt important to my father. Maybe this time, he really did have good intentions. Maybe we really could be a family. Looking back, I think I inherited that same instinct—the idea of trading sweets and gifts for love.

But it didn’t take long for me to see the cracks. My father struggled to keep promises, and his fantasies were miles away from reality. The house was filled with constant yelling and fights with his partner. Thankfully, she had enough backbone to stand up for herself—and to protect her daughter and me. B. was a lawyer, just like my mother had been. She worked from morning until late afternoon. We would see her around dinnertime, and from that moment on, the scenes would unfold night after night, without respite. There was always a reason for the shouting and the slamming doors.

I lived my days on edge, anxious, and my nights were filled with a mix of anger, fear, and excitement—never knowing what would happen next. I wanted B. to punish my father for being immoral and for lying, and I wanted my father to act differently the next day. But that never happened. Everything repeated itself, day after day. I was used to navigating violent environments, always alert, figuring out my next move. This time, I felt like I had to protect C., B.’s daughter. Even though we were both ten years old, our personalities were almost opposite, and I was the one calling the shots. Even now, I notice the same thing—I grow bigger and braver when I step into the role of defender or protector.
summary: The narrator describes being covertly kidnapped by her father at age ten and living with him and his partner B., initially hoping for a real family but soon witnessing instability, conflict, and her own role as a protector amid emotional turmoil.

title: Показ счастливой семьи и последствия
text:
Putting on the show of a happy family

My father took us out every day from morning until B. got back. We’d go to hot springs, rivers, or the pools of his friends. We were always surrounded by a lot of different people, mostly women whose husbands were at work, and who had kids around our age. The idea was that while the adults spent time together, the kids would do the same. But not me. I was always paying attention to what my father was doing. He never missed a chance to get physically close to those women—resting his head on one’s lap “by accident,” pressing up against another in the pool. It was all in broad daylight, and he did it as if it were the most natural thing in the world.

Of course, I wasted no time telling B. about it that same night, and all hell would break loose. Now, looking back, I realize how risky my behavior was. I was alone, surrounded by strangers—including my father—with no one to protect me. But I wasn’t aware of that at the time. I felt like I could handle anything... And honestly, I still do.

Meanwhile, my mother’s family had hired a private investigator to find me. It took about a month. I have some blurry memories of when I finally came home, but I’ll never forget the joy of seeing my grandmother again. Obviously, from that moment on, she denied my father any visits. Still, he managed to track me down two more times when my mother’s family wasn’t around.

My grandmother—the person I felt loved me the most—passed away on October 7, 1985, one day before my fifteenth birthday. In South American culture, a girl’s fifteenth birthday is a big deal, like a mini-wedding but without the groom—complete with a fancy dress, dancing, dinner, confetti, garlands, glitter, etc. Naturally, there was no celebration; just a lot of grief. I remember coming home from school when they told me. I didn’t cry. They didn’t let me see her, didn’t let me say goodbye, didn’t let me touch her one last time. I just froze. I think that was the moment I decided I wouldn’t cry anymore.
