Until that moment, it hadn’t occurred to me that, amid all my searching, what I had truly been longing for was a mentor, a guiding figure. Up until then, I had never felt the need or even the opportunity to admire or look up to anyone. On the contrary, any authority I encountered was quickly repositioned beneath me. Whether through charm, intelligence, competence, or morality, I always managed to feel superior.
summary: Автор описывает своё первое знакомство с Claudio Naranjo через курс по эннеаграмме, сильный культурный и эмоциональный шок от непривычной среды, глубокий эмоциональный отклик на практику, и последующую личную встречу с Наранхо, которая стала началом её духовного и личностного пути.

title: First meeting with Claudio Naranjo
text:
We met at the headquarters of the Claudio Naranjo Foundation. I remember he looked at me and gave me a brief smile. Then, as we walked, he kept his head lowered, glancing at me sideways. First at my hands, then at my neck. I never asked why, but I imagine he was trying to assess my character and had yet to determine which way I leaned. As soon as we exchanged our first words and I told him I wanted to work on an educational research project with him as the foundation for my doctoral thesis, my ambition must have been obvious.

Luckily, there were others around, because I was nearly speechless, only answering his direct questions. Given how much I usually talk, I couldn’t understand what was happening to me. I felt as if I were in shock. He was observant, quiet, speaking without embellishments or the usual pleasantries people exchange upon first meeting. It caught me completely off guard; I wasn’t used to it. I had prepared an entire speech to impress him with everything I had read from his books, to dazzle him with my insights and sharp questions about his ideas. But there was no space for that. Fortunately, others also remained silent, though I worried the meeting would be cut short. Even so, I remained unable to speak, despite the fear that I might be wasting my only chance to talk to him.

But then, Claudio invited me to join them for lunch. The conversation was light and simple; no deep or philosophical discussions. I stayed mostly silent, answering questions while staring at my plate, feeling like a stranger to myself. Then, as dessert arrived, Claudio turned to me and said, “You can check the foundation’s archives. See what you find.” And just like that, our meeting ended. At least it seemed that if I found something worthwhile, I might get another chance to see him.
summary: The narrator describes her first meeting with Claudio Naranjo, noting his quiet, observant demeanor and her own nervous silence despite her preparation. He invites her to explore the foundation's archives, ending the meeting with a simple but meaningful task.

title: Working in the archives and developing a personality test
text:
I went to the archives, where an endless world of boxes filled with papers awaited me. I got comfortable and began sorting through them one by one, coming across various test batteries and a vast array of responses to different questionnaires. I carefully classified and organized them into separate boxes. By the end of the day, I had gathered all the test materials, the responses, the factorial analysis, and copies of nine sets of documents, each containing around three hundred statements grouped according to the nine enneatypes. I had no idea how much this would delight Claudio. The materials dated back to the 1980s and had been typed on a typewriter. I see this now as a small symbolic piece of his legacy, still waiting to be sorted, categorized, and organized, much of it still stored away in boxes, videotapes, or CDs.

I wish I had stayed on this path of research with him. In my fantasy, I could have helped him in this area where he seemingly had no assistance, and I might have even completed my thesis, which remains unfinished to this day. But the neon lights were too enticing, and I stumbled over the same stone more than once.

Fortunately, there would be more opportunities to collaborate with Claudio. His goal was to develop a personality test with 27 scales (one for each enneatype subtype) rather than limiting personality to just five dimensions, as Raymond Cattell had done. So, we began working with 240 items, though in his final months, Claudio was exploring the idea of expanding it to 300. He was convinced that if we carefully selected the right adjectives and phrases he had compiled and cross-referenced them with NEO PI test results organized by subtype, we could create a test that would more precisely confirm specific subtype traits. This instrument does not yet exist but that I hope can be developed in the future through research on his legacy.

We assembled a team (Javier Hernández de la Luz, Susan Sylvester, Mónica Bustos, Antonio Castillo, my husband, and myself) with the aim of enlisting SAT program participants as voluntary test subjects for both the NEO and the 240-adjective test. We gathered in Zamora for this purpose. My husband digitized the test, but we never got to use it. I had a hyper-neurotic creative episode and, without realizing it, veered off in another direction…
summary: The narrator describes her work organizing archival materials related to the nine enneatypes, her regret over not continuing research with Claudio, and their collaborative effort to develop a 27-scale personality test based on enneatypes and subtypes, including team assembly and testing efforts in Zamora.

title: Ongoing collaboration and personal reflections
text:
I still have an email from Claudio from August 2011 in which he wrote: “I would be very interested in hearing your proposals on how to bring teachers closer to the dream of a new education for the renewal of our world in crisis.” And with that one sentence, the floodgates opened. Looking back, I see my voracity. I became an idea machine. For every suggestion he made, I countered with another. Every video of his that I watched or text of his that I found inspired new ideas.

I got so easily carried away with every email, meeting, phone call, or Skype session that I kept wanting more, offering more. I think I became a bit of a stalker. I wrote to him every week. And he, always so kind and quick to reply, overwhelmed me with ideas. Claudio had become a source of boundless inspiration, and I, in turn, became a kind of assistant to his memory, keeping track of his pending projects.

One day, by chance, we ran into each other at the airport. He was headed to Barcelona, and I was on my way to Madrid. There, we arranged our next meeting, just a few days later. By then, I was in the throes of what I can only describe as “Claudio fever.” Every exchange opened a new door. And Claudio never stopped assigning me more and more tasks, many of which I left unfinished or could only complete halfway. I couldn’t keep up with my own life. Thanks to the SAT program, Gestalt therapy, and personal work, I began to see things more clearly—the extent of my ambition and my inability to follow through. Even now, I feel a deep sadness for all the promises I made to Claudio that I was unable to fulfill during his lifetime. And I don’t know if I ever will.
summary: The narrator reflects on her intense, idea-driven collaboration with Claudio Naranjo, describing her overwhelming enthusiasm, frequent communication, and tendency to take on too many tasks. She expresses sadness over unfulfilled promises and recognizes her pattern of ambition without follow-through, despite personal growth through therapy and self-work.

title: Изменения в жизни после прибытия в SAT-школу
text:
My arrival at the SAT school and in Claudio Naranjo’s world brought many changes. First and foremost, on a personal level. But also in my family and professional life. For example, we had always sent our children to expensive schools, such as the Swiss School, where we had an active social life as a family. We organized charity dinners, secondhand fairs to raise funds for soup kitchens, attended embassy gala dinners, and so on.

But by the end of 2013, we had hit rock bottom financially and could no longer sustain the life we were living: renting a penthouse in Las Tablas, two cars, two private school tuitions plus cafeteria fees, extracurricular activities, a downtown parking space, multiple insurance policies, etc. I was no longer working as a freelancer; I had decided to leave all my clients to work solely for the Claudio Naranjo Foundation, as it was the only thing that made sense to me at the time. This, combined with the economic crisis that was also affecting my husband’s business, showed us that we were living beyond our means. For the first time, I lacked the financial security I had always enjoyed.
summary: Описание значительных изменений в личной, семейной и профессиональной жизни автора после вступления в SAT-школу и погружения в мир Клаудио Наранхо, включая финансовый кризис и переосмысление приоритетов.

title: Переезд на Мальорку и новая жизнь
text:
The most important factor in choosing a new city was ensuring our children could continue their education in a school that aligned with our values as a family—a holistic approach to learning, as Claudio advocated in his book Changing Education to Change the World. That’s how we arrived at Sa Llavor, in Mallorca. I had known about the school since 2011 when I was looking for one for my niece after my sister moved to the island.

And so, we began a low-cost life on one of the most expensive islands in Spain. When we told people we were moving to Mallorca to cut costs, they laughed, but in the end, we managed to at least make them question their assumptions. The new school was in a former convent in Mancor de la Vall, a village of fewer than a thousand people, where the road literally ends. We went from a two-bedroom apartment to a four-bedroom house with three bathrooms, a garden in the front and back, stunning mountain views, and even snow in the winter… all for a third less than what we had been paying in Madrid.

The school didn’t allow refined sugars, so our diet changed quite a bit. We walked, biked, or rode scooters to school. No more morning traffic jams, parking fees, extra gas costs, or insurance payments. If we stayed in the area, we could go out to dinner for less than half of what it cost in Madrid. As residents, we got extremely cheap flights… But all this came at a price: the kids struggled to adapt to the new town, we missed being able to go out in Madrid, we missed our family… The beginning wasn’t easy.
summary: Рассказ о переезде на Мальорку ради образования детей в соответствии с ценностями семьи, описание новой жизни в деревенской школе, её плюсах (низкие расходы, природная среда) и трудностях (адаптация детей, тоска по прежней жизни).

title: Личные трансформации и рождение ребёнка
text:
At that time, my husband and I were both going through our own therapeutic processes. And on our last night in Mallorca, before I left for Barcelona and he for Italy, leaving the kids with their grandparents, my husband said to me, “I’m going to give you a baby.” And a few months later, the youngest of our family arrived. I was 45, and he was 46. In that same year, I changed languages, cities, neighborhoods, homes, schools, workplaces, coworkers, routines, and lifestyle pace. And now, on top of it all—a big family!

Choosing this new life wasn’t easy, but now I can embrace my role as a woman more fully. We function as a true family. I’ve come to understand that life doesn’t happen in the grand offices of power but in the everyday moments with the people you truly love. And at last, I’ve found a sense of peace.
summary: Описание рождения ребёнка в зрелом возрасте, множественных жизненных изменений за один год и осознанного принятия новой роли в семье, приводящего к ощущению полноты и мира.

title: Путь к становлению терапевтом
text:
Trying to find myself through being a therapist

Over the years, thanks to my connection with Claudio, his disciples, and the integrative education communities of the Claudio Naranjo Foundation, my interest in one-on-one interactions has gradually grown. Before, I saw them as a waste of time. I found it more practical and far-reaching to address a group rather than a single person. I thought my time was too valuable to invest in just one individual. In a group, there’s a statistical chance of appealing to several people; I might not win over everyone, but at least I’d connect with some. In a one-on-one setting, though, everything hinges on that single connection. Through these years, I’ve worked on my fear of intimacy, allowing myself to truly engage with whatever arises in an encounter with another person. However, I still fear not being a good therapist. As my desire to help others therapeutically has awakened, I also worry that I’m forcing a calling out of sheer desperation.
summary: Постепенное развитие интереса к индивидуальной терапевтической работе, преодоление прежнего предпочтения групповой работы, работа над страхом близости и сомнения в собственной компетентности как терапевта.

title: Страхи и трудности в терапевтической практике
text:
Another fear that once held me back from exploring the possibility of becoming a therapist was the idea of abandonment, absence, rejection, and people leaving. Now, I see these as ghosts that have always haunted my life, both my own fear of leaving and of being left. It’s not the same when a few people leave a large group as when one person walks away from an individual relationship.

My struggles with becoming a one-on-one therapist are fading as I learn to truly see the other person, to listen with presence, to stay silent without interrupting, without trying to impose myself while they speak, to feel committed to their process, to respect their pace, and to prioritize their needs over mine. At times, I feel a pull toward the role of a fortune-teller, astrologer, or seer, and I risk slipping into telling others who they are and what they should do. Being aware of this helps me manage the anxiety I usually feel in the face of slowness, uncertainty, lack of understanding, vulnerability, and unpredictability.
summary: Анализ страха abbandона и отвержения как барьера на пути к терапевтической практике, описание роста навыков активного слушания и осознания собственной тенденции давать советы вместо поддержки процесса клиента.

title: Риски безграничного слушания и терапевтических паттернов
text: I also see the risk of falling into limitless listening, of losing track of time, of not knowing how to say, “See you next time,” either because I get lost in the other person or as a strategy to make them feel intensely listened to (more heard than ever before) or to make them feel treated in a special way by me, proving that I am the best “listener” they have ever had. In my most unbalanced state, I see my fear of the other person’s slowness in the therapeutic process, their difficulty in accepting my “sacred word” right away, their inability to see the light through me.
summary: Автор осознает риски чрезмерного слушания в терапии, включая потерю границ и использование слушания как стратегии для подтверждения собственной значимости, а также страх перед медлительностью клиента и их неспособностью принять терапевтическое вмешательство.

title: Положительный опыт и интерес к групповой терапии
text: However, I recall my experiences with therapeutic listening during my training at the Madrid School of Gestalt Therapy and the rather flattering feedback from my fellow trainees who felt “listened to,” as if I had a natural gift for therapy. And often, it’s true: in certain situations, when someone shares something they’re going through, I start speaking as if the words come out on their own, as if I were delivering a message from somewhere else—not from my reasoning, nor from my need to charm, or any strategy (I usually don’t even remember what I just said). These days, I’m interested in exploring group therapy work with teenagers and with parents of teenagers.
summary: Автор вспоминает положительный опыт терапевтического слушания во время обучения в Мадридской школе гештальт-терапии, отмечая спонтанность своих ответов, и выражает интерес к работе в групповой терапии с подростками и их родителями.

title: Методы активного слушания и работа с границами
text:
I like listening and seeing what comes up. I try to stay aware of my body language and that of others. I use a lot of mirroring: I repeat what others have said as a way to confirm whether I’ve heard correctly, since I tend to interpret and even invent content. I also like summarizing what has been said so far. I like asking about obvious statements; I don’t like leaving things assumed. Even if a question seems silly, I like to ask it, and this makes me aware that I might reveal that I don’t know or don’t understand something.

I’m more than a little confrontational, but I’m working on becoming more compassionate. Sometimes, when listening to someone, I feel an immediate urge to set boundaries, and I usually do. When in doubt, I stay silent. I’m not uncomfortable with the other person’s silence. It’s like practicing giving space. The other person owns their time. They decide how to use it. I have no urgency to move forward if they don’t want to—though, in the end, that can be frustrating for me…
summary: Автор описывает свои техники активного слушания: зеркалирование, резюмирование, уточняющие вопросы, а также баланс между конфронтацией и состраданием, умением держать паузу и уважать tempo другого человека в диалоге.

title: Воссоединение с отцом и его внезапная потеря
text:
Trading a real father for an ideal one

A few months after completing SAT 1, my father coincidentally reappeared in my life. It had been thirty-one years since we had spent more than a brief coffee chat together. It seems he was revisiting his past and suddenly remembered he had a daughter. He went to Salta and somehow managed to convince my lawyer to give him my phone number in Spain. That’s how my husband ended up handing me the phone, simply saying, “It’s your father.”

I froze. I answered the call as if I had spoken to him just yesterday. Then I became demanding and aggressive, scolding him for taking so long to show signs of life. I got no real response, just a simple, “I’m sorry.” We spoke several more times, and whenever I started asking difficult questions about his past or ours, he would say it was better to discuss in person. So we agreed to meet at the end of January 2012. We were in touch, but it was clear that the sensitive topics would be saved for when we saw each other.

We were organizing two conferences at the Complutense University for January 16 and 17, 2012. One with José Antonio Marina and Claudio at the Faculty of Philosophy, and another with just Claudio at the Faculty of Education, where I am still a professor. On the night of the 16th, after the first talk, Asunta Hormaechea asked me to take home the flowers that had been decorating the stage so we could reuse them for the next day’s conference. When I opened my car door, a wave of cemetery-like scent hit me, and I was momentarily stunned. “Of course,” I thought. “They’re flowers…” Two nights later, I got a call from Buenos Aires. It was my father’s wife, telling me that on Monday, January 16, he had passed away.

Three days had already passed. He was already buried. I couldn’t attend the wake or the funeral. I had no one to talk to about it. Everyone in my family would be pleased by the news… I had a flight to Argentina scheduled for twelve days later to see him. All my questions remained unanswered, waiting for a reunion that would never happen.
summary: Автор описывает неожиданное восстановление связи с биологическим отцом после 31 года разлуки, их напряженные телефонные разговоры, планы встречи и шоковое известие о его внезапной смерти незадолго до встречи, что оставило множество unresolved вопросов и чувство вины.

title: Преобразование горя через идеализацию и благодарность
text:
So I tried to see the glass as half full. I thought: My biological father has died, but life has given me a teacher whom I see as an ideal father. That brought me a sense of peace, leading me into a daily fast that lasted twelve days.

Now, years later, having also lost my ideal father, my teacher, I feel a deep sadness, but also faith in the future and immense gratitude. My bond with him helped me heal my bond with my father. I am no longer an orphan.
summary: Автор описывает процесс психологической адаптации к потере отца: идеализация учителя как замены отцу, двенадцатидневный пост как ритуал исцеления, и最终 осознание, что эта связь помогла ей исцелить раннюю травму abbandonmenta и обрести чувство целостности.

title: Эротическая склонность у женщин типа 2 и связь с истерией
text: After years of proto-analytical research, it was found that the majority of those classified as Enneagram Type 2 are women and that their compulsive pursuit of love is often expressed through erotic seduction. In this sense, we can correlate this personality type with the primary trait of hysteria, which frequently manifests in women with a strong erotic inclination.
summary: This chunk discusses how Enneagram Type 2, predominantly found in women, expresses its compulsive pursuit of love through erotic seduction, which correlates with the primary trait of hysteria in women with strong erotic inclinations.

title: Исторические и клинические примеры истерии: от инквизиции до Шарко
text:
Fabio Riemenschneider, in his article Hysteria and Witch Hunts, describes the terror of the Inquisition:

France, 1599. The young peasant Martha Brossier is arrested and tried on charges of witchcraft. For the clergy, the signs of a pact with the devil are undeniable: her body convulses, her muscles twist, her face contorts, she speaks in an altered tone of voice, and she is insensitive to the pricks of long needles. [...] She is found guilty and, as such, executed by the Inquisition.

Women like Martha would later become, in the 19th century, the subject of studies conducted by Jean-Martin Charcot at the French hospital La Salpêtrière. In fact, psychoanalysis emerged from the inquiry into sexuality initiated by Sigmund Freud, one of the doctors who attended Charcot’s research laboratory on hysteria.

Claudio Naranjo observes that, although hysteria was a key area of Freud’s research, his comments on this clinical manifestation were rare, and he did not present his first psychoanalytic descriptions of the hysterical personality until 1930.
summary: This chunk presents historical and clinical examples of hysteria, from the witch trial of Martha Brossier in 1599 to Charcot’s studies and Freud’s delayed engagement with hysteria, highlighting the evolution of understanding this condition.

title: Описание истерического характера: Перлс и Наранхо о диссоциации и компенсации
text:
Perls, Hefferline, and Goodman, describing this character pattern, note that the hysteric has

too much spontaneity and too little control. [...] “I cannot control the impulses that arise”: the body looms in the foreground, he is swept by emotions, his ideas and inventions are capricious, everything is sexualized, etc. [...]. It is just because there is too little self, too superficial desire and too little spontaneity, that the hysteric organizes the experience apparently desired: the feelings are not dominant enough to energize the functions of orientation and manipulation, and thus these are pointless and seem to be “too little.” [...] Therefore, he cannot control his impulses and turns against them, and then his feelings seem to be “too little.” The split of self and ego is mutually disastrous.
summary: This chunk describes the hysteric character through Perls, Hefferline, and Goodman, emphasizing excessive spontaneity, lack of control, bodily expression of emotions, and a painful split between self and ego that leads to mutual disaster.

title: Внешняя образ E2: гордость, соблазн и зависимость от внешней валидации
text: The E2 person typically presents an outwardly proud demeanor, appearing happy, friendly, affectionate, seductive, and eager to please. For them, attention is not enough; they must be the center of it. Their self-esteem relies on external validation through the privileges they feel they deserve. In general, they compulsively seek love, with romantic love serving as their primary motivational drive and the foundation of their self-worth. For this reason, they use seduction (often tied to erotic expression) to secure the validation of their object of desire. They need to feel loved. To achieve this, they are always available, attuned to others’ emotions, and offering love and understanding in an ambiguous way, all while appearing not to need anything themselves. To maintain this illusion, they repress their own needs and construct an inflated self-image, channeling all their energy into avoiding awareness of their fundamental deprivation.
summary: This chunk outlines the outward presentation of Enneagram Type 2: proud, seductive, and eager to please, driven by a need for external validation through love and attention, while internally repressing their own needs and constructing an inflated self-image to avoid confronting their fundamental deprivation.

title: Пride как защита от осознания потребности в любви: взгляд Наранхо и Эдипов конфликт
text:
The conversion symptoms, dramatic performances, and fantasies described in Freud’s studies of hysterics mirror how Enneagram Type 2s uphold their pride by presenting themselves as having an abundance of love to give, while secretly fulfilling their own need for love (Naranjo).

According to Naranjo:

It is easy to see how unawareness of needing—and particularly unawareness of needing love—supports pride, for if pride is built upon self-worth, what measure of worth presents itself more naturally to a child’s mind than being worthy of the love of her parents? To the extent that the proud is implicitly saying “I am worthy of love, and feel loved,” she is saying, “My love wish is satiated, I am not frustrated in my love thirst.” Yet this image of self as not wanting necessarily clashes with the ongoing acknowledgment of want—and the gap is made up by “histrionics.”

Psychoanalytic authors link the hysterical character to unresolved Oedipal conflicts, particularly in relation to genital frustration. Naranjo agrees with this psychoanalytic view of the Oedipal tendencies in hysterics and sees this pattern in Enneatype 2. In his book Character and Neurosis, he includes accounts from protoanalysis sessions where students describe having felt like “daddy’s little girlfriend” or “the favorite.” Some, after experiencing rejection or abandonment, recall fantasizing about waiting for a prince (who would be the father) or being the center of the universe. He explains:

A transition from frustration to a self-satisfied and self- satisfying stance, and self-image generally can be seen, among women, as a shift from the experience of relative rejection by the mother to the development of seductiveness in view of becoming father’s favorite.
summary: This chunk explains how pride in Enneagram Type 2 functions as a defense against unconscious love needs, linking it to Naranjo’s view of self-worth rooted in parental love and the Oedipal dynamic, where early maternal rejection leads to seductive behavior aimed at becoming the father’s favorite.

title: Гистриический характер по Райху: симптомы и проявления
text:
As Alexander Lowen states, the hysterical attitude, rooted in the “Oedipal” dynamic, manifests as conflicting feelings toward the sexual object, mirroring the way the young girl once related to her father.

In his book Character Analysis, Reich outlines the following traits of the hysterical character:

Overtly sexual behavior

Physically expressive movements with a distinctly sexual undertone

Anxiety when sexual conquest is imminent

Mood instability

Coquetry in gait, look, or speech

Fickleness of reactions

High excitability

Susceptibility to suggestion, followed by swift deprecation and groundless disparagement

Baseless feelings of superiority

Pathological lying

Exceptional capacity for sexual attachment of a childish nature

Somatization of psychological conflicts
summary: This chunk details Alexander Lowen’s view of hysteria as rooted in Oedipal dynamics and Wilhelm Reich’s comprehensive list of hysterical character traits, including sexual expressiveness, emotional instability, suggestibility, pathological lying, and somatization of psychological conflicts.

title: Sексуальный E2 и истрионное расстройство: связь с DSM
text:
Sexual E2 and its histrionic traits

The DSM refers to hysterical personality and histrionic disorder, two profiles that, with some caveats, seem to correspond to the sexual Type 2 of the Enneagram.
summary: This chunk notes that the DSM’s hysterical personality and histrionic disorder profiles, with certain caveats, correspond to the sexual subtype of Enneagram Type 2, establishing a diagnostic bridge between typology and clinical psychology.

title: Исторический контекст гистрии и гистрионического расстройства
text:
Hysteria has come and gone as a diagnostic category in the DSM. In the second edition (DSM-II, 1968), hysterical personality was described as a syndrome marked by excitability, emotional instability, hyper-reactivity, self-dramatization, attention-seeking, immaturity, vanity, and excessive dependency.

Histrionic personality disorder

In DSM-III (1980), hysteria-related traits were reorganized under the personality disorder category as histrionic personality disorder, classified under Axis II.
summary: Описывает эволюцию диагностики гистрии в DSM: от hysterical personality в DSM-II до histrionic personality disorder в DSM-III, расположенной по оси II. Подчеркивается связь с Enneatype 2.

title: Клинические критерии и поведенческие проявления гистрионического расстройства
text:
People with this personality type are often stuck in oral frustration, seeking constant compensation. They tend to exhibit excessive attachment, masochistic tendencies, and paranoia. According to DSM-IV, the disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of excessive emotionality and attention-seeking:

Discomfort in situations where the patient is not the center of attention.

Interactions often marked by inappropriate sexual seductiveness or provocative behavior.

Superficial and rapidly shifting emotional expression.

Persistent use of physical appearance to draw attention.

A speech style that is excessively impressionistic and lacking in detail.

Self-dramatization, theatricality, and exaggerated emotional expression.

High suggestibility; easily influenced by others or circumstances.

A tendency to perceive relationships as more intimate than they actually are.

These individuals often come across as vain, self-absorbed, and immature. They tend to speak in an effusive and dramatic manner, exhibit exaggerated emotional expressions, engage in turbulent interpersonal relationships, and display egocentric and manipulative behavior.
summary: Детализирует диагностические критерии гистрионического расстройства по DSM-IV и описывает типичное поведение: потребность во внимании, сексуальная провокативность, поверхностная эмоциональность, драматичность и манипулятивность, что аналогично проявлениям Энеаграммы типа 2.

title: Манипулятивное поведение и поиск новизны у гистрионических личностей и сексуальных Твёрок
text:
Manipulation can take various forms, including threats or suicide attempts, among other attention-seeking behaviors. They have an exaggerated need to present themselves to others as more than they really are. Their expressions are often neither genuine nor spontaneous; instead, they tend to act in a theatrical manner. They crave to be recognized as special and will leverage their full arsenal of verbal and physical seduction to achieve it. The same applies to E2, especially the sexual subtype.

Histrionic personalities, much like sexual Twos, almost always react too quickly in situations that require reflection and analysis. They rarely focus long enough to perceive situational nuances, often responding in broad emotional strokes. When asked to describe something, they tend to prioritize impressions and emotions over objective facts, often prefacing their statements with “I feel.” Their expression is typically grandiose, emphasizing emotional impact over analytical clarity.

People with this type of disorder, much like Twos, operate based on gut feelings. Not only are they easily influenced by others’ opinions, but they’re also highly distractible when under someone’s gaze. It’s easy to catch their attention, and just as easy to lose it. Their behavior, as a result, tends to be scattered. These attention issues make them seem incredibly naive about trivial matters. In their constant search for novelty and intensity, they feel suffocated by stability, which they find monotonous and boring. This leads them to latch onto new situations with great enthusiasm, only to abandon them without much hesitation once they become familiar or predictable.
summary: Сравнивает манипулятивное поведение, поверхностность эмоций, стремление к новизне и поверхностные отношения у гистрионических личностей и сексуальных subtype Энеаграммы типа 2, подчеркивая их зависимость от внешнего одобрения и страх скуки.

title: Сексуальная экспрессия и гендерные проявления у гистрионических личностей и Энеаграммы типа 2
text:
Like histrionic personalities, Twos, especially those of the sexual subtype, feel unloved and may even perceive themselves as rejected if they’re not the center of attention. In response, they try to make themselves sexually irresistible. Their appearance, and often their behavior, tends to be provocative and inappropriately sexualized.

This heightened sexual instinct isn’t just directed at romantic partners. It spills over into many areas of their lives, including friendships, work relationships, and casual interactions. However, despite their overtly seductive demeanor, they rarely desire genuine sexual intimacy.

Women in particular often dress and behave in an overtly flirtatious manner. Their walk, their speech, even the way they make eye contact—there’s a calculated allure in their gaze, aimed at drawing in their next victim.

In men, this often manifests as an excessive softness and courtesy, with delicate, feminine facial expressions and mannerisms. At times, they adopt hyper-masculine attitudes, while at others, they are subtly effeminate and seductive, combining this flirtatiousness with childish behaviors, patterns of sexual promiscuity, and dependent, childlike attitudes toward women.

Their behavior is often erratic; moods shift rapidly, without any external trigger. Sometimes, just a single glance from someone can provoke an exaggerated reaction, designed to win over an audience. They throw themselves so fully into their performances that they end up believing their own act, making it feel strikingly “authentic.” They have a strong tendency to be deceptive; even when they seem compliant or reasonable, they internally oscillate between disapproval and disdain for anything that doesn’t align with their own plans.
summary: Описывает, как гистрионические черты и сексуальный subtype Энеаграммы типа 2 проявляются в сексуализированном поведении, гендерно-специфичных манерах (флирт у женщин, сочетание мягкости и гипермужественности у мжн), драматичности и самообмане, направленных на получение внимания и подтверждения своей привлекательности.

title: Социальная 계산ность эмоций и связь с зависимым расстройством по Миллону и Наранхо
text:
In other cases, their over-the-top emotional displays don’t represent a genuine loss of control but are, in fact, socially calculated. In other words, they don’t lose it just anywhere or in front of just anyone; their most intense outbursts are reserved for close relationships where deeper conflicts exist.

According to Millon’s classification based on his theory of biosocial learning, Enneatype 2 also coincides with histrionic personality disorder, which, as Claudio Naranjo points out in Character and Neurosis, shares significant traits with dependent personality. Dependent personality Naranjo attributes to Type 4, which is directly and inversely related to E2.

These are the characteristics described by Millon, which are similar to those of E2:

Intense need for affection and attention, sought actively and manipulatively

Uses seduction tactics to gain attention

Highly attuned to others’ emotions
summary: Объясняет, что эмоциональные проявления гистрионических личностей часто являются социально выверенными, а не спонтанными. Ссылается на Миллона и Наранхо, связывая Enneatype 2 с гистрионическим и зависимым расстройствами, noting что тип 4 связан обратно с типом 2, и перечисляет общие черты: потребность во внимании, соблазнительные тактики и эмоциональная чувствительность к другим.

title: Hypervigilant and Inconsistent Behavior
text:
Hypervigilant

Inconsistent behavior and emotions

Dissatisfaction in one-on-one relationships, and a constant need for new stimulation

Fickle and moody

Actively takes care of others, but not out of pure altruism; it’s a way to secure their attention, seeking praise and ensuring a constant supply of admiration and gratification

Quickly moves from one romantic partner to the next, with little difficulty finding a new one to fulfill their needs

Physically attractive, charming, and sensual

Popular, extroverted, and outgoing
summary: Describes hypervigilant, emotionally inconsistent, and attention-seeking behaviors of Enneatype 2, including manipulative caregiving, romantic volatility, and external charm used to gain validation.

title: Millon’s Observable and Interpersonal Traits of Histrionic Personality
text:
Millon’s detailed breakdown across different spheres of observation highlights traits that are common with the proud personality:

Observable behavior: dramatic

Hyperactive

Engages in fleeting, provocative interactions

Impulsive, erratic, highly emotional, intolerant of boredom or inactivity

Drawn to short-lived excitements and pleasure-seeking adventures

Naturally talented at expressing emotions and eliciting admiration; exhibitionistic

Emotionally shallow, easily excitable, and prone to whims

Low tolerance for frustration

Interpersonal behavior: attention-seeking

Their main goal is affection and validation

Maintains friendly and service-oriented relationships, selling themselves on their charm

Fun-loving and sexually provocative

Skilled at seduction, flirtation, and flattery

Enjoys playing with romantic or sexual tension but becomes immature or apprehensive when things get serious

Unable to maintain the image they initially project; has many acquaintances but few close friends

Withdraws when relationships demand depth and commitment

Uses their charm as a tool, presenting themselves in an attractive way and performing gestures designed to impress

Hyperaware of potential rejection and skilled at avoiding it

Always eager to please and ready to meet others’ expectations
summary: Details Millon’s clinical breakdown of histrionic traits aligned with E2, covering observable behavior, interpersonal strategies, and emotional patterns focused on attention, charm, and avoidance of depth.

title: Cognitive Style: Frivolous and Externalized Thinking
text:
Cognitive style: frivolous

Avoids introspective thinking.

Easily influenced, integrates experiences poorly.

Speaks in generalities; impressionistic and unreflective.

Behaves like empty vessels, reacting more to external stimuli than internal ones.

Highly attuned to the thoughts of those whose approval and attention they seek.

Their radar picks up on signs of imminent rejection and how to manipulate situations accordingly.

Superficial cognitive style; distracted, frivolous, lacking curiosity and unable to concentrate.

Avoids problematic or disturbing thoughts and feelings.

Dissociates from thoughts, people, and activities that could disrupt their strategy of superficiality.
summary: Describes the frivolous, externally oriented cognitive style of E2, marked by avoidance of introspection, poor concentration, and heightened sensitivity to social cues for manipulation and validation.

title: Self-Image and Object Relations: Superficiality and Fear of Exposure
text:
Self-image: gregarious

Sees themselves as sociable, friendly, conformist, stimulating, and charming.

Skilled at creating an exciting and interesting life.

Suppresses signs of weakness, agitation, or hostility.

Object relations: superficial

Insatiable need for approval, attention, and stimulation.

Feels devoid of an inner self, seeking constant validation from others to fill the void.

Relies on those around them for guidance and protection.

Seduces indiscriminately and persistently, unable to stop.

Indifference or neutrality from others triggers feelings of emptiness and rejection.

Abandons intimate relationships out of fear that their fraud will be exposed, leading to numerous failed attempts at connection.
summary: Covers E2’s self-perception as gregarious and charming, and their object relations marked by insatiable need for validation, fear of exposure, and avoidance of intimate commitment due to inner emptiness.

title: Defense Mechanisms and Morphological Organization: Dissociation and Inner Poverty
text:
Defense mechanisms: dissociation & repression

Their focus on others’ thoughts and feelings makes it difficult to recognize their own.

Represses, blocks, or dissociates memories that cause distress; much of their past is a blank.

Invests energy in crafting and maintaining socially acceptable facades to keep painful thoughts and emotions out of awareness.

Engages in massive repression of the inner self to avoid confronting the triviality, emptiness, and lack of substance in their existence; this sustains their self-esteem. Believes that if they turn their attention inward, they will lose their vigilance over the desires and moods of others.

Morphological organization: disconnected

Their psychological structure and inner world are poorly integrated.

Uses broad, generalized defense mechanisms to maintain overall psychic cohesion.

Struggles with independence, having deprived themselves of previous learning experiences; this makes them even more dependent.

Their internal world is impoverished, deficient, and insubstantial, and remains so as they always occupy themselves with external matters.

To maintain their external vigilance, they suppress internal awareness and actively try to eliminate any consciousness of inner emptiness.

Displaying their inner void feels intolerable, as it would expose conflict, fraud, cognitive sterility, and emotional poverty.
summary: Explains how E2 uses dissociation and repression to avoid inner emptiness, maintains facades for self-esteem, and has a disconnected, impoverished inner world due to external fixation.

title: Mood, Temperament, and Millon’s Instinctual Variants
text:
Mood & temperament: inconsistent

High energy and activation levels with a low threshold for reactivity.

Emotions shift rapidly and remain shallow.

Emotionally facile, highly sensitive to stimuli, with excessive sympathetic nervous system activity and poor cortical inhibition.

Emotional range is unstable, intense, chaotic, and expansive.

It can be inferred that, in infancy and childhood, they exhibited heightened emotional responsiveness and likely encouraged similar reactions in others for stimulation.

Millon extends this classification with variants that reflect the different types we can associate with the various instincts: self-preservation, sexual, and social. These correspond, respectively, to the infantile histrionic, the theatrical histrionic, and the lively histrionic. Or, in other terms, the appeaser, the tempestuous, and the deceitful.

In every aspect Millon describes, we can see the traits of E2 (keeping in mind that he is discussing a personality disorder from a clinical pathology perspective rather than a general character type). While none of these traits can be outright dismissed, some nuances can be added. For example, it’s notable that Millon does not highlight the polarity between pain and pleasure, whereas E2 is a pleasure-oriented personality that actively flees from pain.
summary: Details the unstable mood and temperament of E2, links Millon’s histrionic subtypes to instinctual variants, and notes conceptual alignment with E2 despite clinical framing and omissions like the pain-pleasure polarity.

title: Critique of Millon's analysis of E2
text: Millon also does not explicitly address the E2’s deep need for love, both in giving and receiving it. Lastly, he does not explore the false abundance that is a core characteristic of the Two.
summary: This chunk criticizes Millon's clinical analysis of E2 for overlooking the type's core need for love and the characteristic of false abundance.

title: Self-preservation E2 and childlike traits
text:
Self-preservation E2 and its childlike traits

Self-preservation Twos channel their energy into strategies aimed at fulfilling their need to feel loved. For them, knowing they are special is essential. Otherwise, they risk losing protection and support. Claudio Naranjo refers to this subtype as “2 that goes against” or “anti-2” because, among the proud subtypes, the self-preservation subtype hides their pride behind a childlike attitude. They fulfill the needs of family and friends, often at the expense of their own.

They always have a lot to offer and, paradoxically, believe they deserve preferential treatment simply because they see themselves as special. In extreme cases, their behavior can even resemble exaggerated caricatures.

This dynamic aligns with what Freud described as primary narcissism, which he saw as a projection of parents’ narcissistic ideals onto a child. According to Freud, parents often expect their child to reclaim all the privileges they had to give up. He famously referred to this as “His Majesty the Baby,” because of the pedestal on which the child is placed. This Freudian concept fits well with the kind of pride experienced by self-preservation Twos.

Eric Berne, in his theory of personality, divides the psyche into three ego states: the Parent, the Adult, and the Child. These states influence how a person thinks, feels, and behaves. They manifest concretely and can be assessed through the observation of vocabulary, tone of voice, gestures, and body language.

A healthy psychological dynamic, according to Berne, integrates the positive aspects of all three states while maintaining the Adult’s capacity for rational decision-making. The Child state represents both the playful, innocent aspects of personality and its more problematic, regressive tendencies. In self-preservation Twos, the Child state dominates, overshadowing the Adult state.

Among the hysterical subtypes, self-preservation Twos are undoubtedly the most structured in terms of infantile hysteria and also the most dependent. Some researchers suggest that the term “psychoinfantile,” found in the ICD-10 as a variation of hysteria, may have originated from observations of individuals with this subtype.

Given the characteristic childlike nature of self-preservation Twos, we can identify certain aspects of dependent personality disorder in their behavioral dynamics.
summary: This chunk describes the self-preservation subtype of E2, emphasizing its childlike traits, need to feel special and loved, dominance of the Child ego state, and connections to theories by Freud, Berne, and concepts like psychoinfantility and dependent personality disorder.

title: Reich's analysis and DSM-IV-TR on dependent personality disorder
text:
In Character Analysis, Reich discusses a variant of the hysterical character:

Insofar as mechanisms other than genital mechanisms or their substitute formations are found in the hysterical character, they do not belong specifically to this type. For example, we often encounter depressive mechanisms. In these cases, the genital incestuous fixation is replaced by regressions to oral mechanisms or by new formations in the course of the process. The hysterical character’s strong inclination to regress, especially to oral stages, can be accounted for by the sexual stasis in this zone [...]

Thus, the hysterical character presents himself in a pure form when he play-acts, and is nervous and vivacious. When he is depressive, introverted, autistic, however, he betrays mechanisms other than those which specifically belong to him. Yet one can speak of hysterical depression as opposed to melancholic depression.

By describing this variant of hysteria with an oral fixation, Reich supports the hypothesis that the self-preservation E2 contains intrapsychic elements of histrionic personality disorder along with traits of dependent personality disorder as outlined in the DSM-IV-TR.

However, the description of dependent personality disorder should only be used as a reference, helping us recognize a tendency within this subtype that becomes particularly pronounced in the most pathological cases.

According to the DSM-IV-TR, individuals with dependent personality disorder struggle with everyday decisions, tend to be passive, and rely on others to take initiative and assume responsibility in major areas of their lives. They fear losing approval or support and often avoid expressing disagreement, especially with those they depend on. They have difficulty starting projects or working independently. To obtain affection and support, they may go to extremes, even volunteering for unpleasant tasks if it helps them secure the attention they crave.

People with this disorder feel uncomfortable or helpless when alone, fearing they won’t be able to take care of themselves. To avoid isolation, they may cling to others. When a significant relationship ends, they may desperately seek a new one to provide the care and support they need.

The key distinction between dependent personality disorder and histrionic personality disorder is that dependent individuals exhibit self-effacing and submissive behavior, while histrionic individuals display lively, attention-seeking exuberance.

Like those with dependent personality disorder, self-preservation E2s have difficulty thinking for themselves, making choices, and recognizing their own preferences. Their energy is directed toward compulsively pleasing others, providing services, and forming relationships based on dependency.

And just like histrionic personality, this subtype is highly active, channeling all its energy into maintaining control over relationships and feeling loved. This sets it apart from dependent personality disorder.
summary: This chunk discusses Wilhelm Reich's analysis of hysterical character with oral fixation as relevant to self-preservation E2, details the DSM-IV-TR criteria for dependent personality disorder, and compares/contrasts it with histrionic personality disorder, concluding that self-preservation E2 combines traits of both but is distinguished by its active control over relationships.

title: Самосохранение E2: механизм выживания и потеря связи с собственными потребностями
text:
Just as the E3 has mastered adapting its image to meet external expectations, the self-preservation E2 specializes in recognizing others’ needs as a survival mechanism, a way to receive love and validation by embodying the role of the “good girl.” The consequence is losing touch with their own needs. To avoid facing a deep sense of helplessness and abandonment, they compulsively invest their energy into keeping relationships under control; always being available, showing empathy, and offering love and understanding.

Now, the fundamental structure of self-preservation E2 makes them a dependent person. As long as their strategy for maintaining these dependent relationships is working and everything feels under control (allowing them to feel loved and protected), their hysteric traits will dominate. However, when their efforts fail, they may become overly dependent, submissive, and depressive, with a real risk of self-destructive behavior.
summary: Описывает, как самосохранение E2 использует распознавание чужих потребностей как стратегию выживания, теряя связь с собственными нуждами. При стабильности доминируют истерические черты, при провале стратегии — зависимость, подчинённость и риск саморазрушительного поведения.

title: Теория Карен Хорни: три межличностные стратегии и их связь с самосохранением E2
text:
Psychoanalyst Karen Horney explains that character neurosis develops when a child lacks a nurturing and secure environment, leading to basic anxiety that manifests as feelings of isolation, helplessness, or hostility. This results in a fixed behavioral pattern and three possible personality strategies:

Compliant or submissive (moving toward people);

Aggressive or assertive (moving against people); and

Withdrawn or resigned (moving away from people).

Self-preservation E2 aligns with the first of these interpersonal styles, deeply affected by anxiety about abandonment. Their defense strategy is clinging to others, trying to win favor through flattery, being subservient, and avoiding confrontation. For this personality, being loved is a guarantee that they won’t be left behind.
summary: Объясняет, как самосохранение E2 соответствует compliant-подтипу по Карен Хорни — движется навстречу людям из-за тревоги об abandonment, используя лесть, покорность и избегание конфронтации как защиту.

title: Невротические потребности по Хорни и защита через идеализацию у самосохранения E2
text:
Among Horney’s ten neurotic needs, the need for affection and approval is particularly relevant to the self-preservation E2. These individuals crave love, tend to be people-pleasers, are highly sensitive to criticism, and fear rejection or hostility.

To avoid feelings of abandonment or despair, the self-preservation E2 often throws themselves into a chaotic, euphoric lifestyle. They’re always tuned in to others’ needs, seeking distractions through social events, or constantly surrounding themselves with people. In this sense, their behavior parallels Melanie Klein’s depressive position. Around the second trimester of the first year of life, the infant recognizes their mother as a separate person, seeing her as the “good breast” when she provides comfort and the “bad breast” when she withholds it. This creates an emotional ambivalence of love and hate towards her. The baby also becomes aware of their own aggressive impulses toward the mother, making them feel vulnerable. In the depressive position, the predominant anxiety is the fear of losing this loved object.

To cope, idealization becomes a defense mechanism. The child ignores the negative traits of those they depend on, denying their ambivalent feelings and their own dependency. They exert an illusion of omnipotent control over these figures, treating them with disdain, so that their loss does not lead to guilt or pain.

Self-preservation E2 tends to filter out anything painful or unpleasant, constructing a partial reality where they simply refuse to acknowledge what isn’t positive or pleasurable. Like a child lost in their imagination, they “create” their version of the world that keeps them from truly seeing it, or the people in it.
summary: Детально описывает, как у самосохранения E2 доминирует потребность в привязанности и одобрении, ведущая к людей-угождению и страху отвержения. Их поведение напоминает депрессивную позицию Кляйн, где идеализация служит защитой от амбивалентных чувств и зависимости, приводя к конструированию иллюзорной реальности без боли и неприятного.

title: Терапевтическая склонность и защитные механизмы у самосохранения E2: репрессия и ретрофлексия
text: Among the three subtypes, the self-preservation E2 is the one most likely to go to therapy. According to Claudio Naranjo, the primary defense mechanism of Enneatype 2 is repression. When the self-preservation E2’s strategies become obsolete and they are forced to confront the reality that they are not as irreplaceable as they believed, another defense mechanism often emerges in their intrapsychic dynamics: retroflection, which fuels depressive tendencies.
summary: Указывает, что самосохранение E2 наиболее склонно к терапии среди подтипов. Основная защита — репрессия (по Наранхо), а при неудаче стратегий возникает ретрофлексия, направляющая агрессию внутрь и усиливающая депрессивные тенденции.

title: Нарциссизм у социального E2: проекция зависти и подавление аутентичности
text:
Social E2 and its narcissistic traits

According to Alexander Lowen and Neville Symington, narcissism lies at the root of all psychological disorders. Symington emphasizes that a fundamental aspect of narcissism is self-blindness—using most of one’s psychic energy to conceal one’s true nature.

Symington’s definition of narcissism aligns closely with the psychodynamics of the social E2 :

Essentially envious, they project their own unbearable feelings of envy outward, often becoming individuals who are, ironically, envied by others. They struggle to form authentic connections, relying instead on seduction and manipulation. However, manipulation often triggers guilt, which they vigorously suppress—yet this suppression fuels an endless need for external validation.

Self-awareness is avoided at all costs, and there is an almost total inability (depending on the severity of the narcissistic disorder) to postpone the gratification of personal needs. Ultimately, the inner child is completely repressed.
summary: Описывает нарциссические черты социального E2: основана на зависти и её проекции, приводит к манипуляциям и соблазну вместо подлинных связей. Подавление вины и потребностей ведёт к хронической потребности в подтверждении и полному репрессированию внутреннего ребёнка.

title: Нарциссизм по Лоуэну: отрицание чувств, расщепление реальности и телесная ригидность
text:
The portrait Lowen gives us, in turn, is as follows:

Feelings are continuously denied by the narcissist. Everything they do is meant to reinforce their own image; the denial of feelings results in an indifferent or even ruthless attitude toward others.

The narcissist undergoes a true splitting of reality, accepting certain aspects that become part of their image while rejecting the traits they dislike, projecting them onto others. This also leads to an inability to distinguish between truth and falsehood and a tendency to lie with ease.

Another constant element is bodily rigidity. When the first problems begin to manifest, the narcissist becomes physically rigid as a way of denying their emotions. Later, it is precisely this rigidity that prevents emotions from reaching consciousness. The narcissist expresses only two emotions: rage and sentimentality (which, even then, come across as false), while strongly repressing sadness and fear because they evoke vulnerability, something a narcissist absolutely cannot allow themselves to feel.
summary: Излагает модель нарциссизма Лоуэна: хроническое отрицание чувств для поддержания образа, расщепление реальности (принятие желаемого, проекция нежелательного), телесная ригидность как блокировка эмоций, оставляющая только ложную ярость и сентиментальность при полном подавлении грусти и страха.

title: Классификация нарциссических расстройств по Лоуэну и их связь с социальным E2
text:
Moreover, they place enormous importance on power (over others) and control (over themselves), believing that through them, they can shield themselves from humiliation. However, power is never enough because it feeds the image rather than deep emotions. As a result, the narcissist is always seeking situations where they can gain social power.

Ultimately, the need to feel special manifests as omnipotence, omnipresence, and omniscience, alongside the belief that they are entitled to universal admiration.

Lowen’s multidimensional classification of various narcissistic disorders, shown below, effectively expands and clarifies the overly one-dimensional DSM-IV classification. In particular, his descriptions of the phallic-narcissistic or hypervigilant character and the narcissistic or unaware character seem to align well with the social E2.

Lowen describes phallic-narcissists as individuals who display excessive self-confidence and are overly preoccupied with their image. This personality type includes, at least to some extent, all the defining traits of narcissism: grandiosity, apparent emotional detachment, a lack of true self-awareness, and a distorted sense of reality.

In the narcissistic character, grandiosity is even more pronounced than in the phallic-narcissist. These individuals feel a constant need to be the best at everything; they demand perfection. In fact, they often achieve notable success in various fields, particularly in the workplace, as they navigate power
summary: Продолжает описание модели Лоуэна: нарциссы ищут власть не для глубины, а для образа, стремясь к всевластию и всезнанию из-за права на всеобщее восхищение. Его типология выделяет фаллического нарцисса (образозависимого) и нарциссический характер (с завышенной величием и перфекционизмом), оба resonating с социальным E2.

title: Нарциссизм как стремление к власти и контролю
text:
Moreover, they place enormous importance on power (over others) and control (over themselves), believing that through them, they can shield themselves from humiliation. However, power is never enough because it feeds the image rather than deep emotions. As a result, the narcissist is always seeking situations where they can gain social power.

Ultimately, the need to feel special manifests as omnipotence, omnipresence, and omniscience, alongside the belief that they are entitled to universal admiration.
summary: The chunk describes how narcissists seek power and control to avoid humiliation, but this only reinforces their false image. Their need to feel special leads to fantasies of omnipotence and entitlement to universal admiration.

title: Классификация нарциссических расстройств по Лоуэну и связь с E2
text:
Lowen’s multidimensional classification of various narcissistic disorders, shown below, effectively expands and clarifies the overly one-dimensional DSM-IV classification. In particular, his descriptions of the phallic-narcissistic or hypervigilant character and the narcissistic or unaware character seem to align well with the social E2.

Lowen describes phallic-narcissists as individuals who display excessive self-confidence and are overly preoccupied with their image. This personality type includes, at least to some extent, all the defining traits of narcissism: grandiosity, apparent emotional detachment, a lack of true self-awareness, and a distorted sense of reality.

In the narcissistic character, grandiosity is even more pronounced than in the phallic-narcissist. These individuals feel a constant need to be the best at everything; they demand perfection. In fact, they often achieve notable success in various fields, particularly in the workplace, as they navigate power and money with ease. As a result, their grandiose self-image may, in some ways, be reinforced by how others perceive them. However, this image is ultimately false, far removed from reality. While they may achieve significant career success, they remain powerless in the realm of emotions.

In his description of borderline personality, Lowen also distinguishes two types: One projects an image of great success, marked by pronounced grandiosity—this seems aligned with E2. The other is more withdrawn, vulnerable, and highly dependent on others, resembling E4 more closely.

It is evident that this subdivision reflects the previous distinction between hypervigilant and unaware narcissists. This apparent contradiction is easily explained when considering that in borderline personalities, powerful superiority complexes coexist with equally powerful inferiority complexes. In the first type, the sense of superiority is overt, while inferiority remains hidden. In the second, the opposite occurs.

These individuals find themselves caught in a perpetual and intense dilemma: either they are the best in the world, or they are nothing. The difference between the narcissistic character and the grandiose type of borderline personality lies in the fact that, in the latter, the façade is extremely fragile and can collapse under the slightest stress, revealing the insecure and frightened child it was meant to conceal.

Thus, according to Lowen’s five-character model, social E2 seems to belong to the narcissism of the borderline personality, where a sense of superiority is evident while inferiority remains hidden, confirming that E2 has its roots in E4.
summary: Lowen’s classification of narcissistic disorders is presented, linking phallic-narcissistic and narcissistic characters to social E2. The grandiose subtype of borderline personality is associated with E2 due to overt superiority masking hidden inferiority, suggesting E2 originates from E4.

title: Ранние травмы и формирование нарциссической идентичности
text:
When a proper parent-child relationship is lacking, the self becomes fixated in a narcissistic position. The experience of the self then crystallizes into a defensive stance, assuming the character of a grandiose and omnipotent self. The child, deprived of an empathetic relationship, particularly from their mother and father, cannot develop adequate self-esteem nor invest in the idealization of their parents.

Instead, they invest in themselves, seeking grandiose recognition from the world.

The narcissistic personality transfers the privileged love experienced in childhood to their ideal self. The absence of boundaries and proper guidance from parents leads this personality to identify with their ideal self. Rather than being governed by a controlling and accusatory superego, the self aligns itself as a loving ally to the ideal self.
summary: This section explains how insufficient parental empathy in childhood leads the child to develop a narcissistic self-structure, investing in an idealized self and seeking external validation to compensate for lack of true self-worth.

title: Коут и переосмысление здорового нарциссизма
text:
Kohut’s definition of mental health represents a significant step forward in self psychology compared to classical psychoanalysis. The Austrian psychoanalyst argues that “due to the improper intrusion of the altruistic value system of Western civilization,” narcissism has been completely and unfairly excluded from the concept of psychological health, taking on an exclusively negative and pathological connotation.

Kohut proposes replacing Freud’s definition of mental health, understood as “the ability to love and work,” with the following: “A healthy individual must be capable of loving and working successfully.” This redefinition grants narcissism the possibility of being seen as an integral and fundamental part of an individual’s capacity for positive and healthy potential—a healthy narcissism.

In line with Kohut’s perspective, it is appropriate to support, nurture, and allow the grandiose self to develop naturally as part of the evolutionary process. As narcissistic demands emerge, they can gradually be confronted in therapy and reconciled with the realities of life.
summary: Kohut redefines mental health to include narcissism as a potentially healthy component of personality, advocating for the natural development of the grandiose self and its therapeutic integration rather than suppression.
